The design rules and limits that keep an AI system's behavior within safe and educational bounds; in a tutor, the most important is giving hints instead of answers.

See also: AI Tutoring

docs.title: AI in Education
docs.text:
The use of artificial intelligence in teaching and learning, such as tutoring, feedback, translation and course design, with both promise for reaching more learners and risks of over-reliance and bias.

See also: AI Tutoring, AI Guardrails

docs.title: AI Over-Reliance
docs.text:
Depending on AI tools so heavily that a person stops thinking, practicing or checking for themselves, losing skills and accepting errors.

Example: A student who copies an AI's essay learns nothing about writing one.

docs.title: AI Translation
docs.text:
The use of machine-learning systems to translate speech and writing between languages and to read text aloud or transcribe it.

It could let learners study in their own languages instead of first learning a dominant one.

See also: Mother-Tongue Learning

docs.title: AI Tutoring
docs.text:
The use of AI systems to give individual students explanations, questions, hints and feedback at their own pace, aiming to bring some benefits of one-on-one tutoring to every learner.

See also: AI Guardrails, One-on-One Tutoring

docs.title: AI-Native School
docs.text: A school designed around a clear purpose and way of teaching first and then equipped with the AI that serves them, with mornings of personalized academic work and afternoons of projects and collaboration.

docs.title: AI-Native Schools Companion
docs.text: The companion textbook AI-Native Schools, linked throughout this book, which works out in detail how a school might use AI tutoring and intelligent textbooks well.

docs.title: Alcmaeonids
docs.text:
Say it: alk-MEE-uh-nidz 🔊 Pronounce

A powerful Athenian aristocratic family who, while in exile, rebuilt the front of Apollo's temple at Delphi in fine marble in the 6th century BCE.

Example: Herodotus reports they were also accused of bribing the Pythia.

See also: Bribery of the Oracle

docs.title: Aldine Editions
docs.text:
The books printed by Aldus Manutius's press in Venice, especially its small octavo volumes from 1501, which made classical texts portable and cheaper for students and readers.

Example: A scholar could carry a pocket Virgil instead of needing a heavy manuscript at a desk.

docs.title: Aldus Manutius
docs.text:
Say it: Manutius muh-NOO-shee-us 🔊 Pronounce

A Venetian printer and publisher (about 1450–1515) whose Aldine Press issued the first printed editions of many Greek classics and introduced small, affordable books in italic type.

See also: Aldine Editions, Affordable Course Materials

docs.title: Alexander the Great
docs.text: The king of Macedon (356–323 BCE), taught by Aristotle, who conquered the Persian Empire and lands as far as India, spreading Greek language and culture across the Near East.

docs.title: Alice Kober
docs.text:
An American classicist (1906–1950) at Brooklyn College who studied Linear B for years on thousands of handmade index cards and showed that its words changed their endings like an inflected language.

Her method laid the foundation for the decipherment.

See also: Michael Ventris, Credit for Groundwork

docs.title: Alphabet
docs.text:
A script in which each letter stands for a single consonant or vowel sound, so that a small set of signs can spell any word. Its simplicity made reading far easier to learn.

Example: The Greeks borrowed the Phoenician letters and added vowels, creating the ancestor of the Latin letters used in this book.

See also: Greek Alphabet, Phoenician Alphabet

docs.title: Alphabet Reform of 1928
docs.text:
The law of November 1928 that replaced the Arabic-based Ottoman script with a new Latin-based alphabet of 29 letters for Turkish, designed to match the language's sounds.

Example: Within months, newspapers, street signs and school books switched to the new letters.

docs.title: Altar to an Unknown God
docs.text:
An altar inscription that Paul, in Acts 17, says he saw in Athens, which he used as the starting point of his speech. Ancient writers do mention Athenian altars to unnamed gods.

See also: Meeting People Where They Are

docs.title: Amfissa Olive Groves
docs.text:
Say it: Amfissa AHM-fee-sah 🔊 Pronounce

The broad plain of olive trees below Delphi, stretching from the town of Amfissa to the Gulf of Corinth, one of the oldest continuously cultivated olive landscapes in Greece.

Example: From the theater at Delphi, the groves look like a silver-green sea in the valley.

See also: Olive Oil

docs.title: Amphictyonic League
docs.text:
Say it: Amphictyonic am-fik-tee-ON-ik 🔊 Pronounce

The council of Greek peoples that managed the sanctuary at Delphi, oversaw the Pythian Games and could declare sacred wars against those who violated the sanctuary.

docs.title: Anatolia
docs.text:
Say it: an-uh-TOH-lee-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The large peninsula that forms the Asian part of modern Turkey, between the Black Sea, the Aegean and the Mediterranean. It was home to Hittites, Greek cities, Romans, Byzantines and Ottomans in turn.

Example: Troy, Ephesus and Paul's hometown of Tarsus all lie in this region.

docs.title: Anchoring Change in Culture
docs.text: Making a new practice part of an organization's shared habits, values and stories, so it continues because people believe in it, not because a leader enforces it.

docs.title: Ancient Agora of Athens
docs.text:
The open public square at the foot of the Acropolis that served as the heart of civic life in ancient Athens: market, law courts, council house, temples and covered walkways.

Example: Socrates questioned passersby here, and Paul argued in it with Stoic and Epicurean thinkers.

docs.title: Ancient Greece
docs.text:
The Greek-speaking world of roughly 800 BCE to the Roman conquest, made up of many independent cities around the Aegean and beyond, and famous for its art, theater, philosophy and early democracy.

Example: The Acropolis in Athens and the sanctuary at Delphi are two of the best-known places from this world on our route.

docs.title: Ancient Mediterranean Treasures
docs.text:
The name of Viking's seven-night cruise itinerary from Istanbul to Athens, which stops at sites spanning more than three thousand years, from Troy to Byzantine Constantinople.

Example: In one week the itinerary takes us from the Gallipoli peninsula to Ephesus, Rhodes, Heraklion and Piraeus.

See also: Viking Star Cruise

docs.title: Ancient Prediction Machines
docs.text:
Devices built before the modern era that worked out future events from a model fixed in their structure, rather than from a god's answer or new observation.

Example: The Antikythera mechanism's gears predicted eclipses years ahead.

See also: Antikythera Mechanism

docs.title: Anıtkabir
docs.text:
Say it: ah-nuht-kah-BEER 🔊 Pronounce

The monumental mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk on a hill in Ankara, completed in 1953, visited by large crowds on national days and anniversaries.

Example: On November 10, people across Turkey stop at 9:05 AM while officials gather there.

docs.title: Answer as Start of Inquiry
docs.text:
Treating an answer not as the end of thinking but as a claim to be tested, so that it begins an investigation.

Example: Told that no one was wiser than he, Socrates set out to test the claim by questioning others.

docs.title: Antikythera Mechanism
docs.text:
Say it: Antikythera an-tee-kih-THEER-uh 🔊 Pronounce

A hand-cranked bronze device of interlocking gears, made in the 2nd or 1st century BCE and found in 1901 in a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, that modeled the movements of the sun, moon and probably planets and predicted eclipses.

Example: Its corroded fragments are displayed in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

See also: Ancient Prediction Machines

docs.title: Anzac Cove
docs.text:
The small beach on the west coast of the Gallipoli peninsula where Australian and New Zealand troops landed on April 25, 1915, under steep cliffs held by Ottoman troops.

Example: Visitors read Atatürk's words of reconciliation on a stone memorial above the beach.

docs.title: ANZAC Forces
docs.text:
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, the combined force that landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on April 25, 1915.

Example: April 25, Anzac Day, is a national day of remembrance in both countries.

docs.title: Apollo
docs.text: The Greek god of prophecy, music, healing, light and order, worshipped above all at Delphi, where he spoke through his priestess.

docs.title: Apollo's Winter Absence
docs.text:
The ancient belief that Apollo left Delphi for three winter months each year, traveling to a distant northern land, during which the oracle gave no answers.

Example: The book uses it to show that even the god of prophecy had a season when he could not see ahead.

See also: Prediction Horizon

docs.title: Apollos
docs.text:
Say it: uh-POL-us 🔊 Pronounce

A Jewish believer from Alexandria, described in Acts as eloquent and learned in the scriptures, who taught in Ephesus and Corinth after Priscilla and Aquila instructed him more fully.

Example: One faction at Corinth claimed "I belong to Apollos."

docs.title: Arachova
docs.text:
Say it: ah-RAH-kho-vah 🔊 Pronounce

A mountain town on the slopes of Mount Parnassus about 10 km east of Delphi, known for its stone houses, woven rugs, local cheese and winter ski crowds.

Example: Our day trip stops here for coffee on the way to the sanctuary.

docs.title: Aratus
docs.text:
Say it: uh-RAY-tus 🔊 Pronounce

A Greek poet of the 3rd century BCE from Soli in Cilicia, whose astronomical poem Phaenomena contains the line "For we too are his offspring," quoted by Paul in Athens.

See also: Areopagus Speech

docs.title: Archaeology
docs.text:
The study of the human past through the physical things people left behind, such as buildings, tools, pottery, bones and writing, recovered by careful excavation and survey.

It is the main way we know about periods, like the Bronze Age, that left few or no readable texts.

Example: Digging at Hisarlik revealed nine superimposed settlements, giving a physical history for the place Homer called Troy.

docs.title: Archaic Period
docs.text:
The phase of Greek history from about 800 to 480 BCE, when city-states formed, Greeks founded colonies across the Mediterranean, the alphabet spread and the first stone temples and life-size statues appeared.

Example: The Oracle of Delphi rose to its greatest influence during these centuries.

docs.title: Areopagus
docs.text:
Say it: air-ee-OP-uh-gus 🔊 Pronounce

The rocky hill northwest of the Acropolis, the "Hill of Ares," and the ancient council of former magistrates that met there and judged homicide cases.

Example: Paul's speech to the Athenians is set here in Acts 17.

See also: Areopagus Speech

docs.title: Areopagus Bronze Plaque
docs.text:
Say it: Areopagus air-ee-OP-uh-gus 🔊 Pronounce

The large bronze tablet set into the rock at the foot of the Areopagus steps, engraved with the Greek text of Paul's speech from Acts 17.

Example: Greek school groups and pilgrims often stop to read it in the original words.

docs.title: Areopagus Speech
docs.text:
Say it: Areopagus air-ee-OP-uh-gus 🔊 Pronounce

Paul's address to the Athenians in Acts 17:22–31, which begins with their altar "to an unknown god," quotes Greek poets and proclaims the God who made the world.

Example: It quotes Aratus' line "For we too are his offspring."

docs.title: Aristotle
docs.text:
A Greek philosopher and scientist (384–322 BCE), student of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great, who wrote on logic, biology, ethics, politics and poetry and founded the Lyceum.

See also: Lyceum

docs.title: Artemis of Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The local form of the goddess Artemis worshipped at Ephesus, shown as a stiff standing figure with a tall headdress and many egg-shaped forms on her chest, whose meaning scholars still debate.

Example: Two marble statues of her stand in the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk.

docs.title: Arthur Evans
docs.text:
The British archaeologist (1851–1941) who excavated Knossos from 1900, named the Minoan civilization, classified its scripts as Linear A and Linear B and rebuilt parts of the palace.

Example: The concrete columns painted red at Knossos are his work, not the Minoans'.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text:
The field of computing that builds systems able to do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images, making predictions and solving problems.

Example: A phone app that translates a Turkish menu aloud uses this kind of system.

See also: Machine Learning, AI in Education

docs.title: Asia Minor Refugees
docs.text:
The Greek Orthodox people who fled or were expelled from Anatolia in 1922–1923 and resettled in Greece, many in new neighborhoods around Athens and Piraeus.

Example: Athens suburbs such as Nea Smyrni, "New Smyrna," are named after the towns they left.

See also: Rebetiko

docs.title: Ataturk Memorial Day
docs.text:
Say it: Atatürk ah-tah-TEWRK 🔊 Pronounce

November 10, the anniversary of Atatürk's death at Dolmabahçe Palace at 9:05 AM in 1938, marked across Turkey by a minute of silence at that moment.

Example: At 9:05 AM sirens sound and traffic in Istanbul comes to a stop.

docs.title: Ataturk's Reforms
docs.text:
Say it: Atatürk ah-tah-TEWRK 🔊 Pronounce

The sweeping changes of the 1920s and 1930s that remade Turkish law, education, dress and public life, including abolishing the caliphate, a new civil code, the Latin alphabet, surnames and votes for women.

See also: Secularism in Turkey, Costs of Top-Down Reform

docs.title: Athena
docs.text:
The Greek goddess of wisdom, crafts and strategic war, patron of Athens, often shown with helmet, spear and her sacred bird, the little owl.

Example: The owl on the ancient Athenian silver coin, and on today's Greek one-euro coin, is her bird.

See also: Glaux, Parthenon

docs.title: Athena Pronaia Sanctuary
docs.text:
Say it: Pronaia proh-NAY-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The lower sanctuary at Delphi, about a kilometer from Apollo's, dedicated to Athena "before the temple," which travelers passed on their way to the oracle.

See also: Tholos of Delphi

docs.title: Athenian Citizenship
docs.text: The legal status that gave a person a share in governing classical Athens; after 451 BCE it required both parents to be Athenian, and full political rights belonged only to adult men.

docs.title: Athenian Democracy
docs.text:
The system of government in Athens from about 508 to 322 BCE in which adult male citizens voted directly on laws and war in an Assembly and filled most offices by lottery.

Example: Juries of hundreds of citizens, chosen by a stone allotment machine, decided cases in the Agora.

See also: Pnyx, Who Democracy Left Out

docs.title: Athenian Treasury
docs.text:
The small Doric building on the Sacred Way at Delphi built by Athens around 500–490 BCE to hold offerings, reconstructed by French archaeologists in the early 1900s.

Example: Its walls carry carved hymns to Apollo with signs for musical notes, among the oldest written music.

docs.title: Athens
docs.text:
The capital of modern Greece and in ancient times the leading city of Attica, home of the first democracy, the Parthenon, tragedy and the schools of Plato and Aristotle.

Example: The city's 3.6 million people live around the same rock that held Athena's temple 2,400 years ago.

See also: Acropolis, Athens as Modern Capital

docs.title: Athens as Modern Capital
docs.text:
The choice in 1834 to make Athens, then a small town of a few thousand people, the capital of the new Greek kingdom, because of its ancient prestige.

Example: The neoclassical buildings along Panepistimiou Street were built in this period to give the new capital a classical look.

docs.title: Athens Polytechnic Uprising
docs.text:
The student occupation of the National Technical University of Athens in November 1973 against the military dictatorship, ended on November 17 when a tank broke through the gate.

Example: Every November 17 Athenians march to the US embassy and lay flowers at the Polytechnic gate.

See also: Exarchia

docs.title: Augustine of Hippo
docs.text:
A North African bishop and theologian (354–430 CE) whose reading of Paul on grace, sin and the will shaped Western Christianity, and whose Confessions tells of his own conversion.

Example: He wrote that a passage of Romans, read in a garden in Milan, changed his life.

docs.title: Ayasuluk
docs.text:
Say it: ah-yah-soo-LOOK 🔊 Pronounce

The name for centuries of the town now called Selçuk, a Turkish form of the Greek Hagios Theologos, "the Holy Theologian," the title of the apostle John.

docs.title: Baklava
docs.text:
A pastry of many thin layers of phyllo dough, filled with chopped pistachios or walnuts, baked with butter and soaked in syrup, made across the former Ottoman lands.

See also: Shared Greek-Turkish Dishes

docs.title: Balik Ekmek
docs.text:
A grilled fish sandwich, usually mackerel with onions and lettuce in bread, sold from boats and stalls along the waterfront at Eminönü in Istanbul.

Example: Eating one by the Galata Bridge, with ferries coming and going, is a classic Istanbul lunch.

docs.title: Bargaining in Bazaars
docs.text:
The practice of negotiating a price between buyer and seller in a traditional market, through offers and counter-offers, often with conversation and tea.

Example: In the Grand Bazaar a carpet price is a starting point, while packaged spices in the Spice Bazaar usually have fixed prices.

See also: Grand Bazaar

docs.title: Basic Greek Phrases
docs.text:
A small set of everyday expressions in modern Greek, such as greetings, thanks and requests, that let a visitor show courtesy and handle simple exchanges.

Example: Kalimera, "good morning," and efcharistó, "thank you," are the two most useful phrases in Athens.

docs.title: Basic Turkish Phrases
docs.text:
A small set of everyday expressions in Turkish, such as greetings, thanks and requests, that let a visitor show courtesy and handle simple exchanges.

Example: Saying teşekkür ederim, "thank you," to a shopkeeper in the Spice Bazaar often earns a smile.

docs.title: Basilica Cistern
docs.text:
A vast underground water reservoir built under Justinian in 532 CE across the street from Hagia Sophia, its roof held up by 336 columns.

Example: Visitors walk on raised platforms in dim light over shallow water with fish.

docs.title: Basilica of St. John
docs.text:
The ruins of a large domed church built by Justinian in the 6th century on Ayasuluk hill in Selçuk, over the traditional tomb of John the Apostle.

Example: From its terrace there are views of the Isa Bey Mosque and the lone column of the Temple of Artemis.

docs.title: Battle of Crete
docs.text:
The German airborne invasion of Crete in May 1941, the first major attack by parachute troops, fought against British, Commonwealth and Greek soldiers and Cretan civilians, followed by a harsh occupation.

Example: War memorials in Cretan villages list civilians shot in reprisal for resistance.

docs.title: Battle of Marathon
docs.text:
The battle in 490 BCE in which Athenian and Plataean soldiers defeated a Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon, northeast of Athens.

Example: The legend of a runner carrying news of the victory to Athens inspired the modern marathon race.

docs.title: Battle of Salamis
docs.text:
The sea battle in 480 BCE in the narrow strait between the island of Salamis and the Attic coast, where the Greek fleet led by Athens destroyed much of the Persian navy.

Example: The strait lies just west of Piraeus, where our cruise ends.

docs.title: BCE and CE Dating
docs.text:
The system that numbers years "Before the Common Era" and in the "Common Era," equal to the older BC and AD. BCE years count down toward year 1 CE, and there is no year zero.

Example: A span from 750 BCE to 391 CE is 750 + 391 − 1 = 1,140 years, because the count skips zero.

docs.title: Bloom's 2 Sigma Problem
docs.text:
Benjamin Bloom's 1984 finding that students tutored individually with mastery methods performed about two standard deviations better than students taught in ordinary classes, and the challenge of achieving that result at scale.

Example: That means the average tutored student did better than about 98 percent of the classroom students.

See also: AI Tutoring, Mastery Learning

docs.title: Blue Mosque
docs.text:
The Sultan Ahmed Mosque in Istanbul, built from 1609 to 1616 facing Hagia Sophia, with six minarets and an interior lined with more than 20,000 blue-and-white Iznik tiles.

Example: It remains an active mosque, closed to tourists during the five daily prayers.

docs.title: Book of Acts
docs.text:
The New Testament book, written by the author of the Gospel of Luke, that tells the story of the first Christian communities and of Paul's journeys, trials and voyage to Rome.

Historians use it with care, comparing it with Paul's own letters.

See also: Primary Source

docs.title: Bosphorus Strait
docs.text:
Say it: Bosphorus BOS-fer-us 🔊 Pronounce

The narrow natural channel, about 30 km long, that runs through Istanbul and links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, dividing Europe from Asia.

Control of it made the city rich and strategically vital for over two thousand years.

Example: A twenty-minute public ferry from Eminönü to Kadıköy crosses from one continent to the other.

See also: Golden Horn, Istanbul

docs.title: Bribery of the Oracle
docs.text:
Cases reported by ancient writers in which powerful people paid Delphic staff to obtain the answers they wanted, as when a Spartan king bribed the Pythia, who was then removed.

See also: Who Funds the Model

docs.title: Brier Score
docs.text:
Say it: Brier BRY-er 🔊 Pronounce

A measure of forecast accuracy equal to the average of the squared differences between forecast probabilities and what happened, scored 1 or 0; lower numbers mean better forecasts.

Example: A 70 percent rain forecast on a day it rained adds (1 − 0.7)², or 0.09.

docs.title: Bronze Age
docs.text:
The era, roughly 3200 to 1100 BCE in the Aegean, when tools and weapons were made of bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, and the first palaces, scripts and long-distance trading networks appeared.

Example: The Minoan palace at Knossos and the Troy of the Trojan War legend both belong to this period.

See also: Bronze Age Collapse, Minoan Civilization

docs.title: Bronze Age Collapse
docs.text:
The breakdown of the palace societies of the Eastern Mediterranean around 1200 to 1150 BCE, when many cities were destroyed, trade networks failed and several states, including the Hittites and Mycenaeans, disappeared.

Causes probably combined drought, earthquakes, invasions, revolts and disrupted trade.

See also: Greek Dark Age, Hittite Empire

docs.title: Building a Team
docs.text:
Gathering and developing a group of co-workers with different skills who share responsibility for a change, so that it does not depend on one leader.

Example: Paul relied on Timothy, Titus, Priscilla, Aquila and Phoebe to carry his work.

docs.title: Bull-Leaping Fresco
docs.text:
A Minoan wall painting from Knossos, about 1450 BCE, showing young figures grasping a charging bull's horns and vaulting over its back, probably a ritual or sport.

Example: The original fragments hang in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

docs.title: Burning of Smyrna
docs.text: The fire of September 1922 that destroyed the Greek and Armenian quarters of Smyrna, modern İzmir, after Turkish forces retook the city, while tens of thousands of Christians fled to the waterfront.

docs.title: Byzantine Empire
docs.text:
Say it: Byzantine BIZ-un-teen 🔊 Pronounce

The Greek-speaking, Christian continuation of the Roman Empire in the east, ruled from Constantinople from 330 to 1453. Its people called themselves Romans.

See also: Byzantine Period, Fall of Constantinople

docs.title: Byzantine Manuscript Copying
docs.text:
Say it: Byzantine BIZ-un-teen 🔊 Pronounce

The work of Byzantine scribes, often monks, who copied ancient Greek texts by hand onto parchment, preserving much of classical literature and science that would otherwise be lost.

Example: Most of what we can read of Plato and Homer today passed through these copies.

See also: Scribes and Copyists

docs.title: Byzantine Mosaics
docs.text:
Say it: Byzantine BIZ-un-teen 🔊 Pronounce

Pictures made of small glass and stone cubes, often on gold backgrounds, that decorated Byzantine churches with images of Christ, Mary, saints and emperors.

Example: The Chora Church holds one of the most complete cycles of these images.

See also: Mosaic, Deesis Mosaic

docs.title: Byzantine Period
docs.text:
Say it: Byzantine BIZ-un-teen 🔊 Pronounce

The era of the eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire, from the founding of Constantinople in 330 CE to its capture by the Ottomans in 1453, marked by Greek-speaking Christian rule.

Example: Hagia Sophia, the Basilica Cistern and the Chora Church's mosaics all come from these centuries.

docs.title: Byzantium
docs.text: The Greek city founded around 657 BCE by colonists from Megara on the tip of the peninsula beside the Bosphorus, which later became Constantinople and then Istanbul.

docs.title: Caliphate
docs.text: The office of the caliph, the political and religious successor to the prophet Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community, claimed by Ottoman sultans and abolished by the Turkish Republic in 1924.

docs.title: Call to Prayer
docs.text:
The chanted announcement, made from each mosque five times a day, that the time for prayer has come, recited in Arabic with set phrases praising God.

Example: In Istanbul the calls from many mosques overlap across the city, especially at dusk.

docs.title: Canakkale Martyrs Memorial
docs.text:
Say it: Çanakkale chah-NAHK-kah-leh 🔊 Pronounce

The large four-legged stone monument at the southern tip of the Gallipoli peninsula honoring the Turkish soldiers who died in the 1915 campaign.

Example: Turkish school groups and families visit it in large numbers on March 18 and in spring.

docs.title: Canakkale Today
docs.text:
Say it: Çanakkale chah-NAHK-kah-leh 🔊 Pronounce

The lively provincial capital and university town on the Asian shore of the Dardanelles, whose name means "pottery castle," the base for visits to Troy and Gallipoli.

Example: The wooden horse from the 2004 film Troy stands on its waterfront.

See also: Eceabat

docs.title: Candia
docs.text:
The Venetian name for Heraklion, the capital of Venetian Crete, from the Arabic Khandaq, "moat"; the name was also used for the whole island.

Example: El Greco was born in this city in 1541.

docs.title: Caryatids
docs.text:
Say it: kar-ee-AT-idz 🔊 Pronounce

Carved figures of standing women used as columns to support a roof, best known from the porch of the Erechtheion on the Acropolis.

Example: Five of the originals stand in the Acropolis Museum; the sixth is in London, and copies hold up the porch today.

docs.title: Castalian Spring
docs.text:
Say it: Castalian kas-TAY-lee-un 🔊 Pronounce

The spring at the foot of the cliffs beside Delphi where visitors to the oracle washed to purify themselves before consulting the god.

Example: The remains of its stone fountain basins lie beside the road between the sanctuary and the museum.

docs.title: Cenchreae
docs.text:
Say it: SEN-kree-ee 🔊 Pronounce

The eastern port of ancient Corinth on the Saronic Gulf, home of the church whose leader Phoebe Paul commends in Romans.

See also: Phoebe

docs.title: Chaerephon's Question
docs.text:
Say it: Chaerephon KAIR-uh-fon 🔊 Pronounce

The question that Socrates' friend Chaerephon asked at Delphi, whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, to which the oracle answered that no one was.

docs.title: Change Fatigue
docs.text: The exhaustion and cynicism that build up when people face too many changes too quickly or see past changes abandoned.

docs.title: Change Leadership
docs.text:
The work of guiding an organization or community through a significant change, by setting a direction, building support, managing resistance and helping the change last.

See also: Paul as Change Case Study, Guiding Coalition

docs.title: Charioteer of Delphi
docs.text:
A life-size bronze statue of a chariot driver, made about 475 BCE to celebrate a victory in the Pythian Games, found in 1896, with eyes of inlaid stone and glass.

Example: It stands alone in its own room at the Delphi museum.

docs.title: Chora Church
docs.text:
Say it: Chora KOR-ah 🔊 Pronounce

A Byzantine church in western Istanbul whose mosaics and frescoes of the early 14th century, paid for by the statesman Theodore Metochites, are among the finest late Byzantine art. It reopened as a mosque in 2024.

docs.title: Christian Anti-Judaism
docs.text:
Hostility toward Jews and Judaism in Christian teaching and practice, which drew on readings of Paul and the gospels and contributed to centuries of persecution. Churches have formally rejected it since the 20th century.

Example: The Catholic Church's 1965 declaration Nostra Aetate repudiated blaming the Jews for Jesus' death.

See also: Chrysostom, Nostra Aetate

docs.title: Christianity
docs.text:
The religion centered on the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth, which began as a movement within Judaism in the 1st century CE and spread through the Roman world, partly through Paul's journeys and letters.

Example: Hagia Sophia, the Basilica of St. John at Ephesus and the Orthodox churches of Athens all trace back to this faith.

docs.title: Chrysostom
docs.text:
Say it: KRIS-us-tum 🔊 Pronounce

John Chrysostom, "golden-mouthed" (about 347–407 CE), a celebrated preacher in Antioch and later archbishop of Constantinople, whose sermons included harsh attacks on Jews.

See also: Christian Anti-Judaism

docs.title: Church of Mary at Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

A long church built inside a Roman hall in Ephesus, the first known church dedicated to Mary, where the Council of Ephesus met in 431 CE.

docs.title: City-State
docs.text:
An independent state made up of a single city and the farmland around it, with its own government, laws, army and gods, the normal political unit of ancient Greece.

Example: Athens and Sparta were rival states of this kind, each with only a few hundred thousand people at most.

docs.title: Civilization
docs.text:
A complex society with cities, specialized work, organized government, monumental building and usually a system of writing, sustained over many generations. The book follows several on one route, each building on those before.

Example: The Minoans of Crete had palaces, scribes and long-distance trade, the marks of an early Mediterranean society of this kind.

docs.title: Classical Orders
docs.text:
The standard styles of Greek and Roman column and the beam above it, each with its own proportions and decoration. Recognizing them helps date a building and read its purpose.

Example: The Parthenon uses one style outside and another for some interior columns.

See also: Doric Order, Ionic Order, Corinthian Order

docs.title: Classical Period
docs.text:
The phase of Greek history from the end of the Persian Wars in 480 BCE to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE, the age of Athenian democracy, the Parthenon, tragedy and Socrates.

Example: Nearly every building on the Acropolis today dates from these years.

docs.title: Climate Models
docs.text:
Computer simulations of the atmosphere, oceans, ice and land used to project how Earth's climate will change under different levels of greenhouse gas emissions.

Example: They project hotter, drier summers for Greece and Turkey, with more wildfire risk.

docs.title: Closing of the Oracle
docs.text:
The end of the Oracle of Delphi in the late 4th century CE, when the Christian emperor Theodosius I banned pagan worship and the sanctuary fell silent.

See also: Theodosian Decrees

docs.title: Colossus of Rhodes
docs.text:
A bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 meters tall, completed around 280 BCE to celebrate the city's survival of a siege, and toppled by an earthquake about 54 years later.

It almost certainly did not straddle the harbor, as later pictures show.

Example: Two bronze deer on columns now mark Mandraki harbor where popular legend places it.

docs.title: Compelling Inclusive Vision
docs.text:
A short, vivid picture of a future that people want to belong to, which also names clearly who is included in it, especially those once left out.

Example: "Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female" was one sentence any listener could repeat.

See also: Neither Jew Nor Greek

docs.title: Concentrated AI Risk
docs.text: The danger that knowledge and skills held inside a few AI systems, owned by a few companies, can be lost, priced out of reach or controlled.

docs.title: Confirmation Bias
docs.text:
The human tendency to notice, remember and believe information that supports what we already think, and to overlook evidence against it.

Example: People remembered Delphi's famous hits and forgot its misses.

See also: Track Record and Trust

docs.title: Consent in Mass Prediction
docs.text:
The question of whether the people a predictive system makes forecasts about have agreed to it, or even know about it.

Example: At Delphi every prediction was asked for, while modern systems score millions of people who never asked.

docs.title: Constantine the Great
docs.text:
The Roman emperor (ruled 306–337 CE) who legalized and favored Christianity and refounded Byzantium as his new capital, dedicated in 330 CE.

Example: Hagia Sophia's mosaics show him offering the city to Mary and the Christ child.

docs.title: Constantinople
docs.text: The capital of the eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire from 330 to 1453, built on the site of Byzantium, and capital of the Ottoman Empire after 1453, now called Istanbul.

docs.title: Contested History
docs.text:
An account of the past on which groups disagree, often because the events still matter to national identity, religion or property, so that the same place or date is remembered in conflicting ways.

Example: Hagia Sophia's conversions from church to mosque to museum and back to mosque are read very differently in Athens and in Istanbul.

docs.title: Corinthian Order
docs.text:
The most ornate Greek and Roman column style, with a tall capital carved with rows of acanthus leaves and small scrolls. The Romans favored it for grand public buildings.

Example: The surviving columns of the Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens carry these leafy capitals.

docs.title: Cost of Delaying Technology
docs.text:
What a society loses in the years between the arrival of a better way to store or spread knowledge and its adoption: books not printed, readers not made, ideas that traveled slowly.

Example: The book's clearest case is the roughly 275-year gap between Gutenberg and the first Ottoman Turkish press.

docs.title: Costs of Top-Down Reform
docs.text:
The losses that come with a change decided by a ruler or government and imposed on people without their choice: the knowledge, trust and ways of life that a fast, uniform change sweeps away.

Example: The 1928 alphabet switch cut new generations off from reading their grandparents' letters and books.

See also: Education With Communities

docs.title: Council of Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The church council of bishops held at Ephesus in 431 CE that affirmed Mary's title Theotokos, "God-bearer," and condemned Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople.

docs.title: Council of Jerusalem
docs.text:
The meeting of early church leaders in Jerusalem around 49 CE, described in Acts 15 and Galatians, which decided that Gentile believers did not have to be circumcised or keep the whole Jewish law.

Example: The book reads it as a model for separating what is essential in an institution from what is inherited.

docs.title: Credit for Groundwork
docs.text:
The principle that people who build a discovery's foundations, by collecting, cleaning and organizing evidence, deserve recognition alongside those who make the final leap.

Example: For decades the Linear B story was told as Ventris's alone, leaving out Alice Kober.

docs.title: Cretan Diet
docs.text: The traditional diet of rural Crete, heavy in olive oil, wild greens, legumes, bread, fruit and modest amounts of cheese and meat, whose study in the 1950s helped define the Mediterranean diet.

docs.title: Cretan Renaissance
docs.text:
The flowering of art and literature on Venetian Crete from the 15th to 17th centuries, combining Byzantine and Italian styles in icon painting and producing poetry and drama in the Cretan dialect.

Example: The verse romance Erotokritos is its best-known literary work.

docs.title: Cretan Village Life
docs.text: The way of life in Crete's inland villages, built around family land, olive groves and vineyards, the parish church and its saint's-day festival, and the village coffeehouse.

docs.title: Crete
docs.text:
The largest Greek island, at the southern edge of the Aegean, home to the Bronze Age Minoan civilization and later ruled by Romans, Byzantines, Venetians and Ottomans before joining Greece in 1913.

Example: At Heraklion we can walk the Venetian harbor in the morning and see Minoan gold in the archaeological museum in the afternoon.

docs.title: Croesus of Lydia
docs.text:
Say it: Croesus KREE-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The fabulously rich king of Lydia in western Anatolia (ruled about 560–546 BCE), who sent lavish gifts to Delphi and asked whether he should attack Persia.

docs.title: Croesus Prophecy
docs.text:
Say it: Croesus KREE-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The oracle's reply to Croesus that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire. He attacked, and the empire destroyed was his own.

Example: It is the classic case of an answer that could not turn out wrong.

See also: Hedging Answers

docs.title: Crusades
docs.text:
The series of military expeditions from about 1095 to 1291 launched by Western Christians, with papal support, to seize or defend the Holy Land and other territories.

See also: Fourth Crusade, Knights Hospitaller

docs.title: Cultural Memory
docs.text:
The way a community remembers its past through monuments, ceremonies, stories, school lessons and holidays, which shapes who it believes it is.

Example: Gallipoli is remembered as a founding sacrifice in Turkey and as a coming of age for Australia and New Zealand.

docs.title: Curetes Street
docs.text:
Say it: Curetes kyoo-REE-teez 🔊 Pronounce

The main sloping marble street of ancient Ephesus, running downhill from the upper civic square to the Library of Celsus and lined with statues, fountains, shops and monuments.

Example: Walking down it, visitors pass the Temple of Hadrian and the entrance to the Terrace Houses.

docs.title: Currency and Payments
docs.text:
The money and payment methods used on the trip: the Turkish lira in Turkey and the euro in Greece, with cards widely accepted but cash still needed for small purchases and tips.

Example: A simit from a street cart is paid for in coins, while a museum ticket can be bought by card.

docs.title: Cyclades
docs.text:
Say it: SIK-luh-deez 🔊 Pronounce

The group of Greek islands in the central Aegean arranged roughly in a circle around the sacred island of Delos, including Naxos, Paros, Mykonos and Santorini.

docs.title: Daily Chapter Routine
docs.text:
The habit this book is built around: reading one chapter for each day, at breakfast or the night before, so that each morning we arrive knowing what happened at the place, what to look for, what to eat and who lives there now.

Example: The night before Delphi we read the chapter on the oracle so that the ruins make sense the next day.

docs.title: Daily Life in Athens
docs.text:
The everyday routines of Athenians: late lunches and later dinners, coffee with friends, neighborhood street markets, crowded metro rides and long summer evenings outside.

Example: A freddo espresso at a café can last two hours of conversation.

docs.title: Daily Life in Istanbul
docs.text:
The everyday routines of the city's residents: long commutes by ferry, metro and bus, tea breaks, family breakfasts, neighborhood bakeries and mosques, and a mix of religious and secular lifestyles.

Example: On a Sunday, families fill ferries to the Asian shore simply for the ride.

docs.title: Daily Prayer
docs.text:
The ritual prayer, called namaz in Turkish, that Muslims perform five times a day at set times, facing Mecca, with standing, bowing and kneeling.

Example: Shopkeepers in the Grand Bazaar may step away briefly to pray at midday.

See also: Prayer Times, Ablution

docs.title: Dakos
docs.text:
Say it: DAH-kos 🔊 Pronounce

A Cretan dish of a dried barley rusk topped with grated tomato, crumbled soft white cheese, olive oil and oregano.

Example: Ordered as a starter in Heraklion, it arrives softened by the tomato juice.

docs.title: Dardanelles Strait
docs.text:
Say it: Dardanelles dar-duh-NELZ 🔊 Pronounce

The narrow channel in northwest Turkey that links the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara and separates the Gallipoli peninsula in Europe from Asia. The ancient Greeks called it the Hellespont.

Example: The 1915 Allied attempt to force a fleet through it led to the Gallipoli Campaign.

See also: Gallipoli Campaign, Canakkale Today

docs.title: Data Bias
docs.text:
Systematic distortion in a dataset, caused by who or what was recorded, how and by whom, that leads a system trained on it to make unfair or inaccurate predictions for some groups.

Example: A model trained mostly on English text may translate Greek or Turkish less well.

docs.title: Day Trip to Delphi
docs.text:
Day 12 of our itinerary: a round trip by road from Athens to the sanctuary of Apollo and its museum, about 180 km and two and a half hours each way, with a stop in Arachova.

Example: The road climbs past Thebes and Livadeia into the mountains before the cliffs above Delphi come into view.

See also: Delphi, Arachova

docs.title: Decipherment of Linear B
docs.text:
The 1952 breakthrough that showed the clay tablets of Knossos and Pylos record Greek, pushing the written history of the language back about 600 years before Homer.

Example: Once read, the tablets turned out to be palace bookkeeping, not poetry or history.

docs.title: Decline of the Oracle
docs.text:
The gradual loss of Delphi's influence under Hellenistic kings and Roman rule, when cities no longer made great political decisions on their own and fewer consultants came.

Example: Plutarch, writing around 100 CE, noted that one Pythia was now enough where once two or three had been needed.

docs.title: Deesis Mosaic
docs.text:
Say it: Deesis dee-EE-sis 🔊 Pronounce

A 13th-century mosaic in the upper gallery of Hagia Sophia showing Christ flanked by Mary and John the Baptist, who plead with him on behalf of humanity.

Example: Even damaged, the gentle faces make it one of the finest works of Byzantine art.

docs.title: Delayed Arabic-Script Printing
docs.text:
The gap of about 275 years between Gutenberg's press and the first Ottoman Turkish book press in 1727, explained by scholars through scribal interests, the beauty of handwriting, religious caution and low demand.

See also: Cost of Delaying Technology, Scribal Resistance

docs.title: Delphi
docs.text:
The site of the ancient sanctuary of Apollo on Mount Parnassus, home of the most famous oracle of the Greek world, which the Greeks called the center of the earth.

See also: Oracle of Delphi, Sanctuary of Apollo

docs.title: Delphi Archaeological Museum
docs.text: The museum beside the sanctuary that displays sculpture, offerings and objects found at Delphi, including the Charioteer, the Sphinx of the Naxians and the omphalos.

docs.title: Delphi Reflection Questions
docs.text:
A short set of questions, answered in our own words in the travel journal, about how the oracle's lessons apply to the predictions in our own lives.

Example: The drive back from Delphi to Athens is long enough to answer all of them.

docs.title: Delphic Neutrality
docs.text:
The sanctuary's position as common ground for all Greeks, where rival cities could consult the god and dedicate offerings, which Delphi did not always maintain in practice.

Example: Accusations that the oracle favored Persia in 480 BCE damaged its standing.

docs.title: Demetrius the Silversmith
docs.text: The craftsman in Acts 19 who made silver shrines of Artemis and roused fellow workers against Paul, warning that the new teaching threatened both their income and the goddess's honor.

docs.title: Democratization of Education
docs.text:
The long historical effort to make good learning available to every person, whatever their wealth, birthplace, gender, language or ability.

It depends on quality as well as access, and on working with communities.

Example: Free adult alphabet classes in 1929 Turkey were one large step in this effort.

docs.title: Diffusion of Innovation
docs.text:
The process by which a new idea or practice spreads through a population over time, described by Everett Rogers as moving from innovators and early adopters to the majority and finally to latecomers.

See also: Hub and Spoke Diffusion

docs.title: Dionysus at Delphi
docs.text: The worship of Dionysus, god of wine and ecstasy, at Delphi, where he was believed to preside in winter while Apollo was away, and where his tomb was said to lie in the temple.

docs.title: Direct Instruction
docs.text: A teacher-led method in which the teacher explains and models new content, guides students through practice, checks understanding and then has them practice alone, often summed up as "I do, we do, you do."

docs.title: Disputed Pauline Letters
docs.text:
The letters bearing Paul's name whose authorship scholars debate because of differences in style, vocabulary or ideas, such as Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus.

See also: Letter to the Ephesians

docs.title: Dodecanese Union With Greece
docs.text:
Say it: Dodecanese doh-dek-uh-NEEZ 🔊 Pronounce

The transfer of Rhodes and the other Dodecanese islands from Italian control to Greece after World War II, agreed in the 1947 Treaty of Paris and completed in March 1948.

Example: Rhodes became part of Greece only in 1948, more than a century after Athens.

docs.title: Dolmabahçe
docs.text:
Say it: dol-MAH-bah-cheh 🔊 Pronounce

The European-style Ottoman palace on the Bosphorus to which the sultans moved their court from Topkapı in 1856, and where Atatürk died in 1938.

Example: The clocks in the room where he died are traditionally set to 9:05.

docs.title: Doric Order
docs.text:
The plainest and oldest Greek column style, with a fluted shaft standing directly on the floor without a base and a simple cushion-shaped capital, favored on the Greek mainland.

Example: The outer columns of the Parthenon and the Temple of Hephaestus are of this style.

docs.title: Dress at Sacred Sites
docs.text:
The expected clothing for visitors to mosques, churches and monasteries, usually covered shoulders and knees, and for women a head scarf in mosques.

Example: At the Blue Mosque, staff lend scarves and wraps to visitors who arrive in shorts.

docs.title: Early Jesus Movement
docs.text:
The communities of Jesus' followers in the decades after his death, at first Jewish groups in Judea and Galilee, which spread through Greek-speaking cities and came to include non-Jews.

Example: The small house groups in Ephesus, Corinth and Rome that Paul wrote to belonged to this movement.

docs.title: Eastern Mediterranean
docs.text:
The part of the Mediterranean Sea east of Italy, together with the coastlands around it: Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt. It is the shared stage for every stop on this trip.

Example: Sailing from Istanbul to Athens, the ship never leaves this one connected sea world, where Greeks, Romans, Byzantines and Ottomans all ruled in turn.

docs.title: Eastern Orthodox Church
docs.text: The family of Christian churches, including the Greek Orthodox Church, that grew from Byzantine Christianity, governed by bishops in communion with each other and known for icons and a rich liturgy.

docs.title: Eceabat
docs.text:
Say it: eh-JEH-ah-baht 🔊 Pronounce

A small town on the European shore of the Dardanelles, on the Gallipoli peninsula, linked to Çanakkale by a car ferry of about half an hour.

docs.title: Economics of Resistance
docs.text:
The fact that people resist a change partly because of what it would cost them in income, skill, status or the value of years of training.

Example: Demetrius' silversmiths feared both for their goddess and for their trade.

See also: Riot of the Silversmiths, Scribal Resistance

docs.title: Ecumenical Patriarchate
docs.text:
The office and headquarters of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, honored as first among the Orthodox bishops, based since 1601 in the Fener district of Istanbul.

Example: Its small Church of St. George sits in a quiet neighborhood on the Golden Horn.

docs.title: Education Evangelism
docs.text:
The work of persuading schools, families and communities that a new way of teaching and learning is good news worth adopting, and helping them adopt it.

Example: A teacher who shows colleagues how an AI tutor helped one struggling student is doing this work.

docs.title: Education With Communities
docs.text:
Designing, running and judging an effort to widen learning together with the people it is meant to serve, in their language, with their consent and with their hands on how it continues.

Example: Masakhane's volunteers build translation tools for their own African languages.

See also: Masakhane, Costs of Top-Down Reform

docs.title: Eggplant
docs.text:
A purple-skinned vegetable, first grown in South or Southeast Asia, that reached the Mediterranean through Persian and Arab cooking and appears in more shared Greek and Turkish dishes than any other.

Example: It is one of our favorite foods of the trip, whether as moussaka or as imam bayıldı.

docs.title: El Greco
docs.text:
The painter Domenikos Theotokopoulos (1541–1614), born in Candia, who trained as an icon painter on Crete and moved to Venice, Rome and finally Toledo in Spain.

Example: The Historical Museum of Crete in Heraklion holds two of his small paintings.

See also: Theotokopoulos

docs.title: Elite Knowledge Is Fragile
docs.text:
The lesson that knowledge held by a small group, for a narrow purpose, inside one institution, lives and dies with that institution, while knowledge spread among many people survives.

Example: Linear B vanished with the palaces, while the Greek alphabet, scratched on jugs by ordinary people, lasted.

See also: Palace Scribes, Concentrated AI Risk

docs.title: Eminönü
docs.text:
Say it: eh-MEE-nuh-new 🔊 Pronounce

The busy waterfront district of Istanbul at the mouth of the Golden Horn, home to ferry piers, the Spice Bazaar, the New Mosque and the fish-sandwich boats.

docs.title: Empathy in Travel
docs.text:
The effort to imagine the lives, feelings and concerns of the people who live where we visit, including how our presence affects them, rather than seeing them only as part of the scenery.

Example: A waiter in Çanakkale in November may be earning the last tips before months without tourist income.

docs.title: Empire
docs.text:
A large state in which one ruler or people governs many lands and peoples of different languages and faiths, usually gained by conquest and held by force, taxes and administration.

Example: Istanbul was the capital of two such states in a row, the Byzantine and the Ottoman, for nearly sixteen hundred years.

docs.title: Endowed Free Education
docs.text:
Teaching provided at no cost to students and paid for permanently by income from a charitable endowment rather than by fees or the state budget.

Example: A boy in an Ottoman mosque-complex school learned to read without paying anything.

docs.title: Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

A major ancient city on the west coast of Anatolia, near modern Selçuk, the leading city of Roman Asia and home of the Temple of Artemis, where Paul spent more than two years.

Example: Its marble streets, theater and the facade of the Library of Celsus are among the best-preserved Roman remains anywhere.

See also: Paul in Ephesus, Library of Celsus

docs.title: Ephesus Harbor Silting
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The gradual filling of Ephesus's harbor with mud carried by the Kaystros River, which over centuries moved the coastline several kilometers west and helped end the city's role as a port.

Example: The Harbor Street that once led from the theater to the docks now ends in fields far from the sea.

docs.title: Ephesus Museum
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The archaeological museum in the town of Selçuk, a few kilometers from ancient Ephesus, that displays statues, coins, household objects and portraits found at the site.

Example: The two marble statues of Artemis of Ephesus are its most famous pieces.

docs.title: Ephesus Public Latrines
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The Roman public toilets of Ephesus, a room with rows of marble seats over a channel of running water, where men sat side by side and talked.

Example: Visitors are often surprised that a toilet could be a social space.

docs.title: Epictetus
docs.text:
Say it: ep-ik-TEE-tus 🔊 Pronounce

A Stoic teacher (about 50–135 CE), born enslaved at Hierapolis in Anatolia, who taught in Greece after being freed and stressed focusing only on what lies within our control.

docs.title: Erechtheion
docs.text:
Say it: eh-REK-thee-on 🔊 Pronounce

An unusual Ionic temple on the north side of the Acropolis, built from about 421 to 406 BCE, housing several old cults on uneven ground, including those of Athena and Poseidon.

Example: Its south porch is held up by six statues of young women instead of columns.

docs.title: Erotokritos
docs.text:
Say it: eh-roh-TOH-kree-tos 🔊 Pronounce

A Cretan verse romance of about 10,000 rhyming lines written around 1600 by Vitsentzos Kornaros, telling of young Erotokritos's love for a princess, still recited and sung in Crete.

docs.title: Essential Versus Inherited
docs.text:
The distinction between what an institution exists to do and the particular forms through which it happened to do it.

Example: The Council of Jerusalem treated faith as essential and circumcision as an inherited form Gentiles did not need.

docs.title: Euangelion
docs.text:
Say it: yoo-an-GEL-ee-on 🔊 Pronounce

The Greek word for "good news," used by Homer for a messenger's reward, in a Roman inscription honoring Augustus, and by Paul for his message. It is the source of "evangel" and "evangelical."

See also: Evangelist, Good News Message

docs.title: Evangelism's Shadow
docs.text: The harm that follows when good news is imposed on people rather than chosen by them, or when its carriers treat those who decline it with contempt.

docs.title: Evangelist
docs.text:
A person who carries good news to others; in Christianity, a preacher of the gospel or one of the four gospel writers. In technology it came to mean someone who promotes an idea.

Example: In the 1980s Apple called its staff who championed the Macintosh "software evangelists."

See also: Education Evangelism

docs.title: Evans Reconstructions
docs.text:
The partial rebuilding of Knossos carried out for Arthur Evans in the 1910s to 1930s, using reinforced concrete and repainted copies of frescoes to show how rooms might have looked.

They help visitors imagine the palace but mix evidence with guesswork.

Example: The famous red columns of the north entrance are concrete restorations based on Evans's interpretation.

See also: Restoration and Reconstruction

docs.title: Exarchia
docs.text:
Say it: ek-SAR-khee-ah 🔊 Pronounce

The student neighborhood of central Athens just behind the Polytechnic, known for its bookshops, cafés, graffiti, left-wing politics and occasional clashes with police.

Example: Its square fills with students in the evening, and walls are covered in posters and murals.

See also: Athens Polytechnic Uprising

docs.title: Ezan
docs.text:
Say it: eh-ZAHN 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish word for the Muslim call to prayer, the Arabic adhan, chanted from the minarets of mosques five times a day, now usually through loudspeakers.

Example: In Istanbul the ezan from neighboring mosques overlaps, so the city seems to answer itself.

See also: Call to Prayer

docs.title: Faith in Modern Turkey
docs.text: The place of religion in Turkish life today, where most people are Muslim, practice ranges from devout to secular, and debates over religion's role in public life remain lively.

docs.title: Fall of Constantinople
docs.text:
The capture of Constantinople by the Ottoman army of Mehmed II on May 29, 1453, after a siege of about seven weeks, ending the Byzantine Empire.

See also: Mehmed the Conqueror, Theodosian Walls

docs.title: Family Life Today
docs.text:
The patterns of modern Greek and Turkish family life, where close ties between generations remain strong, young adults often live with parents longer and grandparents help raise children.

Example: A Sunday lunch in Athens may bring three generations around one table.

docs.title: Farewell at Miletus
docs.text:
Say it: Miletus my-LEE-tus 🔊 Pronounce

The scene in Acts 20 where Paul, on his way to Jerusalem, called the leaders of the Ephesian church to the port of Miletus and gave a farewell speech before sailing.

Example: The book reads it as a lesson in handing leadership on to others.

See also: Succession Planning

docs.title: Fear of New Learning Tech
docs.text:
The recurring worry that a new tool for learning will weaken memory, effort or understanding, voiced about writing, printing, calculators, search engines and now AI.

See also: Phaedrus on Writing, AI Over-Reliance

docs.title: Fees and Sacrifice
docs.text: The payments and offerings required to consult the oracle: a cake or money fee, set higher for cities than individuals, and an animal sacrifice before entering the temple.

docs.title: Feta Cheese
docs.text:
A white brined cheese made in Greece from sheep's milk, or sheep's and goat's milk, whose name is legally protected for cheese made in certain regions of Greece.

See also: Greek Salad

docs.title: Filiki Eteria
docs.text:
Say it: fee-lee-KEE eh-teh-REE-ah 🔊 Pronounce

The "Friendly Society," a secret Greek organization founded by three merchants in Odessa in 1814 to prepare an uprising against Ottoman rule, which began the 1821 revolution.

See also: Greek War of Independence

docs.title: First Corinthians
docs.text: Paul's letter to the community at Corinth, written from Ephesus in the mid-50s CE, dealing with divisions, worship and conduct, and including his famous passages on the body and on love.

docs.title: Five Pillars of Islam
docs.text: The five basic practices of Islam: the declaration of faith, the five daily prayers, giving to the poor, fasting in the month of Ramadan and the pilgrimage to Mecca for those able.

docs.title: Food as History
docs.text:
The idea that dishes and ingredients record past trade, conquest, migration and religion, so that what people eat today can tell stories that buildings and texts do not.

Example: Eggplant reached the Mediterranean through Persian and Arab cooking, so Pericles never tasted it.

docs.title: Fourth Crusade
docs.text:
The Western crusade of 1202 to 1204 that, instead of reaching the Holy Land, attacked and sacked Constantinople, deepening the split between Latin and Orthodox Christians.

Example: The four bronze horses taken from the Hippodrome still decorate St. Mark's Basilica in Venice.

docs.title: Frank Calvert
docs.text:
A British resident of the Dardanelles (1828–1908) who owned part of the Hisarlik mound, dug there in the 1860s and persuaded Heinrich Schliemann that it was Troy.

His role was long overshadowed by Schliemann's self-promotion.

See also: Heinrich Schliemann, Credit for Groundwork

docs.title: French Excavation of Delphi
docs.text:
The "Great Excavation" of Delphi carried out by the French School at Athens from 1892 to 1903, after the village of Kastri, which sat on the ruins, was moved to a new site.

Example: The reconstructed Athenian Treasury is one of its lasting results.

See also: Kastri, Modern Delphi Village

docs.title: Fresco
docs.text:
A wall painting made by applying pigment to wet lime plaster, so that the color binds into the wall as it dries and lasts for centuries.

Example: The walls of the Terrace Houses at Ephesus still carry painted birds, muses and garden scenes.

See also: Minoan Frescoes

docs.title: Fresh Fish
docs.text:
Fish caught that day and cooked simply, usually grilled with olive oil and lemon, sold in Greek tavernas by weight and chosen by the diner from the display.

Example: At a Piraeus fish taverna, the waiter may bring the day's catch to the table to choose.

docs.title: Friday Prayer
docs.text: The weekly congregational prayer held at midday on Friday in a large mosque, with a sermon, which adult Muslim men are expected to attend.

docs.title: Galata Tower
docs.text:
Say it: Galata GAH-lah-tah 🔊 Pronounce

A round stone tower about 67 meters high, built by Genoese merchants in 1348 above the Golden Horn, now a viewing point over the old city and the Bosphorus.

docs.title: Gallipoli Campaign
docs.text:
Say it: Gallipoli guh-LIP-uh-lee 🔊 Pronounce

The Allied attempt in 1915 to seize the Dardanelles and knock the Ottoman Empire out of World War I, first by naval attack and then by landings on the Gallipoli peninsula, which ended in Allied withdrawal in January 1916.

More than 100,000 soldiers died on both sides.

See also: ANZAC Forces, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk

docs.title: Gamaliel
docs.text:
Say it: guh-MAY-lee-ul 🔊 Pronounce

A respected Pharisee teacher in Jerusalem in the 1st century CE, under whom Acts says Paul was trained; Paul's own letters do not mention him.

docs.title: Gentiles
docs.text:
People who are not Jewish; in the New Testament, the non-Jewish peoples of the Greek and Roman world to whom Paul saw himself sent.

See also: Neither Jew Nor Greek

docs.title: Geological Fault Theory
docs.text: The modern hypothesis that the Pythia's inspiration came from gases, such as ethylene, rising through faults in the rock beneath the temple, proposed by a geologist and archaeologist around 2001 and still debated.

docs.title: Glaux
docs.text:
Say it: GLOWKS 🔊 Pronounce

The book's mascot, a little owl, the same species that sat on Athena's shoulder and appeared on the silver coins of ancient Athens; its name is the ancient Greek word for that owl.

Example: Glaux appears in boxes through the chapters to welcome readers and point out key ideas.

See also: Athena

docs.title: Golden Horn
docs.text:
The narrow, curved inlet of the Bosphorus that forms a natural harbor on the north side of Istanbul's historic peninsula, separating it from Galata and Beyoğlu.

Example: The Galata Bridge across it is lined with people fishing at almost any hour.

docs.title: Good News Message
docs.text:
A short statement, in our own words, of why something about learning is good news, drawn from one real story and written so that the people it concerns would find it good.

Example: The book asks us to write one on the flight home.

docs.title: Grace and Faith
docs.text:
Two central ideas in Paul's letters: grace, God's free and unearned favor, and faith, a person's trust in God and in Christ, which Paul argues is how people are made right with God.

See also: Letter to the Romans, Protestant Reformation

docs.title: Graffiti
docs.text:
Writing or drawing on public walls without permission, from scrawled names to building-sized murals, for which Athens is known across Europe.

Example: Tags on shutters, political slogans and large murals cover many walls in Exarchia and Psyrri.

docs.title: Grammar of Schooling
docs.text:
The phrase from historians David Tyack and William Tobin for the regular, mostly unnoticed structures of school: periods of time, age-graded classes, one teacher per room and separate subjects.

See also: Seat Time and Carnegie Unit

docs.title: Grand Bazaar
docs.text:
The great covered market in the center of Istanbul's historic peninsula, begun in the 1450s under Mehmed II, with thousands of shops along dozens of vaulted streets.

Example: Carpets, lamps, gold and leather goods fill its lanes, and it is closed on Sundays.

See also: Kapalıçarşı, Bargaining in Bazaars

docs.title: Great Schism of 1054
docs.text:
The break between the Church of Rome and the Church of Constantinople, marked by mutual excommunications in 1054, which divided Western Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christianity.

See also: Eastern Orthodox Church

docs.title: Great Theater of Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

The huge hillside theater of Ephesus, enlarged in Roman times to seat about 25,000 people, used for plays, assemblies and later gladiator shows.

Example: Acts places the riot of the silversmiths here, with the crowd shouting for two hours.

See also: Riot of the Silversmiths, Greek Theater

docs.title: Greco-Turkish War
docs.text:
The war of 1919 to 1922 in which a Greek army, landing at Smyrna, advanced deep into Anatolia and was defeated by Turkish nationalist forces under Mustafa Kemal.

See also: Burning of Smyrna, Megali Idea

docs.title: Greek Alphabet
docs.text:
The script adapted from Phoenician letters around 800 BCE, which added letters for vowel sounds and so became the first full alphabet, able to record any word with about two dozen signs.

Example: Early examples are scratched on pottery jugs, showing it was used by ordinary people, not only scribes.

docs.title: Greek Coffee
docs.text:
Finely ground coffee boiled in a small pot and served unfiltered with its grounds, the same drink as Turkish coffee, renamed in Greece in the 20th century.

Example: Ordering it metrio means medium sweet.

docs.title: Greek Colonization
docs.text:
The founding of new Greek cities around the Mediterranean and Black Sea from about 750 to 550 BCE, often after colonists consulted Delphi about where to settle.

Example: Byzantium was founded by colonists from Megara who, by tradition, followed an oracle's advice.

See also: Oracle as Data Hub

docs.title: Greek Cuisine
docs.text:
The cooking of Greece, built on olive oil, vegetables, legumes, bread, cheese, fish and lamb, flavored with lemon, oregano and herbs and shaped by regional and Ottoman influences.

See also: Mediterranean Diet, Taverna Culture

docs.title: Greek Dark Age
docs.text:
The period in Greece from about 1100 to 800 BCE that followed the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, when population shrank, monumental building stopped and writing was lost.

Example: Stories of Troy survived these centuries only in song, carried by oral tradition.

docs.title: Greek Debt Crisis
docs.text:
The financial crisis that began in 2009 when Greece could not repay its debts, leading to international bailouts, harsh spending cuts, high unemployment and the emigration of many young Greeks.

Example: Shuttered shops and lowered pensions from the crisis years are still remembered in Athens conversations.

docs.title: Greek Islands
docs.text:
The several thousand islands belonging to Greece, grouped into chains such as the Cyclades, the Dodecanese and the Ionian Islands, with Crete as the largest.

Example: Rhodes and Crete are the two that our ship visits.

docs.title: Greek Language
docs.text:
The Indo-European language spoken in Greece and around the Aegean for more than 3,400 years, from Mycenaean records in Linear B through ancient and Koine forms to the Greek spoken today.

Example: A modern Athenian can read many words on an ancient inscription, such as demos, "people."

docs.title: Greek Mythology
docs.text:
The body of traditional stories the ancient Greeks told about their gods, heroes, monsters and origins, passed down by poets and artists and used to explain the world and teach values.

Example: The tale of Theseus and the Minotaur links Athens to the palace of Knossos on Crete.

See also: Myth Versus History, Olympian Gods

docs.title: Greek Philosophy
docs.text:
The tradition of reasoned inquiry into nature, knowledge, ethics and politics begun by Greek thinkers from the 6th century BCE, including Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and the Stoics.

Example: Athens's Agora, Academy and Lyceum were its main teaching places.

docs.title: Greek Salad
docs.text:
The village salad, horiatiki, of tomato, cucumber, onion, peppers and olives topped with a slab of feta and olive oil, served without lettuce.

Example: In November, made with the last good tomatoes of the season, it is still on every taverna menu.

docs.title: Greek Theater
docs.text:
An open-air performance space built into a hillside, with a semicircle of stone seats, a round dancing floor called the orchestra and a stage building behind it.

Example: The Great Theater of Ephesus and the theater at Delphi both follow this plan.

docs.title: Greek Tragedy
docs.text:
A form of serious drama developed in 5th-century BCE Athens, performed by masked actors and a chorus, in which characters face suffering, moral choices and the limits of human power.

Example: Sophocles' Oedipus the King turns on a prophecy from Delphi.

docs.title: Greek War of Independence
docs.text: The uprising that began in 1821 in which Greeks fought to free themselves from Ottoman rule, won with help from Britain, France and Russia and leading to an independent Greek state in 1830–1832.

docs.title: Greek Wine
docs.text: Wine made in Greece from mostly native grape varieties, such as Assyrtiko, Agiorgitiko and Xinomavro, continuing a winemaking tradition older than Homer.

docs.title: Greek-Turkish Relations
docs.text:
The relationship between the two neighboring countries, shaped by shared history, wars, the 1923 exchange, disputes over Cyprus and the Aegean, and periods of cooperation and friendship.

Example: After the earthquakes of 1999, rescue teams from each country helped the other, warming relations.

See also: Shared Greek-Turkish Dishes

docs.title: Guiding Coalition
docs.text: In John Kotter's model of leading change, a group with enough power, expertise and credibility to lead a change effort together.

docs.title: Gulhane Park
docs.text:
Say it: Gülhane gewl-hah-NEH 🔊 Pronounce

A large public park on the slope below Topkapı Palace, once the palace's outer garden, now one of Istanbul's oldest and most popular green spaces.

Example: In April its paths are lined with tulips during the city's tulip festival.

docs.title: Gutenberg
docs.text: Johannes Gutenberg (about 1400–1468), the goldsmith of Mainz, Germany, who developed printing with movable metal type around 1450, producing his famous Bible in the mid-1450s.

docs.title: Hadrian
docs.text:
Roman emperor from 117 to 138 CE, a great traveler and admirer of Greek culture who funded buildings across the Greek world, including the completion of the Temple of Olympian Zeus.

Example: A small temple on Curetes Street in Ephesus was dedicated in his honor.

docs.title: Hagia Sophia
docs.text:
Say it: HAH-yuh soh-FEE-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The great domed church of Holy Wisdom in Istanbul, built by Justinian from 532 to 537 CE, later a mosque, a museum and, since 2020, a mosque again.

See also: Hagia Sophia Dome, Hagia Sophia Status Debate

docs.title: Hagia Sophia as Mosque
docs.text:
Say it: Hagia Sophia HAH-yuh soh-FEE-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The use of Hagia Sophia for Muslim worship, from the Ottoman conquest in 1453 to 1934, and again since 2020, with minarets, a mihrab and large calligraphic roundels added.

Example: During prayers, curtains cover some of the Christian mosaics.

docs.title: Hagia Sophia Dome
docs.text:
Say it: Hagia Sophia HAH-yuh soh-FEE-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The vast central dome of Hagia Sophia, about 31 meters across and 55 meters high, which seems to float on a ring of windows; it partly collapsed in 558 and was rebuilt higher.

Example: Ottoman architects later added buttresses to keep it standing through earthquakes.

docs.title: Hagia Sophia Status Debate
docs.text:
Say it: Hagia Sophia HAH-yuh soh-FEE-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The ongoing disagreement over whether Hagia Sophia should be a museum open to all, a mosque, or both, reignited when Turkey reconverted it to a mosque in 2020.

docs.title: Hall of Tyrannus
docs.text:
Say it: Tyrannus tih-RAN-us 🔊 Pronounce

The lecture hall in Ephesus where, according to Acts, Paul taught daily for two years after leaving the synagogue. Acts calls it a scholē, the root of the word "school."

Its location has not been identified.

docs.title: Hamam
docs.text:
Say it: hah-MAHM 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish word for a public steam bath, where bathers sweat on a heated marble platform and are washed and scrubbed by attendants.

Example: A historic one by Mimar Sinan near Hagia Sophia still serves bathers today.

docs.title: Harem of Topkapi
docs.text:
Say it: Topkapı TOP-kah-puh 🔊 Pronounce

The private quarters of the sultan's family in Topkapı Palace, where his mother, wives, children and women servants lived, guarded by eunuchs, and where much palace politics took place.

Example: Its most powerful figure was the sultan's mother, the valide sultan.

docs.title: Hebrew Press of 1493
docs.text:
The printing press set up in Istanbul in 1493 by the Sephardic brothers David and Samuel ibn Nahmias, the first press in the Ottoman Empire, which printed books in Hebrew.

Example: Jewish printers in the city were producing books more than two centuries before the first Ottoman Turkish press.

docs.title: Hedging Answers
docs.text: Replies worded so they could fit several outcomes, protecting the speaker's reputation whatever happened. Many famous Delphic oracles have this quality.

docs.title: Heinrich Schliemann
docs.text:
Say it: Schliemann SHLEE-mahn 🔊 Pronounce

A German businessman turned archaeologist (1822–1890) who excavated Hisarlik from 1870, publicized it as Homer's Troy and later dug at Mycenae, using fast, destructive methods by modern standards.

Example: His north–south trench destroyed layers that later archaeologists would have studied closely.

See also: Priam's Treasure, Frank Calvert

docs.title: Helios
docs.text:
The Greek god of the sun, who drove his chariot across the sky each day, and the patron god of the island of Rhodes.

Example: The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of him.

docs.title: Hellenistic Kingdoms
docs.text: The states created by Alexander's generals after his death, chiefly Ptolemaic Egypt, the Seleucid Empire in Syria and Mesopotamia and Antigonid Macedon, ruled by Greek-speaking dynasties until Rome absorbed them.

docs.title: Hellenistic Period
docs.text:
The era from Alexander the Great's death in 323 BCE to the Roman takeover of Egypt in 31 BCE, when Greek culture and language spread across kingdoms from Egypt to Afghanistan.

Example: The Colossus of Rhodes was raised early in this period.

See also: Hellenistic Kingdoms, Koine Greek

docs.title: Heraklion Archaeological Museum
docs.text:
Say it: Heraklion heh-RAH-klee-on 🔊 Pronounce

The main museum of Crete, in the city of Heraklion, which holds the world's most important collection of Minoan art and objects, from frescoes and pottery to jewelry and clay tablets.

Example: The Phaistos Disc, the bull's-head rhyton and the original bull-leaping fresco are all on display there.

docs.title: Heraklion Today
docs.text:
Say it: Heraklion heh-RAH-klee-on 🔊 Pronounce

The modern capital and largest city of Crete, a busy port and university city with Venetian monuments, a major museum and lively cafés, home to about 180,000 people.

Example: The 1866 Street market near Lions Square sells herbs, cheese and raki.

docs.title: Herodotus
docs.text:
Say it: heh-ROD-uh-tus 🔊 Pronounce

A Greek writer from Halicarnassus, modern Bodrum (about 484–425 BCE), whose Histories of the Persian Wars made him known as the first historian. He mixes careful inquiry with stories he heard.

Example: Most of the famous Delphic prophecies come to us through his book.

See also: Primary Source

docs.title: Hippodrome
docs.text:
The great chariot-racing stadium of Constantinople, the center of public life and political protest, whose track lies under today's Sultanahmet Square.

Example: An Egyptian obelisk and the Serpent Column from Delphi still stand where its central barrier ran.

See also: Nika Riots, Serpent Column

docs.title: Hisarlik Mound
docs.text:
Say it: Hisarlık hih-sar-LUHK 🔊 Pronounce

The artificial hill near the Dardanelles, built up by thousands of years of settlement debris, which most archaeologists identify as the site of Troy.

Example: Schliemann's great trench still cuts through the middle of it.

docs.title: Historical Timeline
docs.text:
An ordered sequence of dated events and named eras that shows what happened before what and how long each period lasted. It lets a visitor place any ruin or object in its proper century.

Example: On a timeline, the Minoan palace at Knossos sits more than a thousand years before the Parthenon, which sits a thousand years before Hagia Sophia.

See also: BCE and CE Dating, Bronze Age

docs.title: Historicity of Troy
docs.text:
The question of how much of the Trojan War story reflects real events, weighed using the excavations at Hisarlik, Hittite records and the poems themselves.

Most scholars accept a real Bronze Age city and conflicts there, but not the poem's details.

docs.title: Hittite Empire
docs.text:
A powerful Bronze Age state in central Anatolia, about 1650 to 1180 BCE, with its capital at Hattusa, whose clay-tablet archives mention western lands including Wilusa and Ahhiyawa.

Example: A treaty with a ruler of Wilusa named Alaksandu recalls Homer's Trojan prince Alexandros.

See also: Wilusa, Bronze Age Collapse

docs.title: Homer
docs.text:
The name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey, probably composed in the 8th or 7th century BCE from a long oral tradition. Nothing certain is known of his life.

Example: Greek children learned to read from his epics for more than a thousand years.

See also: Iliad, Odyssey

docs.title: Homer Written Down
docs.text:
The turning point at which the songs of the oral tradition were recorded in the Greek alphabet, producing fixed texts of the Iliad and Odyssey. How and when it happened is debated.

Example: One theory holds that a singer dictated the poems to a scribe, as singers in Yugoslavia did for researchers in the 1930s.

docs.title: Horta
docs.text: Boiled wild or cultivated greens, such as dandelion or amaranth, dressed with olive oil and lemon, a staple of Greek and especially Cretan home cooking.

docs.title: Hospital of the Knights
docs.text:
The 15th-century stone building in Rhodes where the Hospitaller knights cared for the sick and pilgrims, their founding purpose. It now houses the island's archaeological museum.

Example: The long upper ward once held beds for about a hundred patients.

docs.title: Hospitaller Rhodes
docs.text:
Say it: Hospitaller HOS-pih-tuh-ler 🔊 Pronounce

The period from about 1310 to 1522 when the Knights Hospitaller governed Rhodes, fortifying the city and building the palace, hospital and inns of the medieval town.

See also: Siege of Rhodes 1522

docs.title: House of the Virgin Mary
docs.text:
A small stone chapel on the mountain above Ephesus that Catholic tradition, since its identification in 1891, holds was Mary's last home. It is visited by both Christian and Muslim pilgrims.

Example: Visitors tie prayer notes to a wall below the house.
