docs.title: Hub and Spoke Diffusion
docs.text:
A pattern in which a change is firmly established at one central place and then carried along connections to other places by people who travel between them.

Example: Paul stayed in Ephesus while co-workers carried the message to nearby towns such as Colossae.

docs.title: Hubris
docs.text:
Arrogant pride or overconfidence that leads a person to overstep human limits and dishonor others or the gods, which in Greek stories brings ruin.

Example: Croesus trusting his own reading of the oracle is often told as a lesson of this kind.

docs.title: Human in the Loop
docs.text:
A design in which a person reviews, and is responsible for, the decisions an automated system recommends, rather than letting the system act on its own.

Example: The Athenian Assembly debated and voted on the oracle's answer before acting.

docs.title: Human Need for Foresight
docs.text: The lasting wish of people and communities to know what will happen, so they can prepare, choose well and reduce fear, which drove visits to Delphi and drives modern forecasting.

docs.title: Hürrem
docs.text:
Say it: hew-REM 🔊 Pronounce

The wife of Suleiman the Magnificent (died 1558), known in Europe as Roxelana, who rose from slavery in the harem to become one of the most powerful women of the Ottoman court.

Example: Her tomb stands beside Suleiman's at the Süleymaniye Mosque.

See also: Harem of Topkapi

docs.title: Ibrahim Muteferrika
docs.text:
Say it: Müteferrika mew-teh-feh-ree-KAH 🔊 Pronounce

A Hungarian-born Ottoman official and scholar (about 1674–1745) who founded the first press to print books in Ottoman Turkish in Istanbul in 1727, with permission from the sultan.

Example: His press published only a few dozen titles, including dictionaries, histories and maps.

docs.title: Iconoclasm
docs.text:
The periods in the 8th and 9th centuries when Byzantine emperors banned religious images and many were destroyed, ending in 843 with the restoration of icons.

Example: Hagia Sophia's earliest figure mosaics were lost or covered in these years.

docs.title: Idea of Human Equality
docs.text:
The belief that all people share equal worth regardless of birth, status, sex or nation, which later movements traced partly to Paul's "neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free."

Paul himself did not call for ending slavery, which is part of his contested legacy.

See also: Neither Jew Nor Greek

docs.title: Iliad
docs.text:
The Greek epic poem attributed to Homer, about 15,000 lines long, telling of a few weeks in the tenth year of the siege of Troy, centered on the anger of the hero Achilles.

Example: The poem ends not with the fall of the city but with the funeral of the Trojan prince Hector.

docs.title: Imaret Soup Kitchen
docs.text:
Say it: imaret ee-mah-RET 🔊 Pronounce

A public kitchen in an Ottoman mosque complex that gave free meals to students, travelers and the poor, paid for by a charitable endowment.

Example: The former kitchen of the Süleymaniye complex is now a restaurant.

docs.title: Implementation Dip
docs.text:
The temporary drop in performance and confidence that often follows the start of a new practice, before people master it and results improve.

See also: Change Fatigue

docs.title: Individual Conscience
docs.text:
A person's own inner sense of right and wrong, which Paul discusses in his letters and which later thinkers made a basis for personal religious and moral freedom.

Example: Paul tells believers not to eat food that would trouble a fellow believer's conscience.

docs.title: Inscription
docs.text:
Text cut into stone, metal or another durable surface, such as a dedication, law, decree, epitaph or honor, which often survives when books are lost.

Example: An inscription on the Library of Celsus records the money its founder's family left for books and upkeep.

docs.title: Insider Change Leader
docs.text:
Someone who leads change from within the institution or tradition being changed, with the knowledge and credibility of a member.

Example: Paul, a trained Pharisee who argued from the Torah, was an insider to the tradition he reshaped.

docs.title: Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
A digital textbook that responds to the reader, with interactive simulations, self-check quizzes and a map of how its concepts depend on one another.

Example: This travel guide is built as one, with MicroSims and a learning graph.

See also: Open Educational Resources

docs.title: Interpreting Ambiguous Answers
docs.text:
The work of deciding what an unclear reply means and how to act on it, which at Delphi fell to the person or city asking, and with AI falls to the person reading the output.

Example: Athenians argued over whether the "wooden wall" meant ships or a palisade.

docs.title: Ionia
docs.text:
Say it: eye-OH-nee-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The central part of Anatolia's Aegean coast and nearby islands, settled by Greeks in the early Iron Age, whose cities, including Ephesus and Miletus, led early Greek science and philosophy.

docs.title: Ionic Order
docs.text:
A slender Greek column style that stands on a molded base and is topped by a capital with two scroll-shaped curls called volutes. It developed in the Greek cities of western Anatolia.

Example: The Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis use these columns.

docs.title: Iron Age
docs.text:
The era that followed the Bronze Age, beginning in the Aegean around 1100 BCE, when iron replaced bronze for everyday tools and weapons because iron ore was common and widely available.

Example: The Greek alphabet and Homer's epics took written form in the early part of this period.

docs.title: Islam
docs.text:
The religion founded in Arabia in the 7th century CE through the prophet Muhammad, centered on submission to one God and on the Quran. It was the faith of the Ottoman state and is the majority religion of modern Turkey.

Example: The call to prayer sounding five times a day over Istanbul is the most audible daily sign of this faith on our trip.

docs.title: Islamic Calligraphy
docs.text:
The art of beautiful handwriting in the Arabic script, used to write the Quran and to decorate mosques, books and objects, valued as the highest visual art in Islamic culture.

Example: Huge round wooden panels in Hagia Sophia carry the names of God, Muhammad and the first caliphs.

docs.title: Istanbul
docs.text: Turkey's largest city, with more than 15 million people, spanning the Bosphorus between Europe and Asia, formerly Byzantium and Constantinople, and capital of empires for nearly 1,600 years.

docs.title: Italian Rule of Rhodes
docs.text:
The period from 1912 to 1943 when Italy held Rhodes and the other Dodecanese islands, building new public buildings and heavily restoring the medieval town.

Example: The Italian-built buildings around Mandraki harbor date from this time.

docs.title: Iznik Tiles
docs.text:
Glazed ceramic tiles made in the town of Iznik in northwest Anatolia, especially in the 16th century, famous for blue, turquoise, green and bright red patterns of tulips, carnations and vines.

Example: The Rüstem Pasha Mosque near the Spice Bazaar is covered inside with some of the finest.

docs.title: Jesus of Nazareth
docs.text:
A Jewish teacher and healer from Galilee, crucified by the Roman authorities around 30 CE, whose followers proclaimed that God had raised him from the dead and that he was the Messiah.

See also: Early Jesus Movement, Christianity

docs.title: Jewish Law
docs.text:
The commandments and teachings of the Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, together with their interpretation, governing worship, diet, Sabbath, purity and daily life.

Example: The early church argued over whether Gentile believers had to keep these rules, such as circumcision.

docs.title: Jewish Quarter of Rhodes
docs.text: The eastern part of the walled medieval town, called La Juderia, where the Jewish community of Rhodes lived for centuries until its deportation in 1944.

docs.title: John the Apostle
docs.text:
One of the twelve disciples of Jesus, whom later Christian tradition places in Ephesus in old age, caring for Mary and buried on the hill of Ayasuluk.

Example: The Basilica of St. John in Selçuk was built over his traditional tomb.

docs.title: Johnnies and Mehmets Words
docs.text:
A short message of reconciliation, traditionally attributed to Atatürk in 1934, telling the families of Allied soldiers buried at Gallipoli that their sons lie in a friendly country, with no difference between them and the Turkish dead.

Historians debate the exact wording, but it is central to how Gallipoli is remembered.

docs.title: Judaism
docs.text:
The religion and way of life of the Jewish people, based on the covenant with one God described in the Hebrew Bible and on the Torah, its law and teaching. Paul was raised in it and never stopped calling himself a Jew.

Example: The Kahal Shalom Synagogue in Rhodes keeps alive the memory of a Sephardic Jewish community that lived there for centuries.

docs.title: Juderia
docs.text:
Say it: hoo-deh-REE-ah 🔊 Pronounce

La Juderia, the Jewish quarter in the eastern part of the medieval town of Rhodes, settled largely by Sephardic families after 1522.

docs.title: Justinian
docs.text: The Byzantine emperor (ruled 527–565 CE) who reconquered parts of the western empire, codified Roman law and rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika Riots.

docs.title: Kafeneio
docs.text:
Say it: kah-feh-NEE-oh 🔊 Pronounce

The traditional Greek coffeehouse, especially in villages, where older men gather to drink coffee, play backgammon, read the news and argue about politics.

Example: In a Cretan village, the coffeehouse on the square is often the first place to ask directions.

docs.title: Kahal Shalom Synagogue
docs.text:
Say it: Kahal Shalom kah-HAHL shah-LOHM 🔊 Pronounce

The synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of Rhodes, built in 1577, the oldest synagogue still in use in Greece, with a small museum of the community's history.

Example: A wall plaque lists the families of Rhodes who were deported in 1944.

docs.title: Kahvaltı
docs.text:
Say it: kah-vahl-TUH 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish word for breakfast, literally "before coffee," referring to the traditional morning spread of many small dishes with bread and tea.

docs.title: Kallimarmaro
docs.text:
Say it: kah-lee-MAR-mah-roh 🔊 Pronounce

The Athenian nickname, "beautiful marble," for the Panathenaic Stadium, an ancient stadium rebuilt in white marble for the first modern Olympic Games in 1896.

Example: The Olympic flame is still handed over here to each host city.

docs.title: Kamares
docs.text:
Say it: kah-MAH-res 🔊 Pronounce

A style of fine Minoan pottery from about 2000 to 1700 BCE, named after a cave on Mount Ida, with thin walls painted white, red and orange on a dark background.

docs.title: Kapalıçarşı
docs.text:
Say it: kah-PAH-luh-char-shuh 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish name for Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, meaning "covered market," from the vaulted roofs that cover its dozens of streets and thousands of shops.

docs.title: Kastri
docs.text:
Say it: kah-STREE 🔊 Pronounce

The mountain village, "the little castle," that stood on top of the ruins of Delphi until it was moved in the 1890s to allow excavation.

Example: Its villagers had reused ancient stones in their house walls.

See also: French Excavation of Delphi

docs.title: Kebab
docs.text:
Any of many Turkish dishes of grilled or roasted meat, such as skewered pieces, minced meat on a skewer or meat sliced from a vertical rotisserie.

Example: Döner kebab, sliced from a turning spit, is the cousin of Greek gyros.

docs.title: Kleroterion
docs.text:
Say it: kleh-roh-TEER-ee-on 🔊 Pronounce

A stone slab cut with rows of narrow slots, used in Athens to choose jurors and officials at random from citizens' name tickets.

Example: A surviving example is displayed in the Agora Museum.

See also: Athenian Democracy

docs.title: Knights Hospitaller
docs.text:
Say it: Hospitaller HOS-pih-tuh-ler 🔊 Pronounce

A Catholic military order, the Order of St. John, founded to care for pilgrims in Jerusalem, which ruled Rhodes from about 1310 to 1522 and then moved to Malta.

Example: Each nationality of knights had its own lodging on the Street of the Knights in Rhodes.

docs.title: Knossos Palace
docs.text:
Say it: Knossos NOSS-us 🔊 Pronounce

The largest Minoan palace, a complex of about 1,300 rooms around a central court on a hill near Heraklion, occupied for centuries and partly rebuilt by Arthur Evans in the early 1900s.

Example: Visitors walk past painted copies of frescoes and huge clay storage jars still standing in its storerooms.

See also: Arthur Evans, Throne Room at Knossos

docs.title: Know Thyself
docs.text:
The maxim gnōthi seauton, said to be inscribed on the porch of the Temple of Apollo, urging people to understand their own nature and limits before asking the god anything.

See also: Nothing in Excess, Values Beyond Prediction

docs.title: Knowledge Gatekeepers
docs.text:
People or institutions that control who can create, copy or reach knowledge, such as scribes, priests, guilds, publishers or, today, technology companies.

See also: Widening the Circle

docs.title: Koine Greek
docs.text:
Say it: Koine KOY-nay 🔊 Pronounce

The "common" Greek that spread across the Eastern Mediterranean after Alexander, used for trade, government and writing from Egypt to the Black Sea, and the language of the New Testament.

Example: Paul could write in it to churches in Galatia, Corinth and Rome and be understood in all of them.

See also: Shared Language Spreads Ideas

docs.title: Komnenos
docs.text:
Say it: kom-NEE-nos 🔊 Pronounce

The name of a Byzantine ruling family that held the throne from 1081 to 1185, restoring the empire's strength for a century.

Example: A mosaic in Hagia Sophia shows Emperor John II of this family with Empress Irene.

docs.title: Koules Fortress
docs.text:
Say it: Koules koo-LESS 🔊 Pronounce

The Venetian sea fortress guarding the entrance to Heraklion's old harbor, built in the 16th century and marked with reliefs of the lion of St. Mark.

Example: From its roof, visitors look back over the harbor where Venetian galleys once docked.

docs.title: Kulliye Mosque Complex
docs.text:
Say it: külliye kewl-lee-YEH 🔊 Pronounce

An Ottoman group of buildings centered on a mosque and paid for by an endowment, including schools, a hospital, a soup kitchen, baths and tombs that served the surrounding neighborhood.

Example: The Süleymaniye is the largest such complex in Istanbul.

docs.title: Kusadasi and Selcuk
docs.text:
Say it: Kuşadası koo-SHAH-dah-suh 🔊 Pronounce · Selçuk SEL-chook 🔊 Pronounce

Two neighboring towns near ancient Ephesus: Kuşadası, the seaside resort and cruise port where the ship docks, and Selçuk, the inland market town beside the ruins and the Ephesus Museum.

Example: Selçuk's weekly market sells local olives, figs and cheeses.

docs.title: Labrys
docs.text:
Say it: LAB-ris 🔊 Pronounce

The Minoan double-headed axe, a sacred symbol carved on palace stones and found in shrines on Crete; some link it to the word "labyrinth."

See also: Labyrinth

docs.title: Labyrinth
docs.text:
In legend, the maze built by Daedalus at Knossos to hold the Minotaur; in general, any confusing network of passages. The name may come from labrys, the double axe.

Example: The palace's many rooms and turning passages may have inspired later Greeks to imagine it as a maze.

docs.title: Ladino
docs.text:
Say it: lah-DEE-noh 🔊 Pronounce

The language of the Sephardic Jews, a form of medieval Spanish written in Hebrew letters, which they brought from Spain to the Ottoman Empire and kept alive for more than four hundred years.

See also: Sephardic Jewish Refugees

docs.title: Laiklik
docs.text:
Say it: lah-eek-LEEK 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish term, from the French laïcité, for the principle that the state and its law are not based on religion.

See also: Secularism in Turkey

docs.title: Large Language Model
docs.text: A machine-learning system trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next word in a sequence, which lets it write, summarize, translate and answer questions in ordinary language.

docs.title: Larnakes
docs.text:
Say it: LAR-nah-kes 🔊 Pronounce

Minoan clay coffins shaped like chests or bathtubs, used from about 1400 to 1200 BCE and painted with octopuses, birds, fish and plants.

Example: Several painted examples stand in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

docs.title: Layers of a City
docs.text:
The idea that a long-lived city is built on top of its own earlier versions, so that streets, walls and buildings from many eras sit above, below and inside one another.

Example: In Istanbul a Byzantine column, an Ottoman fountain and a modern tram stop can share one street corner.

See also: Stratigraphy, Spolia

docs.title: Leadership Reflection
docs.text:
A short written answer, in our own words, to the question of what a day's history means for the changes we are trying to make.

See also: Travel Journal

docs.title: Learning for All
docs.text:
The thread running through this book, a short note at the end of each daily chapter that ties a story from that day's place to the effort to bring a good education to every child on Earth.

Example: At Ephesus, the note asks who could use the Library of Celsus and who could not.

See also: Democratization of Education, Widening the Circle

docs.title: Lecture to Dialogue
docs.text:
The shift from teaching mainly by a teacher talking to a class toward teaching through questions, discussion and conversation among students and teachers.

See also: Socratic Method

docs.title: Legacy Institution
docs.text:
An organization old and established enough that its structures, habits and identity were inherited from an earlier age, and that resists redesign because many people depend on it working as it does.

The term borrows from computing, where "legacy systems" are old software still running critical work.

Example: The book treats the modern school as one.

docs.title: Lessons Across the Route
docs.text: The conclusions drawn by reading all the trip's stories together rather than one at a time, and the final reflection questions they leave for our own work.

docs.title: Letter to the Ephesians
docs.text: A New Testament letter attributed to Paul, possibly written by a later follower, that speaks of the unity of Jews and Gentiles in one church. Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words "in Ephesus."

docs.title: Letter to the Galatians
docs.text:
Paul's letter to the communities of Galatia in central Anatolia, arguing that Gentile believers need not keep the Jewish law and declaring that in Christ "there is neither Jew nor Greek."

See also: Neither Jew Nor Greek

docs.title: Letter to the Romans
docs.text:
Paul's longest letter, written from Corinth around 57 CE to believers in Rome, setting out his thinking on faith, grace, the law and the place of Israel.

Example: It ends with a list of greetings that begins by commending Phoebe of Cenchreae.

See also: Grace and Faith, Phoebe

docs.title: Letters as Teaching Technology
docs.text:
Paul's use of the letter to teach communities he could not visit in person, read aloud, copied and shared, with the strength of reach and the weakness of no immediate conversation.

See also: Pauline Letters

docs.title: Library as Public Access
docs.text:
A collection of books owned in common and opened to readers who could never afford the books themselves, at a time when every book was a costly handwritten scroll.

Example: The Library of Celsus at Ephesus offered its city's readers thousands of scrolls they could not have bought.

See also: Library of Celsus, Philanthropy for Knowledge

docs.title: Library of Celsus
docs.text:
The two-story marble library at Ephesus, completed in the early 2nd century CE by Tiberius Julius Aquila in honor of his father Celsus, a governor of Asia, who was buried beneath it.

Its facade was re-erected by archaeologists in the 1970s.

Example: Statues in its niches represent Wisdom, Knowledge, Intelligence and Virtue.

docs.title: Limits of the Oracle Parallel
docs.text:
The ways Delphi is not like a modern predictive model, and where reading one as a lesson about the other misleads.

Example: The oracle claimed divine authority, while a model claims only measured probabilities.

docs.title: Limits of the Paul Parallel
docs.text:
The ways Paul's mission is not like leading change in a school, and where reading him as a case study misleads.

Example: Paul's hearers chose to join and could leave, while students and teachers often cannot opt out of a school reform.

docs.title: Lindos Acropolis
docs.text:
The rocky citadel above the town of Lindos on Rhodes, crowned by a sanctuary of Athena Lindia and later enclosed by a castle of the Knights Hospitaller.

Example: From the top there is a view down to St. Paul's Bay, a small round cove below the cliffs.

docs.title: Linear A
docs.text:
The undeciphered script of the Minoans, used on Crete from about 1800 to 1450 BCE on clay tablets and ritual objects. Its signs resemble Linear B, but the language it records is unknown.

Example: Tablets in the Heraklion museum show signs we can sound out but whose meaning no one can read.

docs.title: Linear B
docs.text:
The syllable-based script used by Mycenaean palace scribes from about 1450 to 1200 BCE to record an early form of Greek, mainly in lists of goods, people and offerings. It was deciphered in 1952.

Example: One Knossos tablet lists jars of honey sent to "all the gods."

See also: Linear A, Decipherment of Linear B

docs.title: Literacy
docs.text:
The ability to read and write a language with understanding, and in a wider sense the skills needed to use written information in daily life.

Example: In Turkey before the 1928 reform, roughly one person in ten could read.

docs.title: Literacy Rate Uncertainty
docs.text:
The margin of doubt in any count of how many people could read, which comes from how reading ability was defined, who was counted and who did the counting.

Example: Turkey's 1927 census figure of about one in ten readers depends on how the question was asked.

docs.title: Loan and Hiring Algorithms
docs.text: Automated systems that score applicants for credit or jobs from past data, making high-stakes decisions about people that can repeat past discrimination if not checked.

docs.title: Local Guides
docs.text:
Licensed guides who live in the region and lead visitors through sites, bringing knowledge of history, language and present-day life that a printed guide cannot.

Example: A guide from Selçuk can point out which marble blocks at Ephesus were placed by modern restorers.

docs.title: Lokum
docs.text:
Say it: loh-KOOM 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish word for Turkish delight, the soft sweet of cooked sugar and starch, flavored with rosewater, fruit or nuts and cut into cubes.

Example: Shops in the Spice Bazaar offer free samples of pomegranate and pistachio flavors.

See also: Turkish Delight

docs.title: Long-Term Consequences
docs.text:
The effects of a decision that appear years or generations later, which are hard to predict and easy to discount but often matter most.

Example: The silting of Ephesus's harbor came partly from centuries of forest clearing upriver.

docs.title: Loukoumades
docs.text:
Say it: loo-koo-MAH-thes 🔊 Pronounce

Small balls of fried dough soaked in honey or syrup and sprinkled with cinnamon or nuts, a Greek sweet with ancient roots.

docs.title: Love as Greatest Virtue
docs.text:
Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 13 that among faith, hope and love, love is the greatest, describing it as patient, kind and not boastful.

Example: The word he uses is agapē, a love of goodwill shown in action.

docs.title: Lowering the Cost of Reading
docs.text:
Reducing the time, money and training a person needs before they can read, which widens the circle of people able to read at all.

Example: The Greek alphabet's two dozen letters took far less time to learn than Linear B's many signs.

docs.title: Lyceum
docs.text:
The school Aristotle founded in Athens in 335 BCE in a grove sacred to Apollo Lykeios, where he taught while walking with students. Its remains were found in central Athens in 1996.

Example: The excavated site lies in a small park near the Byzantine and Christian Museum.

docs.title: Machine Learning
docs.text: A branch of artificial intelligence in which computer systems learn patterns from examples in data, rather than following rules written by hand, and use those patterns to make predictions.

docs.title: Mandraki
docs.text:
Say it: man-DRAH-kee 🔊 Pronounce

The old harbor of Rhodes town, beside the medieval walls, whose entrance is marked by two bronze deer on columns.

Example: Popular legend places the feet of the Colossus here.

See also: Colossus of Rhodes

docs.title: Manumission Records
docs.text:
Inscriptions at Delphi, many on the Polygonal Wall, that record the freeing of enslaved people through a formal sale to Apollo, often with conditions they still had to meet.

Example: Many name the freed person, the owner and the price, rare records of ordinary enslaved people.

docs.title: Marble Street
docs.text:
The paved street of Ephesus that runs from the Library of Celsus north toward the Great Theater, along the edge of the commercial agora.

Example: A carved footprint on one paving stone is often explained by guides as an ancient advertisement, a claim with little evidence.

docs.title: Marcus Musurus
docs.text:
Say it: Musurus moo-SOO-rus 🔊 Pronounce

A Cretan Greek scholar (about 1470–1517) who worked in Venice as chief editor of Greek texts for the printer Aldus Manutius, preparing first printed editions of Plato and other authors.

docs.title: Masakhane
docs.text:
Say it: mah-sah-KAH-neh 🔊 Pronounce

A grassroots research community, whose name is isiZulu for "we build together," that brings speakers of African languages together to build translation tools for their own languages.

See also: Education With Communities, AI Translation

docs.title: Mastery Learning
docs.text: An approach in which students move to a new topic only after showing they have learned the current one, with extra time and help for those who need it, rather than a fixed pace for all.

docs.title: Measuring Who Is Left Out
docs.text:
Counting the people a system does not reach, group by group, rather than judging the system only by those it serves.

Example: By such a count, only about one in six people in classical Athens could vote.

docs.title: Mediterranean Climate
docs.text:
A pattern of hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters typical of lands around the Mediterranean Sea, which shapes what grows there, above all olives, grapes and wheat.

Example: November falls at the start of the rainy season, so olive harvests are under way while some days bring sudden showers.

docs.title: Mediterranean Diet
docs.text: The traditional eating pattern of Mediterranean countries, rich in vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and fish, with little red meat, linked by researchers to good heart health.

docs.title: Medrese
docs.text:
Say it: med-reh-SEH 🔊 Pronounce

An Islamic college attached to a mosque, where students studied the Quran, law, theology, Arabic and other subjects, often living in small rooms around a courtyard.

See also: Endowed Free Education

docs.title: Medusa Heads
docs.text:
Two large carved stone heads of the Gorgon Medusa, one upside down and one on its side, reused as column bases in the Basilica Cistern.

See also: Spolia

docs.title: Meeting People Where They Are
docs.text:
Starting from the beliefs, concerns, language and experience that people already have, rather than from the leader's own, when introducing a new idea.

Example: Paul began his Athens speech with their own altar and quoted their own poets.

See also: Altar to an Unknown God, Stages of Concern

docs.title: Megali Idea
docs.text:
Say it: meh-GAH-lee ee-DEH-ah 🔊 Pronounce

The "Great Idea," the 19th- and early 20th-century Greek national goal of uniting all Greek-speaking lands in one state with Constantinople as its capital, abandoned after defeat in 1922.

docs.title: Megara
docs.text:
Say it: MEG-uh-ruh 🔊 Pronounce

An ancient Greek city-state on the isthmus between Athens and Corinth, whose colonists founded Byzantium, the future Constantinople, around 657 BCE.

Example: Megara lies about 40 km west of Athens on the road to Corinth.

See also: Byzantium

docs.title: Mehmed the Conqueror
docs.text:
Say it: Mehmed MEH-met 🔊 Pronounce

The Ottoman sultan Mehmed II (1432–1481), who captured Constantinople in 1453 at age 21, made it his capital and began rebuilding and repopulating it.

Example: He ordered the building of Topkapı Palace and the Grand Bazaar.

docs.title: Mehmetçik
docs.text:
Say it: meh-MET-chik 🔊 Pronounce

The affectionate Turkish name, "little Mehmet," for the ordinary Turkish soldier, used especially for the men who fought and died at Gallipoli in 1915.

Example: Statues of these soldiers stand near the memorials on the Gallipoli peninsula.

docs.title: Menenius Agrippa
docs.text:
Say it: meh-NEE-nee-us uh-GRIP-uh 🔊 Pronounce

A Roman senator who, according to the historian Livy, persuaded the protesting common people of Rome to return in 494 BCE with a fable about limbs that refused to feed the belly.

See also: One Body Many Parts

docs.title: Meze
docs.text: A selection of small cold and hot dishes in Turkish dining, such as eggplant purée, white cheese, stuffed vine leaves and seafood, shared before a main course, often with raki.

docs.title: Mezedes
docs.text:
Say it: meh-ZEH-dhes 🔊 Pronounce

Greek small plates, such as olives, cheese, grilled octopus, meatballs or dips, served to share, often with ouzo or wine.

See also: Meze, Ouzo

docs.title: Michael Ventris
docs.text:
An English architect (1922–1956), not a professional classicist, who deciphered Linear B in 1952 by showing that it recorded an early form of Greek, then worked with John Chadwick to publish the proof.

Example: His success is the book's leading case of an outsider solving a problem experts had not cracked.

docs.title: Migration and Refugees Today
docs.text:
The movement of people into and through Greece and Turkey in recent years, especially refugees from Syria, Afghanistan and Africa, and the emigration of Greeks and Turks seeking work abroad.

Example: Turkey hosts several million Syrian refugees, many living in Istanbul.

docs.title: Mihrab and Minbar
docs.text:
Say it: mihrab MEE-rahb 🔊 Pronounce

Two key features of a mosque interior: the mihrab, a niche in the wall that shows the direction of Mecca, and the minbar, a tall stepped pulpit from which the Friday sermon is given.

Example: In Hagia Sophia the mihrab sits slightly off-center in the apse because the church did not face Mecca.

docs.title: Millet Mektepleri
docs.text:
Say it: mil-LET mek-tep-leh-REE 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish name for the Nation's Schools, the free adult literacy classes opened across Turkey in 1929 to teach the new alphabet.

See also: Nation's Schools

docs.title: Millet System
docs.text: The Ottoman practice of organizing non-Muslim subjects into religious communities, such as Orthodox Christians, Armenians and Jews, that ran their own religious, educational and family-law affairs under their leaders.

docs.title: Mimar Sinan
docs.text:
Say it: Sinan see-NAHN 🔊 Pronounce

The chief architect of the Ottoman Empire (about 1490–1588), who designed hundreds of buildings, including the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, and perfected the domed Ottoman mosque.

Example: He called the Süleymaniye the work of his journeyman years and the Selimiye in Edirne his masterpiece.

docs.title: Minaret
docs.text:
The tall slender tower of a mosque from which the call to prayer is given, now usually broadcast by loudspeaker.

Example: The Blue Mosque is known for its six.

docs.title: Minoan Civilization
docs.text:
Say it: Minoan mih-NOH-un 🔊 Pronounce

The Bronze Age culture of Crete, at its height from about 2000 to 1450 BCE, known for large palaces, nature-filled wall paintings, seafaring trade and the undeciphered Linear A script.

The name was given by Arthur Evans, after the legendary King Minos.

Example: The Heraklion Archaeological Museum holds the world's greatest collection of this culture's art.

docs.title: Minoan Frescoes
docs.text:
Say it: Minoan mih-NOH-un 🔊 Pronounce

The wall paintings of Bronze Age Crete, painted on wet plaster in bright colors with scenes of nature, ritual, processions, sea creatures and young men and women.

Example: The Prince of the Lilies and the dolphin fresco are shown as copies at Knossos and in their original fragments in Heraklion.

See also: Bull-Leaping Fresco, Fresco

docs.title: Model Calibration
docs.text:
How well the probabilities a forecaster gives match how often events actually happen; a well-matched forecaster sees rain on about 70 percent of the days it says "70 percent."

See also: Brier Score, Track Record and Trust

docs.title: Modern Delphi Village
docs.text:
The small town just west of the ancient sanctuary, built in the 1890s when the village of Kastri was moved off the ruins to allow excavation, and now a base for visitors.

See also: Kastri, French Excavation of Delphi

docs.title: Modern Greek State
docs.text:
The independent Greek country formed after the war of independence, first a small kingdom in 1832 and later expanding to include Crete, the Dodecanese and other territories.

See also: Megali Idea, Dodecanese Union With Greece

docs.title: Morosini Fountain
docs.text:
The Venetian fountain in Heraklion's Lions Square, built in 1628 under the governor Francesco Morosini, with four stone lions spouting water into a basin.

Example: It is a favorite meeting spot, surrounded by cafés selling bougatsa pastry.

docs.title: Mosaic
docs.text:
A picture or pattern made by setting many small pieces of colored stone, glass or tile, called tesserae, into plaster or mortar on a floor, wall or ceiling.

Example: The gold-glass portraits of Christ, Mary and John the Baptist in Hagia Sophia's upper gallery are among the finest Byzantine examples.

docs.title: Mosque Etiquette
docs.text:
The customs visitors follow in a mosque: removing shoes, dressing modestly, women covering their hair, speaking quietly, not walking in front of people praying and avoiding visits during prayer.

See also: Dress at Sacred Sites

docs.title: Mother-Tongue Learning
docs.text: Teaching and learning in the language a child speaks at home, especially in the early years, so that learning to read and learning new ideas need not wait until a second language is mastered.

docs.title: Mount Parnassus
docs.text:
The mountain in central Greece, about 2,457 meters high, on whose southern slopes the sanctuary of Delphi stands, sacred in myth to Apollo and the Muses.

Example: Snow can appear on its upper slopes by late November.

docs.title: Multi-Faith Empire
docs.text:
A state that rules people of many religions and allows them to practice their faiths, usually with unequal rights, as the Ottoman Empire did with Muslims, Christians and Jews.

Example: In 19th-century Istanbul, mosques, Orthodox churches and synagogues stood within a short walk of one another.

docs.title: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk
docs.text:
Say it: Atatürk ah-tah-TEWRK 🔊 Pronounce

The Ottoman officer who led the defense at Gallipoli and the Turkish War of Independence and became the founding president of the Republic of Turkey (1881–1938).

Example: His portrait hangs in shops, offices and classrooms across Turkey.

See also: Ataturk's Reforms, Anıtkabir

docs.title: Mycenaean Greeks
docs.text:
Say it: Mycenaean my-suh-NEE-un 🔊 Pronounce

The Bronze Age Greek-speaking people of the mainland, about 1600 to 1100 BCE, who built fortified palaces at Mycenae, Pylos and elsewhere and later took control of Knossos on Crete.

They are the likely model for Homer's Achaeans who besieged Troy.

Example: Their palace scribes wrote early Greek in Linear B on clay tablets found at both Pylos and Knossos.

See also: Linear B, Ahhiyawa

docs.title: Myth of the Minotaur
docs.text:
The Greek legend of a monster, half man and half bull, kept by King Minos of Crete in a maze and fed with young Athenians until the hero Theseus killed it with Ariadne's help.

Example: Visitors to Knossos often look for the maze of the story in the palace's confusing corridors.

See also: Labyrinth, Greek Mythology

docs.title: Myth Versus History
docs.text:
The distinction between traditional stories told to explain origins, gods or heroes and accounts of the past that can be checked against evidence. Many sites on our route sit where the two overlap.

Example: The Trojan Horse belongs to legend, while the burned layers of Troy VIIa are physical evidence of a real destruction.

docs.title: Nation's Schools
docs.text:
The free adult literacy classes opened across Turkey on January 1, 1929, to teach the new Latin-based alphabet to the whole adult population.

See also: Millet Mektepleri, Literacy Rate Uncertainty

docs.title: National Archaeological Museum
docs.text:
The largest museum of ancient Greek art in the world, in central Athens, with collections from prehistory to late antiquity, including Mycenaean gold and the Antikythera mechanism.

Example: The gold mask that Schliemann called "the mask of Agamemnon" is displayed here.

docs.title: Neither Jew Nor Greek
docs.text: Paul's declaration in Galatians 3:28 that in Christ the divisions between Jews and Greeks, slaves and free people, and male and female no longer determine who belongs, an early statement of shared standing.

docs.title: New Model Becomes Legacy
docs.text:
The pattern in which a successful reform, once widely adopted, eventually hardens into the established system that a later generation of reformers must change.

Example: The early house churches became, over centuries, the imperial church of Hagia Sophia.

docs.title: New Testament
docs.text:
The second part of the Christian Bible, 27 writings in Koine Greek: four gospels, Acts, letters attributed to Paul and others, and Revelation.

Example: The Book of Revelation addresses seven churches in Asia, starting with Ephesus.

docs.title: Next-Word Prediction
docs.text:
The basic task a large language model is trained on: given the words so far, estimate which word or word-piece is most likely to come next, repeated to produce whole passages.

Example: Given "The oracle of," the model rates "Delphi" far more likely than "Denver."

docs.title: Nika Riots
docs.text:
The uprising of 532 CE in Constantinople, begun by rival chariot-racing fans, that burned much of the city center and was crushed by massacring about 30,000 people in the Hippodrome.

Example: The fire destroyed the earlier Hagia Sophia, giving Justinian the chance to build the present one.

docs.title: Nikos Kazantzakis
docs.text:
Say it: Kazantzakis kah-zahn-DZAH-kees 🔊 Pronounce

A Greek writer (1883–1957) born in Heraklion, author of Zorba the Greek and The Last Temptation of Christ, buried on the city's Venetian walls.

Example: His grave carries the words "I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free."

docs.title: Nine Cities of Troy
docs.text:
The nine main settlement layers at Hisarlik, numbered Troy I (oldest, about 3000 BCE) to Troy IX (Roman), each built on the ruins of the one before.

Example: Signs at the site mark which walls belong to which numbered level.

docs.title: Nostra Aetate
docs.text:
Say it: NOS-trah ay-TAH-tay 🔊 Pronounce

The 1965 declaration of the Second Vatican Council on the Catholic Church's relations with other religions, which rejected blaming Jews as a people for Jesus' death.

docs.title: Nothing in Excess
docs.text: The maxim mēden agan, said to be inscribed at the Temple of Apollo alongside "Know thyself," advising moderation in all things.

docs.title: November Weather
docs.text:
The typical conditions on our route in late autumn: mild days, cool evenings, shorter daylight and a rising chance of rain, cooler in Istanbul and on Mount Parnassus than in Rhodes or Crete.

Example: A sunny afternoon at Rhodes can feel like summer, while the morning at Delphi may need a warm jacket.

docs.title: Odyssey
docs.text:
The Greek epic poem attributed to Homer that follows the hero Odysseus on his ten-year journey home from Troy to the island of Ithaca, and his return to his wife Penelope.

Example: Its tales of guests welcomed and abused make it an early study of hospitality, or philoxenia.

docs.title: Oedipus Prophecy
docs.text:
The oracle in Greek legend that warned King Laius of Thebes that his son would kill him and told Oedipus he would kill his father and marry his mother, both of which came true despite efforts to escape them.

Example: Sophocles' tragedy Oedipus the King turns this story into a study of fate and self-knowledge.

See also: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy, Greek Tragedy

docs.title: Off-Season Livelihoods
docs.text:
The ways people who depend on visitors earn a living in the months when tourists are few, through farming, fishing, other jobs, savings or seasonal migration.

Example: On the Dardanelles, a guide who is busy in April and summer may work an olive harvest in November.

docs.title: Off-Season Travel
docs.text:
Traveling outside the busiest tourist months, which usually means smaller crowds, lower prices and cooler weather, but also shorter opening hours and some closed businesses.

Example: In November the Acropolis is far less crowded than in July, but some island tavernas have already shut for winter.

See also: Overtourism, Off-Season Livelihoods

docs.title: Olive Oil
docs.text:
The oil pressed from the fruit of the olive tree, central to Mediterranean cooking and also used for lamps, medicine, soap and religious ritual since the Bronze Age.

Example: November is olive harvest season, so new oil may appear at markets in Crete and near Delphi.

docs.title: Olympian Gods
docs.text:
The twelve chief gods of Greek religion, believed to live on Mount Olympus, including Zeus, Hera, Athena, Apollo, Artemis and Poseidon, each with their own powers, festivals and sanctuaries.

Example: Athena was honored in the Parthenon, Apollo at Delphi and Artemis at Ephesus.

docs.title: Omphalos
docs.text:
Say it: OM-fuh-los 🔊 Pronounce

A carved stone at Delphi marking the "navel" of the world, where in myth two eagles released by Zeus from the ends of the earth met.

Example: The museum's marble version is carved with a net of knotted bands.

docs.title: One Body Many Parts
docs.text:
Paul's image in 1 Corinthians 12 of a community as a single body made up of different members, each with a different gift, all needed and none to be despised.

Example: He borrowed a familiar political image, used by Menenius Agrippa in Rome, and turned it toward care for the weakest members.

See also: Menenius Agrippa

docs.title: One-on-One Tutoring
docs.text:
Instruction in which a single teacher works with a single student, adjusting explanation, pace and practice to that student, long the privilege of the wealthy.

Example: Aristotle tutoring the young Alexander is the most famous ancient case.

docs.title: Open Educational Resources
docs.text: Teaching and learning materials that are free to use and carry an open license, such as Creative Commons, allowing anyone to copy, adapt, translate and share them without asking permission.

docs.title: Opening Hours and Closures
docs.text:
The days and times that sites, museums, markets and places of worship are open to visitors, which change by season, holiday and prayer times and must be checked before a visit.

Example: The Grand Bazaar is closed on Sundays, so a Sunday in Istanbul is better spent on a ferry or a long breakfast.

docs.title: Oracle as Data Hub
docs.text:
The idea that Delphi worked, among other things, as a meeting point for information, where envoys from across the Greek world brought news that may have informed the answers given.

See also: Greek Colonization

docs.title: Oracle as Living Faith
docs.text:
Understanding the oracle as its users did: a religious act in which a person approached a god with purity, sacrifice and respect and received the god's word, rather than a curiosity or a trick.

Example: For an envoy who climbed to Delphi, consulting Apollo was an act of piety, not a gamble.

docs.title: Oracle Consultation
docs.text:
The process of asking the oracle a question: purification, payment of a fee, a sacrifice whose signs decided whether the god would answer, and the Pythia's reply relayed by priests.

Example: A goat was sprinkled with cold water; if it trembled, the god was ready to speak.

docs.title: Oracle in Verse and Prose
docs.text:
The forms in which the oracle's answers were delivered: in early centuries often as hexameter verse, like Homer's, and later mostly in plain prose.

Example: Plutarch, a priest at Delphi, wrote an essay asking why the Pythia no longer answered in verse.

docs.title: Oracle of Delphi
docs.text:
The institution at Delphi through which people sought answers believed to come from Apollo, spoken by his priestess, the Pythia, from at least the 8th century BCE until the late 4th century CE.

See also: Pythia, Oracle Consultation

docs.title: Oracle's Long Lifespan
docs.text:
The length of time the Oracle of Delphi gave answers, from at least the 8th century BCE until the late 4th century CE, more than eleven centuries.

Example: That is longer than the time from the founding of Oxford University to today.

docs.title: Oral Tradition
docs.text:
The passing of stories, poems, laws or knowledge from one generation to the next by spoken word and memory rather than by writing, often with set phrases that help the performer remember.

Example: Phrases like "rosy-fingered Dawn" in Homer are building blocks that singers used to compose aloud.

docs.title: Orthodox Faith Today
docs.text:
The present-day practice of Greek Orthodox Christianity, which most Greeks identify with, expressed in church festivals, name days, lighting candles and Easter, the year's greatest feast.

Example: People passing a church in Athens often cross themselves without breaking stride.

See also: Eastern Orthodox Church, Orthodox Icons

docs.title: Orthodox Icons
docs.text:
Painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints on wood panels, used in Orthodox worship as windows to the holy, honored with candles, kisses and prayer.

Example: In an Athens church, worshippers light a candle and kiss the icon by the door as they enter.

docs.title: Ostracism
docs.text:
An Athenian procedure in which citizens could vote to send a leading man into exile for ten years by scratching his name on pieces of broken pottery, without any charge of crime.

Example: Hundreds of these pottery ballots, including some naming Themistocles, are shown in the Agora Museum.

docs.title: Ottoman Crete
docs.text: The period from 1669 to 1898 when Crete was an Ottoman province, marked by repeated Greek uprisings, followed by autonomy and union with Greece in 1913.

docs.title: Ottoman Decline
docs.text:
The long weakening of the Ottoman Empire from the late 17th century to its end in 1922, through military defeats, lost territory, debt and nationalist movements.

Example: Greece in the 1820s was among the first provinces to break away.

docs.title: Ottoman Empire
docs.text:
The state founded in northwest Anatolia around 1300 by Osman and his descendants, which conquered Constantinople in 1453 and at its height ruled from Hungary to Arabia and North Africa, ending in 1922.

See also: Ottoman Period, Ottoman Decline

docs.title: Ottoman Mosque Architecture
docs.text:
The style of mosque developed in the Ottoman Empire, with a large central dome supported by half domes, slender pencil-shaped minarets, a courtyard with a fountain and surrounding charitable buildings.

Example: The skyline of Istanbul's old city is shaped by these domes and minarets.

See also: Mimar Sinan, Minaret

docs.title: Ottoman Palace Kitchen
docs.text:
The huge kitchens of Topkapı Palace, which fed thousands of people a day and refined many dishes of Turkish cooking, including stuffed vegetables, pilafs and sweets.

Example: The palace kitchens, with their rows of chimneys, now display Chinese porcelain used at the sultans' tables.

docs.title: Ottoman Period
docs.text:
The centuries of Ottoman Turkish rule over Anatolia, the Balkans and much of the Eastern Mediterranean, from the 14th century to the end of the empire in 1922, with Istanbul as its capital after 1453.

Example: The Blue Mosque, Topkapı Palace and the Grand Bazaar are its landmarks in Istanbul.

docs.title: Ottoman Rhodes
docs.text:
The period from 1523 to 1912 when Rhodes was ruled by the Ottomans, who converted churches to mosques and settled Turks inside the walls while Greeks lived in villages outside.

Example: The Mosque of Suleiman with its pink dome stands at the top of Sokratous Street.

docs.title: Ottoman Rule in Greece
docs.text:
The centuries, from the 14th and 15th centuries to the 1820s and later in some regions, when Greek lands were part of the Ottoman Empire, with Orthodox Christians as a recognized community.

See also: Greek War of Independence

docs.title: Ottoman Turkish Script
docs.text: The Arabic-based script used to write Ottoman Turkish until 1928, a language rich in Arabic and Persian words that took years of study to read and write well.

docs.title: Outsider Breakthroughs
docs.text:
The pattern in which a problem that has defeated a field's experts is solved by someone from outside it, who brings a different skill or does not know what is supposed to be impossible.

Example: Michael Ventris was an architect, not a classicist, when he deciphered Linear B.

See also: Michael Ventris

docs.title: Ouzo
docs.text:
The Greek anise-flavored spirit, usually mixed with water or ice, which turns it cloudy, and drunk slowly with small plates of food.

See also: Raki

docs.title: Overtourism
docs.text:
The condition in which visitor numbers at a place grow so large that they harm residents' daily lives, the environment or the site itself.

Example: Rhodes Old Town can be packed with several cruise ships' passengers on a summer day, pushing up rents for locals.

docs.title: Packing for November
docs.text:
Choosing clothing and gear for a late-autumn Mediterranean trip, based on layers, rain protection and shoes with grip for uneven marble, plus modest clothing for mosques and churches.

Example: A scarf works as warmth on a windy ferry and as a head covering at the Blue Mosque.

See also: Dress at Sacred Sites

docs.title: Palace Economy
docs.text:
An economic system in which a central palace collects, stores, records and redistributes goods such as grain, oil, wine and wool, and directs craftsmen and laborers.

Example: The clay tablets of Knossos list sheep, textiles and rations, the bookkeeping of such a system.

docs.title: Palace of the Grand Master
docs.text:
The fortified residence of the head of the Knights Hospitaller at the top of the Street of the Knights, heavily rebuilt by the Italians in the 1930s as a summer residence for their rulers.

Example: Its floors are paved with Roman and early Christian mosaics brought from the island of Kos.

docs.title: Palace Scribes
docs.text:
The small group of trained record-keepers in Bronze Age palaces who wrote inventories, rations and offerings on clay tablets. Writing was their specialized tool, not a skill shared by ordinary people.

Example: When the palaces fell around 1200 BCE, their knowledge of Linear B died with them.

docs.title: Papoutsakia
docs.text:
Say it: pah-poo-TSAH-kyah 🔊 Pronounce

A Greek dish of halved eggplants stuffed with spiced minced meat and topped with béchamel sauce; the name means "little shoes."

Example: Its Turkish cousin, karnıyarık, has no béchamel.

See also: Eggplant, Shared Greek-Turkish Dishes

docs.title: Parthenon
docs.text:
The marble temple to Athena on the Acropolis, built from 447 to 432 BCE, admired for its refined proportions and sculpture and later used as a church, a mosque and a gunpowder store.

Example: Its columns lean slightly inward and its floor curves upward, so the building looks straight to the eye.

See also: Parthenon Sculptures, Doric Order

docs.title: Parthenon as Church and Mosque
docs.text:
The later lives of the Parthenon, which became a Christian church in late antiquity, a mosque after the Ottoman conquest of Athens in the 15th century, and was wrecked in 1687 when a Venetian shell ignited gunpowder stored inside.

Example: Traces of Christian paintings and a minaret staircase once survived inside the temple.

See also: Layers of a City

docs.title: Parthenon Marbles Dispute
docs.text:
The long disagreement between Greece and the British Museum over sculptures removed from the Parthenon by agents of Lord Elgin between 1801 and 1812. Greece seeks their return.

Example: The Acropolis Museum's top gallery shows plaster copies in pale white where the originals in London would go.

docs.title: Parthenon Sculptures
docs.text:
The carved decoration of the Parthenon: a 160-meter frieze of a procession, 92 square relief panels called metopes, and two pediments with groups of gods.

About half of what survives is in the British Museum and most of the rest in the Acropolis Museum.

docs.title: Paul and the Stoics
docs.text:
The encounter, told in Acts 17, between Paul and Stoic and Epicurean philosophers in Athens, and the wider overlap between some of Paul's ideas and Stoic teaching about conscience and a universal divine order.

See also: Stoicism, Areopagus Speech

docs.title: Paul as Change Case Study
docs.text:
The book's use of Paul's mission as an example of leading change in a long-established tradition, with lessons for turning schools into AI-native learning organizations.

See also: Limits of the Paul Parallel, Insider Change Leader

docs.title: Paul as Persecutor
docs.text:
Paul's early role, by his own account, as a zealous opponent of Jesus' followers who tried to destroy their communities before his change of mind.

Example: In Galatians he writes that he "violently persecuted the church of God."

docs.title: Paul in Athens
docs.text:
Paul's visit to Athens around 50 CE, told in Acts 17, when he argued in the synagogue and the Agora and spoke before the council of the Areopagus.

Example: Acts names two people who joined him there, Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.

docs.title: Paul in Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

Paul's stay of more than two years in Ephesus in the mid-50s CE, when he taught first in the synagogue and then in the hall of Tyrannus, and wrote letters to Corinth.

Example: Acts says that from there "all the residents of Asia" heard the message, an early case of hub-and-spoke spread.

See also: Hall of Tyrannus, Hub and Spoke Diffusion

docs.title: Paul of Tarsus
docs.text:
A Jewish Pharisee and Roman citizen (died about 64–67 CE) who first persecuted Jesus' followers, then became the movement's most influential missionary to non-Jews and the author of the earliest Christian writings.

Example: He lived and taught in Ephesus for more than two years and spoke in Athens.

See also: Pauline Letters, Paul's Missionary Journeys

docs.title: Paul's Contested Legacy
docs.text: The disagreement over how Paul's letters have been used: as a source of equality, grace and community, and also to justify slavery, the silencing of women and hostility toward Jews.

docs.title: Paul's Death in Rome
docs.text: The early Christian tradition that Paul was executed in Rome under the emperor Nero in the mid-60s CE, probably by beheading as a Roman citizen.

docs.title: Paul's Missionary Journeys
docs.text:
The travels by sea and road, described in Acts as three main journeys, in which Paul founded and visited communities across Anatolia, Macedonia and Greece in about the 40s and 50s CE.

Example: His routes touched Ephesus, Troas, Athens, Corinth and Rhodes.

docs.title: Pauline Letters
docs.text: The thirteen New Testament letters that carry Paul's name, written to communities and individuals to teach, correct and encourage them. Scholars agree that he wrote seven of them.

docs.title: Pax Romana
docs.text:
The "Roman peace," about two centuries from the reign of Augustus (27 BCE) to the late 2nd century CE, when the empire was largely free of major wars and trade and travel flourished.

Example: Safe seas and roads in this period made Paul's journeys possible.

docs.title: Pelagius
docs.text:
Say it: puh-LAY-jee-us 🔊 Pronounce

A British monk (about 354–418 CE) who taught that people can choose to do good by their own effort, provoking Augustine's sharp defense of the need for God's grace.

docs.title: Pericles
docs.text:
The Athenian statesman and general (about 495–429 BCE) who led the city at the height of its democracy and power and directed the building program that produced the Parthenon.

Example: He used money from Athens's league of allies to pay for the temples on the Acropolis.

docs.title: Persian Wars
docs.text:
The conflicts of 490 to 479 BCE in which the Persian Empire twice invaded Greece and was defeated, a victory that gave Athens the confidence and wealth for its classical age.

See also: Battle of Marathon, Battle of Salamis

docs.title: Phaedriades
docs.text:
Say it: fee-DRY-uh-deez 🔊 Pronounce

The two great cliffs rising directly above the sanctuary at Delphi, "the Shining Ones," named for how their rock faces gleam in the sun.

Example: The Castalian Spring flows from the gorge between them.

docs.title: Phaedrus on Writing
docs.text:
Say it: Phaedrus FEE-drus 🔊 Pronounce

The passage in Plato's dialogue Phaedrus where Socrates tells a myth warning that writing will weaken memory and give people the appearance of wisdom without real understanding.

Example: The same worry has been raised about printing, calculators, search engines and AI.

docs.title: Phaistos Disc
docs.text:
Say it: Phaistos feh-STOS 🔊 Pronounce

A clay disc about 16 cm across, found in 1908 in the Minoan palace of Phaistos in southern Crete and dated to about 1700 BCE, stamped on both sides with a spiral of 241 signs.

No one has deciphered it, and with so little text it may never be read.

Example: It is one of the most visited objects in the Heraklion museum.

docs.title: Pharisees
docs.text: A Jewish group of the late Second Temple period known for careful study and strict observance of the Torah, including traditions handed down by teachers. Paul calls himself one in his letters.

docs.title: Phidias
docs.text:
Say it: FID-ee-us 🔊 Pronounce

The Athenian sculptor (about 480–430 BCE) who oversaw the sculpture of the Parthenon and made its huge gold-and-ivory statue of Athena, now lost.

Example: The calm, flowing figures of the Parthenon frieze reflect the style of his workshop.

docs.title: Philanthropy for Knowledge
docs.text:
A private fortune given to pay for learning that the giver will never personally use up, such as a library, school or scholarship.

Example: Celsus's son left 25,000 denarii to buy books for the library and maintain the building.

docs.title: Philoxenia
docs.text:
Say it: fee-loh-kseh-NEE-ah 🔊 Pronounce

The Greek ideal of hospitality, literally "love of the stranger," the duty to welcome and care for guests and travelers, honored since Homer's time and still felt in Greek homes and tavernas.

Example: A taverna owner on Rhodes bringing a free dessert at the end of a meal is a small modern form of it.

See also: Turkish Hospitality

docs.title: Phoebe
docs.text:
A woman leader of the church at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, whom Paul calls a diakonos, minister or deacon, and a patron, and who probably carried his letter to Rome.

See also: Cenchreae

docs.title: Phoenician Alphabet
docs.text:
Say it: Phoenician fuh-NEE-shun 🔊 Pronounce

The script of 22 consonant letters developed by the Phoenicians of the Levant coast around 1050 BCE, the source of the Greek, Hebrew, Arabic and Latin scripts.

Example: The Greek letter alpha comes from the Phoenician aleph, "ox."

See also: Greek Alphabet, Alphabet

docs.title: Photography Etiquette
docs.text:
Respectful habits for taking pictures, such as asking before photographing people, avoiding flash where it is forbidden and not photographing worshippers at prayer.

Example: Inside a mosque during prayer, the thoughtful choice is to lower the camera and wait.

docs.title: Pilot School as Hub
docs.text: One school, or a few classrooms, that makes a change work completely and visibly, then serves as the place where teachers from other schools come to watch, practice and take the change home.

docs.title: Piraeus Port
docs.text:
Say it: Piraeus pie-REE-us 🔊 Pronounce

The main port of Athens, about 12 km southwest of the city center, used as a harbor since the 5th century BCE and today one of the busiest passenger ports in Europe.

Example: Our cruise ends here, and a short ride takes us up to central Athens.

docs.title: Plaka Neighborhood
docs.text:
The old residential quarter on the northeast slopes of the Acropolis in Athens, with narrow lanes, neoclassical houses, tavernas, small churches and souvenir shops.

Example: Its upper corner, Anafiotika, has whitewashed houses built by island stonemasons in the 1800s.

docs.title: Plato
docs.text:
An Athenian philosopher (about 428–348 BCE), student of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, who wrote dialogues on justice, love, knowledge and the ideal state and founded the Academy.

See also: Plato's Academy, Phaedrus on Writing

docs.title: Plato's Academy
docs.text:
The school Plato founded around 387 BCE in a sacred grove outside the walls of Athens, where teachers and students studied philosophy and mathematics, a model for later universities.

Example: Its ruins lie in a public park in a northwest Athens neighborhood still called Akadimia.

docs.title: Plutarch
docs.text: A Greek writer and philosopher (about 46–120 CE) from Chaeronea who served for many years as a priest at Delphi and wrote essays on the oracle as well as his famous Lives of Greeks and Romans.

docs.title: Pnyx
docs.text:
Say it: PNIKS 🔊 Pronounce

The hill west of the Acropolis where the Athenian Assembly met to debate and vote, with a speaker's platform cut into the rock.

Example: Thousands of citizens sat on its slope to hear Pericles and Themistocles speak.

docs.title: Polygonal Wall
docs.text:
The 6th-century BCE retaining wall below the Temple of Apollo, built of tightly fitted many-sided stone blocks and covered with hundreds of carved inscriptions.

See also: Manumission Records

docs.title: Population Exchange of 1923
docs.text:
The compulsory transfer agreed between Greece and Turkey in 1923, in which about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Turkey for Greece and about 400,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey, by religion rather than language.

Example: The village of Şirince near Ephesus lost its Greek families and received Muslim newcomers from northern Greece.

docs.title: Port Times
docs.text:
The scheduled arrival and departure times of the ship at each port, together with the all-aboard deadline by which every passenger must be back on the ship.

The ship does not wait for late passengers on independent outings.

Example: On a day exploring Kuşadası on our own, we plan to be back well before the all-aboard time.

docs.title: Prayer Times
docs.text:
The five daily times for Muslim prayer, set by the sun's position: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night, so they shift through the year.

Example: In mid-November in Istanbul the sunset prayer falls around 5 PM, and mosques close to tourists for it.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
A statement about what will happen or what is true but unseen, based on evidence, patterns, models or claimed insight, often with some level of confidence.

See also: Prediction Uncertainty, Predictive Model

docs.title: Prediction Horizon
docs.text:
How far ahead a forecaster can predict with useful accuracy before its forecasts become no better than a guess based on long-run averages.

Example: For daily weather, useful detail fades after about a week or two.

docs.title: Prediction Uncertainty
docs.text:
The range of possible outcomes around a forecast, showing how confident it is; a good prediction states this range rather than offering a single certain answer.

Example: "Between 60 and 80 percent chance of rain" carries more honest information than "it will rain."

docs.title: Predictive Model
docs.text:
A mathematical or computer system that takes information about a case and produces an estimate of an outcome, such as the chance of rain, of a loan being repaid or of a student failing.

Example: A weather app's "70 percent chance of rain at Delphi" comes from such a system.

docs.title: Predictive Policing
docs.text: The use of data and models to forecast where crimes may happen or who may commit them, so police can deploy resources, criticized for repeating biased patterns in arrest records.

docs.title: Priam's Treasure
docs.text:
A hoard of gold, silver and bronze objects that Heinrich Schliemann found at Troy in 1873 and named after Homer's king, though it comes from a level about a thousand years older than any Trojan War.

Smuggled to Berlin, it was taken to Moscow in 1945 and remains there.

Example: The Troy Museum displays copies and asks for the originals' return.

docs.title: Priests Who Framed Answers
docs.text:
The male officials at Delphi who managed consultations, received questions and recorded or shaped the Pythia's words into the reply given to the consultant.

Their role is why historians ask how much of an answer came from the priestess and how much from them.

See also: Interpreting Ambiguous Answers

docs.title: Primary Source
docs.text:
A document or object made at the time being studied, or by someone who witnessed it, such as a letter, inscription, chronicle or coin, as opposed to a later account written about it.

The book's rule for any such text is to ask who wrote it, for whom and why.

Example: Procopius wrote both an official praise of Justinian's buildings and a bitter secret history of the same emperor.

See also: Inscription, Contested History

docs.title: Printing Press
docs.text:
A machine that presses inked type onto paper to produce many identical copies of a text, which after the 1450s made books far cheaper and spread ideas rapidly across Europe.

See also: Aldine Editions, Delayed Arabic-Script Printing

docs.title: Priscilla and Aquila
docs.text:
Say it: Aquila AK-wih-luh 🔊 Pronounce

A Jewish Christian married couple, tentmakers expelled from Rome, who worked with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus and taught the preacher Apollos. Priscilla is often named first, a sign of her standing.

docs.title: Procopius
docs.text:
Say it: pruh-KOH-pee-us 🔊 Pronounce

A 6th-century Byzantine historian from Caesarea who wrote official accounts of Justinian's wars and buildings, and also a hostile Secret History attacking the same emperor and his wife Theodora.

Example: His two portraits of Justinian show why the author of a source matters.

See also: Primary Source

docs.title: Propylaea
docs.text:
Say it: prop-uh-LEE-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The monumental marble gateway at the west end of the Acropolis, built from 437 to 432 BCE, through which visitors and processions entered the sanctuary.

Example: Today's visitors still climb through its columns, the same path the Panathenaic procession took.

docs.title: Protestant Reformation
docs.text: The 16th-century movement, beginning with Martin Luther in 1517, that broke with the Roman Catholic Church over authority and teaching, drawing heavily on Paul's letters on faith and grace.

docs.title: Prytaneion
docs.text:
Say it: pry-tuh-NAY-on 🔊 Pronounce

The city hall of a Greek city, where its sacred hearth of the goddess Hestia was kept burning and where officials met, worked and dined at public expense.

Example: The two statues of Artemis in the Ephesus Museum were found in that of Ephesus.

docs.title: Pythia
docs.text:
Say it: PITH-ee-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The priestess of Apollo at Delphi, a local woman chosen to serve for life, who sat on a tripod in the temple's inner room and spoke the god's answers.

See also: Adyton, Geological Fault Theory

docs.title: Pythian Games
docs.text: The festival of athletic and musical contests held at Delphi every four years in honor of Apollo, second in prestige only to the Olympic Games. Winners received a laurel wreath.

docs.title: Quran
docs.text: The holy book of Islam, which Muslims believe is the word of God revealed in Arabic to the prophet Muhammad, divided into 114 chapters called suras.

docs.title: Raki
docs.text:
Say it: rah-KUH 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish anise-flavored spirit made from grapes, usually mixed with water, which turns it milky white, and drunk slowly with meze and fish.

Example: Turks sometimes call it "lion's milk."

docs.title: Reading a Ruin
docs.text:
The skill of working out what a damaged ancient site once was, how it was used and when it changed, by looking closely at its plan, materials, repairs and reused pieces.

Example: Spotting a Byzantine cross carved on a Roman column tells us the stone was reused centuries after it was first cut.

See also: Spolia, Layers of a City

docs.title: Rebetiko
docs.text:
Say it: reh-BEH-tee-koh 🔊 Pronounce

A form of Greek urban popular music, often called the Greek blues, sung to bouzouki and baglamas in the port cafés and refugee neighborhoods of Piraeus and Athens in the 1920s to 1950s.

Example: Small clubs in Athens still play it late at night.

docs.title: Republic of Turkey
docs.text: The state proclaimed on October 29, 1923, with Ankara as its capital and Mustafa Kemal as president, which replaced the Ottoman Empire.

docs.title: Republic of Venice
docs.text:
The trading city-state on the lagoons of northeast Italy, independent from the early Middle Ages until 1797, whose navy and merchants dominated much of the Eastern Mediterranean for centuries.

Example: The winged lion of St. Mark, Venice's symbol, is carved on fortresses in Crete.

See also: Venetian Crete, Fourth Crusade

docs.title: Restoration and Reconstruction
docs.text:
Two ways of treating damaged monuments: restoration repairs and stabilizes what survives, often re-setting original pieces, while reconstruction rebuilds missing parts, sometimes with new material and some guesswork.

Example: The Acropolis team puts fallen marble back in place, while Arthur Evans rebuilt parts of Knossos in concrete.

See also: Evans Reconstructions

docs.title: Rhodes
docs.text: The largest island of the Dodecanese in the southeast Aegean, and its main city, founded in 408 BCE, later a center of trade, rhetoric, the Knights Hospitaller and Ottoman rule.

docs.title: Rhodes City Walls
docs.text:
The fortifications around the medieval town of Rhodes, about 4 km long, with towers, bastions, gates and a wide dry moat, strengthened by the knights against Ottoman cannon.

Example: A walk through the dry moat shows stone cannonballs still lying on the grass.

docs.title: Rhodes Deportation of 1944
docs.text:
The deportation in July 1944 of about 1,700 Jews of Rhodes and Kos by the German army to Auschwitz, from which only a small number survived.

Example: The Turkish consul Selahattin Ülkümen saved several dozen people by claiming them as Turkish citizens.

See also: Selahattin Ülkümen, World War II

docs.title: Rhodes Medieval Town
docs.text:
The walled old city of Rhodes, built mostly by the Knights Hospitaller in the 14th to 16th centuries and later lived in by Ottoman Turks and Jews, now a living neighborhood and World Heritage site.

Example: Its cobbled lanes hold Gothic inns, Ottoman mosques, fountains and the old synagogue within a short walk.

docs.title: Rhodes School of Rhetoric
docs.text:
The teachers of rhetoric, the art of persuasive speaking, who made Rhodes from the 2nd century BCE one of the best places in the Mediterranean to learn public speaking.

Example: The orator Apollonius Molon taught both Cicero and Julius Caesar there.

See also: Roman Students at Rhodes, Traveling to the Teacher

docs.title: Rhodes Today
docs.text:
The modern island of Rhodes, home to about 125,000 people, whose economy depends heavily on tourism, alongside farming and fishing, with a busy new town beside the walled old one.

See also: Overtourism

docs.title: Rhyton
docs.text:
Say it: RYE-ton 🔊 Pronounce

A ritual pouring vessel, often shaped like an animal's head or a cone, filled through one opening and emptied through another during religious ceremonies.

Example: The black-stone bull's-head one in the Heraklion museum has eyes of rock crystal.

docs.title: Riot of the Silversmiths
docs.text:
The uproar in Ephesus, told in Acts 19, when silversmiths who made shrines of Artemis stirred a crowd against Paul's companions, fearing for their trade and their goddess.

Example: The crowd filled the Great Theater shouting "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians" until the town clerk calmed it.

docs.title: Road to Damascus
docs.text:
The episode, told in Acts and referred to in Paul's letters, in which Paul saw the risen Jesus near Damascus and turned from persecutor to apostle.

The phrase now means any sudden, life-changing change of mind.

docs.title: Roman Bath Culture
docs.text:
The Roman habit of bathing together in large public bathhouses with hot, warm and cold rooms, which served as social centers as much as places to get clean.

Example: The Baths of Scholastica at Ephesus once had heated floors and a large cold pool.

See also: Turkish Bath, Hamam

docs.title: Roman Citizenship
docs.text:
The legal status that gave a person the rights of a Roman, such as protection from certain punishments and the right to appeal to the emperor, gradually extended to many people in the provinces.

Example: According to Acts, Paul used his status to appeal his case to Caesar, which took him to Rome.

docs.title: Roman Empire
docs.text:
The state centered on Rome that, at its height in the 2nd century CE, ruled the whole Mediterranean basin and much of Europe and the Near East under emperors. Its eastern half continued for another thousand years as the Byzantine Empire.

Example: Ephesus was the leading city of Rome's province of Asia, and its marble streets show Roman wealth at its peak.

See also: Pax Romana, Byzantine Empire

docs.title: Roman Period
docs.text:
In the Eastern Mediterranean, the centuries of Roman rule from the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE until the founding of Constantinople in 330 CE, when Greek cities became prosperous provincial centers of the empire.

Example: Most of what visitors walk through at Ephesus, including the Library of Celsus, was built in this period.

docs.title: Roman Province of Asia
docs.text: The Roman administrative region created in 133 BCE in western Anatolia from the former kingdom of Pergamon, one of the richest provinces in the empire, with Ephesus as its leading city.

docs.title: Roman Roads
docs.text:
The network of paved, engineered highways built by Rome to move armies, officials and goods, which also carried travelers, letters and ideas across the empire.

Example: The Via Egnatia, which Paul likely walked, crossed the Balkans from the Adriatic to the Aegean.

docs.title: Roman Students at Rhodes
docs.text:
The young Roman aristocrats who sailed to Rhodes in the 1st centuries BCE and CE to study rhetoric and philosophy with its Greek teachers, finishing their education in a Greek city.

Example: Caesar was captured by pirates on his way to study on the island.

docs.title: Sacred Relics Chamber
docs.text:
The rooms of Topkapı Palace holding objects associated with the prophet Muhammad and earlier prophets, such as his mantle, banner and sword, brought to Istanbul after 1517.

Example: A reciter chants the Quran there throughout the day, and visitors are asked to keep silent.

See also: Mosque Etiquette

docs.title: Sacred Way of Delphi
docs.text:
The zigzag path that climbs through the sanctuary of Apollo from the entrance to the temple, lined with treasuries, statues and monuments dedicated by Greek cities.

See also: Treasuries of Delphi

docs.title: Saffron
docs.text:
The spice made from the dried red stigmas of the autumn-flowering crocus Crocus sativus, picked by hand, about 150,000 flowers per kilogram, which makes it the costliest spice by weight.

Example: We bought a small packet at the Spice Bazaar.

See also: Spice Trade

docs.title: Sanctuary of Apollo
docs.text:
The sacred area at Delphi, enclosed by a wall, holding the temple of Apollo, treasuries, monuments, a theater and the Sacred Way climbing the hillside.

Example: The route up from the entrance rises steeply, so good shoes matter.

docs.title: School as a System
docs.text: Viewing a school as connected parts, such as schedules, tests, budgets, staffing, families and rules, so that changing one part, like adding AI tutors, requires changing others.

docs.title: Scribal Resistance
docs.text:
Opposition to a new technology for storing or spreading knowledge from the people whose skill, income or prestige depended on the older method.

Example: Some Ottoman scribes and calligraphers had good reason to fear the printing press.

See also: Scribes and Copyists, Economics of Resistance

docs.title: Scribes and Copyists
docs.text:
People trained to write documents and copy books by hand, who held a respected and paid place in societies before printing and sometimes opposed new technologies that threatened their work.

See also: Scribal Resistance, Byzantine Manuscript Copying

docs.title: Seat Time and Carnegie Unit
docs.text:
Seat time is the hours a student spends in class, used to measure instruction; the Carnegie unit, defined in 1906, is the high school credit built on it, about 120 hours of class in one subject.

Example: A student who sits through a year of algebra earns the credit whether or not the algebra was learned.

docs.title: Secularism in Turkey
docs.text:
The constitutional principle, adopted in 1937, that the Turkish state and its law are not based on religion, while the state also manages religious affairs through a government directorate.

See also: Laiklik, Faith in Modern Turkey

docs.title: Seeing Past the Tourist Script
docs.text:
The habit of asking, at every stop, what the standard story told to visitors leaves out, especially who got to learn there and who did not.

Example: At the Agora, the guide's story of democracy rarely mentions the women, metics and enslaved people who could not vote.

See also: Who Democracy Left Out

docs.title: Selahattin Ülkümen
docs.text:
Say it: seh-lah-hah-TEEN ewl-kew-MEN 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish consul on Rhodes (1914–2003) who in 1944 insisted to the German commander that Jews with Turkish citizenship and their families were under Turkey's protection, saving several dozen lives.

Example: Israel's Yad Vashem honors him as Righteous Among the Nations.

See also: Rhodes Deportation of 1944

docs.title: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
docs.text:
A prediction that causes itself to come true, because the people who hear it change their behavior in ways that bring about the predicted result.

Example: Telling a student a model predicts failure can lower expectations until the student does fail.

docs.title: Sephardic Jewish Refugees
docs.text:
Say it: Sephardic seh-FAR-dik 🔊 Pronounce

The Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 and Portugal soon after, many of whom were welcomed into the Ottoman Empire and settled in Istanbul, Thessaloniki, Rhodes and other cities.

See also: Ladino, Hebrew Press of 1493

docs.title: Serpent Column
docs.text:
