docs.title: Bribery of the Oracle
docs.text:
Bribery of the oracle means paying or pressuring the Pythia or her officials to give a particular answer. Herodotus reports two cases, and it is telling that he does. The first involves the Alcmaeonids, the exiled Athenian family who had rebuilt the temple's front in marble. Herodotus says that they bribed the Pythia so that whenever Spartans came to consult, on any business, she told them to free Athens from its tyrant, Hippias. The Spartans eventually did, in 510 BCE, and the Alcmaeonids came home. Within a few years one of them, Cleisthenes, gave Athens the reforms that began its democracy.

The second case is about Sparta. Around 491 BCE, Herodotus says, the Spartan king Cleomenes wanted to remove his fellow king, Demaratus, by proving he was not the true son of the previous king. He persuaded a powerful Delphian named Cobon to persuade the Pythia, Perialla, to say so, and she did. When the plot came out, Cobon fled Delphi and Perialla was removed from office. The story shows both the flaw and a defense against it: the oracle could be corrupted, and when it was found out, it punished its own. A century and a half later, as Philip of Macedon came to dominate Delphi, the Athenian orator Demosthenes complained that the Pythia had begun to "philippize," to take Philip's side. The charge was political, but it shows that Greeks always knew the god's voice passed through human hands.

docs.title: The Geological Fault Theory
docs.text:
Ancient writers say that something came out of the ground at Delphi. Strabo describes a cave with a narrow mouth under the temple, from which rose a breath that filled the Pythia with the god; Plutarch, who worked there, mentions a sweet smell like perfume that sometimes filled the room where consultants waited, and suggests that the oracle's decline might come from the vapor growing weaker. Yet when French archaeologists cleared the temple in the 1890s, they found no chasm beneath the adyton, and for most of the 20th century scholars treated the vapor as a myth.

The geological fault theory is the modern hypothesis that the Pythia's inspiration came from gases rising through faults in the rock beneath the temple. In the 1990s, the geologist Jelle Zeilinga de Boer and the archaeologist John Hale studied the site and argued, in a paper published around 2001 with the chemist Jeffrey Chanton and later work with the toxicologist Henry Spiller, that two faults cross beneath the temple; that the local limestone contains petroleum-like material; that springs once flowed through the rock, leaving mineral deposits; and that water from a nearby spring contained traces of light gases, including ethylene, a sweet-smelling gas once used as an anesthetic, which in small doses can bring on a pleasant, detached trance. Earthquakes, they suggested, could open and close the gas's path, which would explain why the oracle seemed to grow weaker or stronger over the centuries. The table below separates the parts of the case by how firm they are.

Claim Evidence Status Ancient writers reported a vapor or breath at the oracle Strabo; Plutarch Certain: they reported it Faults cross beneath the temple Geological mapping by de Boer and Hale Widely accepted Gas escaped there in antiquity Mineral deposits left by springs; traces of light gases in spring water today Plausible The gas was ethylene, strong enough to cause a trance Small traces measured in spring water; comparison with ethylene anesthesia Disputed

The theory was widely reported, and it has been seriously criticized. Later measurements around Delphi found little or no ethylene in the gases escaping from the ground. A toxicologist and a historian argued that the amounts needed to cause a trance in a closed room would have been far larger than any plausible leak, and that the effects did not match the ancient descriptions closely enough. Others point out that the oracle's practical answers, recorded in inscriptions, do not need a drug to explain them. The faults themselves are real; whether anything useful came out of them is debated.

It Is All Right to Leave This One Open

If you finish this section wanting a verdict, that is normal; most readers do, and the scientists still disagree. Sort it the way Part Four sorted the stories: ancient writers did report a vapor, the faults are measured, and the gas is disputed. Two out of three is a good night's work.

docs.title: Part Six: Politics, Seasons, and an Insider
The Amphictyonic League
docs.text:
The oracle needed managers who were not a single city. The Amphictyonic League 🔊 Pronounce am-fik-tee-ON-ik (from Greek amphiktyones, "those who dwell around") was the association of peoples of central and northern Greece that ran the Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi. It had twelve member peoples, among them the Thessalians, the Boeotians, the Phocians, the Dorians, and the Ionians, each with two votes on its council, 24 in all. Its delegates met twice a year, in spring and autumn, at Delphi and at Anthela, near Thermopylae. The League managed the sanctuary's money and property, organized the Pythian Games, oversaw the rebuilding of the temple, and was supposed to protect the sanctuary and the pilgrims' road. It was not a union of equals: Athens took part only through the Ionian vote and Sparta through the Dorian one, while small peoples of the north had votes of their own. The point was not fairness but shared ownership. No one city could claim the god.

Worked example: the Sacred Wars. Let's follow what happened when someone did try. The League fought four wars that ancient writers called Sacred Wars, wars to protect, or to seize, the god's sanctuary.

War Dates What happened What it shows First Sacred War c. 595–585 BCE The League destroyed Kirrha, the port town below Delphi, said to have taxed pilgrims; its plain was dedicated to Apollo and left unfarmed The League's founding story of protecting pilgrims; some historians think it was elaborated later Second Sacred War c. 449–448 BCE Sparta and Athens took turns handing control of the sanctuary to the Delphians and the Phocians The great powers fought over who held the god's house Third Sacred War 356–346 BCE The Phocians seized Delphi and melted the sanctuary's treasures to pay mercenaries, worth more than 10,000 talents by the reckoning of the historian Diodorus; Philip II of Macedon defeated them and took their two votes The treasures were only safe while the rivals agreed to leave them alone Fourth Sacred War 339–338 BCE The League called on Philip against the city of Amphissa; his army came south, and at Chaeronea in 338 BCE he defeated Athens and Thebes A war in the god's name opened Greece to Macedon

docs.title: Delphic Neutrality
docs.text:
Delphic neutrality is the oracle's claim, and its practical need, to stand above the quarrels of the Greek cities, as a sanctuary common to all. The claim was real. Enemies dedicated their victory monuments side by side, as Part Two's scoreboard showed. Treaties often guaranteed free access to Delphi: the Peace of Nicias between Athens and Sparta in 421 BCE begins, Thucydides says, with the right of everyone to visit the common sanctuaries and consult the oracles. A god whom every city consulted could not be seen to belong to one.

The practice was more complicated. Before Xerxes' invasion, Delphi's answers to the Greeks were gloomy and discouraging: it told the Athenians first to flee and, Herodotus says, advised Argos and the Cretans to stay out of the war. Many historians think the oracle expected Persia to win and hedged accordingly, as any sensible institution in the Persians' path might. Herodotus himself tells a different story of 480 BCE: a Persian detachment marching on Delphi was driven off by thunder, by boulders crashing down from Parnassus, and by two giant warriors, local heroes come to life. The god, the Delphians said, had defended his own. After the war, the Serpent Column stood in the sanctuary, and the oracle's wartime caution was quietly forgotten. In the Peloponnesian War, Thucydides says, the god told Sparta it would win if it fought with all its strength, and that he would help, invited or uninvited. Neutrality was the oracle's ideal; leaning toward the likely winner was often its practice.

docs.title: Dionysus at Delphi
docs.text:
Delphi was Apollo's, but not only Apollo's. Dionysus at Delphi refers to the god of wine, theater, and ecstasy, whom Chapter 8 met among the Olympians, and to his strong place in the life of Apollo's sanctuary. Plutarch, writing as a Delphic priest, says that Dionysus had no less share in Delphi than Apollo. Tradition placed Dionysus' tomb in the adyton beside the golden statue of Apollo. The west pediment of the 4th-century temple showed Dionysus with his women followers, facing the setting sun, while Apollo faced the sunrise.

His most vivid worshippers were the Thyiads 🔊 Pronounce THY-yadz, women of Athens and Delphi who, every other winter, climbed Parnassus by night to celebrate Dionysus with dancing and torches. Their leader in Plutarch's day was his friend Clea, to whom he dedicated two of his essays. Plutarch tells of a winter when the Thyiads were caught in a snowstorm on the heights and had to be rescued, the rescuers' cloaks frozen stiff as boards. He also tells how, during the Third Sacred War, a band of Thyiads wandered exhausted into the town of Amphissa at night and fell asleep in the marketplace, and the women of Amphissa stood around them in silence until morning to protect them, then fed them and escorted them home. Two gods shared one sanctuary: Apollo of order and measure and clear speech, and Dionysus of wine, night, and release. The Greeks did not think a holy place needed only one.

Apollo at Delphi Dionysus at Delphi Season Spring, summer, and autumn The three winter months Song The paean The dithyramb Temple pediment East, toward the sunrise West, toward the sunset Worshippers Consultants, pilgrims, and athletes The Thyiads, on the mountain at night What he stands for Order, measure, clear speech Wine, night, release

docs.title: Apollo's Winter Absence
docs.text:
Apollo's winter absence is the belief that Apollo left Delphi for the three winter months, during which the oracle gave no answers and Dionysus held the sanctuary. Plutarch says that in winter the hymns to Apollo, the paeans, gave way to the dithyramb, Dionysus' song. Ancient writers usually said Apollo spent the winter with the Hyperboreans, a happy people who lived "beyond the north wind," the same faraway land to which Bacchylides' Apollo carried Croesus. His return in spring was celebrated, and in early times his birthday, in the month Bysios, was the oracle's one consultation day of the year.

Worked example: would the oracle have been open for us? Let's check our own date against the ancient calendar. Greek months were lunar and began at different times in different cities, so we cannot convert November 22, 2026, exactly into the Delphic calendar. But the three winter months of the oracle's silence are generally put in roughly the period from November or December to February. So if we had arrived tomorrow in the oracle's great days, we would very probably have found the god away and the Pythia silent, with the Thyiads perhaps preparing for their night on the mountain. We would have had to wait until spring to ask our question. There is a lesson about foresight hidden in the myth: even the god of prophecy had a season when he did not answer. Chapter 19 asks what that means for every forecaster.

docs.title: Plutarch
docs.text:
Plutarch (about 46 to after 119 CE) was the Greek philosopher and biographer from Chaeronea in Boeotia, a small town not far from our road tomorrow, who served for about the last thirty years of his life as one of the two priests of Apollo at Delphi. This book has quoted him often: on Pericles and the Parthenon in Chapter 1, on Alexander's birth in Chapter 9, on Cicero's teacher in Chapter 12. He wrote the Parallel Lives, paired biographies of famous Greeks and Romans, and dozens of shorter works on ethics, religion, and nature, collected as the Moralia. He studied in Athens, visited Rome and Egypt, and chose to live in his small hometown, so that it would not become smaller by one. An inscription at Delphi records that the Delphians and the people of Chaeronea set up a portrait of him together.

Worked example: what only an insider could tell us. Let's list what Plutarch adds that no outsider could. Three of his essays are set at Delphi and are called the Pythian dialogues.

  • The E at Delphi discusses the letter carved in the temple porch and records the yearly rhythm of Apollo and Dionysus.
  • The Oracles at Delphi No Longer Given in Verse describes the Pythia of his day as an uneducated farm woman, defends prose answers, and notices the monuments around the sanctuary as an informed guide would.
  • The Obsolescence of Oracles asks why so many oracles had fallen silent, and in answering records the three Pythias of former times, the goat test, the story of the Pythia who died, and the theory that the vapor had grown weaker.

Without Plutarch, we would know the oracle almost entirely from historians who saw it from outside, and the inside view he gives is one of devotion mixed with intelligent doubt. He believed in the god and was honest about the oracle's decline, a combination worth admiring in any insider.

docs.title: Part Seven: Two Sayings Over the Door
Know Thyself
docs.text:
Know thyself (Greek gnōthi seauton) is the most famous of the sayings carved in the porch of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi. Pausanias says the sayings there were attributed to the Seven Sages, a traditional list of wise men of the 6th century BCE whose names vary from writer to writer but usually include Thales and Solon. Visitors read them before they entered the god's house, so the sayings were advice given to everyone, free, before anyone paid for an answer.

Worked example: one saying, three meanings across six centuries. Let's follow how "Know thyself" was read, because its meaning changed with its readers. In the Archaic age, scholars think it meant: know that you are a mortal, not a god; know your place and your limits before you approach Apollo. In Plato's dialogues, around 380 BCE, Socrates turns it inward: to know oneself is to examine one's own beliefs, desires, and ignorance, the work he took up after Chaerephon's answer; in one dialogue he says he cannot yet know himself, so it would be absurd to investigate other things. In Plutarch's The E at Delphi, around 100 CE, one speaker suggests the letter E stands for ei, "you are," the worshipper's greeting to the eternal god, and that "Know thyself" is the god's reply to the mortal: you are not. Across six centuries the saying moved from humility before a god to self-examination to a meditation on what it means to be a changing creature before an unchanging one.

When Reader "Know thyself" means 6th century BCE Visitors to the Archaic temple Know that you are mortal, not a god c. 380 BCE Socrates, in Plato's dialogues Examine your own beliefs and ignorance c. 100 CE A speaker in Plutarch's The E at Delphi Answer the god's "you are" by knowing that you are not eternal

The sayings traveled farther than any pilgrim. In the early 3rd century BCE, a Greek named Clearchus copied a list of Delphic maxims and had them carved on a monument at Ai Khanoum, a Greek city founded after Alexander's conquests in what is now northern Afghanistan, more than 4,000 km from Delphi as the crow flies. The inscription survives. Its last lines give advice for each stage of life: as a child, be well-behaved; as a youth, self-controlled; in middle age, just; in old age, a good counselor; at the end, without grief.

The Free Advice and the Paid Answer

Notice the order of a visit. Before anyone reached the Pythia and paid for a particular answer, they walked past a wall of general advice that cost nothing. The oracle told you what might happen; the porch told you who you were and how to act whatever happened.

docs.title: Nothing in Excess
docs.text:
Nothing in excess (Greek mēden agan) is the second great Delphic saying: the advice to keep a measure in everything, to avoid the extremes of pride, greed, grief, and ambition. Chapter 15 met its opposite, hubris, arrogant overreaching that invites ruin, and saw Xerxes as its great example. The Greek virtue that goes with the saying is sōphrosynē, usually translated as self-control or moderation: the sense of one's limits.

Worked example: Croesus and Solon. Herodotus frames the whole Croesus story with this saying, and the frame is worth testing. He says that Solon, the Athenian lawmaker and one of the Seven Sages, visited Croesus at Sardis. Croesus showed him his treasures and asked who was the happiest man in the world, expecting to hear his own name. Solon named an Athenian who had died bravely for his city after a good life, then two young brothers who had died in their sleep after an act of devotion to their mother. Count no one happy until you see how his life ends, Solon said: the god often gives people a glimpse of happiness and then destroys them root and branch. Croesus dismissed him as a fool. Then came his son's death, the misread prophecy, the fall of Sardis, and the pyre, where he called out Solon's name. It is a perfect story of excess and its price. It is also, very probably, not history. Solon's travels are usually dated before Croesus became king, and Plutarch, writing his Life of Solon, noted that some people rejected the meeting on chronological grounds, but said he would not give up so famous a story, so true to Solon's character, for the sake of some tables of dates. Plutarch, the Delphic priest, chose the saying's truth over the story's accuracy, and told us he was doing it. That is an honest way to keep a myth.

docs.title: Part Eight: Eleven Centuries and an Ending
Decline of the Oracle
docs.text:
The decline of the oracle was the long, slow loss of the oracle's political importance, wealth, and number of consultants, from the 4th century BCE to the 4th century CE. It did not happen at once, and it was never a straight line. Several forces worked together.

  • Power moved away. After Philip of Macedon and Alexander, the great decisions of the Greek world were made by kings and, later, by Rome, who did not need a god's permission to found a city or make war, though they still sent gifts.
  • The treasures were taken. The Phocians melted the sanctuary's treasures in 356–346 BCE. The Roman general Sulla took what remained of value in 87–86 BCE to pay for his war against Mithridates. The emperor Nero, touring Greece in 67 CE, carried off about 500 bronze statues, Pausanias says.
  • Faith in oracles weakened among the educated. In 44 BCE Cicero asked why Delphi's answers had not been given for so long, in his own day or earlier, and why nothing was now more despised.
  • Greece grew emptier. Plutarch explains that in his day one Pythia was enough where three had once been needed, because Greece had far fewer people and far fewer questions.
  • But not yet death. In 279 BCE, a Gaulish army that attacked Delphi was driven off, the defenders said by snow, earthquake, and the god; Plutarch saw new building and a revival of the sanctuary in his own day; and in the 2nd century CE the Roman emperor Hadrian showed Delphi favor. The oracle had become something like a famous old university: still respected, still visited, still answering, but no longer where the world's decisions were made.

docs.title: Closing of the Oracle
docs.text:
The closing of the oracle was the end of consultations at Delphi in the late 4th century CE, as Christian emperors outlawed the old religion. Constantine had already carried off the Serpent Column to his new capital by 330 CE, where Chapter 4 found it. The Theodosian Decrees of 391 and 392, which Chapter 3 told, banned sacrifice and closed the temples. With no goat to sacrifice, there could be no consultation, and the Pythia fell silent. Christian churches were later built at Delphi, and in time a village grew over the ruins, until the French excavation that Chapter 18 describes.

A famous "last oracle" is said to have been given to the emperor Julian, who reigned from 361 to 363 and tried to restore the old gods. His physician, the story says, was sent to Delphi and brought back the answer that the god's hall had fallen: "No longer has Phoebus a hut, nor a prophetic laurel," nor a speaking spring. It is a moving answer, and a suspicious one. It survives only in Christian writers, most fully in a Byzantine chronicle written some seven hundred years later, and it announces exactly what Christian readers wanted to hear. By Chapter 4's test, as Chapter 3 said, it is a legend. The silence was real.

docs.title: The Oracle's Long Lifespan
docs.text:
The oracle's long lifespan is the length of time the Oracle of Delphi gave answers, from at least the 8th century BCE until its closing at the end of the 4th century CE, more than eleven centuries. Using Chapter 1's rule for spans across the line between BCE and CE (add the two years and subtract one, because there was no year zero), a span from 750 BCE to 391 CE is 750 + 391 − 1 = 1,140 years. That is a conservative figure, since legend and some archaeology push the start earlier.

Worked example: putting 1,140 years in perspective. Let's compare the oracle's life with the long-lived institutions on our route. The Byzantine Empire, ruled from Constantinople from 330 to 1453, lasted 1,123 years. The Ottoman Empire, from about 1299 to 1922, lasted about 623 years. The oracle outlived both.

Institution From To Years The Oracle of Delphi c. 750 BCE 391 CE About 1,140 The Byzantine Empire 330 CE 1453 CE 1,123 The Ottoman Empire c. 1299 CE 1922 CE About 623

Through all that time, kings and cities kept sending envoys up the mountain, even after the riddles failed, the treasures were looted, and the critics laughed. Whatever we think of its answers, an institution does not last eleven centuries without giving people something they valued: a place to bring their hardest questions, and a voice they trusted more than their own fear. Chapter 19 asks what earns, and what loses, that kind of trust.

The timeline below sorts fourteen moments of those centuries into signs of the oracle's strength and signs of its weakness.

docs.title: Diagram: Eleven Centuries of the Oracle
docs.text:

(3) Corruption only appears late, when the Alcmaeonid bribery happened at the oracle's height (card 5). docs.title: Questions to Carry Up the Mountain
docs.text:
Tomorrow we will stand in front of the temple where all of this happened. The stories in this chapter raise questions that the drive back, and Chapter 19, will take up with today's prediction machines. We leave them as questions tonight.

  1. Delphi heard questions from cities all over the Greek world for centuries. Did hearing so many questions make it better informed, and did its priests use what they heard?
  2. At Salamis the god gave a riddle and the Assembly decided what it meant. Who was really responsible for the choice, the source that answered or the people who acted?
  3. Croesus heard the answer he wanted to hear. How often do we read an answer in the way that confirms what we already planned?
  4. Oedipus fulfilled his prophecy by trying to escape it. Can a prediction, once spoken, help cause what it predicts?
  5. Croesus' gold and the Alcmaeonids' marble paid for the god's house. Does it matter who pays for a source of answers?
  6. Delphi is remembered for its hits; who remembers its misses? How would we measure whether a source of predictions deserves our trust?
  7. Apollo did not answer in winter. How far ahead, and in which seasons, can any forecaster really see?

The companion book AI-Native Schools asks a version of the Socrates question about AI tutors, whether a good tutor should hand over answers or, as the oracle did for Socrates, start an inquiry, in AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance. Tonight it is enough to notice that the oldest answer in this chapter that is still worth having is the one Socrates refused to take on trust.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The human need for foresight arises whenever an outcome is uncertain, the stakes are high, and we must act before we know. Greeks met it with seers, dreams, lots, oracles, and reasoning.
  • A prediction is a claim, made before the outcome, that some outcome could prove wrong. Commands and hedged answers are not predictions.
  • Mount Parnassus rises to 2,457 m above Delphi, about 180 km from Athens; the sanctuary sits about 550 to 650 m up, so expect it to be several degrees colder than Athens.
  • Apollo, god of prophecy, music, healing, and purification, spoke at Delphi, Didyma, Claros, and Patara. The Sanctuary of Apollo was a walled precinct whose gifts were messages between cities.
  • The Temple of Apollo at Delphi burned in 548 BCE and fell in an earthquake in 373 BCE; the Doric temple we see was finished around 330 BCE.
  • The Oracle of Delphi answered private and state questions for more than a thousand years. Fontenrose found that its best-recorded answers were mostly plain commands, and the riddles mostly legend. For its users it was an oracle as a living faith, an act of piety, and Xenophon shows that the question shapes the answer.
  • The Pythia, a woman of Delphi on a tripod, spoke for the god, and the priests who framed the answers announced and perhaps shaped them. An oracle consultation had eight steps, with fees and sacrifice, a goat test, and a line led by those with promanteia. Answers came in verse and prose, and in prose by Plutarch's day.
  • Greek colonization sought Delphi's approval. Croesus of Lydia tested the oracles and misread the Croesus prophecy. The wooden walls prophecy was decided by the Athenian Assembly on Themistocles' reading. Chaerephon's question made Socrates begin a lifelong inquiry. The Oedipus prophecy comes true through every attempt to escape it.
  • Every famous answer was written down after the outcome. Hedging answers cannot lose. Bribery of the oracle happened and was punished. The geological fault theory of an ethylene vapor is real science and is still debated.
  • The Amphictyonic League ran the sanctuary and fought the Sacred Wars. Delphic neutrality was an ideal often bent toward the likely winner. Dionysus at Delphi shared the sanctuary, and Apollo's winter absence silenced the oracle for three months a year.
  • Plutarch, a priest at Delphi, gives the only insider's view. Know thyself and nothing in excess, carved on the temple, were free advice for everyone.
  • The decline of the oracle took centuries, and the closing of the oracle came with the Theodosian Decrees of 391–392 CE. The oracle's long lifespan, about 1,140 years from 750 BCE, outlasted the Byzantine Empire.

Ready for the Mountain

You can now walk up to the Temple of Apollo and explain how a consultation worked, from the cold-water goat to the prophet's answer, and tell the Croesus and Salamis stories while testing them like a historian. You can also tell a real prediction from a hedge, and you know why the god would probably have been away for our visit. Next stop: Day 12: Delphi, where we walk the Sacred Way under the cliffs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Day 12 (Sunday, November 22) is the day trip by road to Delphi, about two and a half hours each way. The chapter walks the site in order: the Castalian Spring, the Sacred Way and the Athenian Treasury, the polygonal wall and its records of freed slaves, the omphalos, the theater, the stadium of the Pythian Games, and the round Tholos at Athena Pronaia. In the museum it explains the Charioteer, and it traces the Serpent Column we saw in Istanbul back to its original home here. It closes with the French excavation that moved the village, and with modern Delphi, Arachova, the Amfissa olive groves, and mountain honey.

docs.title: Concepts Covered

docs.title: A Sunday on Apollo's Mountain
docs.text:
Day 12, Sunday, November 22, is our day trip from Athens to Delphi, about 180 km and two and a half hours each way by coach. Last night's chapter, Chapter 17, explained the oracle as an institution: the Pythia on her tripod, the steps of a consultation, the famous answers and their flaws, and the league that ran the sanctuary. Today we stand in the place itself. The ruins are not one building but a whole hillside of them, climbing in terraces under the cliffs of Mount Parnassus, and each terrace was built by someone who wanted to be seen there.

So today's chapter is a walk, in the order a pilgrim climbed, from the spring at the bottom to the stadium at the top, then down to Athena's sanctuary and into the museum. It ends where the ancient story meets the modern one: a village that archaeologists moved, a mountain town that lives from snow, and a plain of olives that was once the god's own land.

A Hillside That Talks

Today we follow a bronze snake from Istanbul back to its home, watch a bronze driver hold the reins he has held for about 2,500 years, and read the names of people who bought their own freedom from a god. Every stone on this slope was put there to send a message. By evening we will be able to read a good number of them. Look closer.

The chapter has six parts. Part One covers the drive and the Castalian Spring. Part Two climbs the Sacred Way past the treasuries, the polygonal wall and its records, the Serpent Column's old home, and the omphalos. Part Three explains the Pythian Games and visits the theater and the stadium where they were held. Part Four goes down to the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia and its Tholos. Part Five tours the museum and the Charioteer. Part Six follows Delphi after the oracle: the French excavation, the modern village, Arachova, the olive groves, thyme honey, and honey-soaked loukoumades 🔊 Pronounce loo-koo-MAH-thes.

docs.title: Part One: The Road and the Spring
The Day Trip to Delphi
docs.text:
The day trip to Delphi is Day 12 of our itinerary: a round trip by road from Athens to the sanctuary and its museum, about 180 km and two and a half hours each way, with a stop in the mountain town of Arachova. The road leaves Athens to the north, crosses the plain of Boeotia past Thebes, turns west at Livadeia, and then climbs the flank of Parnassus. Somewhere on this road, ancient writers placed the crossroads where Oedipus met and killed his father, a story Chapter 17 tested. Pilgrims who came from Athens walked or rode much of the same way for several days. We do it before lunch.

A long day by coach has a shape, and our own photos record it. Their timestamps, in Athens time, show where the hours went.

Time (Athens) What our photos show Where this chapter covers it About 11:00 AM The olive plain below Delphi The Amfissa Olive Groves 12:41 PM Columns at the entrance to the sanctuary The Sacred Way of Delphi 12:49 PM The Athenian Treasury The Athenian Treasury 12:57 PM The bronze copy of the Serpent Column The Serpent Column 1:14 PM The theater above the temple The Theater of Delphi 1:44 PM The Pleistos valley The Athena Pronaia Sanctuary About 4:15 PM Arachova, on the road home Arachova

Worked example: budgeting a short winter day. Let's see how much time the table leaves for each part of the visit. Our photos on the site span about an hour, from 12:41 to 1:44 PM. An hour is enough to walk the Sacred Way to the temple and theater at a steady pace, but not to linger at every stone. Add the museum, which deserves at least an hour, and lunch, and the day in Delphi itself runs from late morning to mid-afternoon. With two and a half hours of driving at each end and sunset at about 5:15 PM, much of the drive home is in the dark. The lesson for anyone planning the same day is simple: decide before arriving which three or four things matter most, because there will not be time for everything.

docs.title: The Castalian Spring
docs.text:
The Castalian Spring is the sacred spring that flows from the gorge between the two Phaedriades cliffs, just east of the Sanctuary of Apollo, where pilgrims, priests, and the Pythia purified themselves with water before entering the sanctuary. Two fountain houses survive. The older one, from about 600 BCE, lies lower down by the modern road: a paved court where water poured from spouts into a basin. The later one, cut into the rock face itself, has a long basin, steps, and niches carved for offerings. Because rocks fall from the cliffs above, the upper fountain is often fenced off, and we may have to look at it from the path.

Later stories gave the spring a nymph, Castalia, who leaped into it to escape Apollo, and Roman poets made its water the drink of poetic inspiration, as Parnassus was the home of the Muses. For a pilgrim, though, the point was simpler. Nobody approached Apollo unwashed. A splash of cold mountain water on the hands and hair was the first step of every visit, which is why our walk begins here too.

docs.title: Part Two: Up the Sacred Way
The Sacred Way of Delphi
docs.text:
The Sacred Way of Delphi is the paved processional road that zigzags up through the Sanctuary of Apollo from its main gate at the southeast corner to the great altar in front of the temple. It runs west along the lowest terrace, turns sharply at the Athenian Treasury, climbs back east along the polygonal wall, and turns once more up to the temple. In antiquity it was lined so thickly with statues, bases, and small buildings that walking it was like walking through a crowded museum of Greek rivalry. Our best guide to what stood here is Pausanias, the Greek travel writer of the 2nd century CE, who walked it and described it monument by monument in the tenth book of his Description of Greece. Before the gate lies a paved square with a row of columns, the Roman agora, the market square of Roman times, where pilgrims probably bought statuettes and other offerings before going in.

Columns of the Roman agora at the entrance to the Sanctuary of Apollo. Photo by Dan McCreary

The first stretch inside the gate shows how the monuments argued with one another. Pausanias saw a bronze bull given by the island of Corcyra, statues given by the Arcadians, and the Spartans' monument for their naval victory over Athens in 405 BCE, which Chapter 17 met in its scoreboard of gifts. Across the way stood Athenian and Argive monuments. Rival cities set their victories facing each other on the god's road, so that every pilgrim walked between the claims.

docs.title: The Treasuries of Delphi
docs.text:
The treasuries of Delphi are the small, temple-shaped buildings that Greek city-states built along the Sacred Way to hold their offerings to Apollo and to display their wealth and piety. Archaeologists have found the foundations of more than twenty. A treasury was not a bank. It held gifts of gold, silver, and bronze, ritual equipment, and spoils of war, and its real job was to stand in the god's precinct with the city's name on it.

The treasury of the Corinthians, said to be the oldest, held the gold and silver gifts of Croesus, Herodotus says, and Chapter 17 explained how Croesus earned his answer. The small island of Siphnos built its treasury in marble around 525 BCE with young women, not columns, holding up its porch; its carved frieze is one of the museum's treasures. Most treasuries are now only foundations, so the terraces they stood on are the best guide to how crowded this slope once was.

Sanctuary terraces under the cliffs. Photo by Dan McCreary

docs.title: The Athenian Treasury
docs.text:
The Athenian Treasury is the small Doric treasury of Parian marble, built by Athens around 500 to 490 BCE, that stands at the first bend of the Sacred Way. It is the only treasury at Delphi that we can see standing, because French archaeologists rebuilt it from its original blocks between 1903 and 1906, with money from the city of Athens. Its metopes, the carved panels above the columns, showed the deeds of Heracles and of Theseus, the hero of Athens; the originals are in the museum and copies are on the building.

Worked example: built from the spoils of Marathon? Let's run Chapter 4's test on the building's famous story. Pausanias says the Athenians built the treasury from the spoils of the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, which Chapter 15 told. Beside the treasury, on a triangular terrace, a base still carries an inscription saying the Athenians dedicated the spoils of Marathon to Apollo. That sounds conclusive. But many archaeologists date the building's style to a few years before Marathon, around 500 BCE, and the inscription belongs to the terrace, which may have held a separate monument. So the honest verdict is "possibly." Athens certainly used this spot to remind every visitor of Marathon. Whether the treasury itself was paid for by that victory, or was simply a good place to advertise it afterward, the evidence does not settle.

The Treasury of the Athenians. Photo by Dan McCreary

Its walls also became a public notice board. In the 2nd century BCE, two hymns to Apollo were carved on its south wall with signs written above the words to show the melody. These Delphic Hymns are among the oldest pieces of written music that can still be performed, and the stones are now in the museum.

docs.title: The Polygonal Wall
docs.text:
The polygonal wall is the long retaining wall that holds up the terrace of the Temple of Apollo, built after the temple burned in 548 BCE. Its limestone blocks are not rectangles. Each is cut to an irregular many-sided shape with curving edges, and fitted against its neighbors so closely, without mortar, that the blocks lock one another in place. Masonry like this resists earthquakes well: the temple above it fell in the earthquake of 373 BCE, but the wall has stood for about 2,500 years. Against its lower face the Athenians built a long, narrow porch, the Stoa of the Athenians, to display spoils from their naval victories.

The Sanctuary of Apollo on the slopes of Parnassus. Photo by Dan McCreary

A smooth, prominent wall in the busiest part of the sanctuary was too good to leave blank. Over the centuries its face was covered with hundreds of inscriptions, so many that the wall became the sanctuary's public archive. Most of them record one kind of transaction, the subject of the next section.

Let the Light Skim the Stone

Here's an epigrapher's trick: worn letters show best when light skims across the stone at a low angle, not when it falls straight on. Look at the wall from the side, or shade it with your hand and hold a phone light low and sideways. Rows of letters will appear where we saw only rough stone.

docs.title: Manumission Records
docs.text:
Manumission is the legal act of freeing an enslaved person. The manumission records of Delphi are the inscriptions, more than a thousand of them, most carved between about 200 BCE and 100 CE, that record enslaved men and women gaining their freedom through a sale to Apollo. Many of them are on the polygonal wall. Slavery was normal in the ancient Greek world, and most enslaved people had been captured in war or by pirates, or born to enslaved mothers. A few could save money from their work, and at Delphi they could use it to buy their freedom in a form that the whole community would respect.

The form was a sale to the god. The owner "sold" the person to Pythian Apollo for a price, but the money was the enslaved person's own, saved and handed over through the god. Since no one could claim a god's property, the person became free. The record was dated by the archon, the magistrate who gave his name to the Delphic year, and named a guarantor, a citizen bound to defend the sale if anyone later claimed the freed person as a slave, and witnesses, often including Apollo's priests. Many records add a harder condition, called paramone, "remaining": the freed person had to stay with the former owner and serve, often until the owner's death, before the freedom became complete. Many of the people freed were women.

Worked example: reading a record's parts. Let's take the standard form of a Delphic manumission record, simplified and with the names left out, and ask what each part did. The table follows the record clause by clause.

Part of the record What it says, in substance What it did Date In the year of a named archon, in a named month Made the record findable and checkable Sale A named owner sold to Pythian Apollo Made the god the legal buyer The person freed A named person, with his or her homeland Identified who was freed Price A sum in silver, received in full Recorded that the sale was complete Freedom clause The person trusted the purchase to the god, to be free, claimed by no one, living as they wish Protected the freed person Guarantor A named citizen, by the law of the city Protected the freed person against later claims Paramone (in many records) The freed person stays with the former owner while the owner lives Kept the former owner's control for years Witnesses The priests and named citizens Protected the freed person: people who could testify

The record did two things at once. It gave a person freedom that no one could later deny, written where everyone could read it, and in many cases it also kept them bound to the old household for years. The infographic below lets us take a record apart clause by clause.

docs.title: Diagram: Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall
docs.text:
Run the Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall MicroSim Fullscreen

Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall

Type: infographic sim-id: delphi-freedom-record-reader Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: deconstruct Learning Objective: The learner will deconstruct a simplified Delphic manumission record into its eight clauses, naming each clause and judging whether it protects the freed person, limits the freed person's freedom, or records the facts of the sale, with at least 7 of the 8 judgments correct.

Prerequisites: manumission, manumission records, archon, guarantor, witnesses, paramone, and the sale to the god (all defined in "Manumission Records" above); inscription (Chapter 10); the polygonal wall (defined above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the eight clauses, the learner commits two answers: the clause name (from eight names) and its effect (one of three). A clause is correct when both answers match the Content table. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 clauses correct on the first attempt. Hovering over a clause and reading the glossary terms is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Freedom at Delphi was a gift from the owner, when the price was usually the enslaved person's own savings. (2) A freed person was immediately and completely free, when many records include a paramone clause. (3) The god's role was decorative, when the sale to the god was the legal mechanism that made re-enslavement impossible. (4) The witnesses and guarantor were formalities, when they were the people who could defend the freedom later.

Instructional Rationale: Deconstructing a real document form into its working parts is an Analyze task: the learner must decide what each clause does, not just what it says. Asking for the effect of each clause, with protection and limitation as separate answers, makes the learner confront the record's double character.

Content:

A heading above the record reads: "A simplified record in the standard Delphic form. Bracketed words stand for the names that a real record gives. This is a composite, not a translation of one inscription."

The record, shown as eight clauses in this order:

# Clause text shown Correct name Correct effect Why (shown as feedback) 1 "In the year when [name] was archon, in the month [month]," Date Records the facts Dating by the archon's year made the record findable and checkable by anyone. 2 "[owner's name], son of [father's name], sold to Pythian Apollo" Sale to the god Protects the freed person Once the god owned the person, no human could claim them as property. 3 "a woman named [name], [her homeland] by birth," Person freed Records the facts The record names the person and her origin so that she can be identified later. 4 "for a price of [sum] of silver, and he has received the whole price," Price Records the facts The price was usually the freed person's own savings, and full payment closed the sale. 5 "as [name] entrusted the purchase to the god, on condition that she be free and claimed by no one, doing what she wishes and going where she wishes." Freedom clause Protects the freed person This clause states the freedom itself and forbids anyone to claim her. 6 "Guarantor, according to the law of the city: [name]." Guarantor Protects the freed person The guarantor was legally bound to defend the sale if anyone claimed her as a slave. 7 "[name] shall remain with [owner's name] for as long as he lives, doing what she is told." Paramone Limits the freed person's freedom This condition kept her serving the former owner, often until his death. 8 "Witnesses: the priests of Apollo, [name], [name]." Witnesses Protects the freed person Witnesses could testify to the sale if her freedom was ever challenged.

The eight clause names offered for every clause: Date; Sale to the god; Person freed; Price; Freedom clause; Guarantor; Paramone; Witnesses.

The three effects offered for every clause: Protects the freed person; Limits the freed person's freedom; Records the facts.

Glossary available on hover: archon, guarantor, witnesses, paramone, manumission, each with the definition given in the chapter section "Manumission Records".

Provenance: The clause structure, the sale to Pythian Apollo, the entrusting formula, the guarantor, the witnesses, and the paramone condition come from the chapter section "Manumission Records". The wording is a simplified composite of the standard form; the sim must show the heading in Content saying so.

Rules:

  • The clauses are always shown in the fixed order 1 to 8.
  • Each clause has exactly one correct name and one correct effect, as in the Content table.
  • A clause counts as correct only when both its name and its effect are correct.
  • Each clause name may be used for more than one clause while answering, but the Check reports every duplicate as wrong for all clauses except the one it fits.
  • Score = number of correct clauses, from 0 to 8. Mastery is score >= 7 on the first Check.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the whole record, then selects clause 1.
  2. For the selected clause, the learner chooses a name and an effect. The clause is marked as answered.
  3. The learner repeats step 2 for all eight clauses, in any order.
  4. The learner presses Check. Each clause is marked correct or incorrect, and the "Why" text appears for every clause.
  5. The learner may change answers on incorrect clauses and press Check again; only the first Check counts toward mastery.
  6. After the final Check, a summary line appears under the record: "Four clauses protect her freedom, three record the facts, and one keeps her bound."
  7. The learner should notice that the same document both guarantees and limits freedom.

Feedback: Eight clauses, fixed order, unlimited re-checks. Correct clause: "Correct: [why text]." Incorrect name: "This clause is the [correct name]. [why text]" Incorrect effect only: "Right name, but look again at its effect. [why text]" The score "Clauses correct: n of 8" is shown after each Check. After the second Check, a Show Answers option reveals any remaining correct answers.

Starting State: The eight clauses of the record, unanswered, with the heading from Content and the question "Which words set her free, and which words keep her bound?"

Chapter Anchors: More than a thousand manumission records, most from about 200 BCE to 100 CE; the sale to Pythian Apollo; the paramone condition, "often until the owner's death"; eight parts in the chapter's table, the same eight in this record.

docs.title: The Serpent Column
docs.text:
At the top of the Sacred Way, the road turns onto the temple terrace and reaches the great altar in front of the temple's east end. Here, Herodotus says, stood the golden tripod that the Greeks dedicated after their victory over the Persians at Plataea in 479 BCE, set on a three-headed serpent of bronze. Chapter 4 met what is left of that monument in Istanbul. Today we close the loop.

The Serpent Column is the bronze column of three intertwined snakes, cast for the Greek allies after Plataea from a tenth of the spoils, as Herodotus says, which once supported a golden tripod beside Apollo's altar and has stood in the Hippodrome of Istanbul since Constantine moved it to his new capital by 330 CE. Its coils carry the names of the 31 Greek communities that fought, under the heading "These fought the war." Chapter 17 told how the Spartan commander Pausanias first had his own name inscribed on it, and how the Spartans erased his boast.

Worked example: two ends of one object. Let's put the two ends of the Serpent Column side by side, and ask what each place can show us that the other cannot. On Day 2, in Istanbul, we looked down into a pit in the Hippodrome at a twisted trunk of bronze with no heads, standing on ground that has risen several meters since Byzantine times. On it we could have read, if we had climbed down, the names of the cities. In the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, which Chapter 5 passed at the edge of Gülhane Park, lies the upper jaw of one of the serpent heads. Istanbul has the object.

Delphi has the place. Here the monument's base still lies near the altar, and a bronze copy of the column now stands near it, so that we can see how tall the column rose against the cliffs and how close it stood to the god's altar and temple. Neither city tells the story alone. Istanbul cannot show why the column mattered, and Delphi cannot show the column. The written sources fill in what neither place can show: Herodotus gives the spoils and the place, Thucydides gives the erased boast, and the travel writer Pausanias, in the 2nd century CE, says that the gold of the tripod had been carried off by the Phocian leaders during the Third Sacred War of 356–346 BCE, while the bronze serpent still stood. The table sorts the evidence.

Evidence Where we meet it What it adds The monument's base by the altar Delphi, the temple terrace Where the monument stood, before every pilgrim's eyes The bronze copy of the column Delphi, near the altar How the column looked in its setting The bronze coils with the cities' names Istanbul, the Hippodrome (Day 2) Who fought, in their own inscription The upper jaw of one head Istanbul Archaeology Museums What the lost heads looked like Herodotus, about 430 BCE A written source Made from the spoils of Plataea; the tripod stood on the serpent by the altar Thucydides, about 400 BCE A written source Pausanias' boast inscribed, then erased Pausanias, 2nd century CE A written source The tripod's gold taken in 356–346 BCE; the bronze still in place

The column's life runs across this whole book. It was cast in 479 BCE, the year after Salamis in Chapter 15. It lost its gold in the Third Sacred War of Chapter 17. It stood at Delphi for about eight hundred years and then, by 330 CE, became one of the ornaments Constantine gathered for his capital in Chapter 3. It survived the Byzantine and Ottoman centuries; Ottoman pictures of the 16th century still show its three heads, which broke off at the end of the 17th century or soon after, as different accounts say. One piece of a head came to light again in the 19th century.

A bronze copy of the Serpent Column in the Sanctuary of Apollo. Photo by Dan McCreary

An Object Is Half a Story

Notice that the Serpent Column meant one thing beside Apollo's altar, where every Greek city saw its own name among the victors, and another in an emperor's racetrack, where it said "everything old and holy now belongs to the new capital." The bronze did not change; its place did. Whenever we meet an object far from home, ask what it said where it first stood.

The sorting activity below asks which evidence can be checked at which end of the column's journey.

Misconceptions: (1) Everything about the column can be seen in Istanbul, because the bronze is there. (2) Delphi has nothing left of the monument. (3) Facts in a museum label must come from the object itself, when many come from ancient writers. (4) The column was always headless.

Instructional Rationale: Attributing each claim to its evidence is an Analyze task: the learner must separate what an object shows, what a place shows, and what only a text reports. The three bins mirror the chapter's table, so the learner rebuilds the distinction instead of reading it.

Bins, shown with these labels: "Check it at Delphi"; "Check it in Istanbul"; "Only in a written source".

Claim cards, shown in a shuffled order:

# Claim card Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Bronze coils carry the names of the Greek cities that fought. Check it in Istanbul The inscribed coils stand in the Hippodrome, where Constantine moved them. 2 A stone base by the great altar marks where the monument stood. Check it at Delphi The base never left the sanctuary. 3 A bronze copy shows how the column looked in its setting. Check it at Delphi The copy stands near the altar, close to where the original stood. 4 The upper jaw of one serpent head survives. Check it in Istanbul It is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, beside Gülhane Park. 5 The column stands in a pit because the ground has risen since Byzantine times. Check it in Istanbul The pit is in the Hippodrome, at about the level of the Byzantine track. 6 The temple terrace where the monument stood is held up by the polygonal wall. Only in a written source Thucydides tells this story; the erased verse does not survive on the bronze. 8 A golden tripod once sat on top of the three heads. Only in a written source Herodotus and Pausanias describe the tripod; its gold was taken long ago. 9 The monument was made from a tenth of the spoils of Plataea. Only in a written source Herodotus gives the source of the metal; the bronze itself cannot tell us. 10 The Phocian leaders took the tripod's gold during the Third Sacred War. Only in a written source The travel writer Pausanias reports it, about five hundred years later.

Provenance: All claims come from this chapter's sections "The Serpent Column" and "The Polygonal Wall" and from Chapter 4 (the Hippodrome pit, the Byzantine ground level). Bin assignments follow the chapter's evidence table.

Rules:

  • 10 cards and 3 bins. Each card has exactly one correct bin.
  • Cards are shuffled once when the sim starts; the order is the same after Reset.
  • A card can be moved between bins until Check is pressed.
  • Check is available only when all 10 cards are placed.
  • Score = number of cards in their correct bin, from 0 to 10. Mastery is score >= 8 on the first Check.
