Keep the student in the challenging course and add tutoring when the score is high; hide the score from the student; recompute the score every month Keep the course and add tutoring Adding support instead of lowering the placement replaces link L5's loss of challenging work with more help, so a high score leads to higher grades. Q3 Next Sunday the 9 AM forecast said "heavy traffic," and the road was light. What is the best explanation? Drivers acted on the forecast, so the jam it predicted did not form; the model was badly trained; traffic is purely random Drivers acted on the forecast In a balancing loop a useful forecast can look wrong, because people change their behavior to avoid what it predicts.

Provenance: The loops are simplified from the chapter sections "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy," "Student Risk Prediction," and "Predictive Policing." The link directions are the chapter's qualitative claims, not measured effects; the sim labels the diagram "Simplified causal model: directions only, no sizes."

Rules:

  • Links are labeled one at a time in the order L1 to L10 (fixed). Each link has one scored attempt; after it, the correct label and Why text are shown and the link displays its correct sign.
  • A loop can be classified only after all of its links are labeled. Each loop has one scored attempt.
  • The loop questions are answered after all three loops are classified, in the order Q1, Q2, Q3, one scored attempt each.
  • Scoring: links 0 to 10, loops 0 to 3, questions 0 to 3. Mastery requires links >= 9, loops = 3 and questions >= 2.
  • The counting rule is shown only after the learner's first loop classification, whether right or wrong.
  • Start Over resets every label, classification, answer and score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the definitions of same-direction and opposite-direction links and sees Loop 1 with its three links unlabeled.
  2. The learner labels L1, L2 and L3; after each, the feedback appears and the sign is drawn on the link.
  3. The learner classifies Loop 1 as reinforcing or balancing; the feedback and the counting rule appear.
  4. The learner repeats steps 2 and 3 for Loop 2 (L4 to L7) and Loop 3 (L8 to L10).
  5. The learner answers Q1, Q2 and Q3.
  6. The learner should notice that Loop 2 contains two opposite links and still reinforces, and that the loop which looks like a failed forecast, Loop 3, is the one in which the forecast worked.

Feedback: Correct link: "Correct:" plus the Why text. Incorrect link: "This link runs the [same/opposite] way:" plus the Why text. Correct loop: "Correct:" plus the Why text. Incorrect loop: "Count the opposite links: [n]. This loop is [classification]:" plus the Why text. Questions: "Correct:" or "The best answer is: [choice].", plus the Why text. Running scores "Links n of 10, Loops n of 3, Questions n of 3" are shown throughout. At the end, if mastery is met: "You can read a feedback loop: a prediction about people can make itself come true, or keep itself from coming true."; otherwise: "Look again at Loop 2: count its opposite links before deciding."

Starting State: Loop 1 is shown with its three nodes, the outside factor, and three unlabeled links. The question on screen is "If the model predicts more crime here, what happens next?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter describes the predictive policing loop (patrols where crime is predicted, more crime discovered, more records, higher prediction), the student risk loop (a high-risk label leading to a less demanding class, lower learning and a higher score), and a self-defeating traffic forecast for 9 AM on the road to Delphi. It names Merton (1948) and the Lum and Isaac Oakland study (2016), which the sim does not need to show.

docs.title: Who Funds the Model
docs.text:
Who funds the model is the question of who pays to build and run a prediction system, and how that payment might shape whose interests it serves. Delphi answers the question vividly. Croesus' gold bought his Lydians the right to consult first and pay no fees. The Alcmaeonids, Herodotus says, rebuilt the temple's front in marble and also bribed the Pythia to tell every Spartan who came, on any business, to free Athens; the Spartans eventually did. Chapter 17 showed the defense too: when the Spartan king Cleomenes' bribery was found out, the Pythia was removed from office.

Building a large AI model today costs so much in computing, energy, and expert labor that only a small number of companies, and a few governments and research groups, can do it. That does not make the models corrupt. It does mean that four questions belong with every answer we get from one: Who built it? How does it earn money: subscriptions, advertising, selling to businesses, or public funding? What would it gain by steering our choice, toward a product, a store, or simply toward spending more time with it? Who checks it from outside, as the Amphictyonic League was supposed to check the sanctuary? For schools the question is sharper still, because a free tutoring app may be paid for with students' data. Some models are released openly, so that anyone can run and inspect them; others are closed. Neither kind is automatically trustworthy, but a source that can be inspected can be checked.

docs.title: Model Calibration
docs.text:
Model calibration is how well the probabilities a forecaster gives match how often things actually happen. A forecaster is well calibrated if, of all the days on which they said "70 percent chance of rain," it rained on about 70 percent. Chapter 17 noted that a percentage forecast cannot be proven wrong by a single day; calibration is how it can be tested over many. A forecaster who says 90 percent when the true frequency is 60 percent is overconfident; one who says 60 percent when the true frequency is 90 percent is underconfident. Calibration is not the same as being right: a forecaster who says "30 percent" every day in a place where it rains on 30 percent of days is perfectly calibrated and not very helpful. The best forecasters are both calibrated and sharp, willing to say 90 or 10 percent when they have reason to.

Worked example: two forecasters, ten rainy-season days each. Let's compare two forecasters for Delphi, with illustrative records. Forecaster A said "70 percent chance of rain" on ten days, and it rained on 7 of them. Forecaster B said "90 percent" on ten other days, and it rained on 6. A said 70 and got 70: well calibrated. B said 90 and got 60: overconfident. We can put a number on the difference with the Brier score 🔊 Pronounce BRY-er, the average of the squared differences between the forecast probability and what happened (1 if it rained, 0 if not). Lower is better; 0 is perfect.

Forecaster A Forecaster B Forecast 70 percent, 10 days 90 percent, 10 days Days with rain 7 6 Calibration Well calibrated Overconfident by 30 points Score on a rainy day \( (0.7 - 1)^2 = 0.09 \) \( (0.9 - 1)^2 = 0.01 \) Score on a dry day \( (0.7 - 0)^2 = 0.49 \) \( (0.9 - 0)^2 = 0.81 \) Brier score \( (7 \times 0.09 + 3 \times 0.49) \div 10 = 0.21 \) \( (6 \times 0.01 + 4 \times 0.81) \div 10 = 0.33 \)

B's confident forecasts look impressive on the six rainy days, but they are punished heavily on the four dry ones, and A wins. For comparison, a forecaster who said "50 percent" every day would score exactly 0.25, so B did worse than not forecasting at all. Studies since the 1970s have found that professional weather forecasts are among the best-calibrated predictions people make, largely because forecasters get fast, public feedback every day. Most of us are less calibrated: when we say we are "90 percent sure" of a fact, we are usually right less often than that.

Probabilities Feel Slippery at First

If "70 percent" still feels like a vague hunch rather than a claim that can be checked, that is normal; most people need to keep score for a while before it clicks. Start the way the forecasters do: write down a percentage for a few small things each day, then count how often the 70s came true. The game below does the counting for you.

The MicroSim below turns this into a game: we give probabilities for twelve statements from this book, and it tells us how calibrated we were.

docs.title: Diagram: How Calibrated Are You?
docs.text:
Run the How Calibrated Are You? MicroSim Fullscreen

How Calibrated Are You?

Type: microsim sim-id: calibration-confidence-game Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/confidence-calibration-challenge Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess whether their own probability judgments, and those of two weather forecasters, are overconfident, underconfident, or well calibrated, by stating probabilities for twelve statements and judging the results against a reliability table, with all three assessments correct.

Prerequisites: probability, prediction uncertainty, model calibration, overconfident, underconfident, Brier score (defined in "Prediction Uncertainty" and "Model Calibration" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Three committed judgments, each with one attempt: (1) after stating probabilities for the twelve statements and seeing their reliability table, the learner judges their own record as overconfident, about right, or underconfident; it is correct when it matches the verdict computed by Rules; (2) the learner judges which of Forecaster A and Forecaster B is better calibrated; (3) the learner judges whether Forecaster B was overconfident or underconfident. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Stating the twelve probabilities is the data for judgment 1, not itself evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Being confident is the same as being well calibrated (Forecaster B; statements answered at 100 percent). (2) A 70 percent forecast is "wrong" whenever the event does not happen (Forecaster A). (3) Saying 50 percent on everything is a safe strategy (the 0.25 baseline). (4) Twelve answers are enough to know one's calibration for sure (the small-sample note).

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work asks the learner to judge a record against a standard. Generating their own record first makes the judgment personal and exposes overconfidence directly, and the two forecasters give a second, cleaner case in which the standard can be applied without the learner's own stakes.

Content:

Part A: twelve statements, shown one at a time in this order. The learner states the probability that each statement is true.

# Statement True or false Why (shown after the learner commits) 1 Mount Parnassus rises more than 2,000 m above sea level. True It rises to 2,457 m (Chapter 17). 2 Delphi is more than 300 km by road from Athens. False It is about 180 km, about two and a half hours by coach (Chapter 18). 3 The Oracle of Delphi gave answers for more than 1,000 years. True From at least about 750 BCE to 391 CE, about 1,140 years (Chapter 17). 4 The Byzantine Empire lasted longer than the oracle did. False The Byzantine Empire lasted 1,123 years; the oracle about 1,140 (Chapter 17). 5 Herodotus wrote down the Croesus prophecy within 20 years of the fall of Sardis. False He wrote about 115 to 120 years later (Chapter 17). 6 Joseph Fontenrose collected more than 500 Delphic responses. True He collected about 535 (Chapter 17). 7 More than 4,000 lead question tablets survive from the oracle of Zeus at Dodona. True More than 4,000 survive (Chapter 17). 8 The Temple of Apollo whose ruins we saw at Delphi was finished in the 6th century BCE. False It was finished around 330 BCE, in the 4th century; the 6th-century temple burned in 548 BCE (Chapter 17). 9 At Salamis, Athens supplied almost half of the Greek ships. True 180 of 378 ships, about 48 percent (Chapter 15). 10 The council of the Amphictyonic League had 24 votes. True Twelve member peoples with two votes each (Chapter 17). 11 Fewer than 100 records of freed slaves survive at Delphi. False More than a thousand manumission records survive (Chapter 18). 12 The Athenian Treasury at Delphi was rebuilt from its original blocks in the 20th century. True French archaeologists rebuilt it between 1903 and 1906 (Chapter 18).

Totals: 7 true (1, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12) and 5 false (2, 4, 5, 8, 11).

Part B: two forecasters' records (illustrative), shown after Part A.

Forecaster Forecast Days Days with rain Brier score A 70% chance of rain 10 7 0.21 B 90% chance of rain 10 6 0.33

Judgment questions:

# Question Choices Correct Why (shown as feedback) J1 Looking at your reliability table, how calibrated were you? Overconfident; about right; underconfident The verdict computed by Rules Your average confidence was [c]% and you were right [h]% of the time. J2 Which forecaster is better calibrated? A; B A A said 70% and it rained on 7 of 10 days; B said 90% and it rained on 6 of 10. J3 Was Forecaster B overconfident or underconfident? Overconfident; underconfident Overconfident B's 90% came true only 60% of the time, so B claimed more certainty than the record supports.

Notes always shown with the results: "Twelve answers is a small sample; forecasters are judged over hundreds." and "Saying 50% on everything scores 0.25: never wrong, never useful."

Provenance: Statements 1 to 12 and their reasons come from Chapters 15, 17 and 18 of this book, as cited in each row; the sim copies them verbatim. Forecaster records are illustrative and labeled "Illustrative records." The Brier score values are computed from the Rules and match the chapter's worked example in "Model Calibration."

Rules:

  • Probability input for each statement: minimum 0, maximum 100, step 10, default 50, unit percent; it means "the chance this statement is true."
  • The learner must commit a probability before the answer and reason are shown; a committed probability cannot be changed.
  • Brier score: the mean over all twelve statements of (p − o)², where p is the probability as a fraction (0.0 to 1.0) and o is 1 if the statement is true and 0 if false. Range 0.00 to 1.00, shown to two decimals; lower is better. Baseline for always answering 50 percent: 0.25.
  • Leaning: p > 50 means the learner leans "true" with confidence p; p < 50 means the learner leans "false" with confidence 100 − p; p = 50 means no lean. A leaned statement is a hit when the lean matches the truth.
  • Reliability table: one row for each confidence level 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 percent, showing the number of leaned statements at that level, the number of hits, and the percentage of hits; a row with no statements shows "none."
  • Verdict for J1: compute c = mean confidence of leaned statements and h = percentage of leaned statements that were hits. Overconfident if c − h > 10 percentage points; underconfident if c − h < −10; about right if −10 <= c − h <= 10.
  • J1 unlocks only if at least 6 of the 12 statements are leaned (p ≠ 50). If fewer are leaned, the sim says "Lean one way on at least 6 statements so there is a record to judge," and offers Try Again.
  • The verdict, c and h are shown only after J1 is committed; the reliability table and Brier score are shown before.
  • Try Again clears all twelve probabilities, the judgments and the scores.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads statement 1 and sets a probability that it is true.
  2. The learner presses Commit; the truth and the reason appear.
  3. The learner continues through all twelve statements.
  4. The sim shows the learner's Brier score, the 0.25 baseline, and the reliability table.
  5. The learner answers J1, judging their own calibration from the table; the verdict with c and h appears.
  6. The learner sees the two forecasters' records and answers J2 and J3.
  7. The learner should notice whether their 90 and 100 percent answers were right as often as they claimed, and that Forecaster B's confident record scored worse than the 50 percent baseline.

Feedback: For each statement after Commit: "True." or "False." followed by the reason, and "Your score on this one: [(p − o)² to two decimals]." For J1, J2 and J3: correct shows "Correct:" plus the Why text; incorrect shows "Not quite:" plus the Why text. One attempt each; the correct answer is shown after the attempt. At the end: if J1, J2 and J3 are all correct, "You can judge a forecaster, including yourself: confidence has to be earned by the record."; otherwise, "Compare the stated percentage with the percentage that came true, row by row."

Starting State: Statement 1 is shown with the probability set to 50 percent, a Commit control, and the question "How likely is this to be true?"

Chapter Anchors: Forecaster A: 70 percent on ten days, rain on 7, Brier score 0.21. Forecaster B: 90 percent on ten days, rain on 6, Brier score 0.33, overconfident by 30 points. Always saying 50 percent scores 0.25. Twelve statements from this book.

docs.title: Track Record and Trust
docs.text:
Track record and trust is the principle that a source of predictions deserves trust in proportion to its record of predictions made, and written down, before the outcomes were known. Chapter 17 asked who remembers Delphi's misses. Nobody kept a scorecard. Every famous prophecy in Chapter 17's table was first written down after it "came true," and the oracle's 1,140 years of trust rested on stories of hits, while the misses, if there were any, were forgotten or explained away. Croesus came closest to a scorecard. Before trusting any oracle, he tested seven of them with a question whose answer he alone knew, what he was doing on the hundredth day, and only Delphi passed. In modern terms, he ran a benchmark: a test with known answers, used to compare sources before relying on them. And his story shows the benchmark's limit: an oracle that could see a tortoise boiling in Sardis still gave him an answer he misread about the future.

AI systems are judged the same way today, on benchmarks of questions with known answers, and the same limits apply. A model can do well on a test it has, in effect, seen before, and a high score on one kind of task says little about another. The track records worth trusting are public, cover many predictions, include the misses, and were scored by someone other than the forecaster.

docs.title: Testability of Predictions
docs.text:
Testability of predictions is the property of a claim that lets the world prove it wrong: it says clearly enough what will happen, and when, that a later observation could contradict it. Chapter 17's test was "a prediction has to be able to lose." Testability adds what is needed to check that it lost: a claim recorded before the outcome, an outcome that can be observed, a deadline, and, for a probability, many such claims to score. A hedge cannot be tested at all; a single probability can be tested only as part of a record; a clear, dated, recorded claim can be tested by anyone.

Worked example: rewriting the Croesus answer so it could lose. Let's take the most famous untestable answer and make it testable, one step at a time.

Version The claim Could it lose? The oracle's "If you make war on the Persians, you will destroy a great empire." No: either empire's fall fulfills it Name the empire "If you make war on the Persians, you will destroy the Persian Empire." Yes, but only someday Add a deadline "If you cross the Halys this year, Persia will fall within three years." Yes, and soon enough to check Add a probability "If you cross the Halys this year, there is a 30 percent chance that Persia falls within three years." Only as part of a record of many such forecasts Record it in advance The same, carved on a dated stone before Croesus marches Yes, and no one can rewrite it afterward

The last row is what Delphi never did, and it is what makes a modern forecast trustworthy: the prediction is fixed before the outcome. The same rewriting works on claims about AI. "AI will transform education" cannot lose. "By the end of 2028, a majority of the public schools in our state will give every student access to an AI tutor during the school day" can, and in three years someone can check.

docs.title: Prediction Horizon
docs.text: The prediction horizon is how far ahead a forecaster can predict with useful accuracy before its predictions become no better than a guess based on long-run averages. Chapter 17 ended with Apollo's winter absence: for three months of the year, even the god of prophecy did not answer. Every forecaster has its own winter. For daily weather, useful detail fades after about a week to ten days. In the 1960s the meteorologist Edward Lorenz showed why: the atmosphere is chaotic, so small errors in today's measurements double and double again until, after roughly two weeks, the forecast says nothing that a calendar of average weather could not. Beyond the horizon, the honest forecast is the long-run average: "Delphi in late November is usually cold, often wet." Different questions have different horizons. A train timetable can be trusted for months; the result of an election can be forecast only roughly a year out; a single coin toss cannot be predicted at all. A good forecaster knows its horizon and says so. A bad one answers every question at the same confident length, which is one more thing to check about a chatbot asked about next week.

docs.title: AI Capability Forecasting
docs.text: AI capability forecasting is predicting what AI systems will be able to do in the future, so that schools, companies, and governments can plan. It is hard for all the reasons in this part: the systems change quickly, their builders have reasons to promise much, and "capability" is hard to measure. One careful approach comes from METR, a nonprofit research organization that studies what advanced AI systems can do on their own. Instead of a test score, METR measures the length of task, in the time a skilled person would need to do it, that an AI system can complete about half the time, which it calls the 50 percent time horizon. Measured this way, the horizon has been growing quickly: in its 2025 study, METR found that the length of task the best systems could complete had been doubling every several months for several years. That is a measured trend, not a promise. AI-Native Schools explains how METR produces the number, and why a 50 percent success rate is a coin flip rather than a reliable worker, in Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies.

docs.title: AI Doubling Curves
docs.text: An AI doubling curve is a chart of some measure of AI, such as the task horizon, computing power, or cost, that grows by doubling at a steady interval, and the projection made by extending that doubling into the future. Doubling is deceptive. Something that doubles every five months grows about fivefold in a year and nearly 150-fold in three years, so a curve that looks flat for years can suddenly seem to explode. The forecast's weakness is the one Part Two gave every prediction: it assumes the forces behind the trend continue. Many curves that looked like endless doubling turned out to be the early part of an S-shape that levels off when it meets a limit, such as energy, money, or data. And a small change in the doubling time changes the long-range answer enormously. AI-Native Schools works through these projections and their uncertainty, and how a school can plan with a range of scenarios instead of one line, in Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty. By the measure of this chapter, the honest AI forecast states its range, names its horizon, and gets checked.

docs.title: Part Six: An Answer as the Start of an Inquiry
Answer as Start of Inquiry
docs.text: An answer as the start of an inquiry is an answer treated not as the end of thinking but as a claim to be tested, which then becomes the beginning of an investigation. Chaerephon's question is the model. Told that no one was wiser than Socrates, Socrates did not accept the compliment, and he did not dismiss it. He set out to test it, questioning politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and concluded that his only wisdom was knowing what he did not know. Chapter 17 noted that of all the famous answers, this is the only one whose questioner treated it as a beginning. It is also the only one that has lasted as a way of life: the Socratic method of Chapter 9, teaching by questions, grew out of it. An answer that is tested teaches us something whether it passes or fails. An answer taken on trust teaches us only what the source already believed.

docs.title: AI as Thinking Partner
docs.text:
AI as a thinking partner is using an AI system to help us think, by asking it to question our reasoning, argue the other side, explain a step, or suggest what to check, rather than to think for us by handing over a finished answer. It is the Socrates habit applied to a machine. The difference is not in the technology but in how we ask.

Asking for an answer Asking for a thinking partner "Write our Delphi travel journal entry." "Ask me five questions about today that would help me write it." "Was the oracle a fraud?" "Give me the strongest case that the Pythia was sincere, then the strongest case against, and tell me what evidence would settle it." "Which Athens museum should we see tomorrow?" "Here is what we loved this week. What should we ask ourselves before choosing a museum?" "Explain the geological fault theory." "I think the ethylene theory was disproved. Check my reasoning and tell me where I'm wrong."

Worked example: one question, asked two ways. Let's take the second row and imagine the replies. Asked "Was the oracle a fraud?", a chatbot will produce a balanced paragraph, and we will remember whichever half confirmed what we thought, Croesus' error again. Asked for both cases and the deciding evidence, it gives us Fontenrose's plain historical answers, Plutarch's sincere priesthood, the Alcmaeonid bribery, and the disputed gas, and then the question becomes ours to weigh, as it was for Socrates. The second way takes longer, and it is the way that leaves us knowing more. AI-Native Schools builds this idea into the design of AI tutors, which offer hints and questions rather than answers, in AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance, and tomorrow, at the Lyceum, Chapter 20 picks up tutoring and the old fear that a new tool will think for us.

docs.title: Part Seven: What Prediction Cannot Decide
Values Beyond Prediction
docs.text:
Values beyond prediction is the principle that a prediction can tell us what is likely to happen if we act, but not what we ought to want; deciding what matters is a question of values, and no model can answer it for us. Chapter 17 showed that "Know thyself" was carved on the porch, free, before anyone reached the Pythia's paid answer: know who you are and what you care about before you ask what will happen. Philosophers since the 18th-century Scottish thinker David Hume have pointed out that no amount of facts about what is adds up to a conclusion about what ought to be. A model can predict that a child will score higher on next year's test if she drops music for extra math; whether that trade is worth it is a question about what a good education is for. Recommendation systems predict what we will click, not what we would choose on reflection. The temple's order is still the right one: the free advice first, then the paid answer.

The Porch Before the Tripod

Think of every AI question as a visit to Delphi with two stops. At the tripod, we ask what will happen. At the porch, which comes first, we have to answer for ourselves what we want to happen, and no machine can stand there for us.

docs.title: Climate Models
docs.text:
A climate model is a computer simulation of the Earth's climate system, the atmosphere, oceans, ice, and land, built from the laws of physics and used to project how the climate will change over decades under different assumptions about future emissions of greenhouse gases. Climate models are cousins of weather models, but they answer a different question. A weather forecast predicts the state of the atmosphere on a particular day, and its horizon is about two weeks. A climate model does not try to say whether it will rain at Delphi on November 22, 2060; it projects the long-run average, which is predictable for the same reason that we can be sure the coming July will be hotter than January without knowing the weather on any day of it.

Two terms keep climate forecasts honest. A projection is a forecast that depends on a stated condition: "if emissions follow this path, global warming will be about this much by 2100." A scenario is the stated path. Climate scientists publish several scenarios, from rapid cuts to continued growth in emissions, because the biggest uncertainty about the climate of 2100 is not the physics but what people will choose to do. That makes climate projections the opposite of a self-fulfilling prophecy: they are made so that the worst ones will not come true.

Worked example: testing old climate models. Let's apply Part Five's test of a track record. A prediction earns trust when it was recorded before the outcome and later checked. Climate models have been making projections since the 1970s, so we can now check the old ones against the warming that followed. A 2020 study did exactly that for a set of models published between 1970 and 2007, and found that most of them had projected the warming that actually occurred, once differences between the emissions they assumed and the real emissions were taken into account. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the United Nations body that assesses climate science, reported that by the decade 2011–2020 the Earth's surface had warmed by about 1.1 °C since the late 19th century. In the 2015 Paris Agreement, nearly every country agreed to aim to hold warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Scientists describe the Mediterranean as a climate-change hotspot, warming faster than the global average, and the dry hills we have driven through this week are part of that story.

"Nothing in excess," the second saying on the temple, is a fair summary of what climate models ask of us: a sense of limits. The models can tell us roughly what each path is likely to bring. They cannot tell us which path to take, which returns us to the porch.

docs.title: Acting on Foresight
docs.text:
Acting on foresight is making a decision now, at a known cost, because of a prediction about the future, before the predicted outcome is certain. The hardest part of foresight is not seeing what may come but acting on it. Chapter 15 gave us the classic case: in 483 BCE, when the silver mines at Laurion struck a rich vein, Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to build 200 warships instead of sharing out the money, and three years later those ships won at Salamis. The citizens gave up ten drachmas each, a sure cost, against an uncertain threat. Had Persia never come, the ships would have looked like a waste.

Worked example: the umbrella rule. Let's make the logic exact with a decision we face every morning. Suppose carrying an umbrella costs us a little bother, which we will call 1 unit, and getting soaked on a day out costs us much more, say 4 units. If the chance of rain is \( p \), then not carrying the umbrella costs us \( 4p \) on average, and carrying it costs 1 every time. Carrying it is worth it when \( 4p > 1 \), that is, when \( p > 1 \div 4 = 0.25 \), or 25 percent. So with a 30 percent chance of rain at Delphi, we carry the umbrella; with 20 percent in Athens tomorrow, we leave it. The general rule is to act when the probability is greater than the cost of acting divided by the loss it prevents. The rule explains why sensible people act on predictions that will "probably not" come true: when the loss is large and the precaution cheap, a small probability is enough. It is the reasoning behind flood barriers, vaccines, insurance, and Themistocles' ships, and it is why a calibrated forecast is so valuable, because the rule only works if the probability can be trusted.

Divide the Cost by the Loss

Here's a shortcut for any precaution: divide what it costs by what it would save, and act if the forecast's chance is higher than that fraction. A cheap precaution against a big loss is worth taking at quite low odds. If you cannot put numbers on either one, at least ask which is bigger.

docs.title: Long-Term Consequences
docs.text: Long-term consequences are the effects of a decision that arrive years, generations, or centuries after it is made, often long after the people who made it are gone. They are hard to weigh because they fall beyond every prediction horizon, and because the people who will bear them cannot vote today. Our route is full of decisions made for the long term. After the First Sacred War, Chapter 17 told, the plain below Delphi was dedicated to Apollo and left unfarmed, a rule meant to bind every later generation. The Ottoman vakıf endowments of Chapter 5 were written to run forever, and some ran for four hundred years. The carbon dioxide we emit on this trip will go on warming the planet for centuries. "Nothing in excess" is, among other things, advice about the long term: the excess that seems harmless this year is the one our grandchildren inherit. For education, the long term is the whole point, since a school's choices about AI today shape what its five-year-olds can do when they are thirty.

docs.title: Part Eight: Who Asked, and Where the Parallel Breaks
Consent in Mass Prediction
docs.text:
Consent in mass prediction is the question of whether the people a predictive system makes predictions about have agreed to it, or even know about it. At Delphi, every prediction was asked for. A consultant climbed the mountain, paid the fee, and put a question; no one received an oracle about themselves without asking. Today the arrangement is reversed. Predictions about us are made constantly, by systems we never consulted, from data we may not know we gave.

Worked example: the predictions made about us today. Let's count the predictions that were probably made about us on this one Sunday, without our asking.

  • The bank card we used for lunch in Arachova was checked by a fraud model that predicted whether the purchase was really ours.
  • The phone's keyboard predicted our next word in every message home.
  • The map app predicted the drive time back to Athens from the movements of thousands of other phones.
  • The streaming service in the hotel will predict what we want to watch tonight.
  • The airline may already be predicting, from our booking and browsing, which seat upgrade we might pay for on the flight home.
  • Advertising systems predicted, from our searches about Delphi, which hotels and tours to show us next.

Most of these are helpful, and the fraud check protects us. We agreed to many of them, technically, by accepting terms we did not read. But we asked for none of them, and we can see the workings of none. When predictions decide matters that are more serious, a loan, a job interview, a child's school placement, the question of consent becomes urgent. European data-protection law gives people some rights not to be subject to important decisions made solely by automated systems, and to an explanation of them, and other places are debating similar rules. Students cannot really consent for themselves at all, which is why their data needs special protection; AI-Native Schools sets out the laws and the governance practices in Student Privacy and Data Governance. The question to carry home is simple: who asked for this prediction, and who gets to see it?

docs.title: Limits of the Oracle Parallel
docs.text:
The limits of the oracle parallel are the ways in which Delphi is not like a modern predictive model, and where reading one as a lesson about the other misleads. The parallel has carried this chapter, so it is fair to end by saying where it breaks.

The Oracle of Delphi A modern predictive model What it was A religious institution, a living faith for its users A tool, built from data and arithmetic Who asked Only those who chose to come Often no one; predictions are made about us without asking How many answers A few per consultation day, nine months a year Millions a day Its typical answer Mostly commands and approvals, by Fontenrose's count Mostly probabilities and generated text Can it be tested? Barely; famous answers were written down afterward Yes, at scale, if someone records and scores its predictions Who stood behind it People, the Pythia and the priests, with their own judgment and interests Companies and institutions; the model itself has no aims of its own, as far as we know How it could be checked By the Amphictyonic League, and by its consultants' choice to stop coming By audits, regulators, published evaluations, and the law

Three of these differences matter most. First, respect: for the people who climbed to Delphi, consulting Apollo was an act of piety, as Chapter 17 insisted, and reducing it to "an early algorithm" misses what it meant to them. Second, testability: we can do something with models that no one ever did with the oracle, which is to keep score, so the lessons of Part Five are not only possible but expected. Third, scale and consent: the oracle answered the few who asked; models predict the many who did not. In that respect, the modern situation is harder than the ancient one, and the old wisdom, test the answer, own the decision, know yourself, and keep a measure, is needed more, not less.

docs.title: Delphi Reflection Questions
docs.text:
Delphi reflection questions are a short set of questions, in our own words, about how the oracle's lessons apply to the predictions in our own lives. Chapter 2 set up the travel journal for exactly this kind of writing. Each question takes a sentence or two, and the drive back to Athens is long enough for all of them.

  1. What did I ask a machine this week, and did I treat its answer as a verdict or as the start of an inquiry?
  2. Where did I read an answer the way Croesus did, hearing the reading I already wanted?
  3. Which prediction about me, made without my asking, would I most like to see, and who could show it to me?
  4. When did I last act on foresight, paying a small cost now against a larger loss later, and when did I fail to?
  5. What source do I trust most for news about the future, and what is its track record of predictions written down beforehand?
  6. Know thyself: what do I want my own learning, or my grandchildren's, to be for, before any model tells me what is likely?
  7. For Dan, the evangelist's question: if AI can bring something like a personal tutor to every child, as Chapter 20 will discuss, what would it take for families to trust it, and which of tonight's tests, calibration, track record, consent, a human in the loop, would it have to pass first?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Machine learning finds patterns in examples instead of following written rules; a predictive model turns present facts into a probability about an unknown outcome, assuming the future resembles the past.
  • A model is only as good as its training data. Data bias, from sampling, history, or measurement, makes predictions worse or unfair for the people the data left out. Loan and hiring algorithms can learn old discrimination through proxies even when protected traits are removed.
  • Weather forecasting runs ensembles of physics-based models and states its prediction uncertainty as a probability; an honest source shows its range.
  • A large language model writes by next-word prediction, choosing each word from probabilities shaped by temperature. Likely is not the same as true, and whether these models understand is an open debate.
  • The oracle as a data hub heard from the whole Greek world, but mostly from those who could afford the trip. Interpreting ambiguous answers, as the Assembly did with the wooden wall, keeps a human in the loop who owns the decision. Confirmation bias made Croesus hear what he wanted.
  • A self-fulfilling prophecy comes true because it was made, as Oedipus' did. Student risk prediction and predictive policing can feed their own predictions through feedback loops.
  • Ask who funds the model, as Croesus' gold and the Alcmaeonids' bribe show. Model calibration measures whether a source's percentages come true, and the Brier score rewards calibrated forecasts. Track record and trust depend on predictions recorded before the outcome, and testability of predictions needs a clear, dated, recorded claim.
  • Every forecaster has a prediction horizon, as Apollo had his winter. AI capability forecasting, such as METR's task horizon, and AI doubling curves are measured trends with wide uncertainty, not promises.
  • Chaerephon's question shows the answer as the start of an inquiry, and AI as a thinking partner applies Socrates' habit to machines.
  • "Know thyself" points to values beyond prediction. Climate models project long-run change under scenarios, and their early projections have held up. Acting on foresight means paying a known cost against an uncertain loss, as Themistocles did; long-term consequences fall beyond every horizon.
  • Consent in mass prediction is the modern reversal of Delphi: we are predicted without asking. The limits of the oracle parallel are respect for a living faith, the new power to keep score, and the scale of prediction today. Delphi reflection questions carry the lessons into our own decisions.

From the Tripod to the Algorithm

You can now explain how a machine learns from examples and where its data can mislead it, set a language model's temperature and say what it changes, and score a forecaster, yourself included, for calibration. You can also trace a prediction that feeds itself, rewrite a hedge so that it can lose, and put the oracle's old questions to any AI you meet. Next stop: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today, where an ancient bronze machine that predicted the sky waits in the National Archaeological Museum.

docs.title: The Last Day in Athens
docs.text:
Day 13, Monday, November 23, is the last day of the trip, and a day on our own. Tomorrow we fly home. Today belongs to three things that do not fit on a cruise program: a great museum, a philosopher's school, and the living city around them. In the morning we can stand among the columns of the Temple of Olympian Zeus, which took about 650 years to finish, and walk through the National Garden to the ground where Aristotle taught. In the afternoon, in the National Archaeological Museum, we can look at a corroded lump of bronze from a shipwreck that turned out to be the oldest known geared calculating machine: the Antikythera mechanism 🔊 Pronounce an-tee-kih-THEER-uh, the ancient prediction machine that Chapter 19 left waiting for us. In the evening we can walk down into Plaka for Greek coffee, fresh fish, and perhaps a night of rebetiko, the music the refugees of 1922 carried to Athens.

This is the guide for the day as we planned it. In practice we saw the museum earlier. On Day 11, after we left the ship, we walked through the National Garden in the late morning, past the Parliament on Syntagma Square, and up Panepistimiou Street to the neoclassical "trilogy" of the Academy, the University, and the National Library, and then spent from about 1:45 to 2:15 PM in the National Archaeological Museum. Half an hour is not enough for a museum this size, so the plan below gives it a whole afternoon. The chapter also asks the questions a last day raises. Who gets a good tutor? What do our tools do to our memories? And what is life like now for the people of this city, who in one lifetime have lived through a dictatorship, a debt crisis, and the arrival of hundreds of thousands of refugees?

A Machine, a Tutor, and a City That Talks Back

Today we meet a box of bronze gears that could tell its owner the month of the next eclipse, more than a thousand years before anyone built its equal. We also meet the most famous tutor in history, hired by a king for his thirteen-year-old son, and ask whether every child might now have one. Then the city itself takes over, with its coffee, its fish, its music, and the writing on its walls. Look closer.

The chapter has five parts. Part One visits the National Archaeological Museum and its bronze prediction machine. Part Two walks from Hadrian's Temple of Olympian Zeus to the Lyceum, where Aristotle taught. Part Three reads the city today: the Polytechnic uprising, the debt crisis, daily and family life, faith, migration, and graffiti. Part Four spends the evening in Plaka with coffee, fish, and music. Part Five closes the trip where it began, with Greece and Turkey. After the Practical Notes, the Learning for All section tells two Athenian stories: Aristotle tutoring Alexander, and Plato's warning that writing would weaken memory.

docs.title: The National Archaeological Museum
docs.text:
The National Archaeological Museum is Greece's largest archaeological museum, on Patission Street about 2 km north of the Acropolis, and the home of the most important finds from sites all over the country, from the Stone Age to the end of antiquity. Its neoclassical building went up between 1866 and 1889. The Acropolis Museum (Chapter 15) holds what was found on one rock, and the Delphi museum (Chapter 18) what was found in one sanctuary; this museum gathers the whole country, which makes it the best place to review the trip in a single afternoon.

Worked example: a route through the museum that reviews the trip. Let's walk the galleries in the order they are laid out and stop at objects that close threads from earlier chapters. The central hall just past the entrance holds the Mycenaean collection, with the gold death mask that Heinrich Schliemann, whom Chapter 8 met at Troy, found at Mycenae in 1876 and called the mask of Agamemnon. It was made about three centuries before the dates usually given for a Trojan War, so the name belongs to the myth, not the history. In the early Greek galleries we can look for the Dipylon jug that Chapter 2 promised, with one of the oldest known Greek alphabetic inscriptions, scratched around 740 BCE, offering the jug as a prize to the best dancer. Among the Classical sculptures stands a small Roman copy of Phidias' Athena Parthenos, about a meter tall, the closest thing we have to the lost statue Chapter 15 described.

The museum's bronzes are much rarer than its marbles, because most ancient bronzes were melted down for their metal; the best survivors come from shipwrecks, where no one could reach them. From a wreck off Cape Artemision, in northern Euboea, came two of the museum's stars. One is a bearded god, more than 2 m tall, striding forward to hurl a weapon that is now lost, made about 460 BCE; scholars still argue whether he is Zeus with a thunderbolt or Poseidon with a trident. The other is the Jockey, a small boy clinging to a galloping horse, made about 140 BCE, whose pieces were raised from the seabed in the late 1920s and 1930s and later reassembled.

The Jockey of Artemision, bronze, about 140 BCE. Photo by Dan McCreary

The Classical grave reliefs are the museum's quietest rooms and, for many visitors, its most moving. From the late 400s BCE until a law of about 317 BCE limited lavish tombs, Athenian families set carved marble slabs, called stelai, over their graves. The figures are calm. A seated woman clasps the hand of a standing man; a servant holds out a jewelry box; a father, a mother, and a grown child stand together. The handshake joins the living and the dead, and the faces show no grief: the sorrow is in the stillness.

A Classical grave stele. Photo by Dan McCreary

Horses appear in these galleries again and again, on reliefs, in bronze, and on painted vases, because in ancient Greece a horse was the clearest sign of wealth. Athens's cavalry came from its richest families, who kept their own mounts, and only the rich could enter a horse at the games. The boy on the Artemision racehorse rode for an owner like that, and families who could afford horses liked to be remembered with them.

Marble relief of a horse and its handler. Photo by Dan McCreary

The Hellenistic galleries turn playful. A marble group from the island of Delos, made about 100 BCE, shows Aphrodite raising her sandal to swat the goat-legged god Pan, who has grabbed her wrist, while a small winged Eros pushes Pan away by one horn. It was found in the clubhouse of a guild of merchants from Berytus, modern Beirut, who did business on Delos when it was the busiest free port in the Aegean: a reminder that Hellenistic art was made for a trading world that stretched from Italy to Syria.

Aphrodite, Pan, and Eros, marble group from Delos. Photo by Dan McCreary

Check Monday's Hours the Night Before

A common last-day trap is to plan the big museum for the afternoon and find it closing at 3:30 PM, because Greek state museums keep short winter hours and Monday hours often differ from the rest of the week. Check the museum's official hours the night before. If it opens late, do the Temple of Olympian Zeus first; if it closes early, swap the morning and the afternoon.

docs.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
docs.text:
The Antikythera mechanism is the remains of a hand-cranked device of bronze gears, made in the 2nd century BCE, that modeled the cycles of the Sun and the Moon, and probably the planets, so that its owner could turn a crank and read the sky on any date, past or future. In 1900 sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete, found a Roman-era shipwreck that had sunk about 70–60 BCE. Over the next year they brought up bronze and marble statues, among them the bronze Antikythera Youth that now stands in the museum, and a lump of corroded bronze and wood that no one noticed until 1902, when the archaeologist Valerios Stais saw a gear wheel in one of its broken pieces.

What survives is 82 fragments holding at least 30 gears, from a wooden box about the size of a shoebox, with a dial on the front, two on the back, and a crank on the side. The gears were cut by hand from thin bronze sheet, and every surface carried tiny Greek inscriptions, a built-in user's manual. The historian of science Derek de Solla Price called it "an ancient Greek computer" in 1959, and X-ray scans made in 2005 let researchers count teeth and read letters hidden inside the corroded lumps. The table lists the questions its owner could ask.

Question the owner could ask Dial that answered Cycle set into the gears Where are the Sun and the Moon among the stars on this date? Front: zodiac and calendar rings The solar year and the Moon's monthly circuit What will the Moon look like that night? Front: a turning half-silver, half-black ball The month from new moon to new moon Which month of the calendar is it, and are the Olympic Games this year? Back, upper: a spiral of 235 months and a games dial 19 years = 235 lunar months; the four-year games cycle Could there be an eclipse that month, and at about what hour? Back, lower: a spiral of 223 months The Saros, 223 lunar months, about 18 years

Who built it, and why the skill vanished for so long, is a story of its own, told in the appendix Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism; the evidence points to a workshop, quite possibly on Rhodes, using the lunar theory of the astronomer Hipparchus. The MicroSim below lets us see how tooth counts turn one turn of a crank into different speeds for the Sun, the Moon, and a planet. Its gear ratios are simplified for teaching and do not reconstruct the real mechanism.

Run the Antikythera Gears MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: Ancient Prediction Machines
docs.text:
Ancient prediction machines are devices built before the modern era that worked out the future from a model fixed into their structure, rather than from a god's answer or a new observation. The Antikythera mechanism is the most complex survivor, but the idea behind it was older and simpler. For centuries Babylonian astronomers had kept nightly records of the sky, and from them they had found that eclipses and the positions of the Moon and planets repeat in regular cycles, such as the 223-month Saros. Once a cycle is known, prediction becomes counting, and counting can be written on clay, carved in stone, or cut into gear teeth. Greek cities also set up the parapegma, a stone calendar with a hole for each day into which a peg was moved, listing the yearly risings and settings of the stars and the weather that was expected to come with them.

Set beside the oracle of Chapter 17, the mechanism changes three things. Its answer was the same for everyone who turned the crank, rich or poor, king or farmer. Its answer was fixed before the event, so it could be checked: an eclipse happens or it does not. And its answer came from a model that a person could inspect, gear by gear, rather than from the Pythia's trance and the priests' verses. Set beside the models of Chapter 19, it lacks one thing. Its rules were set once by its maker from centuries of records, and they never changed; a wrong ratio stayed wrong for as long as the gears turned. A machine-learning model, by contrast, adjusts its own rules from examples. One ancient device, then, sits between the tripod and the algorithm.

Gears for What Repeats

Notice which half of the stone peg calendar worked. Star risings repeat exactly every year, so a fixed model could predict them for centuries; the weather does not, so the forecasts tied to the stars were far less reliable. Before trusting any prediction machine, ancient or modern, ask whether the thing it predicts actually repeats.

The sorter below asks us to tell the three ways of predicting apart by how each answer is produced, not by how old or impressive the source looks.
