        height="1060px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare the Acropolis of about 406 BCE with the rock a visitor climbs today, and for each of five monuments name what has been lost, rebuilt, replaced, or removed on purpose.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult travelers on the trip (Mediterranean Travels).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The Acropolis and the Parthenon, from Chapter 15.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Hover over both panels, click each one, and read its infobox. Follow one monument, such as the Erechtheion, across both panels.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Pick one change on the rock and decide which kind it was: lost, rebuilt, replaced, or removed on purpose. Say how you know.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Switch to Quiz mode and answer all ten questions.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner answers at least 9 of the 10 quiz questions correctly on the first try and can say, for the Parthenon, what is original, what is new marble, and what is gone.

docs.text: Try The Parthenon's Five Lives, Agreed Fact or Position?, Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian?, and Xerxes' Road to Salamis.

  2. Acropolis of Athens — Wikipedia.
  3. Parthenon — Wikipedia.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare the Acropolis of about 406 BCE with the rock a visitor climbs today, and for each of five monuments (the path and gateway, the temple of Athena Nike, the Parthenon, the Erechtheion, and the open-air statue) name what has been lost, rebuilt, replaced, or removed on purpose.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Nearly everyone on the trip stands on the rock on Day 10, and orientation is practical: the gateway, the small temple on its bastion, the Parthenon, and the Erechtheion are met in that order, and the chapter ties each step to a different century. One aerial view drawn twice lets a reader hold the whole building program in mind and see the later layers (an explosion in 1687, a clearing in the 1830s, restoration since 1975) as changes to the same rock. The chapter's reading-a-ruin questions from Chapter 4 ("Added? Taken away? Restored, and what did they choose to show?") are the questions the picture asks.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Two tall panels side by side, one zone per panel. The idea entry in Poster Ideas also asks for "a matching set of call-outs inside each panel": the gateway, the small temple, the Parthenon, the Erechtheion, and the path up. I did not build ten small zones, one per monument per panel, for three reasons.

  1. An image tool will not place monuments reliably enough for ten small rectangles, and the zones would be re-measured against the picture anyway.
  2. Small zones overlap a great deal in an aerial view. The Parthenon alone crosses several of the others.
  3. The comparison the poster exists for is between the two panels. Two big zones, with the five monuments in the same order inside each zone's facts, keep that comparison on the screen.

To keep the call-outs available later, the prompt fixes the position of each of the five monuments, as a percentage of the panel, and asks for the same position in both panels (see image-prompt.md). If the author wants numbered markers, a second poster on the call-out engine, with one picture and five markers, can reuse the same image without a new prompt.

The camera is also a change from the idea entry. The entry says "from the northwest". The prompt asks for a view from the west, a little north of west, because that is the direction a visitor climbs from, so the gateway, the small temple on the bastion to its right, and the Parthenon ahead and to the right all appear in the order the chapter describes.

Left panel Right panel 1. Late 5th Century BCE: the rock rebuilt, with its parts painted and bronze 2. Today: a restored ruin with visitors, a gap in the Parthenon, and the later layers cleared

docs.title: What Each Zone Says
docs.text:
Both zones present the five monuments in the same order, so a reader can read one monument across both zones.

Monument Then, about 406 BCE Today Chapter 15 sections Path and gateway The west slope, the Panathenaic procession, the Propylaea built 437 to 432 BCE and left unfinished Odeon of Herodes Atticus, Beulé Gate, ceiling beams reset, the tower removed in 1874 The Acropolis; The Propylaea Temple of Athena Nike Small Ionic temple, 427 to 424 BCE, wingless Victory Dismantled in 1686, rebuilt in the 1830s, 1930s, and early 2000s The Temple of Athena Nike The Parthenon Complete, painted sculpture, gold-and-ivory Athena No roof, middle of both sides gone in 1687, new marble among the old The Parthenon; The Parthenon Sculptures; The Parthenon as Church and Mosque The Erechtheion New, about 421 to 406 BCE, gathering the old cults Caryatids replaced by copies in 1979 The Erechtheion; The Caryatids The open-air statue Bronze Athena Promachos An empty base; the statue is known only from descriptions Phidias

The draft facts are in data.json. Each fact is taken from those chapter sections, so the poster repeats what the book already says.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Mark the reconstruction. The left panel is a reconstruction, and its zone says so in a fact that begins "Where the picture breaks down". Color is limited to muted accents on the sculpted parts, because the chapter says only that the sculpture was painted and that faint traces remain.
  2. No ladder and no decline. The right panel is not a fallen version of the left. The chapter's point is that the bare classical rock we admire is itself a 19th-century choice, and the zone says so.
  3. Neutral on the Marbles. The Today zone says where the Caryatids and the sculpture are (Athens, London, and elsewhere) and takes no side. The argument belongs to Agreed Fact or Position?.
  4. No regret, no triumph. The Parthenon was a church and a mosque. The Today panel shows no minaret or tower, because they were cleared from 1835, and the zone's fact "what was erased" describes that choice without judging it.
  5. No brands or signs. The flag is plain stripes, the guide's paddle is blank, and nothing on the rock carries lettering.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: Ten questions are drafted in data.json, five per panel. They ask about ideas (a procession bringing a robe, a cleared rock, a restoration method), not about what is drawn on which side. The sample question in the idea entry ("Which monument stands on the bastion at the right of the entrance?") has a monument as its answer, so it does not fit a two-zone poster. It belongs on the call-out version if one is built.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
These are not in the chapters, so none of them is in data.json.

  1. Colors on the sculpture. The chapter says only that the sculpture was painted and that faint traces remain. The prompt's dusty blue and warm red are an illustrator's choice and must stay labeled as a reconstruction.
  2. Scaffolding and a crane on the Parthenon today. The chapter says restoration continues but does not describe equipment on the rock. The picture's scaffold and crane are illustrations of that, and may not match the site in November 2026. The author can drop them.
  3. The aerial geometry. The relative positions of the Erechtheion, the Parthenon, and the bastion, as drawn from the west, rest on common knowledge of the site, not on a chapter figure. Check them against a plan.
  4. Details of the statue. The chapter gives the Promachos's material (bronze) and a spear tip visible from Cape Sounion. The pose, shield, and height in the image are not sourced.
  5. The 5th-century procession. The chapter describes the Panathenaia procession but not how large it was, so the picture's size is an illustration.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Call-outs on top? If you want the five monuments clickable, a call-out version can reuse the same image, as described under Layout Decision.
  2. Camera. West-northwest (the prompt) or the idea's northwest.
  3. A third panel? The chapter's Parthenon had a church and mosque life between the two views (see The Parthenon's Five Lives). A third panel for about 1674, before the explosion, would show the mosque and minaret, but it would make three panels of 480 px.
  4. Companion sims. The lesson page should link The Parthenon's Five Lives, Agreed Fact or Position?, Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian?, and Xerxes' Road to Salamis.

  2. Re-measure the two rectangles with main.html?edit=true once the image exists.
  3. Create index.md with status: scaffold, then built. Only the author sets approved.

docs.title: Anatomy of an Ottoman Mosque

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
We plan to be in Istanbul on a Friday, and a visit to a working mosque is easier when you know the building. This cutaway follows a visitor from the courtyard and its ablution fountain, past the shoe racks, into the prayer hall, and up to the dome. It ends at the mihrab, the minbar, and the minaret that carries the call to prayer.

Each marker says what the part is for and what a respectful visitor does there, including dress, shoes, and photography. The prayer times in the chapter are its own calculation, so check the day's times on arrival.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default): hover over a numbered marker or its label to read about that part. The marker and its label light up together.

Quiz mode: press Quiz. The labels disappear and a description appears. Click the marker that matches it. A correct answer scores a point; a wrong one lets you try again. Try Again starts a new round.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the markers, then press Copy JSON and paste the positions into data.json.

docs.title: The Numbered Parts
docs.text:
1. Courtyard (avlu)
  2. Ablution fountain
  3. Entrance and shoe racks
  4. Prayer hall and visitors' area
  5. Dome and semi-domes
  6. Calligraphy and tiles
  7. Mihrab and qibla wall
  8. Minbar
  9. Minaret

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 5 teaches the vocabulary of a mosque (courtyard, ablution, minaret, mihrab, minbar, qibla) across four separate sections, and the etiquette list sits in yet another. Day 3 falls on a Friday, so everyone on the trip will need these words in the same hour. One cutaway lets a reader follow a worshipper's path from the courtyard to the qibla wall, with the practical rule for visitors attached to the part where it applies: shoes at the door, quiet in the hall, no photographs of washing or of people at prayer.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
One cutaway, call-out engine. Numbered markers with leader lines, in the order a person walks: courtyard, fountain, door and shoes, hall, dome, walls, then the qibla end of the hall (mihrab, minbar), and last the minaret outside. The numbered order follows the idea's "outer gate, fountain, shoe racks, hall, qibla wall" path. The picture is a longitudinal section with the courtyard on the left and the qibla wall on the right, which makes the qibla direction the natural end of the walk.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. A living faith, not an exhibit. The poster describes a working place of worship. Say what visitors do, not what worshippers "should" do. The cutaway shows worshippers standing in a row and nothing more intimate; no one is drawn bowing or prostrating.
  2. No decoration that looks like writing. The prompt forbids Arabic calligraphy in the picture, since the generator would make nonsense letters. The band on the wall is abstract looping curves.

1. Women's prayer area. The chapter says women cover their hair and that Friday prayer is required of men and optional for women, but it does not describe a women's gallery or rear section. The idea asked for one. It is left out of data.json; see "To verify" below.

docs.title: The Antikythera Mechanism, Opened Up
docs.text: Run the The Antikythera Mechanism, Opened Up MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Antikythera mechanism is the bronze machine we see at the National Archaeological Museum, an ancient prediction machine that could tell its owner the Moon's phase and the next eclipse. This picture opens it up: the crank, the gear train, the front dial with its zodiac and calendar rings, the back dials, and the corroded fragments that survive.

The picture is an orientation, not a reconstruction. Which dials and pointers survive, and which are reconstructed, is not settled by the chapter, so the drawing shows them complete.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default): hover over a numbered marker or its label to read about that part. The marker and its label light up together.

Quiz mode: press Quiz. The labels disappear and a description appears. Click the marker that matches it. A correct answer scores a point; a wrong one lets you try again. Try Again starts a new round.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the markers, then press Copy JSON and paste the positions into data.json.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 20 lists the dials in a table and sends readers to the Antikythera Gears MicroSim to see tooth counts at work. The MicroSim is a simplified teaching model of three outputs, and it says plainly that it omits lunar phases, eclipse prediction, and the calendar spirals. The poster fills the gap by orientation: what the whole object looked like, which dial answers which question, and what survives. It is the picture a reader needs before the sim makes sense. It also sets up the "ancient prediction machine" idea that connects the oracle chapters to the algorithm chapters.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Call-out engine, one exploded view. The picture has three groups: the front dial lifted away on the left, the open wooden case with the gear train and crank in the middle, and the two back panels stacked on the right, with a few corroded fragments on the ground at lower left. Keeping the groups apart gives each dial a clear place for a marker. The picture is schematic, not a reconstruction of the actual gear layout, and the lesson page should say so. The poster does not repeat the sim's gear arithmetic; the crank marker points to the sim.

The engine is layout: "side-panel", orientation: "landscape", showNumbers: true. Marker positions in data.json are estimates taken from the positions stated in image-prompt.md. They must be calibrated with ?edit=true once the image exists.

Every marker rests on Chapter 20 for its core claim: the crank, the dial and the cycle it answers, and the fragments. Some added detail is only in the appendix: the pin-and-slot Moon gears and the Hipparchus link (2), the Egyptian calendar and the planets in modern reconstructions (3), the five-turn arithmetic (5), the Halieia reading (6), the prime 223 and the eclipse symbols (7), and the whole exeligmos dial (8). The appendix is part of the book, but it is not a chapter. See "To Verify" below.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Say what is certain. Each marker states only what Chapter 20 or the appendix says, in the chapter's own terms. Nothing about the mechanism is drawn from outside the book.
  2. Do not call it a modern computer. The tip on marker 9 repeats the appendix's warning: it was a calculator with one job, and a wrong ratio stayed wrong.
  3. Contested origin is a labeled tip. Marker 6's tip says that where it was made is argued, and what points away from Rhodes.
  4. No ladder. The poster ties the device to the oracle and the algorithm as a point on a line of ways to predict, not as the better way.
  5. No lettering. The real dials are covered in tiny Greek text. The picture shows tick marks and dots only.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: The call-out engine's built-in quiz mode asks "Click on: " from the hint text. A written question bank is drafted here for the lesson page or a later extension. Each marker answers at least one. # Question Answer marker 1 Which dial predicts eclipses? 7 2 Which part do you turn to read the sky on a future or past date? 1 3 Where does the Moon's phase show? 4 4 Which dial tracks 235 lunar months, so the Moon calendar keeps in step with the solar year? 5 5 Where would an owner check whether the Olympic Games fall in a given year? 6 6 Where are the Sun and the Moon among the stars on a given date? 3 7 Which part did the Moon's changing speed make hardest to build? 2 8 Which small dial tells the user how many hours to add to an eclipse time? 8 9 What is left of the device that divers found in 1900? 9 10 Which marker shows the cycle Babylonian astronomers found from centuries of records? 7

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
The chapters and the sim give the 82 fragments, at least 30 gears, the 2nd century BCE date, the about 70 to 60 BCE wreck date, and the dial table, so those are in data.json. These are not in the chapters, and are not stated as facts there.

  1. Which parts are certain and which are reconstructed. The idea calls for "fragments versus reconstructed parts." Chapter 20 does not say which dials or pointers survive and which are inferred. The appendix says only that the five planets appear "in modern reconstructions." The image prompt draws the dials complete; the lesson page needs a source before it marks any of them as reconstructed.
  2. Details from the appendix, not a chapter. The exeligmos dial (marker 8), the Halieia reading (6), the pin-and-slot Moon gears (2), the Egyptian calendar (3), and the 235 = 5 × 47 and prime-223 arithmetic (5, 7) come only from the appendix. If the author wants chapter-only facts, drop or relocate them.
  3. Layout details in the image. The Metonic spiral drawn with five turns comes from the appendix (235 = 5 × 47). The Saros spiral's number of turns, the two front pointers, the case's open sides, the crank's side, and the number of gears drawn are illustrative and not in the book.
  4. "A main drive wheel." The idea lists one. Neither the chapter nor the appendix names it, so there is no marker for it.
  5. Dimensions. Chapter 20 says "about the size of a shoebox"; the appendix gives 34 × 18 × 9 cm. The picture is not to scale and states neither.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Keep the appendix-only details (markers 2, 3, 5 to 8)? The alternative is a smaller poster with six markers from Chapter 20 alone.
  2. Link the appendix? The lesson page should link Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism and the Antikythera Gears MicroSim, and note that the sim's ratios are not a reconstruction.
  3. Oracle thread. Chapter 20 sets the mechanism between the oracle and the learned model. A tenth marker could carry that link, but nothing in the picture suggests where it would sit. The lesson page can say it instead.

docs.title: Roman Bath and Turkish Hamam
docs.text: Run the Roman Bath and Turkish Hamam MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A visitor may well book a hamam in Istanbul, and the chapter reads the bath as a story that runs from Rome to the Ottomans. This poster stacks two cutaway floor plans on the same footprint: a Roman bath above, with its changing room, cold, warm, and hot rooms, and the hypocaust under the floors, and a Turkish hamam below, with its cool hall, warm room, and hot steam room. Reading down a column compares one stage of the bath in the two cultures.

The claim the chapter makes is modest. The hamam is descended from the Roman and Byzantine baths and adapted to a new culture, not copied from them. In the lower plan the cool hall runs across the first two columns, because the hamam has three main rooms and the Roman bath four. That is the first place the parallel breaks, and each zone says where it breaks again.

docs.title: The Five Columns
docs.text:
1. Changing Room: where both baths begin, and where the hamam's cool hall also serves as a place to rest.
  2. Cold Room: the Roman cold room, and the second half of the hamam's cool hall.
  3. Warm Room: the middle step of both baths.
  4. Hot Room: the Roman hot room, and the hamam's steam room with its heated central stone.
  5. Heat Source: the furnace, with the Roman hypocaust under the floors.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a column to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a column to open an infobox below the image with its details. On a tablet or phone, tap a column instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the column that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the column so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult travelers on the trip (Mediterranean Travels).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Hover over all five columns, then click each one and read its infobox. For each, find the line that says where the parallel breaks.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Walk the upper plan from left to right, then the lower one. Where does the hamam skip a step, and where does it add one?

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare the rooms of a Roman bath with the rooms of a Turkish hamam, and for each of five stages state what the two share, where the match breaks, and why the hamam is best described as adapted from the Roman and Byzantine baths, not copied from them.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 6 covers the bath in two short sections, Roman Bath Culture and The Turkish Bath, and the reader has to hold the Roman sequence in mind while reading the Turkish one. A visitor may well book a hamam on Day 4, so this is also a practical poster: it shows what the rooms are, what is worn, and what happens on the heated stone. Two plans on the same footprint, one above the other, let the eye run down a column and see the pair at once. The modest claim the chapter makes, "descended from the Roman and Byzantine baths but adapted", is the thread of every zone.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
The first sketch in Poster Ideas allowed "two cutaway panels stacked or side by side". This spec uses two stacked floor plans (Roman above, hamam below), each a wide strip with the roof removed, with the rooms in the order a bather walks through them, left to right. Stacked strips make the five columns line up, so a zone is one column through both plans and one hover compares the pair. This is the same idea as the diptych tiles in Oracle and Algorithm, turned on its side. Image generators keep two wide strips aligned far better than two squarish plans.

Column Roman bath Hamam Zone id 1 Changing room, with a garden court beside it Cool domed hall, first half changing 2 Cold room (frigidarium) Cool domed hall, second half cold 3 Warm room (tepidarium) Warm room warm 4 Hot room (caldarium) Hot steam room with the göbek taşı hot 5 Furnace, with the hypocaust shown under the floors Furnace area (generic) heat

The hamam has three main rooms in the chapter and the Roman bath has four, so in the lower plan the cool hall is drawn as one wide room across columns 1 and 2, with no wall between them. That is deliberate: it shows the first place where the parallel breaks. The poster says so in the changing and cold zones.

docs.title: Sources and Where Each Zone Comes From
docs.text:
All facts in data.json are from these sections of the book.

Zone Chapter sections Changing Room 6: Roman Bath Culture, The Turkish Bath (and its Glaux tip, "A Hamam Before Boarding"). Cold Room 6: Roman Bath Culture, The Turkish Bath. 4 for the Hippodrome stop on Day 2. Warm Room 6: both sections. 5: The Külliye Mosque Complex, the bath's fee. 12: Ottoman Rhodes, the 16th-century bath. Hot Room 6: The Turkish Bath (göbek taşı, kese, foam). Roman Bath Culture (caldarium, hypocaust). Heat Source 6: Roman Bath Culture, The Turkish Bath. 5: The Külliye Mosque Complex, the complex's public bath (Day 3).

Companion sims that exist: What Did the Külliye Do? (its "public bath" card makes the point that a bath was a source of income), and Read the Ruin - Which Layer? for the ruins we walk at Ephesus.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Keep the continuity claim modest. Say "descended from" and "adapted to", as the chapter does. Never "the hamam is a Roman bath" and never "a direct copy". No zone says which people invented which room.
  2. Say where each pair breaks. Every zone has a "Where the parallel breaks" fact or a fact that makes the break plain: three rooms against four, a shared pool against flowing water, a hypocaust against a heated stone.
  3. Everyone is covered. Bathers in both plans wear a wrap, a towel, or a short tunic. No nudity. Drawn from above they are small, simplified, and dignified.
  4. Bathing is ordinary and respectful. The hamam is a living practice and a place visitors can go. Etiquette appears as practical facts only (the cloth, the locker, the booking), with no gender jokes and no orientalizing.
  5. No ladder. The Roman plan is not the "early version" of the hamam. They are two designs for related habits.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: Nine questions are drafted in data.json, covering all five stages. They ask about ideas and features (which room matches the caldarium, which stage had the hypocaust, why the hamam is "adapted") and not about what is drawn. Two of them (the cold room, the "adapted" idea) depend on understanding where the parallel breaks, not on matching names.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
The chapter does not give these, so none of them are in data.json.

  1. How a hamam is heated. The chapter names the heated göbek taşı but does not describe a furnace, flues, or an underfloor system for a hamam. The image shows a generic furnace area in column 5, which may overstate a link to the Roman system. Check a source on Ottoman hamam heating before approval, or redraw column 5 with only a service room.
  2. Turkish room names. The usual Turkish names for the three rooms (the cool hall, the warm room, the hot room) are not in the chapter. Add them only after checking a source.
  3. A cold plunge pool in the Roman cold room. The chapter only says that Islamic ideas of cleanliness prefer flowing water to "sitting in a shared pool". The prompt draws a pool in the Roman cold room to match that line. Confirm that a pool in the frigidarium is a fair picture.
  4. What the warm room was for. In both baths, the chapter names the warm room but gives it no job of its own, and it does not say in which room the scrubbing and soaping took place. The prompt puts that scene in the hot room, around the stone. Check where it happened.
  5. The Roman changing room's Latin name (apodyterium) and whether the garden court beside it matches the chapter's "exercise courts, gardens".
  6. Dates and sizes for the Baths of Zeuxippus beyond what the chapter gives (beside the Hippodrome, decorated by Constantine, burned in 532), and which hamams by Sinan are open. The poster gives none of them.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Two zones per column? One zone per column compares the pair on one hover. If you want the Roman and the hamam halves clickable on their own, split each column at the gap between the plans (ten zones). The facts would need to be split too, and chip labels like "Roman: Hot Room" fit in 300 px.
  2. How much of the Roman bath? The chapter mentions exercise courts, gardens, libraries, and snack sellers. The prompt shows a garden court and a snack stall in column 1 only, to keep the footprints equal. Add a library and a courtyard if you want the Roman plan to look larger than the hamam's.
  3. Which hamam? The poster draws a generic hamam. The chapter says two historic hamams by Sinan are open to visitors. If you visited one, a plan of that bath would be more personal, but then the poster is about one building.
  4. Canvas. If your image tool can produce 1792 x 1024, the columns would be about 350 px wide and the figures larger. If you switch, tell me and I will recompute the zones and the prompt.

docs.title: The Colossus, Popular Picture and Likely Truth
docs.text:
title: The Colossus: Popular Picture and Likely Truth description: Hover over and click six scenes, the popular picture of the Colossus of Rhodes on the left and what the evidence supports on the right, for its pose, its place, and its end, then test yourself in Quiz mode. status: built image: /posters/colossus-myth-and-evidence/colossus-myth-and-evidence-thumb.jpg og:image: /posters/colossus-myth-and-evidence/colossus-myth-and-evidence-thumb.jpg twitter:image: /posters/colossus-myth-and-evidence/colossus-myth-and-evidence-thumb.jpg social: cards: false

Run the The Colossus: Popular Picture and Likely Truth MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Everyone knows the Colossus of Rhodes as a giant with a foot on each side of the harbor. This poster puts that popular picture on the left and what the evidence supports on the right, for three parts of the story: the pose, the place, and the end. It applies the book's myth versus history test from Chapter 4: find the earliest source, and ask how long after the event it was written.

The right-hand figure is an artist's guess, drawn pale to say so. The evidence gives the god, the sculptor, the height, and the dates, but not the pose.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a zone to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a zone to open an infobox below the image with its details. On a tablet or phone, tap a zone instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the zone that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the zone so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Zones
docs.text:
1. Popular: The Figure: The famous engravings show a giant with a foot on each side of the harbor entrance, and the book's evidence does not support it.
  2. Likely: The Figure: The evidence gives the god, the sculptor, the height, and the dates, but not the pose.
  3. Popular: The Site: The popular story places the statue's feet at the entrance to Mandraki, the old harbor.
  4. Likely: The Site: Scholars think it more likely stood on land, near the harbor or in a sanctuary of Helios higher in the city.
  5. Popular: The End: A Byzantine chronicle says the bronze was sold and carried away on hundreds of camels.
  6. Likely: The End: An earthquake brought it down after about 54 years, and a Roman writer saw the fallen pieces.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will separate what most people imagine about the Colossus of Rhodes from what the book's evidence supports, and apply the myth versus history test from Chapter 4 (find the earliest source and ask how long after the event it was written) to three parts of the story: the pose, the place, and the end.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 4 teaches a habit for the whole trip: ask when a story first appeared, and who wrote it. The Colossus is the cleanest case on the route. Nearly everyone knows the picture of a giant straddling a harbor, and the book says it almost certainly is not true. The poster puts the picture and the evidence side by side so the habit can be seen working, and it is honest about the rest: the evidence also leaves things open (the pose, the exact site), and the poster says where. It is the poster for the myth versus history concept (Chapter 4, Myth Versus History).

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Poster Ideas asked for two panels, "What most people imagine" and "What the evidence supports". This spec keeps the two panels (the left column and the right column of the image) and divides each into three tiles, one under the other, so the same question is asked of both versions at the same scale. A zone is one tile, as in the Oracle and Algorithm poster, so six zones.

Row The question Left tile: popular picture Right tile: likely truth Idea's topics covered 1 The figure A giant astride the harbor entrance, ships beneath A standing Helios, about 33 m, drawn as a pale reconstruction pose, height, how built 2 The site The harbor mouth, one foot on each side The same harbor from above; the statue on land, in one of two possible places location 3 The end The bronze carried off on camels The fallen pieces, and a visitor at the thumb how it fell, what became of the bronze

Tiles are 744 x 320 px, wide strips, which suit a harbor and a caravan better than tall panels would. Row 2 is drawn from above, so the "too wide" argument is a picture, not only a sentence.

docs.title: What Each Zone Says
docs.text:
Zone The point Chapter sections Popular: The Figure The straddle is the picture people carry. Chapter 12 gives two reasons against it, and Chapter 1 says "almost certainly". Includes Chapter 4's test. 12: The Colossus of Rhodes. 1: Hellenistic Period. 4: Myth Versus History. Likely: The Figure Helios, about 33 m, by Chares of Lindos over about twelve years, paid for by the sold siege machines. The pose is not described, so the figure is a guess. 12: Helios, The Colossus of Rhodes. Popular: The Site The popular story puts the feet at the Mandraki entrance. It was far too wide. Rhodes had several harbors. 12: The Colossus of Rhodes, Rhodes. Likely: The Site More likely on land, near the harbor or in a sanctuary of Helios. No one knows. 12: The Colossus of Rhodes, Helios, Rhodes. Popular: The End The camel story, from a Byzantine chronicle written centuries later. 12: The Colossus of Rhodes. 4: Myth Versus History. Likely: The End An earthquake about 226 BCE, after about 54 years. Pliny saw the pieces. Nothing survives. 12, 1, 10 (Seven Wonders table).

The draft facts are in data.json. Each fact is taken from those chapter sections.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Say clearly what is not known. Every "likely" tile ends with a "where the evidence stops" fact. The right-hand figure is a reconstruction, drawn pale and soft-edged on purpose, so that the "truth" column does not look more certain than it is.
  2. Do not make the myth a joke. The popular picture has a real history as an image, and Chapter 4 says myths tell us what later people believed or wanted. The popular tiles are drawn with the same care as the others.
  3. No claim the chapters do not make. The idea entry says "no source describes the straddling pose". The chapters do not say that, so the data gives the reasons the chapters do give (the height and the width of the entrance). See below.
  4. Same scale and same camera in each row, so differences come from the subject, not from the artist.
  5. No faith claims. Helios is treated as the sun god of a Greek city, described as the book does. No modern religious symbols.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: Nine questions are drafted in data.json, covering all six tiles, with two tiles asked about twice. They ask about ideas (what rules the straddle out, why a late chronicle is weak, why a myth is not worthless) and not about what is drawn. One asks how the statue was paid for, which leads into the book's story of the siege.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
The chapters do not give these, so none is in data.json.

  1. "No source describes the straddling pose." This is the idea entry's claim. Chapter 12 gives different reasons: the height and the width of the harbor entrance. Check whether any ancient text describes the pose or the appearance of the statue before saying so.
  2. The famous engravings. The chapter refers to "the famous engravings" but does not say who made them or when. A date would make the Chapter 4 test sharper (how long after the event?). Do not add one without a source.
  3. How it was built. The chapters give the maker (Chares of Lindos), about twelve years, a finish of about 280 BCE, and how it was paid for. They give no method, no scaffolding, no base, and no foundation. The idea entry's scaffolding and stone base are not drawn in the prompt, except a plain low platform under the right-hand figure.
  4. How it fell. The chapters give an earthquake about 226 BCE and an interval of about 54 years. Where the statue broke is not given, and the prompt does not say.
  5. Pliny and the chronicle. The chapters do not date Pliny's visit or name the Byzantine chronicle or its author. They say only "hundreds of camels" and "written centuries later". The data does not add a number.
  6. The pose and crown. The right-hand figure is standing, with rays around the head borrowed from Helios on Rhodian coins (the chapter's evidence for coins, not for the statue). Check how scholars reconstruct the figure before approval.
  7. Candidate sites. The chapters name only "near the harbor" and "a sanctuary of Helios higher in the city". No other names or locations are in the data.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Two zones or six? The poster could have just two zones, the left panel and the right panel. Six tiles answer the idea's list of topics one by one. Two would be simpler to build and weaker for the quiz.
  2. The ghost figure. The prompt draws the right-hand statue as a pale, translucent bronze with soft edges, to mark it as a guess. Image models do not always honor this. If it comes out solid, we can accept it and let the text carry the caveat.
  3. Row 2 diagram. A bird's-eye harbor with footprints and a translucent band is the riskiest tile for a text-to-image model. If it fails, the fallback is a plain aerial harbor in both tiles with the figure's footprint in a different place.
  4. Companion sims. The lesson page should link Source, Myth, or Contested?, Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence?, and Who Built What We See in the Old Town?.
  5. Canvas. If your image tool can produce 1792 x 1024, the tiles would be wider (about 872 px). If you switch, tell me and I will recompute the zones and the prompt.

docs.title: The Three Classical Orders
docs.text: Run the Three Classical Orders MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Greek architects worked in three related systems of design, called the classical orders: the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. Each order fixes the shape of a column's base, shaft, and capital, the parts of the beam it carries, and its proportions. This infographic shows one column of each order side by side, drawn to the same height, so their differences are easy to compare. Each column also carries a short piece of its own entablature.

The capital is the quickest clue. A plain cushion means Doric, a pair of spiral scrolls means Ionic, and a bell of acanthus leaves means Corinthian. The base, the flutes, and the proportions then confirm the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a column to see a short tooltip with its name and key feature.
  2. Click a column to open an infobox below the image with its base, shaft, capital, frieze, proportions, origins, and where we see it on our route. On a tablet or phone, tap a column instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the column that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the column so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each column's zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Three Columns
docs.text:
1. Doric: no base, about 20 sharp-edged flutes, a cushion capital under a square slab, and a frieze of triglyphs and metopes. Sturdy, about 4 to 6 diameters tall. The Parthenon.
  2. Ionic: a molded base, about 24 flutes separated by flat strips, and a capital with two spiral volutes. Slender, about 8 to 9 diameters tall. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus and the Erechtheion.
  3. Corinthian: an Ionic-like base and shaft with a tall bell-shaped capital wrapped in acanthus leaves. The most slender, about 9 to 10 diameters tall. Roman Ephesus and the Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Delphi is a steep hillside, and the sanctuary is scattered across it, so a plan helps. This view follows the climb: the Castalian Spring, the Sacred Way, the treasuries, the Athenian Treasury, the Polygonal Wall, the Temple of Apollo, the theater, and the stadium, with the round tholos at the Athena Pronaia sanctuary below the road.

Each marker says what a petitioner or an athlete did there and what is left to see. The picture is stylized: the real distances and heights are not drawn to scale.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will name nine places on the Delphi hillside in the order a visitor climbs them, say what a petitioner or an athlete did at each, and say what survives to see today.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 18 is a walk, and Chapter 17 is the explanation of what the walk was for. A reader on Day 12 will have about an hour on a steep slope with ruins scattered up it, and a list of names does not tell them which stone is which or what is above what. One elevation shows the whole climb at once, with the Sacred Way as a visible zigzag, and each marker names what was done there and what is left.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
One hillside elevation, call-out engine. Numbered markers with leader lines, in the order of the chapter's walk: Castalian Spring, Sacred Way, treasuries, Athenian Treasury, polygonal wall, the temple terrace, theater, stadium, then down to Athena Pronaia and its Tholos. The picture is stylized and not to scale, but the relative order is the one the chapters give, and the prompt fixes it:

  • The sanctuary gate is at the southeast corner; the Sacred Way runs west along the lowest terrace, turns at the Athenian Treasury, climbs east along the polygonal wall, and turns up to the temple (Chapter 18, The Sacred Way).
  • The stadium is the highest feature, above the theater and outside the wall (Chapter 18, The Stadium; Chapter 17, The Sanctuary of Apollo).
  • The Castalian Spring is just east of the sanctuary; Athena Pronaia is a short walk further east, below the modern road (Chapter 18).

East is therefore on the right, as if looking north up the slope from the valley.

# Marker Chapter section Petitioner or athlete 1 Castalian Spring 18: The Castalian Spring Washed before entering 2 Sacred Way 18: The Sacred Way of Delphi Walked it, between rival monuments 3 Treasuries 18: The Treasuries of Delphi Looked at, not entered 4 Athenian Treasury 18: The Athenian Treasury The one still standing 5 Polygonal Wall 18: The Polygonal Wall; Manumission Records Read the records of freedom 6 Temple of Apollo and altar 17: The Temple of Apollo; The Oracle Consultation Sacrificed, then asked 7 Theater 18: The Theater of Delphi Musical contests 8 Stadium 18: The Stadium of Delphi Athletic contests 9 Athena Pronaia and Tholos 18: The Athena Pronaia Sanctuary; The Tholos First shrine from the east

Marker positions in data.json are estimates from the positions stated in image-prompt.md. They must be calibrated against the real image with main.html?edit=true. Markers are at least 8 percentage points apart.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: All facts in data.json come from Chapter 18 (Parts One to Four) and Chapter 17 (The Sanctuary of Apollo, The Temple of Apollo at Delphi, The Pythia, The Oracle Consultation). The drawing's only inventions are details of how a building looks, not claims about it.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Say what is standing and what is not. Only the Athenian Treasury stands, rebuilt in 1903 to 1906. The temple is foundations and six re-erected columns. The markers say so.
  2. Keep the uncertain parts uncertain. The Athenian Treasury is "possibly" built from the spoils of Marathon. The Tholos has no known purpose. The omphalos is a copy and the original is lost.
  3. Treat the oracle as a living faith of its own time, as Chapter 17 does. No "primitive superstition" wording, and no foaming Pythia: the prompt draws no Pythia at all.
  4. No ladder, no ranking of sites. The poster does not say Delphi was better or more important than the other places on the trip.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions are drafted here. The call-out engine builds its own quiz mode from each marker's hint, and its data.json has no quiz[] field, so these are for the author's review and for any companion page.

# Question Answer Explanation 1 Where would a petitioner have washed before entering the sanctuary? 1, Castalian Spring Nobody approached Apollo unwashed; purifying with its water was the second step of a consultation. 2 Which road did rival cities line with monuments facing each other? 2, Sacred Way Pilgrims walked between the claims, as Pausanias described monument by monument. 3 Which buildings held gifts, but were mainly there to carry a city's name? 3, Treasuries A treasury was not a bank; it displayed a city's wealth and piety. 4 Which building stands today because archaeologists rebuilt it from its original blocks? 4, Athenian Treasury French archaeologists rebuilt it between 1903 and 1906, with money from Athens. 5 Which wall is fitted without mortar, survived the earthquake of 373 BCE, and carries records of freedom? 5, Polygonal Wall The interlocking blocks resist earthquakes; the smooth face became the sanctuary's archive. 6 Where was the goat sacrificed before a consultation? 6, temple terrace On the great altar before the temple's east front. 7 Where were the musical contests of the Pythian Games held? 7, Theater Music came first in the program; the athletics followed higher up. 8 Which structure is the highest, and lies outside the sanctuary wall? 8, Stadium It is about 178 m long, and in winter the path up is not always open. 9 Which shrine was the first a pilgrim reached on the road from the east? 9, Athena Pronaia Its name means "before the temple." 10 Which building is one of the most admired in Greece, though nobody knows why it was built? 9, Tholos No ancient writer says what it was for.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Scale and honesty. The picture squeezes the slope and enlarges buildings. The relative order is right. If you would rather add a small sidebar ("about 100 m of climb from entrance to stadium", from Chapter 17) on the lesson page, say so.
  2. Marker order. The numbering follows our climb and puts Athena Pronaia last, as Chapter 18 does. A pilgrim arriving from the east would have met Pronaia first. Keep the chapter's order, or renumber to the pilgrim's?
  3. Left or right. East on the right is what the chapter's directions give when viewed from the valley. A generator may mirror the picture; if so, the markers need only be moved, but the compass note in the lesson should be edited.
  4. Companion sims. The lesson page should link A Day at the Oracle, Two Ends of the Serpent Column, Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall, and Eleven Centuries of the Oracle.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
• The real relative positions and heights of the terraces. The chapters give the order, not the distances, and the prompt only places the features by order.
  • Where the Siphnian Treasury stood on the Sacred Way. The chapters name it but do not locate it, so marker 3 is a general marker for the row.
  • Where the Stoa of the Athenians and the Castalian Spring's older fountain stand in relation to the road. The prompt draws them as the chapters word them.
  • The current state of the upper paths and the stadium climb on the day.

docs.title: Five Classrooms Across Three Thousand Years
docs.text: Run the Five Classrooms MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Almost every stop on our route holds a story about who got to learn and who was shut out. This poster puts five of those places in one row, in date order, drawn at the same scale so that you can compare who is in the room, what the learners hold, and how close the teacher stands.

Each classroom follows the four-step pattern from Chapter 2: learning is locked up, a new technology or institution opens it, someone resists, and the circle widens but never all the way. The five are not steps on a ladder. Several widened access while others kept narrowing it, and every panel ends with the same question: who was still left outside?

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a classroom to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a classroom to open an infobox below the image with the four steps and where we meet it on the route. On a tablet or phone, tap a classroom instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the classroom that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the classroom so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each classroom's zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Five Classrooms
docs.text:
1. The Lyceum, about 335 BCE: Aristotle's research school in a public gymnasium, run by a foreigner who could not own land in Athens.
  2. Rhodes, first century BCE: the school of rhetoric that Cicero sailed to, the old pattern of traveling to the teacher.
  3. A Venetian print shop, about 1500: Aldus Manutius and the small, plain, portable book.
  4. A medrese at the Süleymaniye, 1550s: free higher education paid for by an endowment.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Learning for All is the book's third thread, and it ends nearly every daily chapter. Each chapter runs the same four-step pattern from Chapter 2: learning is locked up, a new technology or institution opens it, someone resists, and the circle widens but never all the way. The pattern is spread over five chapters. A single row of five rooms lets a reader see it at once, and the zones keep asking the same question of each room: who is still outside?

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Five tall panels in a single row, all drawn at the same scale, from the same camera height, with the floor at the same level. Side by side is the point: the reader compares who is in the room, what the learners hold, and how close the teacher stands. A zone is one whole panel, so this uses the same grid engine as the Three Classical Orders and Oracle and Algorithm posters. The panels are narrow (288 px wide on a 1536 px image), so the prompt asks for people drawn large and stacked toward the foreground.

Panel Room Date Chapter 1 The Lyceum about 335 BCE 20 2 Rhodes, a rhetoric school first century BCE 12 3 A Venetian print shop (Aldus Manutius) about 1500 14 4 A medrese at the Süleymaniye 1550s 5 5 A learning room with a tutor today 20, 21

The order is chronological left to right, but it is not a staircase of progress. Several rooms widened access while others kept narrowing it, and the zones say so.

docs.title: What Each Zone Says
docs.text:
Panels 2, 3, 4, and 5 follow the chapters' own four steps, so a reader can read down one step across the whole row.

Step Rhodes Aldine Press Medrese Modern Tutor Locked up Advanced rhetoric lived with a few teachers in a few cities Plato in Greek needed a manuscript collection, a scribe, and a Greek teacher Advanced study needed years that poor families could not afford One-to-one tutoring went to princes, as with Alexander and Aristotle Opened Rich Romans could sail to the teachers, who built schools for many students Printed Greek authors with grammars; the 1501 octavo a student could own and carry An endowment paid tuition, room, meals, and a stipend AI tutoring, tried in a Harvard physics course and in Edo State, Nigeria Resisted The Senate expelled Greek teachers in 161 BCE Collectors scorned print; Aldus's own privileges forbade copying his type Inertia: the curriculum stayed as founded while the world moved to print Wrong answers, low use, and a Turkish study showing harm Never all the way Families who could pay for a voyage and a tutor; daughters almost never Men who had been to school; few women learned Greek; villagers could not read Only boys and men; Arabic; Muslim subjects Children with no connection, device, or tutor in their language

The draft facts are in data.json. Each fact is taken from those chapter sections, so the poster repeats what the book already says.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. No ladder. Do not draw or word the five as stages leading up to the modern tutor. The last panel ends with the same "never all the way" step as the others.
  2. Draw the exclusions honestly. The Lyceum and Rhodes show men, because that is who the chapters say attended. The medrese panel includes the neighborhood primary school with girls and boys, because the chapter says so.
  3. Keep the human in the last panel. The chapter's closing idea is learning with communities, not to them. The adult sits beside the child and looks at the child, not the screen.
  4. No brands. No logos, no robots, and no recognizable product screens.
  5. Respect for each tradition. The medrese is drawn as the serious college it was, not as a foil for the modern room.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The dome of Hagia Sophia, about 31 m across and about 55 m high, is the structure that made the building famous. This cutaway shows how it stands: four piers, four pendentives, a ring of 40 windows, the half-domes, and the buttresses that hold it. It also marks the collapse of the first dome in 558 and its rebuilding in 562, and the minarets the Ottomans added outside.

It is the companion to Hagia Sophia: One Building, Four Lives: that poster shows what happened to the building, and this one shows how it stays up. The chapter does not say which buttresses are Byzantine and which are Sinan's, so the drawing does not claim to.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: All facts come from Chapter 4 and from the comparison in Chapter 5, "Ottoman Mosque Architecture" and "Mimar Sinan". Chapter 4 states the dimensions (about 31 m across, about 55 m high), the ring of 40 windows, and the dates of the collapse and rebuild (558 and 562), so these are in data.json and not under "To Verify". The two Isidores, the earthquakes of 553, 557, 989 and 1346, and the Fossati restoration of 1847 to 1849 are also Chapter 4's.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Hagia Sophia is a working mosque. The minaret marker says so, once, and says who uses it and what it means to them is where contested history lives, as Chapter 4's own method does. No wording that takes a side on its status.
  2. No hero-worship of Justinian. Procopius wrote for the emperor, and the window marker says to read his "golden chain" with that in mind.
  3. No "ladder." The Süleymaniye is compared, not ranked: narrower, steeper, with hidden buttresses, a different answer to the same problem.
  4. The faint ghost arc is a drawing aid. The chapter says only that the first dome was shallower, and marker 7's tip says so.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions are drafted here. The call-out engine builds its own quiz mode from each marker's hint, and its data.json has no quiz[] field, so these are for the author's review and for any companion page.

# Question Answer Explanation 1 Which element turns a square room into a round base for a dome? 2, pendentives A curved triangle of masonry fills each corner between two arches, so the dome sits on the ring they make. 2 Which element makes the dome seem to float, and what did Procopius call the effect? 3, window ring Its 40 windows flood the base with light and hide the supports; he wrote of a golden chain. 3 Which elements carry the four great arches? 1, piers Four arches rise from four piers, and everything above rests on them. 4 Which marker is about 31 m across and about 55 m high? 4, central dome For its time it was a daring piece of engineering. 5 Which elements extend the space east and west into one continuous room? 5, half-domes Two half-domes open the central space. 6 Which element stops the walls spreading under the dome's weight? 6, buttresses Every builder after Justinian has held the walls in, and Sinan added more in the 1570s. 7 When did the first dome fall, and why was the new one built higher? 7, collapse and rebuild Its eastern part fell in May 558; the rebuilt dome was steeper and pushed outward less. 8 Which parts show Hagia Sophia's Ottoman layer outside? 8, minarets Four, each built by a different sultan; two of them by Sinan in the 1570s. 9 What did Sinan's later domes learn from the rebuilt dome? 7 A steeper curve pushes outward less. 10 Which marker shows a source we should read with its purpose in mind? 3, window ring Procopius wrote his praise for Justinian.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Hagia Sophia is the clearest city of layers on the trip, and we visit it on Day 2. This poster draws the same view of the nave four times, from the same camera: as Justinian's cathedral, as an Ottoman mosque after 1453, as a museum, and as a mosque again since 2020. A tall cross-section beside them shows what stayed through all four lives: the dome, the pendentives, and the ring of windows.

This is a living religious site and a politically contested one. The zones state the agreed dates and facts, and keep the argument over what the changes mean in clearly labeled contested-history notes, with each reading held sincerely.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a zone to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a zone to open an infobox below the image with its details. On a tablet or phone, tap a zone instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the zone that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the zone so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Zones
docs.text:
1. Cathedral: For more than nine centuries the building was the seat of the Patriarch of Constantinople and the coronation church of emperors.
  2. Mosque: Mehmed II made the cathedral a mosque in 1453, and nearly five centuries of Ottoman additions followed.
  3. Museum: For 85 years the building was a museum, and the plastered-over Byzantine mosaics were uncovered and restored.
  4. Mosque Again: Since July 2020 the building has been a mosque again, with the ground floor kept for worshippers and a route for visitors through the galleries.
  5. What Stayed: The 562 dome on its four pendentives has been repaired and buttressed through all four lives, but not replaced.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Hagia Sophia is the clearest "city of layers" subject on the route, and Chapter 4 already gives its four lives in a single table. The facts are spread over six sections, and the chapter's own advice is to read the building as a document with many authors. One picture that holds the room fixed and changes only what was put into it or taken out of it lets a reader see each author's hand. It is also a living religious site and a contested one, so the poster needs a place where the dates (which are agreed) are kept apart from their meaning (which is not).

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Four interior tiles in a 2 × 2 block, plus one tall cross-section panel at the right. The idea entry in Poster Ideas calls for the same interior view drawn four times, with an optional fifth zone for what never changed. A fifth zone cannot be a rectangle on top of the four tiles, so the fifth zone gets its own panel. The panel is a vertical cross-section of the dome, pendentives, and ring of windows, which a tall shape fits better than another interior view would.

Column 1 Column 2 Column 3 (tall) 1. Cathedral, 537 to 1453 2. Mosque, 1453 to 1934 5. What Stayed 3. Museum, 1935 to 2020 4. Mosque Again, 2020 to today (spans both rows)

All four tiles share one camera position, from the nave floor looking east. The prompt asks the image tool to draw the architecture once and change only the furnishing layer, because tools do not hold a room fixed across four tiles reliably. If the tiles drift, the zones still work. A zone is one whole tile.

docs.title: What Each Zone Says
docs.text:
Zone What was added What was covered What was revealed Chapter 4 sections 1. Cathedral Gold mosaics with figures after 843; Komnenos panel (about 1122); Deesis (about 1261) Nothing yet Justinian's dome, rebuilt 562 Hagia Sophia; The Hagia Sophia Dome; Byzantine Mosaics; The Fourth Crusade 2. Mosque Mihrab, minbar, minarets, fountain (1740), roundels (about 1850) Figural mosaics, gradually, under plaster Some mosaics, briefly, by the Fossati brothers (1847 to 1849) Hagia Sophia; Restoration and Reconstruction; Byzantine Mosaics 3. Museum Restoration work Nothing new The plastered mosaics, from the 1930s Contested History; Mosaic; Byzantine Mosaics 4. Mosque Again Carpets on the ground floor Some images, by curtains or lighting during prayers Nothing new Hagia Sophia; Dress at Sacred Sites 5. What Stayed Buttresses, over the centuries Nothing The 562 dome on its pendentives The Hagia Sophia Dome

The draft facts are in data.json. Each fact is taken from those chapter sections, so the poster repeats what the book already says.

docs.title: Contested History: A Labeled Note
docs.text: The chapter's own words for this are: the dates are agreed, the meaning is not. Following that, the zone summaries and facts state only dates and physical changes. The two zones where a decision changed the building's status, Museum (1934) and Mosque Again (2020), each carry one fact that begins "Contested history note:". It gives the readings that the chapter gives and no others. The chapter gives readings for 2020 and a single reading of 1934. It gives none for 1453, so the Mosque zone has no such note (see the open questions). Quiz questions on these decisions ask for the dates and the physical consequences, and never ask the learner to say which reading is right.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Living faiths. Hagia Sophia is a working mosque and a church that Orthodox Christians call their mother church. People in the image are small and seen from behind, and no face is drawn in detail. No scene shows prayer in close view.
  2. No ladder and no verdict. The four lives are in date order, but the poster never ranks them or says which is the building's true purpose.
  3. Neutral verbs. The chapter's verbs are used as written: "made a mosque", "made a museum", "returned to use as a mosque". The poster does not use "converted back", "restored", or "reclaimed", because each of them carries a side.
  4. Honest about 537. The cathedral tile shows the later Byzantine state, with figural mosaics. Justinian's own mosaics had only crosses and patterns, and a fact in the zone says so.
  5. No calligraphy in the image. The roundels are drawn as abstract flourishes on discs, because the image tool will garble real lettering.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: Ten questions are drafted in data.json, two per zone. They ask about ideas and features (what a mihrab and minbar mark, what a cabinet decision changed, how a pendentive works), not about which tile is drawn where. Every zone is the answer to two questions.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
These are not in the chapters, so none of them is in data.json.

  1. The mihrab and minbar. The chapter lists them as signs of the mosque life but gives no dates, no builders, and no position. The image shows a prayer niche in the apse and a stepped pulpit beside it, which is the usual arrangement and needs a source.
  2. The museum years, floor and roundels. The chapter does not say whether the floor was bare or carpeted between 1935 and 2020, or whether the roundels stayed on the piers. The image shows bare marble and roundels in place.
  3. The 2020 changes in detail. The chapter says "curtains or lighting over some images during prayers". It does not say which images or how. The image shows one pale curtain over the apse mosaic, which is an illustration, not a claim.
  4. The scaffold in Tile 3. The chapter mentions "restoration work" for the museum life but not scaffolding. If the author prefers, the tile can drop the scaffold.

docs.title: Walk Down the Hippodrome
docs.text: Run the Walk Down the Hippodrome MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Walking down the old Hippodrome square in Istanbul, we pass three monuments along the old track line: an Egyptian obelisk, a twisted bronze column, and a rough masonry obelisk. None was made for this place. This poster reads them as three borrowed layers, a picture of the word spolia, and asks of each where it came from, who set it up here, and what has happened to it since.

The heights and the north-to-south order in the picture are illustrative. The chapters list the monuments but give no distances, and say only that the base carries a portrait of Theodosius.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 4 spends a worked example reading Sultanahmet Square layer by layer, and then a MicroSim asks readers to place each layer in its era. A single annotated view keeps the whole row in sight at once: an Egyptian obelisk raised by a Roman emperor in 390 CE, a Greek victory monument carried from Delphi, and a rough tower that a Byzantine emperor sheathed in bronze and Crusaders stripped in 1204. That is spolia made visible, and it is the first thing the group sees on Day 2. The Serpent Column's second end is at Delphi on Day 12, so the poster also closes a loop that Chapter 18 opens.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Call-out engine, one wide elevation. The picture is one flat side view of the square, with the three monuments standing clear of each other along the track line, so each can carry a numbered marker without crossing the others. The fountain and the Blue Mosque are included for context, and the pit gets its own marker because it shows a layer literally. The poster does not retell the Serpent Column's two ends; the Two Ends of the Serpent Column MicroSim does that, and the Serpent Column marker's tip points to it.

The engine is layout: "side-panel", orientation: "landscape", showNumbers: true. Marker positions in data.json are estimates taken from the positions stated in image-prompt.md. They must be calibrated with ?edit=true once the image exists.

docs.title: The Eight Markers
docs.text:
# Marker Source section Day 1 The long square: track, Hippodrome, Blues and Greens, Nika Riots Chapter 4: "The Hippodrome", "The Nika Riots", worked example "standing in the Hippodrome"; "Following four horses" 2 2 German Fountain, 1900 Chapter 4: layer table in "Layers of a City" and the MicroSim card list 2 3 Obelisk of Thutmose III Chapter 4: worked example, "Spolia" 2 4 The marble base carved with Theodosius I Chapter 4: worked example 2 5 Serpent Column Chapter 4: worked example, "Spolia"; Chapter 18: "The Serpent Column" 2, 12 6 The pit Chapter 4: worked example; Chapter 18: "The Serpent Column" 2 7 Walled Obelisk Chapter 4: worked example, table of layers 2 8 Blue Mosque Chapter 4: worked example; Chapter 5: "The Blue Mosque" 2, 3

The order is the order a visitor reads the square: the whole shape first, then the row from the north end to the south, then the mosque beside it. Justinian and the Nika Riots live in marker 1, because they explain why the square is still a shape on the map.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Spell out which layer, and why. Each monument marker names the layer by when it arrived, not when it was made. The trap statement from Chapter 4 is in marker 3's tip.
  2. Contested items go in a tip. The 30,000 death toll is one writer's count; who should keep the four bronze horses is opinion. Neither is stated as plain fact.
  3. The Blue Mosque is a working mosque. It is drawn with respect and no figures on the roofs. Its tip points readers to Chapter 5 for etiquette.
  4. No ladder, no villains. The Crusaders' removal and the Venetians' taking of the horses are stated as events; the poster does not rank eras.
  5. No photo-realism, no lettering. The obelisk's faint carving is drawn as squiggles, not hieroglyphs.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
The call-out engine's built-in quiz mode asks "Click on: " using the labels and the hint text. A written question bank is also drafted here for the lesson page or a later extension. Each marker is the answer to at least one. # Question Answer marker 1 Which monument was first set up at Delphi? 5 2 Which monument was carved in Egypt about 1450 BCE but is a Byzantine layer here? 3 3 Which monument shows a layer of removal, where gilded plates were melted down in 1204? 7 4 Why does the Serpent Column stand below the level of the surrounding ground? 6 5 Which marker shows the oldest layer, the outline of the Roman racetrack? 1 6 Which part of the square is its newest layer, a gift from 1900? 2 7 Where does a reused monument carry the face of the emperor who raised it? 4 8 Which building stands on part of the site of the Byzantine Great Palace? 8 9 Where did the Nika Riots of 532 begin, and where were the rioters trapped? 1

Explanations for each, from the same chapter sections, go in the lesson page.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
These details are in the idea entry or the image prompt but not in the chapters, so they are not in data.json.

  1. Order and spacing of the row. Chapter 4 lists the obelisk, the Serpent Column, and the Walled Obelisk in that order but does not say they are arranged north to south, or how far apart. The image prompt draws them that way, with the fountain at the north end and the Blue Mosque on the east side.
  2. Relative heights. The prompt makes the Walled Obelisk tallest and the Serpent Column about a third of the Egyptian obelisk. The chapters give no heights or pit depth.
  3. The carved base. Chapter 4 says only that the base is carved with Theodosius's portrait. The prompt draws one simplified crowned figure; the real carving's scenes are not in the book.
  4. Stone colors and the bare holes. The obelisk's color and the pattern of fixing holes on the Walled Obelisk are illustrative.
  5. Where the horses and the kathisma stood. The chapter says the horses stood "probably above the starting gates" and the kathisma joined the Great Palace. Neither is drawn, because the chapters give no position.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. A ninth marker for the empty place of the horses? It would carry the 1204 taking to Venice, but nothing in the picture marks where they stood. Currently the story is in marker 1's tip.
  2. Add Hagia Sophia in the background? It stands to the north in reality, so it would sit left of the fountain and crowd marker 2.
  3. Companion links. The lesson page should link Two Ends of the Serpent Column and Read the Ruin - Which Layer?, and Chapter 18's Delphi section for the other end of the column.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The front of the Library of Celsus is the best-known view in Ephesus. This picture reads it part by part: the steps and statue bases, the two storeys of columns with their Corinthian capitals, the niches with statues, the doorway to the reading room, and the burial chamber of Celsus under the building. It also marks the Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates beside it.

It was a public library built as a son's memorial and a tomb, which makes it a stop in our Learning for All thread. Part of what we see was put back together in modern times, and marker 8 shows that as a drawing device, not as a map of which stones are new.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will read the front of the Library of Celsus part by part: say which parts are original design, which are copies or reconstruction, and what the building was for, a public library built as a son's memorial and a tomb.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 10 teaches the classical orders and the reading of inscriptions on Day 7, then uses the library as the place to use both skills at once ("One square, and every skill of the day is in use"). It is also the book's example of library as public access in the Learning for All thread. A straight-on drawing with markers lets the reader find the capitals, the niches, the statue bases, and the removed bronze letters on one front, before standing in front of the real one. The Three Classical Orders poster teaches the orders on a single column each; this poster shows them in use on a building. See The Three Classical Orders.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
One straight-on view, call-out engine. The idea asked for two layers (before the earthquake and as reassembled). The chapter says only that the building burned in the 3rd century CE, that an earthquake later brought down the façade, and that it was re-erected in 1970 to 1978, so there is no detailed "before" to draw. The picture shows the front as it stands now, with one marker (8) for what was reassembled, and the "before" layer is dropped. Markers run from the street, up the front, then to the hidden chamber and the neighboring gate.

# Marker Chapter 10 section 1 Curetes Street and the square Curetes Street; Hadrian; The Temple of Hadrian at Ephesus 2 Steps and statue bases Inscription; The Library of Celsus 3 Podium and lower columns The Library of Celsus ("The trick"); The Corinthian Order 4 Niches with statues The Library of Celsus ("The statues") 5 Upper story and Corinthian capitals Classical Orders; The Corinthian Order 6 Reading room doorway The Library of Celsus; Learning for All 7 Burial chamber of Celsus The Library of Celsus 8 What was reassembled The Library of Celsus; Chapter 4, Restoration and Reconstruction 9 Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates The Library of Celsus ("The inscriptions")

Marker positions in data.json are estimates from the positions stated in image-prompt.md. They must be calibrated against the real image with main.html?edit=true. Markers are at least 8 percentage points apart.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: All facts come from Chapter 10: The Library of Celsus, Curetes Street, Hadrian, The Temple of Hadrian at Ephesus, Inscription, Classical Orders, The Corinthian Order, and "Learning for All: A Son's Gift of Books"; plus Chapter 4 for the restoration versus reconstruction distinction.

docs.title: What the Chapter Does Not Say
docs.text: The idea asked for several details that Chapter 10 does not give, so they are not in data.json; see "To Verify Before Approval". Hadrian does not appear on the facade: the chapter dates the library to around 110 CE and Hadrian's reign to 117 to 138 CE, so he appears only in marker 1, through the Temple of Hadrian on Curetes Street.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Mark reconstruction as reconstruction. Marker 8 and marker 4 say what is a copy and what was put back, in the chapter's words.
  2. The 12,000 scrolls are a modern estimate, not an ancient number. The marker says so.
  3. Corinthian "type". The chapter says both stories have capitals "of the Corinthian type", and data.json repeats that.
  4. No ladder. The library is not ranked above the Library at Alexandria or any other. The marker ends on the book's own question, who was still outside the door.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions are drafted here. The call-out engine builds its own quiz mode from each marker's hint, and its data.json has no quiz[] field, so these are for the author's review and for any companion page.

# Question Answer Explanation 1 Which order of capital stands on the front, in both stories, according to Chapter 10? 5, upper story Both stories have paired columns with capitals of the Corinthian type, the Roman favorite. 2 Who is buried beneath the reading room, and why is that unusual? 7, burial chamber Celsus lay in a marble sarcophagus; Romans did not normally bury the dead inside a city. 3 Which feature tells us who paid for the library's books and upkeep? 2, steps and bases The inscription records Aquila's 25,000 denarii, and the bases name Celsus in Greek and Latin. 4 Which feature shows four virtues, and what is true of the ones we see? 4, niches They are copies, and the originals went to Vienna. 5 Which marker shows work done in 1970 to 1978? 8, reassembly Austrian archaeologists re-erected the front from its fallen pieces. 6 Why does the front look taller and grander than its width? 3, podium Podium under the lower columns, and slightly larger columns and spaces near the center. 7 Which feature is the best example of "what was removed"? 9, the gate The holes are where bronze letters were once pinned. 8 About how many scrolls is the library said to have held, and how do we know? 6, doorway About 12,000, a modern estimate from the size and number of the niches. 9 Which street leads down to the library, and what is the footing like? 1, Curetes Street Marble-paved and polished smooth, so slippery when wet. 10 Which feature shows a gift of knowledge that reaches only as far as readers' means? 6, doorway A reader had to walk in and be able to read, and most people in Roman Ephesus probably could not.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. The "before" layer. Drop it, as drafted, or add a note to Chapter 10 about how the façade fell, so a second layer is possible?
  2. Marker 8 position. The prompt asks for a few paler blocks near the upper right corner as a visual device. Chapter 10 does not say which parts of the front are new, so move the marker, or drop the paler blocks, if the real image suggests a claim.
  3. Companion pages. The lesson page should link Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian?, One Walk, Seven Centuries, and Documented, Debated, or Tradition?. The first uses the same orders wording.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
• The lower-story order. Chapter 10 says both stories carry Corinthian-type capitals. The idea entry asked which order is on the lower story, and published descriptions of this façade differ. Check a source before approving question 1.
  • Doors, windows, roofline, and relief detail. The chapter does not describe the entrance doors, the upper windows, or the pediment, so no marker names them and the prompt draws them generically.
  • Which parts of the front are original and which are new stone. Not in the chapter.
  • The date of the earthquake that brought down the façade. Not in the chapter.
