docs.title: One Table, Two Names
docs.text: Run the One Table, Two Names MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Turkey and Greece share many dishes and quarrel over their names. This poster shows one long table seen from above: Turkish dishes in the top row, Greek in the bottom row, and six pairs lined up in columns. Click a pair to see both names, what the chapters say about it, and where the two versions differ.

This is an empathy poster, not an argument about who invented what. The two kitchens grew from a shared Ottoman and Byzantine past, and from the population exchange of 1923, which sent families and their recipes across the Aegean. Each country calls its own version its own, and each is right to.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a zone to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a zone to open an infobox below the image with its details. On a tablet or phone, tap a zone instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the zone that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the zone so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Zones
docs.text:
1. Vine Leaves: One small plate, two names, on a table both kitchens share.
  2. Yogurt Dip: Cool yogurt with cucumber and garlic, a little thinner on the Turkish table.
  3. Eggplant: A smoky eggplant salad, and a family of cousins, found on both sides of the Aegean.
  4. Anise Spirit: Two clear aniseed spirits that turn milky white with water and belong to a long meal.
  5. Baklava: The dish is agreed on, and the argument is over whom it belongs to.
  6. Coffee: The same coffee, made the same way, under a name that changed because a word can carry a wound.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will match six Turkish and Greek dish pairs, give both names for each, and explain, without taking a side, why the two kitchens share so many dishes: one empire for centuries, and the population exchange of 1923.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: The trip begins at a Turkish meze table on Day 4 and ends with Greek coffee on Day 13, and the book keeps noticing the same dishes under two names. The matched list sits in one table in Chapter 15 (Shared Greek-Turkish Dishes), and the rest is spread over Chapters 3, 6, 16, and 20. A single picture of one table, with the same plate on both sides, makes the point before any text does. It is an empathy poster: the aim is that a traveler sits down on either shore and recognizes the food. The 1923 exchange is the reason the two tables are so alike, and also a loss that both communities still remember (Chapter 7).

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
The idea in Poster Ideas put the Turkish half on the left and the Greek half on the right. This spec turns the table the other way: one long table seen from above, with a thin runner down its length, the Turkish dishes above the runner and the Greek dishes below it, so each pair sits in the same column, one over the other. Reasons:

  • A zone must be one rectangle, and a pair that crosses the runner is then one tall column. A left/right split would need a wide row for each pair and chips too small to read.
  • Six columns leave room for a chip over each pair at the top of the table.
  • Diners facing each other across a table is the picture the poster wants.

The order of the columns follows a meal: three cold meze, the drink that goes with them, the sweet, and the coffee.

Column Turkish Greek Zone id Main chapters 1 Yaprak sarma, dolma Dolmades vine-leaves 6, 15 2 Cacık Tzatziki yogurt-dip 15, 12, 3 3 Patlıcan salatası, karnıyarık Melitzanosalata, papoutsakia eggplant 6, 15, 7 4 Rakı Ouzo anise-spirit 6, 16, 14 5 Baklava Baklavas baklava 5, 15, 3 6 Türk kahvesi Ellinikós kafés coffee 3, 20

The pairs were chosen because the chapters themselves pair them. The table in Chapter 15 also pairs gyros with döner, keftedes with köfte, and loukoumi with lokum. They are left out to keep six columns. See the open questions.

docs.title: What Each Zone Says
docs.text:
Each zone has the same shape: both names, what the dish is, one shared root, one place the pair breaks, and where we meet it on the route. The break is a different kind in each column, so the poster avoids saying that every pair is the same dish.

Zone Where the pair breaks Vine leaves Hardly at all. The names differ. Yogurt dip The Turkish version is often thinner (Chapter 15). Eggplant Papoutsakia wear béchamel and karnıyarık does not; Greek moussaka's béchamel is credited to the early 20th century. Anise spirit Strength (about 45 and about 40 percent), and the Cretan raki that has no anise. Baklava The names match but the ownership claims are argued among Turks, Greeks, and Arabs. Coffee The drink is the same, but "Greek coffee" is a name that replaced an older one after 1974.

The draft facts are in data.json. Every fact is from the cited chapter sections, and none claims who invented what.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Never argue about who invented what. The chapters say that this is asked in both countries, often with feeling, and that the honest answer is that each dish belongs to everyone who cooked it. The poster repeats that and goes no further.
  2. Same plates, both sides. The dishes are drawn as near twins, with only the differences the chapters give (a thinner dip, a béchamel on one stuffed eggplant, a glass of water beside the Greek coffee). No difference the chapters do not give.
  3. No national symbols. No flags, crescents, crosses, national colors, or costume. The tablecloth is the same on both halves.
  4. The 1923 exchange is a loss on both sides. Say that families on both shores were uprooted, as Chapter 7 does. Never use it as a punchline or frame one side as the victim.
  5. The Cyprus fact is stated as the chapter states it, as the reason the name came to feel wrong to many Greeks. The zone does not say who was right.
  6. Alcohol is a choice. The spirit zone says many Turks do not drink and declining is polite, as Chapter 6 does.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: Ten questions are drafted in data.json, at least one per zone, with three zones asked about twice. They ask about ideas (contested ownership, a name that changed, one word with two drinks) and not about what is drawn.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
None of these is in data.json.

  1. Preparation differences beyond the few the chapters give. Fillings of vine leaves, how rakı and ouzo are distilled, the syrup and nuts of each baklava, and the thickness of both dips are not in the chapters, apart from the one-line differences listed above. The idea entry called baklava a "honey pastry". The chapters say syrup, so the data does too.
  2. A kebab or döner pair. Chapter 15 pairs gyros with döner, and Chapter 15 also says gyros reached Greece in the 20th century, probably first with refugees from Anatolia ("probably" is the chapter's word). If you add the pair, keep that hedge.
  3. Greek spellings. Chapter 15 uses "Elliniko kafe", Chapter 20 uses ellinikós kafés. The data uses the Chapter 20 form for the coffee, and Chapter 15's forms for the rest. Check the transliterations in one pass.
  4. The Turkish half of "Greek coffee". Chapter 20 says Greeks "usually called it Turkish coffee too" until the 1970s. How and when the Turkish name arose in Greek is not given. Do not add a date before 1970.
  5. Day numbers. The coffee route fact uses Day 1 for Turkish coffee because Chapter 3 describes it. Change it if your own coffee was on another day.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Six columns or seven? Seven pairs would make each column 215 px wide and the chips would need labels of about nine characters. The strongest candidates are döner and gyros, and lokum and loukoumi. If you prefer a kebab pair, I would swap it for the yogurt dip, not add a seventh column.
  2. Add people? The prompt draws no people, so no skin tones, clothes, or faces need to be chosen. If you want hands passing a plate across the runner, say so, and the prompt will add two hands in the baklava column, below the plain label band.
  3. Left and right instead of top and bottom? Possible, with six wide rows and chips over each row. The dishes would be smaller. I recommend the top-and-bottom layout above.
  4. Where does the 1923 story live? It appears in the vine-leaves and eggplant zones and is the topic of a sim. A seventh zone for "the table itself" is possible but does not fit the one-pair-per-zone rule.
  5. Companion sims. The lesson page should link Reading Food in Layers, Who Was Exchanged in 1923?, and Source, Myth, or Contested? for the baklava question.
  6. Canvas. If your image tool can produce 1792 x 1024, the columns would be about 290 px wide. If you switch, tell me and I will recompute the zones and the prompt.

docs.title: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Side by Side
docs.text: Run the Oracle and the Algorithm Side by Side MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
For about eleven centuries, people climbed to Delphi to ask Apollo's priestess what their choices would bring. Today we ask machine-learning models the same kind of question. Chapters 17 and 19 walk through the parallel in detail. This poster puts it in one picture: six tiles, each with Delphi on the left and today on the right, following the life of a single question.

Each tile also says where the parallel breaks. For the people who climbed to Delphi, consulting the god was an act of piety, and calling it "an early algorithm" misses what it meant to them. The six comparisons are lenses for asking better questions of any source, not a claim that the two are the same thing.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a tile to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a tile to open an infobox below the image with what happened at Delphi, what happens today, and where the parallel breaks. On a tablet or phone, tap a tile instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the tile that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the tile so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each tile's zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Six Tiles
docs.text:
1. Who asks: a petitioner who climbed, paid a fee, and sacrificed an animal, and a user typing a prompt, while others are scored without asking.
  2. Where knowledge comes from: envoys bringing news from many cities, and training data from many voices. Both know the most about those who can reach them.
  3. The form of the answer: a verse that came true whichever side won, and a fluent, hedged paragraph. An answer that cannot lose predicts nothing.
  4. Who interprets: the Athenian Assembly arguing over the wooden wall, and a human in the loop who is, or is not, free to disagree.
  5. How we mishear: Croesus hearing the victory he wanted, and a leading question that gets an agreeable answer.
  6. When the answer changes the future: Oedipus at the crossroads, and a prediction that feeds, or defeats, itself.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
The first sketch in Poster Ideas used six horizontal rows across a split scene. Image generators do not keep six rows aligned, so this spec uses six tiles in a 3 × 2 grid, each a small diptych with Delphi on the left and today on the right. A zone is one whole tile, so one hover compares both halves. This matches the grid engine used by the Three Classical Orders poster.

Column 1 Column 2 Column 3 1. Who asks 2. Where knowledge comes from 3. The form of the answer 4. Who interprets 5. How we mishear 6. When the answer changes the future

The reading order follows the life of one question: someone asks, a source knows, an answer comes back in some form, someone interprets it, we hear what we want, and the answer changes what happens next.

docs.title: A Scribe's Page and an Aldine Page
docs.text: Run the A Scribe's Page and an Aldine Page MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapters 6 and 14 tell how a hand-copied book gave way to the small printed book that Aldus Manutius made in Venice. This poster sets the two side by side in six matched tiles: the writing surface, the hand or the type, the page and its size, who made it, how long it took, and who could own one.

Each tile says where the comparison stops being fair. A scribe is cheaper for one copy and a press for a hundred, and Aldus widened the circle of readers without opening it to everyone. All the text in the pictures is blurred on purpose, so the poster shows the form of a page, not its words.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a zone to see a short tooltip with its name and its idea.
  2. Click a zone to open an infobox below the image with its details. On a tablet or phone, tap a zone instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the zone that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the zone so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Zones
docs.text:
1. Writing Surface: A Byzantine page was parchment from animal skin, an Aldine page was handmade paper, and paper was still one of the biggest costs of a printed book.
  2. Hand or Type: A scribe's hand and Aldus's italic type were both writing, and the type was modeled on the hand.
  3. Page and Size: Aldus made a classic small enough for a coat pocket through two choices: a small fold and a dense, plain page.
  4. Who Made It: A scribe's book was one skilled hand's work. An Aldine book was the work of many hands, and each depended on the copyists before.
  5. How Long: For one copy the scribe is cheaper. For a hundred copies the press wins overwhelmingly, because most of its cost is paid before the first page.
  6. Who Could Own: Aldus widened the circle, but only to men who had been to school, and he built a gate of his own.

docs.title: Why This Poster

Chapter 6 gives the cost of copying and the press's fixed cost. Chapter 14 gives Aldus, the octavo, and the many hands behind an Aldine book. They are Day 2, Day 4, and Day 9, so a reader meets them a week apart. One picture puts the two pages side by side and asks the book's third-thread question of each feature: who is still outside?

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Six small diptychs in a 3 × 2 grid, not one picture of two open books. The idea entry in Poster Ideas pictures two open books of the same size, with a zone for each feature. Features such as "how long it took" and "who could afford it" are not parts of a page, so they have no place on two open books. They would need captions or labels, which the image cannot carry. The Oracle and the Algorithm poster met the same problem and solved it with six diptychs, so this poster follows it. Each tile keeps the book idea: a gold seam, like a book's gutter, runs down the middle, with the scribe's page on the left and the Aldine page on the right. A zone is one whole tile.

Column 1 Column 2 Column 3 1. Writing Surface 2. Hand or Type 3. Page and Size 4. Who Made It 5. How Long 6. Who Could Own

The left half is a Byzantine monastery workshop, because Chapter 4's chain (papyrus, Byzantine minuscule, Italian print) is the one that ends in the 1513 Aldine Plato. The Ottoman copyists of Chapter 6 appear in the facts for tiles 4 and 5.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. No lettering, anywhere. Every page, sign, and slip is drawn as blurred gray bars. The prompt forbids decorative letters too, so the decorated initial is an abstract square of pattern.
  2. No ladder. The scribe's page is not the "before" of a better after. The chapter says copyists decided what the future could read, and also that print multiplied errors as freely as truth.
  3. Break each pair. Every zone carries a fact that begins "Where the pair breaks down", as the Oracle and the Algorithm poster does. Tile 3's comes before its route line.
  4. Illustrative numbers are labeled. Tiles 1, 3, and 5 carry numbers from the chapters' illustrative models, and each fact says "illustrative" or "in the chapter's example".
  5. Respect for the Islamic calligraphic tradition. The Ottoman copyists appear in facts as skilled calligraphers, not as a foil for print.

The sample question from the idea entry ("Which feature let a scholar carry a classic in a pocket?") is question 1.

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
These are not in the chapters, so none of them is in data.json.

  1. Whether parchment is a fair "scribe" surface. The chapters give Byzantine parchment, but they do not say which manuscripts used paper instead. Scribes also wrote on paper, so the surface pair is not strictly a scribe against a press. The zone says only that Aldus changed the number of sheets.
  2. A wide margin and a decorated initial. The chapters do not describe a Byzantine page's layout. The picture's large margin and initial are an illustrator's choices for tile 3.
  3. Sizes and prices. The chapters give formats (folio, quarto, octavo) and the "portable little books" description but no centimeters, no price of an Aldine octavo, and no price of a manuscript.

docs.title: A Trireme at Salamis
docs.text: Run the A Trireme at Salamis MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Athenian fleet won the battle of Salamis in 480 BCE, and this cutaway shows what it was won with. It shows the trireme, with its oarsmen on three levels, its bronze ram, and its officers and marines, and the fleet and the narrows beyond it, and the seat of Xerxes on the hill above.

The point the poster makes is about democracy. The ships were rowed by many of the poorest citizens, and that gave them a claim on the city. The chapters give the ram, the three levels, and the numbers of rowers, but not the oar arrangement or the steering oars, so the drawing is illustrative there.

docs.title: Spec: A Trireme at Salamis
docs.text: Status: built (2026-11-25). The image is generated, the marker positions are calibrated to it, and the page is in the nav at A Trireme at Salamis. It is built, not approved: the author approves it after trying the controls.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will explain how the Athenian trireme linked a sea victory to a change in who held power, by naming what the ship was made of, who rowed it, and how Athens's fleet gave the poorest citizens a claim on the city.

docs.title: Why This Poster
docs.text: Chapter 15 gives the trireme in three numbers and the battle in five moves, and ends the worked example with a promise: about 30,000 oarsmen, "a fact whose consequences for democracy Chapter 16 follows." Chapter 16 keeps the promise in the next chapter, in the worked example "why the rowers had a vote that counted." A single cutaway puts the ship, the crew, the silver, and the narrows in one picture, so the reader sees the whole chain: the silver bought the ships, the ships needed the poor, and the poor gained power. The chapters support leading with that link, so marker 1 is the oarsmen and tells the democracy story first.

docs.title: Layout Decision
docs.text:
Call-out engine, one cutaway in a scene. The hero is a large trireme in side view with the hull cut away in the middle, so three ranks of oarsmen, the oar openings, the deck, and the ram all show on one ship. Behind it, small and hazy, are the Athenian line on the left, the Persian ships crowded in the narrows in the middle, and Xerxes' seat on the mountain on the right. That keeps the battle in view without a second panel.

The engine is layout: "side-panel", orientation: "landscape", showNumbers: true. Marker positions in data.json are estimates taken from the positions stated in image-prompt.md. They must be calibrated with ?edit=true once the image exists.

docs.title: The Eight Markers
docs.text:
# Marker Source section Day 1 The Oarsmen: who rowed, and what it did for democracy Chapter 16: worked example "why the rowers had a vote that counted", "Who democracy left out"; Chapter 15: "Themistocles", worked example "a war play in the war's own city" 11 2 Three Levels of Oars: size and crew Chapter 15: worked example "what the silver bought"; "Piraeus" 10 3 Bronze Ram Chapter 15: "what the silver bought"; "The Battle of Salamis"; Part Two map table 10 4 Officers and Marines Chapter 15: "what the silver bought", Part Two table, "Themistocles"; Chapter 16: the list of institutions 11 5 Silver Behind the Fleet Chapter 15: "Themistocles"; Chapter 16: "Who democracy left out", ostraka of Themistocles 11 6 The Athenian Fleet Chapter 15: "what the silver bought", "The Persian Wars", "The Battle of Salamis"; Chapter 17: "The Wooden Walls Prophecy" 10, 12 7 The Narrows Chapter 15: "The Battle of Salamis" 10 8 Xerxes' Seat Chapter 15: "The Battle of Salamis", "a war play in the war's own city" 10

The order follows the chain: crew, ship, weapon, command, money, then the fleet and the battle. The Oracle thread appears once, in marker 6, where Themistocles' reading of the wooden wall is mentioned and sent to Chapter 17.

docs.title: Tone Rules
docs.text:
1. Lead with the link, then say where it stops. Marker 1's tip names who democracy left out: women, metics, and enslaved people, and the enslaved miners who dug the silver. The poster does not say the rowers made Athens a fair city.
  2. Fair to the Persians. The Persian ships are drawn as capable ships caught in a bad place, and marker 8 uses the chapter's own point that Athenians watched their victory as the enemy's tragedy. Marker 7's tip asks which shore Herodotus stood on.
  3. No blood, wounds, or bodies. The scene is the start of the battle.
  4. No invented detail. The chapters give three numbers for the ship. The image shows more (deck, steering oars, benches), but data.json states none of it.
  5. No ladder. The poster does not frame Athenian democracy as the goal toward which history was heading.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: The call-out engine's built-in quiz mode asks "Click on: " from the hint text. A written question bank is drafted here for the lesson page or a later extension. Each marker answers at least one. # Question Answer marker 1 Which part of the fleet gave poor citizens a claim on power in Athens? 1 2 Which part of the ship did the actual damage in a fight? 3 3 Where were the roughly 170 rowers of a ship seated, in how many levels? 2 4 Who paid for the fleet, and where did the money come from? 5 5 Which part of the picture shows Athens providing almost half of the Greek ships? 6 6 Why did the Persians' larger numbers not help them at Salamis? 7 7 Who watched the battle from the shore, and what did Athens later make of his defeat? 8 8 Which office stayed elected while most others were chosen by lot, and why? 4 9 Which marker shows the weapon that decided the battle in the narrows? 3

docs.title: To Verify Before Approval
docs.text:
These details are in the idea entry or the image prompt but not in the chapters, so they are not in data.json. The chapters do give the three levels of rowers, the ram at the bow at the waterline, and the crew of about 170 rowers and about 30 others, so those stay.

  1. How the three levels were arranged and named. The prompt draws staggered ranks stacked diagonally with a row of oar openings per level. The chapters say only "three levels."
  2. Steering oars, the deck's shape, and crew by role. The idea lists steering oars and "crew by role." Chapter 15 gives only "officers, deckhands, and marines." There is no steering-oar marker; add one only after a source is named.
  3. Whether anyone but citizens rowed. The chapters say "many of them from the poorest citizens." They do not say whether foreigners or enslaved men also rowed. The picture avoids marking status.
  4. Where Xerxes' seat stood and whether the chair was gilded. The chapter says "a seat at the foot of Mount Aigaleo." The prompt draws it halfway up the slope, with a canopy and attendants.
  5. The crew total of about 200. It is 170 plus 30 from the chapter, but the chapter does not add them.

docs.title: Open Questions for the Author
docs.text:
1. Photo of the replica? The chapter names the replica Olympias, built in the 1980s. If the author has a photo or a visit planned, a second layer could compare the cutaway with it.
  2. Marker 4 is the thinnest. The chapters say little about the deck. It could be dropped, or replaced by a steering-oar marker once a source is chosen.
  3. Companion links. The lesson page should link Xerxes' Road to Salamis and Who Could Vote in Athens?.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small interactive tools, such as maps and timelines, that help us see where we are going and how the places fit together. Each one can also be embedded in a daily chapter. Click a card to open the MicroSim.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

  • A Day at the Oracle

    Put the eight steps of a consultation at the Oracle of Delphi in order, from arriving on the seventh of the month to carrying the answer home, then walk through the day and predict what happens at three checkpoints - the goat test, the line, and the form of the answer.

  • Agreed Fact or Position?

    Sort twelve statements about the Parthenon Marbles dispute into agreed facts, the British Museum's position, and the Greek government's position, and see how each side builds its case from the same facts.

  • Antikythera Gears

    Explore how gear tooth counts produce simplified Sun, Moon, and Mars cycles.

  • Can This Answer Lose?

    Sort eight answers, from the Croesus prophecy and the "wooden wall" to a modern weather forecast, into answers that could be proven wrong, answers that come true either way, and answers that are not predictions at all, then test each one against two possible outcomes.

  • Crack Linear B Like Ventris

    Replay a simplified version of the 1952 decipherment of Linear B, from the sign count and Kober's triplet to the place-name guess, then test the values on the Pylos tripod tablet, whose pictograms confirm the reading.

  • Delphi After the Oracle

    Predict the stage of nine events in Delphi's history after the oracle closed, from the Theodosian Decrees of 391-392 CE to the UNESCO listing of 1987, as silenced, found, dug up, or shown, and watch each drop onto a timeline that squeezes the empty thousand years between them.

  • Democracy's Workplaces in the Agora

    Match nine jobs of Athenian public life, from posting notices to filing the charge against Socrates, to the building on a schematic plan of the Ancient Agora where each was done, and see the democracy's street of offices emerge along the west side.

  • Documented, Debated, or Tradition?

    Rate the evidence for ten claims about the Christian sites of Ephesus and Selçuk as documented, debated, or tradition only, and choose the reason that justifies each rating.

  • Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian?

    Compare one part at a time across the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders, then classify twelve column features and real buildings from our route, from the Parthenon to the Basilica Stoa of Ephesus.

  • Eleven Centuries of the Oracle

    Judge fourteen dated events from c. 750 BCE to 391-392 CE as signs of the Oracle of Delphi's strength or of its weakness and decline, watch each drop onto a timeline of the oracle's 1,140-year life, and find where the signs of decline begin to cluster.

  • Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline

    A to-scale timeline of the nine periods of Eastern Mediterranean history, from the Bronze Age to today, with six proportion questions to answer before the band lengths are revealed.

  • Essential or Inherited?

    Judge twelve school practices, from the Carnegie unit to being known by a caring adult, as an essential purpose of schooling or an inherited form that served that purpose under earlier constraints, and separate the trap pair of checking mastery and the same test on the same day.

  • Events of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline

    A to-scale timeline of the nine periods of Eastern Mediterranean history with 29 key events on the trip route, each linked to the chapter that covers it, and six proportion questions to answer before the events are revealed.

  • Finish the Line Like a Homeric Singer

    Complete six Homeric hexameter lines by choosing the name formula for Achilles or Odysseus whose syllables exactly fill the space left at the end of the line, and discover Milman Parry's rule that the meter, not the moment, chooses the epithet.

  • Folding the Sheet: Folio, Quarto, Octavo

    Calculate the pages and sheets of paper in one copy of Virgil printed as a folio with commentary, a plain octavo, and an Aldine-style octavo in compact italic, and see a sheet fold into 2, 4, or 8 leaves.

  • From the Schism to the Sack, 1054–1261

    A clickable timeline of seventeen events from the excommunication of 1054 to the recovery of Constantinople in 1261, with four cause questions on how a crusade bound for Egypt ended by sacking Constantinople in 1204.

  • How Calibrated Are You?

    State the probability that each of twelve statements from this book is true, see your Brier score, reliability table and calibration chart, judge whether you were overconfident, then judge two weather forecasters whose 70 and 90 percent forecasts came true 7 and 6 times in 10.

  • How Paul's Words Traveled

    Sort twelve dated events from 386 to 1999 into four strands of Paul's later influence (grace and faith, conscience and equality, contempt and its repudiation, rereading Paul) and see one man, Martin Luther, land in three of them.

  • Istanbul's Three Shores

    Classify twelve Istanbul places, from Hagia Sophia to Rumeli Hisarı and Kadıköy, as on the historic peninsula, in Galata, or on the Asian shore, then see each one appear on a satellite map.

  • Knossos From Village to Decipherment

    A to-scale timeline of Knossos from its first village about 7000 BCE to the reading of Linear B in 1952, filled in one prediction at a time so the long gaps between the volcano, the fires, and the decipherment stand out.

  • Knossos: Minoan, Evans, or Copy?

    Sort ten features a visitor sees at Knossos, from the gypsum throne to the red columns, into Minoan originals, Arthur Evans's reconstructions, and modern copies of paintings now in the Heraklion museum.

  • Layers of the Theodosian Walls

    Place the five layers of Constantinople's land walls, from the moat to the inner wall, on a schematic cross-section in the order an attacker from the west met them, then answer three questions on why the design worked.

  • Learning Graph Viewer

    An interactive viewer for the Mediterranean Travels learning graph of 598 concepts, with search, category filters, and node sizes scaled by each concept's impact.

  • Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence?

    Judge eight stories about Troy and Gallipoli as firm history, a real core with a shaped telling, or late or unsupported, by predicting and then measuring on a timeline the gap between each event and its earliest surviving evidence, and weighing the author's stake.

  • Next-Word Prediction and Temperature

    Predict what the temperature setting does to a language model's choice of the next word, then reveal the adjusted probabilities and a draw of 20 sampled words, for four prompts from "Know " to "On Sundays the Grand Bazaar is ."

  • November Weather at Our Stops

    Predict November temperature and rainfall at six stops on our route before the climate chart reveals the answer, then explore each stop's twelve-month climate.

  • One Walk, Seven Centuries

    Walk downhill through Ephesus monument by monument, predicting whether each one was begun before or after the one just passed, and watch the timeline zigzag across seven centuries.

  • Oracle, Gears, or Data?

    Sort twelve predictions, from Delphi's oracle, the Antikythera mechanism, Babylonian tablets, a stone peg calendar, and modern phones and apps, by how each answer was produced, as an oracle's answer, a cycle model, or a learned model.

  • Paul's Journeys and Our Route

    Classify twelve places by the journey on which the Book of Acts first brings Paul there, then reveal Paul's three journeys and his voyage to Rome on one map with our own November 2026 route.

  • Paul's Speech Through Stoic Ears

    Read ten lines of the speech Acts gives Paul on the Areopagus, predict for each whether a Stoic listener would hear common ground or something new, and see where the speech turns and where Luke says the audience scoffed.

  • Place the Site in Its Era

    Sort 15 sites and objects from our trip into eight period bins, from the Bronze Age to the Ottoman period, by the date each was built.

  • Planning Day 3 Around the Prayer Times

    Drag Topkapı Palace, three mosques and lunch onto a Friday in Istanbul so that every mosque visit misses the prayer closures, then press Check to see each broken rule named.

  • Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall

    Take apart a simplified Delphic manumission record, the kind carved by the hundreds on the polygonal wall below the Temple of Apollo, naming each of its eight clauses and judging whether it protects the freed woman, limits her freedom, or records the facts of the sale.

  • Read a Greek Sign

    Type twelve Greek signs from our route, from ΑΘΗΝΑ to ΚΛΕΙΣΤΟ, in Latin letters, with a letter key, trap-letter hints and a letter-by-letter breakdown.

  • Read the Olive Oil Label

    Judge whether nine illustrative olive oil labels support the claims on their fronts, using the EU acidity limits, the 27 °C rule for "cold extraction", harvest dates, and origin wording.

  • Read the Ruin: Which Layer?

    Place twelve things seen on Day 2 in Istanbul, from the Hippodrome's Egyptian obelisk to the Basilica Cistern's new walkways, into the Roman, Byzantine, Latin, Ottoman or Republic layer in which they arrived.

  • Reading Food in Layers

    Sort fourteen foods found in Istanbul, from olives and yogurt to coffee, tomatoes and tea, into the five historical layers they arrived with, and read a Turkish table like a history book.

  • Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map

    An atlas-style map of the regions, island groups, seas, and straits named in Chapter 1, with hover infoboxes, a 12-region exploration checklist, a Find the Region challenge, and a live stream of xAPI learning events.

  • Reinforcing or Balancing? Loops From Ephesus to the Staff Room

    Classify six causal loops, two from Paul's world and four from school change, as reinforcing or balancing by counting the minus signs around each one, and see that harmful loops can be reinforcing and that the Ephesus riot has the same structure as a rollout pushback.

  • Rhodes Changes Hands, 1912–1948

    A two-row timeline of who governed Rhodes from 1910 to 1949, Italy, Germany, Britain and Greece, with thirteen events and five questions on which power was in charge at each turning point.

  • Scribe or Press?

    Predict how many copies of a 200-page book it takes before printing becomes cheaper than hand-copying, for an ordinary copyist and a master calligrapher, then move a slider to watch the fixed-cost and per-copy lines cross.

  • Sort the Scripts

    Sort twelve writing systems, from Egyptian hieroglyphs and Linear B to Greek and modern Turkish, into logographic, syllabary, abjad and alphabet bins by what one sign stands for.

  • Source, Myth, or Contested?

    Classify ten statements about Byzantine Constantinople, from Procopius's golden chain to the bronze horses of Venice, as a primary source, a myth, contested history or settled history.

  • Sèvres or Lausanne?

    Predict, term by term, which of ten terms of the 1920 Treaty of Sèvres the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne reversed and which it kept, then name the rule behind the pattern, the National Pact.

  • The Olympian Gods at Troy

    Predict, then sort the twelve Olympian gods by the side each took in Homer's Iliad (the Greeks, the Trojans, or outside the fight), and discover that the gods chose sides for human reasons such as pride, old debts, and favorites.

  • The Parthenon's Five Lives

    Classify twelve events from 447 BCE to 2009 CE by which of the Parthenon's five lives it was living, temple, church, mosque, ruin or protected monument, and watch each card drop onto a timeline from 500 BCE to 2030 CE.

  • The Right Words at the Right Moment

    Choose the right Turkish phrase, with its pronunciation guide, in ten everyday Istanbul situations, from breakfast at a café to thanking a home cook, and finish with a phrase sheet for the trip.

  • The Siege of 1453, Step by Step

    Step through eight turning points of the 1453 siege of Constantinople on a schematic map, and for each one say which of the city's defenses it defeated, or whether the defenders held.

  • Thoughtful Traveler Choices

    Judge which of three responses best fits the six thoughtful-traveler principles in eight situations on our route, from a simit seller's photo to a closed Grand Bazaar.

  • Trade Routes of the Eastern Mediterranean

    Predict five route-based outcomes, then watch four simplified trade routes from the Bronze Age to Venetian Crete appear on a map of 16 ports and chokepoints.

  • Tutoring Effect Size Explorer

    Predict the percentile that five reported effect sizes for tutoring, mastery learning, and an AI tutor pilot put the average student at, then watch two normal curves separate to check, and explore how effect size in standard deviations turns into percentiles.

  • Two Ends of the Serpent Column

    Sort ten claims about the Serpent Column, the bronze monument to the Greek victory at Plataea that stood at Delphi and now stands in Istanbul's Hippodrome, by where their evidence can be checked, at Delphi, in Istanbul, or only in an ancient written source.

  • Viking Cruise Map

    An interactive map of the Viking Star Ancient Mediterranean Treasures cruise from Istanbul to Athens and our day trip to Delphi, with the route, times, key sights, and a tip for each of the seven stops.

  • Walking Venetian Candia

    Locate eight landmarks of Venetian and Ottoman Heraklion, from the Morosini Fountain and the Loggia to Koules Fortress and the Martinengo Bastion, by clicking an unlabeled street map of the old town.

  • What Did the Külliye Do?

    Sort twelve buildings of the Süleymaniye mosque complex by the public need each one served, from worship and learning to health, food, income and remembrance, and see the külliye as a whole system of public services.

  • When a Prediction Feeds Itself

    Label every link in three prediction loops, from predictive policing and student risk scores to a traffic forecast on the road to Delphi, as same or opposite direction, then classify each loop as reinforcing (self-fulfilling) or balancing (self-defeating).

  • When Printing Arrived

    A bar chart of the years from Gutenberg's Bible to the first printing in ten scripts and places, from Mainz to Istanbul, with an infobox for every bar and four questions that show who printed in Istanbul long before Müteferrika's press of 1729.

  • Where in Paul's Life Was Each Letter Written?

    Drag the seven undisputed letters of Paul onto a timeline of his life, using one clue from inside each letter, and see that most of them come from the years around Ephesus while the prison letters remain debated.

  • Where the Empire Withdrew, 1683–1923

    Classify fourteen places of the former Ottoman Empire, from Buda and Crimea to Mecca and Damascus, by the era in which they left Ottoman rule, then replay the four eras on a map to see the shape of the retreat.

  • Who Built What We See in the Old Town?

    Attribute twelve buildings and features of the city of Rhodes, from the Temple of Aphrodite to the Liberty Gate, to the Ancient, Knights, Ottoman or Italian builders who made what stands today.

  • Who Could Vote in Athens?

    Calculate what share of Attica's people could vote around 431 BCE from scholarly estimates for four groups, push the estimates to their limits, and compare a full Assembly of 6,000 with everyone it governed.

  • Who Made a Greek Book in Venice?

    Attribute ten contributions to Greek printing in Venice around 1500 to Aldus Manutius, Marcus Musurus, Francesco Griffo, Zacharias Kallierges, and six others, and watch the network of editors, printers, financiers, and patrons grow one link at a time.

  • Who Says So? Sorting Claims About Paul

    Sort fourteen familiar claims about the apostle Paul by their source (Paul's own letters, Acts only, scholars' inference, or later tradition) and see which parts of his story he told himself.

  • Who Was Exchanged in 1923?

    Apply five simplified rules of the 1923 Greek–Turkish population exchange convention to ten illustrative households and decide whether each was sent to Greece, sent to Turkey, or not exchanged.

  • Why Athens Looks the Way It Does

    Match eight things a visitor sees in Athens today, from the Polytechnic gate to euro prices and a Syrian bakery, to the events in modern Greek history from 1967 to 2023 that explain them, on an interactive timeline.

  • With or To?

    Judge eight efforts to widen or control learning, six from the trip and two imagined AI projects, as done with the people they affected or done to them, using four questions about who chose, whose language, who was consulted, and who keeps it going.

  • World Literacy Over Two Centuries

    Predict how many of the world's people could read in 1820, when more than half first could, and what share of adults still cannot, then see each answer on two centuries of literacy data.

  • Xerxes' Road to Salamis

    Step through ten places of the Persian Wars, from Sardis and Marathon to Thermopylae, Salamis and Mycale, and predict at five of them why the fighting or the crossing happened there.

docs.title: Democracy's Workplaces in the Agora
docs.text: Run the Democracy's Workplaces in the Agora MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Walking the Ancient Agora today, we see a park of foundations. This MicroSim turns those foundations back into a working government. A schematic plan shows ten places, and nine job cards ask where an Athenian would go to do each job of public life.

# Job card Where it was done 1 Read a proposed new law, or check the army call-up lists Monument of the Eponymous Heroes 2 Prepare the agenda for the next Assembly Bouleuterion 3 Eat dinner at public expense as a councillor on duty Tholos 4 Look up the exact wording of an old decree Metroon 5 File a charge of impiety, as Meletus did against Socrates Royal Stoa 6 Sit in the shade and talk with Socrates Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios 7 Hear Zeno teach beside the painting of Marathon Stoa Poikile 8 Buy goods in a shop given by a king of Pergamon Stoa of Attalos 9 Pray to the god of the forge Temple of Hephaestus

The tenth place, the boundary stone of about 500 BCE, can be clicked and read, but it is never the answer.

Card 5 is the key card. Many people expect a trial to begin in a courtroom. In Athens a charge of impiety was a matter of religious law, so it was filed first with the King Archon at the Royal Stoa, where Plato sets the opening of his dialogue Euthyphro. Card 8 is a time trap: the Stoa of Attalos, the one building we can walk into, was built about 150 BCE, some 250 years after Socrates.

At the end, six of the nine badges cluster along the west side, outlined in gold: archive, council hall, dining hall, notice board, the King Archon's office, and Socrates' favorite stoa. This was the democracy's street of offices.

Notes on the evidence. The plan is schematic: it places buildings by side of the square, not by measured position, and it leaves out many buildings, including the Middle Stoa, the Odeon of Agrippa, and the law courts, whose locations are less certain. Some of the buildings also changed over time:

  • The Monument of the Eponymous Heroes whose foundations we see dates from about the 330s BCE; an earlier version stood somewhere in the Agora in the 5th century, probably in a different spot.
  • The city archive moved into the Old Bouleuterion at the end of the 5th century BCE, when a new council hall was built behind it. The Metroon whose foundations we see is a Hellenistic rebuilding of the 2nd century BCE.
  • Ancient writers, Xenophon and Plato among them, place Socrates in conversation at the Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios; he also talked in workshops, gymnasia, and private houses.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any place on the plan to read about it in the yellow strip. Reading is free and does not count.
  2. Read the job card. Click the place where that job was done, or choose it in the list, then press Answer. Only the first answer counts.
  3. The correct place turns green, a wrong choice turns red, and the card's number is pinned beside the correct place: green if you got it right, red if you missed it.
  4. Press Next card. After card 9, press See the plan to see all nine badges and the street of offices.
  5. On the final plan, click a numbered badge to read its job again. Try Again repeats all nine cards.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 16, "Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus", before or after walking the Agora. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: the Ancient Agora of Athens, stoa, Royal Stoa, Metroon, Bouleuterion, Tholos, Monument of the Eponymous Heroes, Stoa Poikile, Stoa of Attalos, Temple of Hephaestus, the Council of 500, and the trial of Socrates. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify nine jobs of Athenian public life by the Agora building or monument where each was done, choosing correctly for at least 7 of 9 on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (2 min): Click all ten places and read their descriptions. Which ones were offices of government, and which were for shopping, teaching, or worship?
  2. Classify (6 min): Work through the nine cards.
  3. Walk it (2 min): On site, start at the boundary stone and walk north along the west side. Name what happened in each building as you pass it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 7 of 9 correct on the first attempt, including card 5, the impiety charge. A follow-up question: Why did a charge against Socrates go to a stoa rather than a court? A strong answer says that impiety was religious law, handled by the King Archon, whose office was the Royal Stoa; the trial before a jury came afterward.

docs.text:

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. John McK. Camp II, The Athenian Agora: Site Guide, 5th ed. (Princeton: American School of Classical Studies at Athens, 2010). The standard guide to every building on the plan, with dates and functions.
  2. John McK. Camp II, The Athenian Agora: Excavations in the Heart of Classical Athens (London: Thames and Hudson, 1986). The democracy's buildings and the finds from the excavation, including the boundary stone.
  3. Agora Excavations — American School of Classical Studies at Athens. The excavation's site, with descriptions of the monuments.
  4. Ancient Agora of Athens — Wikipedia. Overview of the buildings, the Panathenaic Way, and the excavation since 1931.
  5. Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 43–44 and 53.4 — The Council of 500, the councillors on duty (prytaneis) who dined in the Tholos with some staying overnight, and notices posted at the Eponymous Heroes.
  6. Plato, Euthyphro 2a — Socrates at the Royal Stoa, the King Archon's office, to answer the charge of impiety.
  7. Xenophon, Oeconomicus 7.1 — Socrates in conversation in the Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios.
  8. Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 7.5 — Zeno teaching in the Stoa Poikile, and the Stoics named after it.
  9. Stoa of Attalos and Temple of Hephaestus — Wikipedia. The stoa's 42 shops and its rebuilding of 1953–1956; the temple begun about 449 BCE.

docs.title: Antikythera Gears
docs.text: Run the Antikythera Gears MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A gear train turns tooth counts into a calculation. Here, three expanded trains share the same time input: every tan gear on the left turns once per model year. The colored output gears represent simplified Sun, Moon, and Mars cycles. Numbers inside the gears are tooth counts; the dark spokes show rotation. The counters show total output turns since the starting position, ignoring direction.

For two meshing gears, the output speed is the input speed multiplied by the number of driver teeth divided by the number of driven teeth. The direction reverses at each mesh. A larger gear driving a smaller gear increases speed.

Output Tooth-count calculation Turns per model year Sun 48 / 48 1 Moon (48 / 12) × (39 / 12) 13 Mars 24 / 48 0.5

The Moon's 12-tooth intermediate gear and 39-tooth driver share a rigid axle, so they turn together. They are drawn apart and joined by a dashed line to make both stages visible. The dashed line represents that shared axle, not another pair of meshing gears. Likewise, the three left input gears are separated for readability; their common drive is omitted.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave the model paused and drag Year to compare any time from zero to two years. The slider also works backward.
  2. Use +1 month to advance by one twelfth of a model year. Each step pauses playback.
  3. Press Start to watch the meshing gears. Adjust Speed to change playback speed without changing any ratios.
  4. Press Pause to inspect a position, or Reset to restore time zero and the default speed. Playback stops at two years; Start then begins again at zero.

At one year, the output counters read 1, 13, and 0.5. At two years, they read 2, 26, and 1. The small Moon gear moves quickly because both stages multiply its speed.

docs.title: What We Simplified
docs.text:
This is an Antikythera-inspired teaching model, not a reconstruction of the ancient gear arrangement. Its tooth counts were chosen for easy arithmetic. The annual Sun cycle, 13 lunar circuits per year, and two-year Mars orbital cycle are rounded teaching values. The lunar circuit is a circuit relative to the stars, not a new-moon-to-new-moon phase cycle. Mars's orbital cycle is not its apparent geocentric motion or its interval between oppositions.

The model omits lunar phases, variable orbital speed, retrograde motion, eclipse prediction, calendar spirals, and the other planets. Gear rotation direction is a mechanical consequence of meshing, not a prediction of which way a body moves across the sky. The triangular teeth are a schematic drawing, not a manufacturing template.

Read the Antikythera mechanism appendix for the historical setting and the more complex functions of the original.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers and introductory science learners. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: fractions, multiplication, and the idea of a rotating axle. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Calculate output turns from gear tooth counts and test the calculation by changing the model's time input.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict: Before moving the time slider, calculate the three output counts after half a year.
  2. Test: Set Year to 0.500. Compare the counters with your prediction: Sun 0.50, Moon 6.50, Mars 0.25.
  3. Trace: Follow the Moon train. Explain why the dashed axle connection preserves speed while each meshing pair changes it.
  4. Compare: Advance to one year, then two years. Identify which output completes a turn last.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: If the Mars driver had 48 teeth instead of 24, how many turns would its 48-tooth output make in one year? Explain using the ratio before answering: 48 / 48 gives one turn. This is a paper calculation; the model's tooth counts remain fixed.

docs.title: Paul's Speech Through Stoic Ears
docs.text:
Run the Paul's Speech Through Stoic Ears MicroSim Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Acts 17:22–31 gives Paul a speech to the Athenians on the Areopagus, with Stoic and Epicurean philosophers among his listeners. It is a lesson in persuasion: it starts from what the audience already believes and only later asks them to accept something new. This MicroSim lets us find the turn ourselves.

Ten lines, paraphrased from the speech, come one at a time in speech order. For each, we predict how a Stoic listener would hear it:

  • Common ground: a Stoic could already agree with the words.
  • Something new: a Stoic would hear a claim his philosophy did not make.

After each prediction, the answer appears with a short note on the Stoic background, and the line is placed on a strip from the beginning of the speech to its end, in the upper lane for common ground or the lower lane for something new.

# Line (paraphrase) Acts Answer Stoic or Epicurean echo 1 "I see that in every way you are very religious." 17:22 Common ground Stoic respect for piety 2 God does not live in shrines made by human hands. 17:24 Common ground Zeno: no need for temples 3 God is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything. 17:25 Common ground Stoics and Epicureans: the divine needs nothing 4 From one ancestor God made every nation. 17:26 Common ground One human community, citizens of one world 5 God is not far from each one of us. 17:27 Common ground Seneca: God is near you, with you, within you 6 "For we too are his offspring." 17:28 Common ground Aratus, Phaenomena 5; Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus 7 The divine is not like an image of gold, silver, or stone. 17:29 Common ground Stoic criticism of images 8 God now commands all people everywhere to repent. 17:30 Something new A command from a personal God 9 God has fixed a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed. 17:31 Something new Stoics: endless cycles of fire, no single judgment 10 God has given proof by raising that man from the dead. 17:31 Something new No school expected a body raised to life

The tally is seven and three. After line 10, the sim shows what Acts says happened next: at the mention of the resurrection some scoffed, others said they would hear him again, and a few joined him, among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris. The scoffing comes exactly at the break.

Reading the answers carefully. "Common ground" means that a Stoic could assent to the words, not that Paul and the Stoics meant the same thing by them. For a Stoic, the divine reason pervades the world and is in a sense the world; in the speech, God made the world and is distinct from it. Some scholars, such as C. Kavin Rowe, argue that the speech uses Greek vocabulary to say something quite different from the start, so the overlap is in the words more than in the worldview. Nearly every idea in lines 2 to 7 also has roots in the Hebrew scriptures, which the speech does not quote. The answers follow the usual scholarly reading, and the sim says so; Stoics were not all alike.

Two readerships. For many Christian readers, this is Paul's own proclamation and a model for speaking about faith to people of another culture. Most historians read it as a speech Luke composed, as ancient historians commonly did, to give the sense of what Paul said; its themes still match what Paul's letters say he told Gentiles. The sim works the same way for both readings: it asks only how the lines would sound to a Stoic in the audience Luke describes.

The quotations. "For we too are his offspring" is from Aratus of Soli, Phaenomena line 5, a 3rd-century BCE poem written under Stoic influence; Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus has a similar line. The line before it, "In him we live and move and have our being," is attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides only by much later Christian writers, and that attribution is uncertain, so the sim does not use it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the line in the panel and its reference in Acts.
  2. Predict with 1 Common ground or 2 Something new (or press 1 or 2). Only the first prediction counts.
  3. Read the feedback and the Stoic background. The line joins the strip in its lane, with a green border if you were right and a red dashed border if not. The tally beside each lane appears after each reveal.
  4. Press Next line (or Enter). After line 10, press See the reaction.
  5. On the final screen, click any line on the strip to read it again. Try Again repeats all ten lines.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 16, "Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus", before or after climbing the Areopagus. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: Stoicism, the Epicureans, Paul in Athens, the Areopagus, Paul and the Stoics, the Areopagus speech and its five moves, and Aratus. Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate the lines of Paul's Areopagus speech that build on what Stoic listeners already believed from the lines that ask them to accept something new, judging at least 8 of 10 lines correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (8 min): Work through the ten lines. Before each answer, ask: Could Zeno, Seneca, or Epictetus have said this?
  2. Find the turn (2 min): On the final strip, where does the speech change lanes? Which of the chapter's five moves does that match?
  3. Discuss (5 min): Why might a speaker build seven lines of common ground before asking for anything? Is the common ground only in the words, or in the ideas too? Think of a time you had to persuade someone who did not share your starting point.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt, including lines 9 and 10. A follow-up question: Line 6 quotes a Greek poet. Why would quoting Aratus persuade this audience more than quoting scripture? A strong answer says that Aratus was the listeners' own poet, writing under Stoic influence, so the quotation starts from what they already accepted.

docs.title: Who Could Vote in Athens?
docs.text: Run the Who Could Vote in Athens? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Athens called itself a democracy, a city ruled by its people. This MicroSim asks how many of its people that was. One stacked bar shows everyone living in Attica around 431 BCE, at the start of the Peloponnesian War, in four groups. Only the first group, the adult male citizens, could vote. A thick line divides them from the three groups who could not. A second bar shows a full Assembly of 6,000 on the Pnyx against the same total.

Group Estimate range Default Could vote? Adult male citizens 30,000–50,000 40,000 Yes Citizens' wives, daughters, and young sons 70,000–130,000 100,000 No Metics, of all ages 20,000–40,000 30,000 No Enslaved people 60,000–100,000 80,000 No

The calculation is simple: the voting share is the citizens divided by everyone, times 100. At the defaults that is 40,000 ÷ 250,000 = 16 percent, about one person in six. With these ranges the share can never rise above 25.0 percent (50,000 ÷ 200,000) or fall below 10.0 percent (30,000 ÷ 300,000).

Every number here is an estimate. No ancient census of Attica survives. Historians build these figures from scattered evidence: Thucydides' count of Athens's soldiers in 431 BCE (2.13), the size of the meeting place on the Pnyx, grain imports, and remarks by ancient writers. The ranges are the chapter's rounded summary of most modern estimates, and the sim labels them as such. A range is not a mistake; it is an honest report of how thin the evidence is.

Some estimates fall outside these ranges, and it is worth knowing which way they pull:

  • Citizens. A. W. Gomme (1933) estimated about 43,000 adult male citizens in 431 BCE. Mogens Herman Hansen argued for a higher figure, perhaps as many as 60,000, before the plague and the war cut the number sharply. With 60,000 citizens and the other groups at their minimums, the share would reach about 29 percent: still fewer than one person in three.
  • Enslaved people. Estimates vary more than for any other group, from about 20,000–30,000 (A. H. M. Jones) to about 115,000 (Gomme). The orator Hyperides spoke of 150,000 enslaved people in Attica in the 4th century BCE, which historians treat as an impression, not a count.
  • The Pnyx. In its first form the Assembly place probably held about 6,000 people, the number required for certain votes; estimates for its capacity run from about 6,000 to 13,000.

The sim's conclusion survives every one of these alternatives: the people who voted were a minority of the people who lived under their decisions.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the bar. Each segment shows its estimate; the share of voters is hidden as ? until you work it out.
  2. Challenge 1: type the percent of everyone who could vote, then press Check (or Enter). You have two attempts; the first wrong answer gives a hint, the second shows the worked answer.
  3. Challenge 2: the four sliders unlock. Set them to give voters the largest share the evidence allows, watching the share update, then press Check.
  4. Challenge 3: the estimates return to their defaults. Type the percent of everyone who sat in a full Assembly of 6,000.
  5. Press Explore freely to unlock the sliders and test the limits yourself. Try Again repeats the three challenges.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 16, "Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus". Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: Athenian democracy, the Assembly, the Pnyx, Athenian citizenship, metics, enslaved people, and the idea of an estimate given as a range. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Calculate the share of Attica's population that could vote around 431 BCE from estimated ranges for four groups, to within one percentage point, and identify the combination of estimates that gives the largest possible share.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (1 min): Before touching the sim, guess: what share of the people of Athens could vote? Write the guess down.
  2. Calculate (5 min): Work through the three challenges. Compare your prediction with the answer to challenge 1.
  3. Test the limits (2 min): In free exploration, find the smallest share the ranges allow. Which group's estimate moves the share most?
  4. Discuss (2 min): A full Assembly was about one person in forty. In what sense was Athens ruled by its people, and in what sense was it not?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges, each within two attempts: 16.0 percent (±1.0), the settings 50,000 / 70,000 / 20,000 / 60,000 for 25.0 percent, and 2.4 percent (±0.2). Moving the sliders freely is exploration, not evidence. A follow-up question: A historian proposes 60,000 citizens. Does that overturn the chapter's point? A strong answer computes the new maximum, about 29 percent, and notes that voters remain a minority.

  2. A. W. Gomme, The Population of Athens in the Fifth and Fourth Centuries B.C. (Oxford: Blackwell, 1933). The classic reconstruction from Thucydides' military figures: about 43,000 adult male citizens and about 115,000 enslaved people in 431 BCE.
  3. Mogens Herman Hansen, The Athenian Democracy in the Age of Demosthenes (Oxford: Blackwell, 1991), and Three Studies in Athenian Demography (Copenhagen, 1988). The case for a larger citizen body in 431 BCE and for a Pnyx holding about 6,000.

  6. Pnyx — Wikipedia. The three building phases of the Assembly place and estimates of its capacity, from about 6,000 to 13,000.
  7. Metic and Slavery in ancient Greece — Wikipedia. The legal status of resident foreigners and enslaved people in Athens.

docs.title: How Calibrated Are You?
docs.text: Run the How Calibrated Are You? MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A forecaster is well calibrated when the things they call "70 percent likely" happen about 70 percent of the time. This game turns that standard on ourselves. We state the chance that each of twelve statements from this book is true, from 0 to 100 percent in steps of 10, and commit before the answer appears. Then the sim scores the record two ways.

The Brier score is the average, over all twelve statements, of \( (p - o)^2 \), where \( p \) is our probability as a fraction and \( o \) is 1 if the statement was true and 0 if false. Lower is better: 0 is perfect, 1 is the worst possible. Saying 50 percent on everything scores exactly 0.25 every time, which makes 0.25 the baseline to beat: never wrong, never useful. The Brier score rewards both calibration and sharpness, being willing to say 90 or 10 percent when we have reason to.

The reliability table groups our answers by confidence. An answer above 50 percent leans "true" with that confidence; an answer below 50 leans "false" with confidence 100 minus the answer (so 30 percent counts as a 70 percent lean toward false); 50 percent has no lean. For each confidence level from 60 to 100 percent the table shows how many answers we gave and how many leaned the right way. The calibration chart (also called a reliability diagram) plots the same rows: stated confidence across, percent right up. Points on the dashed diagonal are well calibrated, points below it are overconfident, and points above it are underconfident.

To judge our own record (J1), the sim compares our average confidence \( c \) with the percentage of leaned answers that were right, \( h \). If \( c \) is more than 10 points above \( h \) the verdict is overconfident; more than 10 points below, underconfident; otherwise about right. At least 6 of the 12 answers must lean one way, or there is no record to judge.

Part B shows two illustrative forecasters for Delphi, from the chapter's worked example:

Forecaster Forecast Days Days with rain Brier score A 70% chance of rain 10 7 \( (7 \times 0.09 + 3 \times 0.49) \div 10 = 0.21 \) B 90% chance of rain 10 6 \( (6 \times 0.01 + 4 \times 0.81) \div 10 = 0.33 \)

A is well calibrated. B is overconfident by 30 points, and B's confident record scores worse than the 0.25 a forecaster would get by always saying 50 percent.

The twelve statements, with the chapters they come from:

# Statement True? 1 Mount Parnassus rises more than 2,000 m above sea level. True (2,457 m, Chapter 17) 2 Delphi is more than 300 km by road from Athens. False (about 180 km, Chapter 18) 3 The Oracle of Delphi gave answers for more than 1,000 years. True (about 1,140 years, Chapter 17) 4 The Byzantine Empire lasted longer than the oracle did. False (1,123 years against about 1,140, Chapter 17) 5 Herodotus wrote down the Croesus prophecy within 20 years of the fall of Sardis. False (about 115 to 120 years later, Chapter 17) 6 Joseph Fontenrose collected more than 500 Delphic responses. True (about 535, Chapter 17) 7 More than 4,000 lead question tablets survive from the oracle of Zeus at Dodona. True (Chapter 17) 8 The Temple of Apollo whose ruins we saw at Delphi was finished in the 6th century BCE. False (about 330 BCE, Chapter 17) 9 At Salamis, Athens supplied almost half of the Greek ships. True (180 of 378, Chapter 15) 10 The council of the Amphictyonic League had 24 votes. True (Chapter 17) 11 Fewer than 100 records of freed slaves survive at Delphi. False (more than a thousand, Chapter 18) 12 The Athenian Treasury at Delphi was rebuilt from its original blocks in the 20th century. True (1903–1906, Chapter 18)

What is uncertain. Twelve answers is a small sample; forecasters are judged over hundreds. With so few answers, luck alone can move the percent right by 10 points or more, so the J1 verdict describes this one record, not a lasting trait. The 10-point band for "about right" is a rule of thumb, not a statistical test. The forecasters' records are illustrative, not real data. Some numbers in the statements are approximate in the sources, such as the oracle's start date (at least about 750 BCE) and the count of Fontenrose's responses.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the statement and move the Chance true slider to the probability that it is true. The gauge shows which way we lean and how confidently.
  2. Press Commit (or Enter). The answer, its reason, and our score on that statement appear. A committed probability cannot be changed.
  3. Press Next statement and continue through all twelve. The strip at the top keeps each answer, green when the lean was right, red when wrong, gray at 50 percent.
  4. After statement 12, press See my record. Study the Brier score, the reliability table and the chart, then answer J1 (keys 1 to 3). The verdict with our average confidence and percent right appears.
  5. Press The forecasters and answer J2 and J3. Finish shows the result. Try Again clears all twelve answers and the judgments.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers who have read the Delphi chapters. Duration: 15 minutes. Prerequisites: probability, prediction uncertainty, model calibration, overconfident, underconfident, and Brier score (Chapter 19, "Prediction Uncertainty" and "Model Calibration"). Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Assess whether one's own probability judgments, and those of two weather forecasters, are overconfident, underconfident, or well calibrated, by stating probabilities for twelve statements and judging the results against a reliability table, with all three assessments correct.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Play (8 min): State a probability for each statement. Use 50 percent only when we truly have no idea, and 100 percent only when we would bet anything on it.
  2. Judge yourself (3 min): Before answering J1, look at the 90 and 100 percent rows. Were those answers right as often as claimed?
  3. Judge the forecasters (2 min): Answer J2 and J3. Why does B score worse than always saying 50 percent?
  4. Discuss (2 min): A chatbot states a museum's closing time in the same confident tone whether it is sure or guessing. What would a calibrated chatbot do differently?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 3 of 3 judgments correct on the first attempt. Stating the twelve probabilities is the data for J1, not itself evidence. As a follow-up, ask: A forecaster said "70 percent chance of rain" and it stayed dry. Was the forecast wrong? A strong answer says that one day cannot show it, because a 70 percent forecast expects dry weather about 3 days in 10; only the record over many such days can.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Glenn W. Brier, "Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability," Monthly Weather Review 78, no. 1 (1950): 1–3. The paper that introduced the Brier score.
  2. Brier score — Wikipedia. The formula, its range, and its decomposition into reliability, resolution and uncertainty.
  3. Allan H. Murphy and Robert L. Winkler, "Reliability of Subjective Probability Forecasts of Precipitation and Temperature," Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C (Applied Statistics) 26, no. 1 (1977): 41–47. Evidence that professional weather forecasters are well calibrated.
  4. Sarah Lichtenstein, Baruch Fischhoff and Lawrence D.   6. Chuan Guo, Geoff Pleiss, Yu Sun and Kilian Q. Weinberger, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks," Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning (2017). Reliability diagrams for machine learning models, and the finding that many modern networks are overconfident.
  7. Saurav Kadavath and others, "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know" (2022, arXiv:2207.05221). Measures how well large language models' stated confidence matches their accuracy.
  8. p5.js — p5.js 2.3.4, the library used to draw the MicroSim.

docs.title: Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian?
docs.text: Run the Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The classical orders are the three related systems of design that Greek architects used for a column and the beam it carries: the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. Each order fixes the shape of the base, the shaft, and the capital, and of the three layers of the entablature above: the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice.

This MicroSim is the practice partner of the Three Classical Orders poster, which Chapter 10 embeds a few paragraphs earlier. The poster reads one whole column at a time. This sim reads one part at a time across all three orders, and then asks us to use what we have read.

  • Explore parts reuses the poster's drawing. Choose Base, Shaft, Capital, Architrave, Frieze, or Cornice, and the part is outlined on all three columns, with a one-sentence definition for each order underneath. It opens on the capital, with the question What does the top of a column tell you?
  • Quiz gives twelve cards in a fixed order. The first six are isolated features, such as a fallen drum or a capital; the last six are real buildings on or near our route. Each card has one first attempt.

Three patterns should stand out by the end. The capital decides most cards. The flute count separates Doric (about 20 flutes meeting in sharp edges) from the other two (about 24 flutes separated by flat strips), but it cannot separate Ionic from Corinthian, so card 6 accepts either answer. And the buildings of Ionia, the coast around Ephesus, are Ionic.

The sim also targets four common mistakes: that any capital with scrolls is Corinthian (cards 2 and 11), that flutes alone name the order (card 6), that all Greek temples are Doric (card 9), and that a smooth, unfluted shaft belongs to one particular order (card 12). The features described are those of the Greek orders; the Romans later gave some Doric columns a base.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. In Explore parts, choose a part with the buttons above the drawing, or click a part on any column. Read the three definitions underneath and compare them.
  2. Press Start the quiz (or the Quiz tab).
  3. Read the card and choose Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian, with the buttons or the keys D, I, and C. Feedback appears at once.
  4. Each card joins the summary below, in the column of its correct order, marked ✓ or ✗; a wrong card also shows what we chose.
  5. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 12 the score appears: You classified n of 12. Mastery is 10. Below 10, Try again restarts from card 1 in the same order.
  6. We can return to Explore parts at any time. Answers already given do not change.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to walk through Ephesus and, later, the Acropolis of Athens. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: classical orders, base, shaft, flutes, capital, volute, acanthus, entablature, architrave, frieze, triglyph, metope, and the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders (Chapter 10, Part Three). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify twelve described column features and buildings from our route as Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Step through the six parts. For each one, say aloud whether it separates all three orders, only Doric from the others, or none of them. (The capital separates all three; the base, the shaft, and the frieze separate Doric from the other two.)
  2. Classify (7 min): Work through the twelve cards. Before each answer, name the part of the column that the card describes.
  3. Read the summary (3 min): Which cards needed the capital? Which could be settled by the base or the flutes? Why does card 6 have two right answers?
  4. Transfer (2 min): Picture the front of a courthouse, bank, or state capitol near home. Which order are its capitals?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up on site, ask: On Curetes Street a column has lost its capital, but its shaft has 24 flutes with flat strips between them, and it stands on a molded base. What can we say, and what can we not say? A strong answer says it is not Doric, because of the base and the flute pattern, but it could be Ionic or Corinthian until the capital is found.
