docs.title: Crack Linear B Like Ventris
docs.text: Run the Crack Linear B Like Ventris MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
In 1952 Michael Ventris showed that the Linear B tablets from Knossos and Pylos were written in an early form of Greek. He did it without a bilingual text: Alice Kober's patterns and his own grid of signs that shared a consonant or a vowel let one good guess unlock dozens of signs at once. This MicroSim replays a small, real piece of that work in five steps.

Step What the learner does Scored? 1. Count the signs Decide from "about 90 sound-signs" what kind of script this is Practice 2. Kober's triplet Decide what the changing signs of a-mi-ni-so, a-mi-ni-si-jo, a-mi-ni-si-ja share; two signs join one grid row Practice 3. Guess the place names Match three sign groups found only at Knossos to Knossos, Amnisos, and Tylissos (Phaistos is a distractor) using three clues Yes, first Check 4. Unlock the grid Watch eight signs get values from the place names, then the signs of the next tablet No 5. Read the tripod tablet Predict the objects named by four words, then see the scribe's pictograms Yes, first Check

The signs are real Linear B characters from the Unicode Linear B Syllabary block, drawn with the Noto Sans Linear B font and labeled with their sign numbers from Emmett Bennett's catalog (B070 is ko, B052 no, B012 so, and so on). They gain sound values only when the learner unlocks them. The values are the ones Ventris and Chadwick published.

Step 3 is labeled "a simplified version of Ventris's test." Ventris's real grid grew over 20 Work Notes and had many more rows; the three clues here stand in for that pattern work. Step 5 uses the tablet Carl Blegen dug up at Pylos in 1952 and read with Ventris's values in 1953, now known as PY Ta 641. Its words are ti-ri-po-de (two tripods), qe-to-ro-we (a four-handled cup), ti-ri-o-we-e (two three-handled cups; the chapter quotes the stem ti-ri-o-we, and the same tablet also writes ti-ri-jo-we), and a-no-we (a cup with no handles). The pictograms are simplified drawings after the tablet, with the count written, as the scribe did, in short upright strokes.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Step 1: Look at the sixteen unread signs, then choose the kind of script with the buttons. A wrong answer gives a hint; try again.
  2. Step 2: Compare the three words. The highlighted sign changes from word 1 to words 2 and 3. Choose what the two signs probably share. Watch them move into one row of the grid on the right.
  3. Step 3: Read the three clues and choose a place name for each group from its menu, then press Check. Only the first Check counts; you can change wrong answers and check again for practice.
  4. Step 4: See the eight values in the grid, then press Unlock the tablet signs.
  5. Step 5: Use the word bank and the values under each sign to choose an object for each word, then press Check. The pictograms appear beside the words.
  6. On a narrow screen, and in step 5, tick Show the grid to see the grid in place of the puzzle. Start over returns to step 1.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the Linear B tablets in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum on Day 9. Duration: 15–20 minutes. Prerequisites: syllabaries and the sign-count rule (Chapter 2); Linear B and its spelling rules, including the worked example "spelling Knossos the Mycenaean way"; Alice Kober's triplets, Ventris's grid, and the place-name guess. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Solve a simplified version of the 1952 decipherment by matching three Linear B sign groups to Cretan place names with grid clues and then using the resulting sound values to predict four objects on the Pylos tripod tablet, getting all three place names and at least 3 of 4 objects right on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (2 min): Spell Knossos, Amnisos, and Tylissos the Mycenaean way on paper, using the chapter's spelling rules.
  2. Solve (10 min): Work through the five steps. In step 3, say aloud which clue rules out each wrong name before you check.
  3. Reflect (3 min): In step 4, find si in the grid. Why did it need no new guess?
  4. Discuss (5 min): Why did the tripod tablet convince the doubters when the place names alone did not? (The scribe's pictures were independent evidence that no one could have arranged to fit Ventris's values.)

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is all three place names right on the first Check in step 3 and at least 3 of 4 objects right on the first Check in step 5. Follow-up question: A friend says Ventris "just guessed" the decipherment. What would you answer? The guess was a tested hypothesis: Kober's patterns and the grid meant one correct guess gave values to many signs, and those values then read new tablets, like the tripod tablet, correctly.

docs.title: Planning Day 3 Around the Prayer Times
docs.text: Run the Planning Day 3 Around the Prayer Times MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Day 3 of the trip, Friday, November 13, 2026, is the Ottoman day in Istanbul, and it falls on the day of congregational prayer. Mosques welcome visitors, but not during prayer, and on a Friday the midday closure is the longest of the week. This MicroSim turns that into a real planning problem: fit five activities into a day from 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM so that every mosque visit lands in an open window.

The grid shows the three prayers that fall inside our day, at the times the chapter calculates from the sun's position for Istanbul on that date:

Prayer Time Mosques closed to visitors (in this exercise) Friday prayer (in place of noon prayer) about 12:55 PM 11:30 AM to 2:30 PM Afternoon prayer about 3:25 PM 3:00 to 4:00 PM Sunset prayer about 5:50 PM 5:30 to 6:00 PM

The closure windows and Topkapı's hours are illustrative, chosen to match the usual pattern: about an hour around each prayer, longer at Friday noon. On the day, check the Diyanet's prayer times and each site's posted hours.

The five activities are Topkapı Palace with the Harem (3 hours, Sultanahmet), the Blue Mosque (1 hour, Sultanahmet), the Süleymaniye Mosque and its courtyard (1 hour, Süleymaniye), the Rüstem Pasha Mosque (30 minutes, Süleymaniye) and lunch (1 hour, either area). The rules are:

  • A mosque visit may not touch any shaded closure band.
  • Topkapı is not affected by prayer, but it must finish by 5:00 PM.
  • Activities may not overlap.
  • Walking between Sultanahmet and Süleymaniye takes 30 minutes, so two sights in different areas need at least one empty slot between them. Lunch can be eaten in either area, so it never needs a walk of its own.
  • All five activities must be placed.

More than one schedule is valid. After three unsuccessful checks, Show One Solution reveals one of them.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question in the panel: It's Friday. When can we visit the mosques?
  2. Drag each card from the right onto the day grid. A dashed outline shows the 30-minute slot where the card will snap. Each placed block shows its start and end times.
  3. To move a block, drag it again. To remove it, drag it off the grid.
  4. Press Check. A valid plan turns every block green. Otherwise the panel lists every broken rule, and each block that breaks one gets a red border and a "!".
  5. Adjust and check again. The counter in the control row counts your checks.
  6. Reset clears the grid and the counter.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 3 in Istanbul. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: daily prayer, prayer times, Friday prayer and mosque etiquette; where Topkapı Palace, the Blue Mosque, the Süleymaniye and the Rüstem Pasha Mosque stand. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Solve the Day 3 scheduling problem by placing five activities into a 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM day so that every mosque visit falls inside a window when mosques are open to visitors, producing a valid schedule within three checks.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the bands (2 min): Before dragging anything, find the three dashed prayer lines and the shaded closures around them. Which closure is longest, and why?
  2. Solve (6 min): Build a full schedule and press Check. Read every message before moving a card. Aim for a valid plan within three checks.
  3. Find the windows (3 min): When your plan is valid, list the open windows a mosque visit can use on a Friday. Only two are long: the morning, and 4:00 to 5:30 PM.
  4. Change the day (3 min): Suppose Day 3 were a Saturday, with an ordinary noon prayer and a closure of about an hour around it. Which of your constraints would relax, and how would you rearrange the day?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is a valid schedule within three checks. Follow-up questions:

  • Why is a list of prayer times from last week not good enough for this plan? (Prayer times follow the sun, so they shift a few minutes every day.)
  • Why is noon on Friday a poor time to visit a famous mosque, even though the mosque is full of people? (It is closed to visitors for the congregational prayer and sermon.)

docs.title: Delphi After the Oracle
docs.text: Run the Delphi After the Oracle MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The ruins we walk at Delphi were not always visible. After the oracle closed, the sanctuary was built over, and for centuries it lay under a mountain village called Kastri. Its return happened in four stages:

Stage What happens to the site Silenced The oracle closes and the sanctuary is abandoned or built over. Found Travelers identify the site from ancient texts and inscriptions. Dug up Excavation reveals and recovers the sanctuary and its finds. Shown The site and its finds are rebuilt, displayed, performed in, or recognized for visitors.

This MicroSim reveals nine events one at a time, in date order. Each starts with only its date and label. We predict its stage first; then the description, the correct stage, and the reason appear, and the event drops into its stage's row on the timeline.

# Date Event Stage 1 391–392 CE Theodosian Decrees: sacrifice banned, temples closed, the oracle falls silent Silenced 2 1436 Cyriac of Ancona visits and copies inscriptions Found 3 1676 Jacob Spon and George Wheler identify the village of Kastri as Delphi Found 4 1892 The French School at Athens, led by Théophile Homolle, begins the great excavation after Kastri is moved west Dug up 5 1896 Excavators find the bronze Charioteer buried near the temple Dug up 6 1903 The first museum opens to display the finds Shown 7 1903–1906 The Athenian Treasury is rebuilt from its original blocks, paid for by the city of Athens Shown 8 1927 Angelos and Eva Palmer-Sikelianos stage Prometheus Bound at the first Delphic Festival Shown 9 1987 Delphi is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site Shown

Two patterns stand out at the end. More than a thousand years separate the silence from the first rediscovery: from 392 to 1436 CE is 1,044 years. And four of the nine events are about how Delphi is shown, not how it was found. What we see today was shaped by museums, rebuilding, and festivals as well as by the excavators.

About the time scale. No events fall between 400 and 1400 CE, so the timeline squeezes those 1,000 years ten to one into a hatched band. Everything else is drawn to scale, and the final view labels the full length of the gap. The modern events crowd together, so from event 4 on the timeline moves to a close-up of 1880–2000; Full span and Close-up switch between the two.

Notes on the evidence. The dates follow the chapter. The French excavation is often called the Grande Fouille, "the great dig", and ran from 1892 to 1903; the moving of Kastri's houses to the new village took several years around the start of the dig, so "after Kastri is moved" is a simplification. The Delphic Festivals were held twice, in 1927 and 1930; the timeline shows the first. A Christian town occupied the site in late antiquity before the village of Kastri grew on its ruins, so "silenced" means the end of the oracle, not of all life on the slope.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the four stages on the colored buttons.
  2. Read the event's date and label. Press the stage you predict (or keys 1 to 4). Only your prediction counts, and it cannot be changed.
  3. The description, the correct stage, and the reason appear. The event's badge moves from the Next row into its stage's row; a dashed red outline marks a missed prediction.
  4. Press Next event (or Enter). After event 9, press See all stages to see every event by stage with the 1,044-year silence marked.
  5. Hover over or click any badge to read it again. Restart clears all predictions.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 18, "Day 12: Delphi", before walking from the modern village to the site. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: the closing of the oracle and the Theodosian Decrees (Chapters 3 and 17), the village of Kastri, the French excavation of Delphi, the Athenian Treasury, the Charioteer of Delphi, the Delphi Archaeological Museum, and the Delphic Festivals in the Theater of Delphi (Chapter 18). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify nine events in Delphi's history after the oracle into the four stages silenced, found, dug up, and shown, with at least 8 of 9 correct, predicting each event's stage before its description is revealed.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the stages (1 min): Say in your own words the difference between found and dug up.
  2. Predict (6 min): Work through the nine events in order.
  3. Discuss (3 min): On the final view, why might travelers in 1436 and 1676 have recognized Delphi without digging at all? What did the people of Kastri lose so that event 4 could happen?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 8 of 9 predictions correct. A follow-up question: Is the rebuilt Athenian Treasury part of how Delphi was found, or how it is shown? A strong answer says shown: it was already found and dug up, and rebuilding it from its blocks made it something visitors can see.

docs.title: A Day at the Oracle
docs.text: Run the A Day at the Oracle MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A consultation at Delphi was not a matter of walking in and asking. It was a sequence of ritual steps, and several of them were gates that could stop a consultant before the god was ever asked. No ancient writer sets out the whole procedure in one place, so the order used here is the chapter's reconstruction, pieced together from Plutarch, Herodotus, Euripides, Aeschylus, inscriptions and the plan of the temple.

The MicroSim has two parts.

Part 1: put the day in order. Eight step cards appear shuffled. We click them into eight slots and press Check order. Each broken rule is named, for example The goat is tested before it is sacrificed, and each card is marked green if it sits in a place it can hold in a valid order. Steps 2 and 3 (purifying at the Castalian Spring and paying the fee) may come in either order; every other step has one place. After a second invalid Check, the sim shows the chapter's order so the walk can begin.

Step What happens Main source 1 Arrive on a consultation day, usually said to be the seventh of the month, in one of the nine months when Apollo was present Plutarch, Greek Questions 9 (originally only on the seventh of Bysios) 2 Purify with water from the Castalian Spring Euripides, Ion 3 Pay the fee (pelanos); a foreigner comes through a Delphian sponsor (proxenos) Euripides, Ion; Delphic inscriptions 4 The priests sprinkle a goat with cold water to test whether the god is present Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles 5 The goat is sacrificed on the great altar before the temple's east front Plutarch; the altar of the Chians 6 Wait for a turn: those with promanteia first, the rest by lot Herodotus 1.54; Aeschylus, Eumenides 7 Enter the temple, make an offering, and ask; the Pythia answers from the tripod in the adyton Plutarch; the Aegeus cup in Berlin 8 Receive the answer from the prophet, write it down, and carry it home Herodotus 7.142

Part 2: walk through the day. The consultation then plays out one step at a time. At steps 4, 6 and 8, a checkpoint stops the walk and asks us to commit to one of four answers before the outcome is shown:

  • A, the goat test. The goat does not tremble. What happens? There is no consultation: the god is absent. Plutarch tells of priests who pressed on after poor omens; the Pythia answered in a strange voice, rushed out screaming, and died a few days later.
  • B, the line. A Lydian envoy of Croesus and a farmer from Attica are both waiting. The Lydian goes first: Herodotus says the Delphians gave Croesus and all Lydians promanteia, the right to consult first, and freedom from fees.
  • C, the answer. About 100 CE, the answer comes in plain prose. By Plutarch's day the god no longer answered in hexameter verse, and Plutarch wrote a dialogue defending the change.

What is uncertain. The step order is a modern reconstruction. The monthly calendar is the usual reading of the sources, but it rests on late and scattered evidence; Plutarch says that in early times the god answered only once a year. How much the prophets and other officials shaped the Pythia's words is still debated, and the step 8 card follows the chapter in having the prophet hand over the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over a card on the right to read it in full in the panel below.
  2. Click a card to put it in the next empty slot on the left. Click a placed card to take it back. Clear empties all the slots.
  3. When all eight are placed, press Check order (or Enter). Fix any broken rules and check again; there are two Checks.
  4. Press Begin the walk, then Next step (or Enter) to move through the day.
  5. At a checkpoint, choose one of the four answers (or press keys 1 to 4). Only one answer counts. Read the outcome and the source, then go on.
  6. After step 8, press See the summary. Try Again reshuffles the cards and starts over.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to visit Delphi. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Pythia, the adyton, the pelanos, the proxenos, promanteia, the prophet, the Castalian Spring, the goat test, and verse and prose answers (Chapter 17, Parts Two and Three). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Explain the sequence of a Delphic consultation, from arrival to the written answer, by placing eight steps in a valid order and choosing the correct outcome at three checkpoints.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict the gates (2 min): Before touching a card, list what could stop a consultant from ever reaching the god.
  2. Order the day (5 min): Place the eight cards and check. For each broken rule, explain why that step has to come first.
  3. Walk and predict (5 min): At each checkpoint, commit to an answer before reading the outcome, then connect the outcome to its source.
  4. Discuss (3 min): Who benefited from each gate: the god, the priests, the town of Delphi, or the favored consultants?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is a valid order within two Checks and at least 2 of 3 checkpoints correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: Name two gates that could keep a consultant from hearing the god's answer, and say who controlled each. A strong answer names the calendar (only consultation days, only nine months a year), the goat test (controlled by the priests), or the line (promanteia for favored cities and people, the lot for everyone else).

docs.text:
1. Pythia — Wikipedia. The priestess of Apollo at Delphi, the consultation calendar, the goat test, and the debate over the officials who framed the answers.
  2. Herodotus, Histories 1.54 and 7.140–143 (Perseus Digital Library). The privileges granted to Croesus and the Lydians, including promanteia and freedom from fees, and the Athenian envoys who wrote down the "wooden wall" answer.
  3. Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles (De defectu oraculorum) 46–51, in Moralia vol. V (LacusCurtius). The goat that must tremble, and the Pythia who died after a forced consultation.
  4. Plutarch, Greek Questions (Quaestiones Graecae) 9, in Moralia vol. IV. The god's birthday, the seventh of Bysios, once the only day of consultation.
  5. Plutarch, The Oracles at Delphi No Longer Given in Verse (De Pythiae oraculis), in Moralia vol. V. Why the answers came in prose by Plutarch's day.
  6. Euripides, Ion and Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–33. Purification in the Castalian Spring, the pelanos, and consultants admitted "by lot, as is the custom."
  7. Delphi — Wikipedia. The sanctuary, the Castalian Spring, and the altar of the Chians before the temple's east front.
  8. Michael Scott, Delphi: A History of the Center of the Ancient World (Princeton University Press, 2014). A modern reconstruction of the consultation procedure and its uncertainties.
  9. H. W. Parke and D. E. W. Wormell, The Delphic Oracle (Blackwell, 1956), vol. 1. The classic account of the consultation procedure and its sources.

docs.title: Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall
docs.text: Run the Read a Freedom Record on the Polygonal Wall MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The polygonal wall below the Temple of Apollo carries hundreds of inscriptions, and most of them record the same transaction: an enslaved person gaining freedom through a "sale" to Pythian Apollo. More than a thousand such manumission records survive at Delphi, most of them carved between about 200 BCE and 100 CE. They follow a standard form, and once we know the form we can read any of them.

This MicroSim shows that form as eight clauses of one record. The record is a simplified composite, not a translation of a single inscription, and the bracketed words stand for the names a real record gives. For each clause the learner chooses two answers: its name and its effect.

# Clause Name Effect 1 "In the year when [name] was archon, in the month [month]," Date Records the facts 2 "[owner's name], son of [father's name], sold to Pythian Apollo" Sale to the god Protects the freed person 3 "a woman named [name], [her homeland] by birth," Person freed Records the facts 4 "for a price of [sum] of silver, and he has received the whole price," Price Records the facts 5 "as [name] entrusted the purchase to the god, on condition that she be free and claimed by no one, doing what she wishes and going where she wishes." Freedom clause Protects the freed person 6 "Guarantor, according to the law of the city: [name]." Guarantor Protects the freed person 7 "[name] shall remain with [owner's name] for as long as he lives, doing what she is told." Paramone Limits the freed person's freedom 8 "Witnesses: the priests of Apollo, [name], [name]." Witnesses Protects the freed person

The totals carry the lesson: four clauses protect her freedom, three record the facts, and one keeps her bound. The same document guaranteed a freedom no one could later deny and, in many cases, kept the freed person serving the old household for years.

Clause 2 is the key to the whole form. The money was usually the enslaved person's own savings, handed over through the god, but the buyer on the record is Apollo. Since no human could claim a god's property, the sale itself made re-enslavement impossible. The guarantor and the witnesses were not formalities either: they were the living people who could defend the freedom if anyone challenged it.

Notes on the evidence. The clause wording follows the standard Delphic formula in simplified English. The Greek formula's key phrases are the sale to "Pythian Apollo", the entrusting of the purchase to the god (episteuse tōi theōi tan ōnan), the freedom clause "free and untouchable by anyone, doing what she wishes and going where she wishes", the guarantor "according to the law", and the paramone condition "let her remain with ... as long as he lives, doing what she is told". Real records vary: the order of clauses differs, some name two or more guarantors, many have no paramone clause at all, and some add penalties or arrangements for buying out the paramone early. Counts of the records differ between studies; "more than a thousand" is the safe figure.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the whole record. Hover over (or tap) a dotted word in the glossary line or in the record to read its definition.
  2. Clause 1 is selected. Choose its name from the eight name buttons and its effect from the three colored effect buttons. The choices appear as tags beside the clause, and the selection moves to the next unanswered clause.
  3. Click any clause to change its answers. When all eight are answered, press Check. Only the first Check counts toward mastery.
  4. Each clause is marked green or red. Click a red clause to read why: a name crossed out means the name is wrong; an effect crossed out means the name is right but the effect is wrong. Correct clauses lock.
  5. Change the red clauses and press Check again as often as you like. After the second Check, Show Answers fills in any that remain. Start Over clears everything.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 18, "Day 12: Delphi", before or after walking past the polygonal wall. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: manumission, manumission records, archon, guarantor, witnesses, paramone, and the sale to the god (Chapter 18, "Manumission Records"); inscription (Chapter 10); the polygonal wall (Chapter 18). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Deconstruct a simplified Delphic manumission record into its eight clauses, naming each clause and judging whether it protects the freed person, limits the freed person's freedom, or records the facts of the sale, with at least 7 of the 8 judgments correct.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read first (2 min): Before answering, read the record aloud and underline the single clause that sounds least like freedom.
  2. Take it apart (8 min): Name every clause and judge its effect, then press Check once and note the first score.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Why did the record need a god as the buyer? What could a former owner's heir do if the record had been a private promise instead?
  4. On site (2 min): At the polygonal wall, use the low-light trick from the chapter to find a line of letters, and imagine it as one clause of a record like this one.

docs.title: Eleven Centuries of the Oracle
docs.text: Run the Eleven Centuries of the Oracle MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Oracle of Delphi answered questions from at least the 8th century BCE until the Theodosian Decrees of 391–392 CE banned sacrifice and closed the temples. Counting across the line between BCE and CE (there was no year zero), 750 BCE to 391 CE is 750 + 391 − 1 = 1,140 years. Its peak came in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, when cities asked it where to found colonies and kings and allied Greek states filled the sanctuary with gifts. Its decline was not sudden, and it did not begin with Christianity.

This MicroSim shows fourteen dated events one at a time, deliberately out of time order. For each, we decide whether it shows the oracle's strength or a weakness or decline. Feedback gives the reason, and the event drops onto a timeline from 800 BCE to 450 CE in the row of its correct category. Each category has three cues, not only color: its own row, a triangle (▲ for strength, ▼ for weakness), and a color. A shaded band marks the oracle's 1,140-year life.

# Date Event Category 1 c. 750 BCE The sanctuary grows; the earliest dedications accumulate Strength 2 c. 630 BCE Settlers from Thera found Cyrene after repeated answers from Delphi Strength 3 548 BCE The temple burns; the Greek world and the king of Egypt pay to rebuild it Strength (trap) 4 c. 550 BCE Croesus sends a gold lion and great mixing bowls Strength 5 c. 510 BCE The Alcmaeonids bribe the Pythia, Herodotus says Weakness (trap) 6 479 BCE The Greek allies dedicate the Serpent Column after Plataea Strength 7 279 BCE A Gaulish army attacks Delphi and is driven off Strength (trap) 8 356–346 BCE The Phocians seize Delphi and melt its treasures Weakness 9 c. 87–86 BCE Sulla takes the remaining valuables Weakness 10 44 BCE Cicero writes that the oracle's answers are long silent and despised Weakness 11 67 CE Nero carries off about 500 bronze statues Weakness 12 c. 100 CE Plutarch: one Pythia is now enough where three were needed Weakness 13 by 330 CE Constantine moves the Serpent Column to Constantinople Weakness 14 391–392 CE The Theodosian Decrees end sacrifice; the Pythia falls silent Weakness

Three cards are traps. The fire of 548 BCE was damage, but the rebuilding that followed shows how much the whole world valued the oracle. The Alcmaeonid bribery happened at the height of the oracle's power, but shows its voice could be bought. The defeat of the Gauls in 279 BCE is late, but it added to the god's prestige. After card 14, a final question (not scored) asks when the signs of weakness begin to cluster: from the Third Sacred War, about 360 BCE, they run one way, yet the end took more than 700 more years.

What is uncertain. Several dates are approximate and are shown with "c.": the beginning of the oracle (legend and some archaeology push it earlier than 750 BCE), the foundation of Cyrene, and the date of Croesus' gifts, which Herodotus places before the fire of 548 BCE. The Alcmaeonid bribery and the Gauls' defeat by snow and earthquake are Herodotus' and later writers' reports, not independent records. The famous "last oracle" said to have been given to the emperor Julian (361–363 CE), announcing that Apollo's hall had fallen, survives only in much later Christian writers and is best treated as a legend; the silence after 391–392 is what the evidence supports.

Some modern writers have linked the oracle's ups and downs to geology. The geologist Jelle Zeilinga de Boer and the archaeologist John Hale, with the chemist Jeffrey Chanton and the toxicologist Henry Spiller, argued around 2001 that faults cross beneath the temple and that light gases, possibly ethylene, once rose through them, with earthquakes opening and closing their path. The faults are widely accepted, but later measurements found little or no ethylene and critics doubt any gas could have caused a trance, so the gas explanation remains debated. This timeline does not depend on it: every event here is political, financial, or religious.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card: its number, date, and event. The cards are not in time order.
  2. Choose Shows strength or Shows a weakness or decline (or press keys 1 and 2). Only the first answer counts.
  3. Read the feedback. The card appears on the timeline in its correct row; a red dashed border marks a card you missed.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 14, press Final question and answer it with the buttons or keys 1 to 4.
  5. Use Full span and Close-up: 750–250 BCE to change the view, and drag the timeline to move it. Hover over or click a card to read it again.
  6. Try Again clears all fourteen cards.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to visit Delphi. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Oracle of Delphi, Greek colonization, Croesus of Lydia, the Temple of Apollo, bribery of the oracle, Delphic neutrality, the Amphictyonic League and the Sacred Wars, Plutarch, the decline and closing of the oracle, and the oracle's long lifespan (Chapter 17). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Distinguish events that show the Oracle of Delphi's strength from events that show a weakness or decline, classifying at least 12 of 14 dated events correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before card 1, guess when the oracle's decline began. Many people guess "when Christianity arrived."
  2. Classify (8 min): For each card, ask what the event says about the institution, not just whether something bad happened.
  3. Read the shape (3 min): After card 14, look at where the ▼ markers crowd together and answer the final question.
  4. Discuss (2 min): Compare the oracle's 1,140 years with the Byzantine Empire (330–1453, 1,123 years). What kept people climbing the mountain after the treasures were gone?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 12 of 14 correct on the first attempt, with at least two of the three trap cards (3, 5 and 7) correct. As a follow-up, ask: Did the oracle decline suddenly when Christianity arrived? A strong answer says no: signs of decline begin with the Third Sacred War in 356–346 BCE, about 700 years before the Theodosian Decrees, and even then there were revivals, such as the defeat of the Gauls and the new building Plutarch saw around 100 CE.

  2. Delphi — Wikipedia. The sanctuary, the fire of 548 BCE and the rebuilding, the Serpent Column, the Gaulish attack of 279 BCE, and the plundering by Sulla and Nero.
  3. Herodotus, Histories 1.50–51, 2.180, 4.150–158, 5.62–63 and 9.81 (Perseus Digital Library). Croesus' gifts, the temple fire and Amasis' contribution, Cyrene, the Alcmaeonid bribery, and the dedication after Plataea.

docs.title: Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline
docs.text: Run the Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
More than five thousand years separate the first Bronze Age villages from our trip, and that span is hard to feel. This timeline draws the nine periods of Eastern Mediterranean history to scale, from the Bronze Age (c. 3200 BCE) to the modern era (2026 CE), so their lengths can be compared by eye. The Bronze Age fills almost half the line. The Classical period, the age of the Parthenon and Socrates, is a thin sliver, and the Byzantine period is longer than most travelers expect.

The timeline shows periods only. Events are left out on purpose, so the band lengths are the one thing to look at. Clicking a band names one or two sites on our route from that period. The full version, with 29 events and the chapter that covers each, is the Events of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline in the appendix.

The timeline is also a short quiz. It asks six questions about proportion, one at a time. Each answer is committed before the relevant bands are highlighted and their lengths shown, so the display checks the learner's mental picture instead of handing over the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Answer question 1. The nine bands are visible at full scale. Choose an answer by judging the band lengths.
  2. Read the feedback. The bands named in the question are highlighted, their lengths in years appear on the bands, and the timeline zooms to them. The feedback explains the answer either way.
  3. Press Next. The view returns to the full span and the next question appears.
  4. After question 6 the right-hand panel shows the final score. Press Full span to see all nine periods, then click any band to read its dates, length, and the sites on our route from that period.
  5. Restart clears the score and returns to question 1.

Drag the timeline sideways to pan. The mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the timeline.

docs.title: Reading the Dates
docs.text: Years BCE are counted down and years CE are counted up, and there is no year zero. The axis marks the line between them as BCE | CE. The quiz uses the chapter's rule for spans that cross that line: add the two numbers and subtract one. From 31 BCE to 330 CE is 31 + 330 − 1 = 360 years. Dates marked "c." (circa) are approximate. Period boundaries are rounded and vary from place to place, so each band's infobox says so.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults who love the history of civilization, culture, and food.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Compare the order and length of the nine periods of Eastern Mediterranean history by answering six proportion questions before the answers are revealed, scoring at least 5 of 6 (Bloom: Understand, verb: compare).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The sections "The Historical Timeline" and "BCE and CE Dating" in Chapter 1: historical timeline, period (era), BCE and CE dating, no year zero, and the names of the nine periods.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): Answer the six questions in order by eye, without working out the numbers first. Note which answers surprised you.
  2. Explore (3 min): After question 6, click each band and find the period of the site you most want to see.
  3. Reflect (2 min): Using the 24-hour clock from the chapter, say in one sentence why the Classical period feels long but is not.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Exploring the timeline and clicking bands are practice, not evidence. Each question targets a misconception:

Question Misconception it tests 1. Bronze Age or Classical? The Classical period was long because it is famous. 2. How much of the timeline is the Bronze Age? Prehistory is a short prelude to "real" history. 3. Byzantine or Ottoman? The Byzantine period was a short epilogue to Rome. 4. Classical + Hellenistic + Roman, or Byzantine? The Byzantine period was a short epilogue to Rome. 5. Length of the Roman period, 31 BCE to 330 CE? Spans across the BCE/CE line are found by subtracting. 6. When was writing almost unknown? Writing in Greece was continuous from the Bronze Age on.

docs.title: Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map
docs.text: Run the Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapter 1 opens with a map because almost every later chapter leans on it. This MicroSim is that map, drawn like an atlas plate from Natural Earth coastlines. Only the places named in "Part One: The Map" carry labels, along with the seas and the two countries we travel through, Greece and Turkey.

Twelve places are key regions, the ones the rest of the book keeps returning to:

Kind Key regions Seas Eastern Mediterranean, Aegean Sea Straits Bosphorus, Dardanelles Land regions Thrace (European Turkey), Anatolia, Ionia, Attica and Central Greece Islands Crete, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese, the North Aegean Islands

Nine more places are labeled as context and can also be clicked: the Black Sea, the Sea of Marmara, the Ionian Sea, the Sporades, the Saronic Islands, the Ionian Islands, Cyprus, the Levant, and Egypt.

Historic regions such as Ionia and Thrace never had fixed borders, so their inland edges are drawn as dashed lines and called approximate. Their coastlines are exact.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  • Hover over any region, sea, or strait to see an infobox: what kind of place it is, its other names, a one-line summary, and which of our stops are in it.
  • Click a key region to explore it. It turns olive green, gets a ✓ on the map and on the checklist, and a small burst of confetti marks the find. The detail panel below the map gives the fuller story.
  • Explore all 12 and a confetti cannon fires.
  • Can't find one? Click its name on the Checklist and the map zooms to it and makes it flash. That gives no credit: the region still has to be clicked on the map.
  • Drag to pan, and use + and − to zoom in on the islands. The mouse wheel scrolls the page as usual, not the map.

Find the Region mode hides the names of the 12 key regions and asks for them one at a time, in random order:

  • A correct click turns the region green and moves on.
  • A wrong click names the place that was clicked and gives a hint about where to look.
  • After two misses, or after pressing Show me, the answer flashes yellow and must be clicked to continue. It then counts as found, but not on the first try.
  • The score is the number found on the first try. Finishing fires the confetti cannon.

Keyboard users can Tab to each region and press Enter to click it.

docs.title: Learning Events (xAPI)
docs.text:
This MicroSim records what a student does as xAPI statements, the standard format a Learning Record Store reads. It does not send them anywhere yet.

Students never see the statements. To watch them arrive, add ?show-events=true to the URL, either the sim's own URL or the URL of a page that embeds it, such as this page. An Event stream tab then appears under the map, already open. Copy JSON copies every statement.

Verb When it is emitted What it carries initialized The map loads, or a Find challenge starts — experienced A hover of at least 0.6 seconds in Explore mode how long the hover lasted interacted A click on a region in Explore mode, or a mode change first visit or revisit, count explored asked Show me, or a click on a checklist name which region answered A click in Find mode correct or not, what was clicked, attempt number completed All 12 explored, or the Find challenge finished first-try score out of 12

Shorter hovers are treated as the mouse passing over, not as evidence, and are not recorded. The actor is always anonymous. Each statement is also announced to the page in three ways a future connection can use: a microsim:xapi window event, a postMessage to the page that embeds the iframe, and window.MicroSimEvents.statements().

  2. Notice the straits (2 minutes). Zoom in on the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. Explain to a travel partner why whoever held these two narrow waters could "tax, feed, or starve" the cities of the Black Sea.

docs.title: Trade Routes of the Eastern Mediterranean
docs.text: Run the Trade Routes of the Eastern Mediterranean MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
In the Eastern Mediterranean, the cities that grew rich, and the cities that were fought over, sat on the sea lanes. This map shows 16 places, from Venice to Alexandria and from Chersonesos in Crimea to Byblos in Lebanon. Gold dots are stops on our trip; dark blue dots are places we will not visit but that explain the ones we will.

Four trade routes are hidden at the start, one from each of four eras:

Route Era Path Cargo A Bronze Age, c. 1300 BCE Byblos → Enkomi → Uluburun wreck → Rhodes → Knossos → Mycenae Copper, tin, glass, ivory, ebony B Classical, 5th century BCE Chersonesos → Byzantium → Troy → Piraeus Black Sea wheat for Athens C Hellenistic, 3rd century BCE Byzantium → Troy → Rhodes → Alexandria Grain, wine, and goods passing Rhodes's harbor D Byzantine and Venetian, 13th–15th centuries CE Venice → Heraklion → Byzantium Silk and spices from the Silk Roads; Cretan wine and grain

Each route appears only after we answer the question about it, so we have to reason from the map first: where are the narrow places, and who sits on them? Once drawn, a route stays visible, and an arrow on each leg shows the direction of travel.

These are simplified routes, not records of single voyages. Each line runs through the listed places in order, with a few unmarked turning points added so that it stays on the water rather than cutting across Cyprus, the Peloponnese, or Anatolia. Real ships hugged the coasts and waited out the winter storms.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read question 1 and look at the map before answering. Each question has one attempt.
  2. Click an answer. The correct choice turns green, a wrong choice turns red, the explanation appears, and the related route is drawn.
  3. Press Next question. Questions 2 and 3 both use route B, the grain route to Athens.
  4. After question 5, press See result for your score. All four routes are then on the map.
  5. Click any dot to read what the place was and which day of our trip it falls on. Click a route to read its era and cargo.
  6. Zoom with the + and − buttons and drag to pan; the mouse wheel scrolls the page instead of the map.
  7. Restart hides the routes, clears the score, and shuffles the order of the answer choices.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: trade route, chokepoint, the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, the Uluburun shipwreck, and the Bronze Age, Classical, Hellenistic, and Byzantine periods. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Infer why places on chokepoints and sea lanes became rich or fought over, by predicting the outcome of five route-based questions before each route is revealed, scoring at least 4 of 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): Answer the five questions in order, committing to an answer before each route appears. Say the reason aloud or jot it down before clicking.
  2. Look for repeats (3 min): With all four routes drawn, find the places that appear on routes from more than one era. The Bosphorus at Byzantium and the Dardanelles at Troy lie on routes B, C, and D.
  3. Find the crossings (3 min): Locate Rhodes and Crete. Explain why an island where routes cross could grow rich without ruling much land.
  4. Connect to the trip (3 min): Click the gold dots. For each trip stop, name the route it sits on and the cargo that passed it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: The Isthmus of Corinth is a chokepoint of a different kind, a narrow strip of land between two seas. What could a city there profit from? A strong answer names harbor fees and tolls on cargo and ships carried across the isthmus, and control of the only land road into the Peloponnese.

  2. Battle of Aegospotami — Wikipedia. The 405 BCE defeat that cut Athens's grain route through the Dardanelles.
  3. Byzantine–Rhodian War (220 BC) — Wikipedia. The war over Byzantium's Bosphorus tolls, reported by Polybius.

docs.title: Documented, Debated, or Tradition?
docs.text:
Run the Documented, Debated, or Tradition? MicroSim Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Ephesus and nearby Selçuk hold some of the most visited Christian sites in Turkey: the Church of Mary, where a council met in 431 CE; the Basilica of St. John on the hill of Ayasuluk; the House of the Virgin Mary on Bülbül Dağı; and a hilltop tower called St. Paul's Prison. Guides tell all of their stories in the same confident voice. This MicroSim asks us to separate them by the strength of the evidence, using three ratings:

Rating Definition Documented Contemporary or near-contemporary written or archaeological evidence supports it. Debated Some early evidence supports it, but scholars disagree about whether it is reliable. Tradition only First recorded long after the events, with no early evidence for or against.

Ten claims appear one at a time, in a fixed order. For each one we choose a rating, then one of two reasons, shown in random order. A card counts only when both the rating and the reason are right, because a correct label reached for the wrong reason is a lucky guess, not a judgment. Five claims are documented, two debated, and three tradition only.

The sim targets four common mistakes:

  • A real ancient building proves the story attached to it. Claims 3 and 4 are about the same tower. The tower is securely dated to the city wall of Lysimachus, early 3rd century BCE; the name "Paul's Prison" is a later local tradition, since Acts mentions no imprisonment in Ephesus.
  • "Tradition" means "false." It does not. It means the evidence cannot settle the question either way (claim 9).
  • Papal visits prove an identification. Three popes have visited the House of the Virgin Mary, but the Catholic Church has not ruled on whether Mary lived there (claim 8).
  • Everything in Acts is either proven or invented. The riot of the silversmiths is told only in Acts, a generation later, but its local details fit the city: plausible, not proven (claims 6 and 7).

One detail is worth knowing for claim 1: the council's acts name the church "called Mary" in which it met. Identifying that church with the ruined church near the harbor is the standard view, though archaeologists have debated exactly when the older Roman hall was converted into a church.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the three rating definitions under the colored headings.
  2. Read the claim in the white panel and ask: how strong is the evidence?
  3. Choose a rating with the buttons below the columns, by clicking a column, or with keys 1 to 3.
  4. Two reasons appear inside the panel. Choose the better one by clicking it or pressing A or B.
  5. Read the feedback. The correct reason is outlined in green, and a wrong choice in red. The card joins the column of its correct rating, marked ✓, ✗, or "reason ✗" when the rating was right but the reason was not.
  6. Press Next card (or Enter). After claim 10, press See result: You judged n of 10. Mastery is 8. Hover over any card to review it. Judge again restarts from claim 1.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Ephesus, the Basilica of St. John, and the House of the Virgin Mary. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: primary sources and myth versus history (Chapter 4); the Book of Acts and Paul in Ephesus (Chapter 9); the Church of Mary, the Council of Ephesus, John the Apostle, the Basilica of St. John, the House of the Virgin Mary, St. Paul's Prison Tower, and the riot of the silversmiths (Chapter 10). Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Judge the strength of the evidence for ten claims about the Christian sites of Ephesus and Selçuk, rating each as documented, debated, or tradition only, with at least 8 of 10 correct and the reason chosen for each.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (2 min): Before starting, name the oldest source you can think of for any one of the sites. How many years after the event was it written?
  2. Judge (8 min): Rate the ten claims. Before choosing a reason, say aloud who first made the claim and when.
  3. Compare cards 3 and 4 (2 min): Why does one tower get two different ratings?
  4. Plan the visit (3 min): Choose one site we will visit. Write one sentence a guide could say there that is true by the historian's test and respectful of the pilgrims around us.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 cards with both rating and reason correct, on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: A guide at the Basilica of St. John says, "This is the tomb of John the Apostle, who wrote his Gospel here." Rate each part of the sentence and give the evidence. A strong answer says the basilica is documented (Procopius), the tomb is tradition first written down about 190 CE, and John's life and writing at Ephesus are debated, resting on Irenaeus about 180 CE.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Council of Ephesus — Wikipedia. The council of 431 CE, summoned by Theodosius II, which met in the church of Mary and approved the title Theotokos.
  2. Procopius, Buildings 5.1, trans. H. B. Dewing and Glanville Downey (Loeb Classical Library 343, Harvard University Press, 1940). Justinian's rebuilding of the church of St. John on the hill above Ephesus; see also Procopius — Wikipedia.
  3. Irenaeus and Polycrates of Ephesus — Wikipedia. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.1.1, about 180 CE) on John publishing his Gospel at Ephesus, and Polycrates' letter (about 190 CE, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 5.24) saying John was buried there.
  4. Basilica of St. John — Wikipedia. The 6th-century basilica over the traditional tomb of John.
  5. House of the Virgin Mary and Anne Catherine Emmerich — Wikipedia. The visions published in 1852, the 1891 rediscovery, and the papal visits of 1967, 1979, and 2006.
  6. Lysimachus — Wikipedia. The successor of Alexander who refounded Ephesus and walled it in the early 3rd century BCE.
  7. Acts 19–20 and 1 Corinthians 16:8, in any modern translation, for example the New Revised Standard Version. Paul's two to three years in Ephesus, the riot of the silversmiths, and Paul writing from Ephesus.
  8. Clive Foss, Ephesus After Antiquity: A Late Antique, Byzantine and Turkish City (Cambridge University Press, 1979). The Christian city, its churches, and its pilgrim sites.

docs.title: One Walk, Seven Centuries
docs.text: Run the One Walk, Seven Centuries MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The standard walk through Ephesus runs downhill, from the upper city past Curetes Street to the Library of Celsus, then along Marble Street to the Great Theater. It is easy to assume that the monuments we pass are about the same age, or that the walk runs steadily from older to newer. Neither is true.

This MicroSim takes nine monuments in the order we pass them. Each one gets its own row on a timeline from 300 BCE to 500 CE. For monuments 2 to 9 we predict, before its date appears, whether it was begun earlier (older) or later (younger) than the monument we just passed, shown as a gold bar. Then its bar appears with the reason.

# Monument Date Bar 1 Memmius Monument Late 1st century BCE c. 40–1 BCE 2 Gate of Hercules 4th–5th century CE, built with older reliefs c. 350–450 CE 3 Fountain of Trajan Early 2nd century CE c. 102–114 CE 4 Temple of Hadrian Dedicated before 138 CE c. 117–138 CE 5 Terrace House 2 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE c. 25 BCE – 270 CE 6 Library of Celsus Begun c. 110 CE c. 110–125 CE 7 Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates 4–3 BCE c. 4–3 BCE 8 Great Theater First built 3rd century BCE; rebuilt 1st–2nd century CE c. 290–250 BCE and c. 41–117 CE 9 Harbor Street (Arcadiane) Rebuilt c. 400 CE c. 395–408 CE

A monument is compared by the year its first bar begins. The bars are rounded for display, and every one is marked "c." Most monuments were built over years and repaired for centuries. The Library's end date, 125 CE, is illustrative only: its completion date is not known exactly. The Gate of Hercules is dated by when it was assembled, although its carved reliefs are older blocks reused as spolia.

After the ninth monument, a reference row adds Paul's years in Ephesus, about 52 to 55 CE, and the riot of the silversmiths, about 55 CE. The riot filled a theater whose Roman rebuilding was still under way.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the first stop, the Memmius Monument, and its bar. Press Walk on.
  2. For each new stop, read its name and where it stands, then predict Older or Younger than the gold bar (keys O and Y). One prediction per stop; it cannot be changed.
  3. The bar appears with feedback, and the row label is marked ✓ or ✗. The score counts correct predictions out of 8.
  4. Press Walk on (or Enter) for the next stop. After stop 9, press See the whole walk.
  5. Drag the timeline sideways, or use +, −, and Full span, to compare bars. Hover over a bar for its date and reason. Walk again restarts from the first stop.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to walk through Ephesus. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: reading a ruin and spolia (Chapter 4); the Memmius Monument, Curetes Street, the Gate of Hercules, the Fountain of Trajan, the Temple of Hadrian, the terrace houses, the Library of Celsus, the Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates, the Great Theater, and the Harbor Street (Chapter 10). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Compare the construction dates of nine monuments passed on the downhill walk through Ephesus, predicting for each one whether it was begun before or after the monument passed just before it, with at least 6 of 8 predictions correct.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict the pattern (2 min): Before starting, guess whether the walk will run from older to newer, from newer to older, or neither.
  2. Walk (8 min): Make the eight predictions. Before each one, say which emperor or king the monument belongs to, if you know.
  3. Read the finished timeline (3 min): Trace the bars from row 1 to row 9 and count how many times the walk jumps back in time. Which two neighbors are furthest apart in date?
  4. Connect to Paul (2 min): Find the reference row. Which monuments on the walk already stood when Paul was in Ephesus?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 6 of 8 correct predictions. As a follow-up, ask: A guide says, "Everything you see on Curetes Street is Roman, from the 2nd century." Use three monuments from the walk to correct the statement. A strong answer names the Augustan Memmius Monument, the 2nd-century Fountain of Trajan and Temple of Hadrian, and the late-antique Gate of Hercules built of older blocks.

docs.text:

  2. Ephesus — Wikipedia. The city's history and its main monuments, including the theater, the terrace houses, and the Arcadiane.
  3. Library of Celsus — Wikipedia. Commissioned in the 110s CE by Tiberius Julius Aquila in memory of his father, and completed under Hadrian, after Aquila's death.
  4. Hadrian — Wikipedia. The emperor (117–138 CE) to whom the small temple on Curetes Street was dedicated, and Trajan's successor.
  5. Helmut Koester, ed., Ephesos, Metropolis of Asia (Harvard Theological Studies 41; Trinity Press International, 1995). Essays by the excavators on the city's buildings, inscriptions, and religion, including the theater and the Roman rebuilding of the city center.
  6. Arcadius — Wikipedia. The emperor (395–408 CE) whose name the rebuilt Harbor Street carries.

docs.title: Essential or Inherited?
docs.text:
Run the Essential or Inherited? MicroSim Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
At the Council of Jerusalem, the leaders of the early Jesus movement decided what Gentile believers had to keep and what they did not: faith was the purpose, and circumcision and the whole law were the inherited form of belonging that could not be imposed on newcomers. Chapter 11 argues that every redesign of a school turns on the same distinction:

  • Essential: part of what a school is for.
  • Inherited: one way of doing it that answered the constraints of an earlier age.

This MicroSim gives twelve practices, one at a time, and asks for a judgment on each. Every card carries the chapter's test: What problem did this solve, and does that problem still exist in the same form? Six practices are essential and six inherited. Four of the inherited forms come straight from the chapter: the Carnegie unit, which the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching defined in 1906 as about 120 hours of class in one subject; grading by age, which spread with schools such as Boston's Quincy Grammar School in 1848; the 50-minute period; and explaining new material to a whole room at one pace.

"Inherited" does not mean worthless. Each inherited form solved a real problem and may still be useful, and each one on this list serves an essential purpose on the same list, which is exactly why it is hard to change. The hardest cards are a trap pair: card 5, someone checks that a student has really learned a skill before building on it, is essential; card 11, every student takes the same unit test on the same day, is one inherited way of doing it. After the last card the two are linked by a line labeled "purpose and form."

The judgments follow this chapter's criterion. Reasonable people may weigh some forms differently; rows of desks, for instance, still suit a lecture. The point is to name the purpose before defending or discarding a form.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the criterion at the top: what essential and inherited mean.
  2. Read the practice in the white panel and ask the chapter's test.
  3. Judge it: press Essential or Inherited, click a column, or press E or I. Only the first choice counts.
  4. Read the feedback. The card joins the column of its correct judgment, marked ✓ or ✗. Press Next card (or Enter).
  5. After card 12, read the score and look for the line linking cards 5 and
  6. Hover over any card to review it; inherited cards also show the purpose they serve. Try again repeats all twelve.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers, especially teachers and school leaders, who have read Part Five of Chapter 11. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: essential versus inherited, the Council of Jerusalem, the grammar of schooling, seat time and the Carnegie unit, direct instruction, and the AI-native school (all in Chapter 11). Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Judge whether each of twelve school practices is an essential purpose of schooling or an inherited form that served that purpose under earlier constraints, judging at least 10 of 12 correctly, including both items of the trap pair.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 min): Name one practice from your own schooling that felt permanent. Was it a purpose or a form?
  2. Judge (6 min): Work through the twelve cards. For each, say aloud what problem the practice solved when it began.
  3. Discuss the trap pair (4 min): Why is checking mastery essential while the shared test date is inherited? What other ways could a school check that a student has learned?
  4. Map the dependencies (3 min): Hover over each inherited card and read the purpose it serves. Pick one and describe a different form that could serve the same purpose, as the AI-native morning does for explanation.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt, with cards 5 and 11 both correct. As a follow-up, ask: A colleague says, "If we drop the unit test, we stop checking learning." What would you answer? A strong answer separates the purpose (checking that each student has learned) from the form (one test for everyone on one day) and names another form that keeps the purpose.

docs.text:

The source of the essential-versus-inherited distinction as applied to schools.
  2. David Tyack and William Tobin, "The 'Grammar' of Schooling: Why Has It Been So Hard to Change?" American Educational Research Journal 31, no. 3 (1994): 453–479. The periods, age grades, and self-contained classrooms that organize nearly every school.
  3. David Tyack and Larry Cuban, Tinkering Toward Utopia: A Century of Public School Reform (Harvard University Press, 1995).
  4. Elena Silva, Taylor White, and Thomas Toch, The Carnegie Unit: A Century-Old Standard in a Changing Education Landscape (Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, 2015). The 1906 origin of the unit and its link to faculty pensions. See also Carnegie Unit and Student Hour — Wikipedia.

docs.title: Folding the Sheet: Folio, Quarto, Octavo
docs.text: Run the Folding the Sheet MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Early books were printed on large sheets of handmade paper, then folded and cut. The number of folds sets the format:

Format Folds Leaves per sheet Pages per sheet Folio 1 2 4 Quarto 2 4 8 Octavo 3 8 16

Paper was one of the largest costs of an early book, so the number of sheets a copy needs is close to a measure of its price. This calculator holds the text fixed, Virgil's Eclogues, Georgics, and Aeneid, about 12,900 lines in all, and asks us to work out the paper for three editions:

  1. A folio with the verses surrounded by commentary, 15 lines of Virgil per page.
  2. An octavo with the same 15 lines per page.
  3. An Aldine-style octavo in compact italic with no commentary, 30 lines per page.

Two rules do all the work. Pages equal the lines divided by the lines per page, and sheets per copy equal the pages divided by the pages per sheet. Both round up, because a part-page is still a page, and a part-sheet still has to be bought. Challenge 2 changes only the fold, and challenge 3 changes only the page density, so we can see how much each choice saves: the fold cuts the paper from 215 sheets to 54, and the denser page halves it again to 27, about one-eighth of the folio.

When we press Check, a drawing folds a sheet into the challenge's format, draws one leaf at the same scale, and lists the two pages printed on each leaf. The lines per page are illustrative round numbers, not measurements of real editions.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge: the format and the lines of Virgil per page.
  2. Type the pages per copy and the sheets per copy, then press Check (or Enter). Each challenge allows two attempts.
  3. A wrong first attempt gets a hint. A wrong second attempt shows the worked calculation, and the challenge counts as missed.
  4. Press Next challenge. The bars at the bottom fill in as each challenge is settled, and "Challenges correct" counts the ones you got right.
  5. After challenge 3, press Start exploring. The format menu and the sliders for lines per page (10 to 40) and copies (100 to 2,000) unlock, and the pages, sheets per copy, and sheets per edition update at once.
  6. Reset starts the three challenges again.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 to 15 minutes. Prerequisites: sheet, folio, quarto, octavo, italic type, commentary, and Aldine editions. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Calculate the number of pages and sheets of paper needed for one copy of Virgil's works in folio, quarto, or octavo format at a given number of lines per page, getting all three challenge calculations exactly right within two attempts each.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Fold a real sheet (3 min): Take a sheet of printer paper and fold it once, twice, and three times. Count the leaves after each fold, then number the pages front and back. Compare with the table above.
  2. Calculate (6 min): Work the three challenges without a calculator first, then check. Write down which rule caught you: the fold, or the rounding.
  3. Explore (4 min): With the format on Octavo, move the lines per page from 15 to 30 and watch the sheets per copy halve. Then set Folio, 15 lines, and 1,000 copies, and compare the sheets per edition with Octavo, 30 lines.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is all three challenges correct within two attempts each. As a follow-up, ask: A quarto Virgil prints 20 lines per page. How many sheets does one copy need? A strong answer finds 12,900 ÷ 20 = 645 pages, then 645 ÷ 8 = 80.6, rounded up to 81 sheets.

docs.text:
1. Book size — Wikipedia. Folio, quarto, and octavo as one, two, and three folds of the sheet, giving 2, 4, and 8 leaves.
  2. Aldine Press — Wikipedia. Aldus Manutius's small octavo classics, beginning with the Virgil of 1501.
  3. Italic type — Wikipedia. The italic cut for Aldus by Francesco Griffo and first used for a whole book in the 1501 Virgil.
  4. Aeneid — Wikipedia. The poem's length of 9,896 lines.
  5. Georgics and Eclogues — Wikipedia. The Georgics run to 2,188 lines and the ten Eclogues average about 83 lines each, so the three works total about 12,900 lines.

docs.title: Reading Food in Layers
docs.text: Run the Reading Food in Layers MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A Turkish meal can be read like an archaeological site, in layers. Each ingredient arrived at a particular time, brought by particular people. This MicroSim sorts fourteen foods we will meet in Istanbul into five layers:

Layer What it means 1. Ancient Mediterranean and Anatolia Grown or caught here since long before Byzantium 2. Turkic herders from Central Asia Brought by Turkish-speaking herders who moved into Anatolia after 1071 3. Ottoman trade and court Arrived through the empire's trade routes and palace kitchens, often from the Arab and Persian worlds 4. The Americas, after 1492 Arrived through the Columbian Exchange 5. The Turkish Republic, after 1923 A 20th-century change

The cards mix the familiar and the surprising. Tomatoes and red pepper flakes feel as old as the Mediterranean, but both are American plants. Tea feels like the most Turkish thing on the table, but it is the newest layer of all: the Ottomans drank coffee, and the tea plantations at Rize date from the 1930s and 1940s. The cards come in a fixed shuffled order, the same for every learner, so a group can compare answers card by card.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the food on the card in the white panel.
  2. Press the button for the layer you think it belongs to (or press 1 to 5). Each card has one attempt.
  3. The correct layer is outlined in green, a wrong choice in red, and the card settles into its correct bin. The feedback gives the reason.
  4. Press Next card to continue. The score in the top right counts correct first placements.
  5. After the fourteenth card, press See result. Hover over any card in the bins to read its reason again; missed cards have a red border.
  6. Restart clears the bins and starts over in the same order.

docs.title: Who Made a Greek Book in Venice?
docs.text: Run the Who Made a Greek Book in Venice? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Aldus Manutius's name stands on the title pages, but a Greek book printed in Venice around 1500 was the work of a team: an editor to prepare the text, a punchcutter to make the letters, a partner to put up the money, teachers who had trained the editors, authors who came to the press, and patrons who rewarded it. Venice also had Greek presses besides Aldus's.

The sim starts with ten people as unconnected boxes, showing only their names and dates. Ten contribution cards come in a fixed order, and for each one we choose who did that job. Only the first choice is scored; after a wrong choice we keep choosing until we find the right person. Each correct answer shows the person's role in their box and, for eight of the cards, draws a link between two people:

Link Card Musurus edited for Aldus The first printed Plato, 1513 Griffo cut type for Aldus The italic and the Greek types Torresani financed Aldus Partner and father-in-law Lascaris taught Musurus Greek lessons for the young editor Kallierges printed for Vlastos The Etymologicum Magnum, 1499 Erasmus was printed by Aldus The Adagia, 1508 Bembo edited for Aldus Petrarch and Dante in small format Leo X was the patron of Musurus The Plato dedication and the call to Rome, 1516

As the cards are answered, the network grows around Aldus, with a separate pair, Kallierges and Vlastos, beside it. After card 10 a last question asks how many of the ten were born on Crete. The answer is three, Musurus, Kallierges, and Vlastos, and their boxes then get gold borders: Cretans worked both inside Aldus's circle and in a rival press.

Notes on the facts. Life dates for Griffo, Kallierges, and Vlastos are approximate, so the sim shows them with "about" or "active." Sources differ on two details. Musurus is said to have been born in Rethymno in some accounts and in Candia (Heraklion) in others; either way he was a Cretan. And the 1499 Etymologicum Magnum was published by Kallierges and Vlastos with the patronage of Anna Notaras, so Vlastos was its financier and publisher, but not its only backer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card below the network, for example Cut the punches for the italic type and for Greek types.
  2. Press the name of the person who did that job. A wrong choice turns red and stays disabled; keep choosing until the right person turns green.
  3. When you are right, the person's role appears in their box and the card's link is drawn. Press Next card (or Enter).
  4. The score in the top right counts the cards you got right on your first choice.
  5. After card 10, press Last question, type how many of the ten were born on Crete, and press Check.
  6. Click any person you have placed to read about them. Zoom with + and −, and Reset view fits the whole network again. Try Again clears the links and the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: Aldus Manutius, Marcus Musurus, Janus Lascaris, Andrea Torresani, Francesco Griffo, Zacharias Kallierges, Nikolaos Vlastos, Erasmus, Pietro Bembo, Pope Leo X, Aldine editions, and collation and emendation. Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Attribute ten contributions to Greek and humanist printing in Venice around 1500 to the people who made them, attributing at least 8 of 10 correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Name the jobs (2 min): Before starting, list the jobs a printed book needs: editing, publishing, type cutting, financing, teaching, writing, and patronage. Guess which of the ten people did each.
  2. Attribute (6 min): Work through the ten cards. Before each choice, say which job the card describes, then which person.
  3. Read the network (2 min): On the finished network, count the people linked to Aldus and to Musurus. Notice that the Cretan editor is linked to the publisher, a teacher, and a patron, and that the second press stands apart from Aldus's.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first choice, plus the answer 3 to the Crete question. As a follow-up, ask: Why does the name of Aldus stand on the 1513 Plato, when Musurus prepared its text? A strong answer separates the publisher, who chose the book and paid for its printing, from the editor, who compared the manuscripts and corrected the Greek.

docs.title: Finish the Line Like a Homeric Singer
docs.text: Run Finish the Line Like a Homeric Singer Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Homer's heroes come with fixed name phrases: "swift-footed Achilles," "much-enduring Odysseus." In the 1920s the American scholar Milman Parry showed that the choice between them follows the meter, not the meaning. The Iliad and the Odyssey are composed in dactylic hexameter, a line of six feet made of long and short syllables, and each name formula fills a different-sized space at the end of that line. For each hero there are three:

Hero Formula Translation Syllables Pattern Achilles dios Achilleus brilliant Achilles 5 – ⏑ ⏑ – – Achilles podas ōkus Achilleus swift of feet, Achilles 7 ⏑ ⏑ – ⏑ ⏑ – – Achilles podarkēs dios Achilleus swift-footed, brilliant Achilles 8 ⏑ – – – ⏑ ⏑ – – Odysseus dios Odysseus brilliant Odysseus 5 – ⏑ ⏑ – – Odysseus polymētis Odysseus Odysseus of many counsels 7 ⏑ ⏑ – ⏑ ⏑ – – Odysseus polytlas dios Odysseus much-enduring, brilliant Odysseus 8 ⏑ – – – ⏑ ⏑ – –

(– long, ⏑ short.) The MicroSim draws each line to scale on a six-foot ruler, counting a long syllable as two beats and a short as one, so a foot is four beats. The opening of the line is shown as already sung; the empty slots at the end are the space the singer must fill. When a formula is chosen, its syllables drop into the space. The right one fits exactly. A formula that is too long runs past the end of the line, and one that is too short leaves a gap.

Four of the six lines are real Homeric lines, given in the chapter's English paraphrase: Iliad 1.84, Odyssey 6.1, Iliad 1.121 and Iliad 1.7. Lines 2 and 6 use real formulas with openings typical of Homer and are labeled "pattern example." The long and short marks are simplified: the last syllable of a line, which can be long or short, is always shown as long.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the line's English opening and the hero's name, and count the empty slots at the end of the line.
  2. Compare the three formula cards, which show each formula split into syllables, and press the button for the one with the same number of syllables (or press 1, 2 or 3).
  3. A right choice completes the line in green and shows the full English line with its source. A wrong choice shows where the syllables fail to fit and tells you how to count. You get two tries; after a second miss the right formula is placed for you.
  4. Press Next line (or Enter) to go on. The counter at the top shows lines composed on the first try.
  5. After line 6, answer the last question: why is Achilles "swift of feet" while he sits in his hut? It is not scored.
  6. Start over begins again at line 1.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 6 at Troy. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: oral tradition, formula, dactylic hexameter, long and short syllables, Achilles and Odysseus. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Use the size of the metrical space left at the end of a line to choose the Homeric name formula that completes it, for six lines naming Achilles or Odysseus, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Count first (2 min): On line 1, count the empty slots aloud before looking at the buttons.
  2. Compose (6 min): Finish all six lines. Notice that lines 1 and 2 have the same space but different heroes, and lines 3 and 4 the same.
  3. Answer the last question (2 min): Explain in one sentence why Achilles is "swift of feet" while sitting still.
  4. Connect (3 min): Using the chapter's section on Parry and Lord, explain why a singer who stored formulas, not a fixed text, could compose at the speed of performance.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is at least 5 of 6 lines composed on the first try. A follow-up question: If a singer needed to end a line about Odysseus with seven syllables, how many choices would the tradition give him? One: polymētis Odysseus. For each hero and each space there is usually just one formula, which is the economy Parry discovered.

Common misconceptions this activity targets:

  • Homer chose each epithet for its meaning at that moment, so "swift-footed" means Achilles is running.
  • The singers memorized a fixed text word for word.
  • Any adjective could fill any gap.

The analysis of noun-epithet formulas and their metrical positions on which the six formulas here are based.
  2. Albert B. Lord, The Singer of Tales (Harvard University Press, 1960). Parry and Lord's fieldwork with South Slavic singers and the theory of oral-formulaic composition.
