docs.title: How Paul's Words Traveled
docs.text: Run the How Paul's Words Traveled MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Paul's letters did not carry one message down the centuries. The same few chapters of Romans and Galatians fed movements that freed people and arguments that harmed them. This MicroSim lays out twelve moments from 386 to 1999 on a timeline with four strands:

Strand What belongs in it Grace and faith Events in which Paul's teaching that people are put right with God by grace, through faith, was received or argued over Conscience and equality Events in which Paul's words were used for, or against, individual conscience or the equal worth of people Contempt and its repudiation Events in Christian treatment of Jews that drew on, or later corrected, readings of Paul Rereading Paul Scholarly work that changed how Paul is read

Every card's date is fixed. The only choice is the strand, so the task is to break each event down to the Pauline idea it carried. Martin Luther appears three times, in three different strands, which is the clearest picture of what Chapter 11 calls Paul's contested legacy. The contempt strand turns toward repudiation only after the Holocaust, shown as a gray band.

To keep events a few years apart from piling on top of each other, the axis hides three long stretches with no events (430–1500, 1560–1725, and 1820–1925). Hatched marks show where each gap falls, so distances on the axis are not to scale across them.

docs.title: Before the strands: how the letters themselves traveled
docs.text: None of these twelve events could have happened unless Paul's letters had first survived as letters. Paul wrote to particular communities, but his letters were read beyond them: Colossians asks that it be passed to the church at Laodicea (Colossians 4:16), and 2 Peter, probably written in the early 2nd century, already speaks of "all his letters" (2 Peter 3:15–16). By about 140 CE, Marcion of Sinope had assembled a collection of ten letters of Paul. The oldest surviving copy of a collection is Papyrus 46, a papyrus codex (a bound book, not a scroll) now divided between the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin and the University of Michigan. It is usually dated about 200 CE, though proposals range from the late 2nd to the 3rd century, and an early date near 80 CE put forward in 1988 has not won acceptance. It contains Romans, Hebrews, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Galatians, Philippians, Colossians, and part of 1 Thessalonians; its last leaves are lost, so whether it ever held 2 Thessalonians, Philemon, or the letters to Timothy and Titus is debated. Lists of accepted books followed: the Muratorian fragment names thirteen letters of Paul and is usually dated to the late 2nd century (a minority of scholars place it in the 4th), and in 367 CE Athanasius of Alexandria's Easter letter listed the 27 books of today's New Testament, including fourteen letters under Paul's name, counting Hebrews. Augustine's book in the garden in Milan, the first card on the timeline, was a copy at the end of that chain.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the four strand definitions in the key under the timeline. The colored lanes on the timeline are the same four strands.
  2. Choose an event card in the tray. Its full text and date appear in the panel at the top.
  3. Place the card: drag it onto a strand, or click a strand on the timeline while the card is selected. Keys 1 to 4 also place the selected card, and the arrow keys move between cards. A numbered chip appears in that lane at the event's date. We can move a card as often as we like.
  4. When all twelve are placed, press Check. Correct chips turn green; wrong ones turn red, and a dashed green chip appears in the strand where the event belongs. Luther's three events get gold rings.
  5. Select any card to read why it belongs where it does. Try again returns every card to the tray in the same order.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers who have read Chapter 11 before the voyage to Rhodes. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: grace and faith, individual conscience, the idea of human equality, Christian anti-Judaism, the New Perspective on Paul, Augustine of Hippo, and the Protestant Reformation (all in Chapter 11). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Organize twelve dated events from 386 CE to 1999 into four strands of Paul's later influence, placing at least 10 of 12 in the correct strand.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before placing anything, guess which strand will hold the most events, and whether any one person will appear in more than one.
  2. Sort (6 min): For each card, ask one question: which of Paul's ideas did this event carry, or fight over? Grace, conscience and equality, the treatment of Jews, or the way scholars read him.
  3. Check and read (4 min): Press Check and read the reason for every red chip. Notice the two easy confusions: Luther at Worms is about conscience, not grace, and Stendahl's essay is about conscience but is scholarship about Paul, so it belongs in Rereading Paul.
  4. Look at the pattern (3 min): Follow the gold rings across three lanes. Then follow the contempt strand from Chrysostom to Nostra Aetate and notice where the gray Holocaust band falls.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first Check. As a follow-up, ask: Is it fair to call Paul's influence good or bad? A strong answer uses the timeline: the same letters fed the Reformation, the defense of conscience, and the teaching of contempt, and the repudiation of that teaching in 1965 quoted Paul's own Romans 11.

docs.text:

  2. Adversus Judaeos — Wikipedia. John Chrysostom's eight homilies in Antioch, 386–387.

docs.title: Istanbul's Three Shores
docs.text: Run the Istanbul's Three Shores MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Istanbul is split by two bodies of water into three parts. The Bosphorus divides Europe from Asia, and the Golden Horn, a curved inlet off the Bosphorus, divides the European side in two. That leaves three shores:

Shore Where it is What stands there Historic peninsula European side, south of the Golden Horn Greek Byzantium, Constantine's city, and the early Ottoman capital Galata European side, north of the Golden Horn The Genoese merchants' colony and its tower Asian shore East of the Bosphorus Kadıköy (ancient Chalcedon) and Üsküdar (ancient Chrysopolis)

The map starts with only the three shores and three bodies of water labeled. The satellite imagery carries no place names, so the map cannot give away the answers. Twelve places are asked in a fixed order. We choose a shore first, and only then does the place's dot appear at its true location, colored by its shore, with a short note about it.

Two places target common mix-ups. Galata Tower stands across the Golden Horn from the old city, but both are in Europe; the Golden Horn is an inlet, not the strait. Rumeli Hisarı, Mehmed II's 1452 fortress, stands far up the Bosphorus on the European shore; for this quiz, all of the European side north of the Golden Horn counts as Galata.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question below the map, for example Sarayburnu (Seraglio Point): which shore? Each place has one attempt.
  2. Press Historic peninsula, Galata, or Asian shore (or press 1, 2 or 3). The correct shore turns green and a wrong choice turns red.
  3. The place's dot appears on the map with a note about it. When the place lies outside the current view, the map widens to show it.
  4. Press Next place (or Enter). The score in the top right counts correct first answers.
  5. After place 12, press See result. Every dot is shown together. Click any dot to read its note again, zoom with + and −, and drag to pan; the mouse wheel scrolls the page instead of the map.
  6. Restart hides the dots and clears the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: strait, the Bosphorus Strait, the historic peninsula, Galata, the Asian shore, and the Golden Horn. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify twelve Istanbul places by the shore they stand on (the historic peninsula, Galata, or the Asian shore), with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Find the water (2 min): Before answering, trace the Bosphorus from the top of the map to the Sea of Marmara, then trace the Golden Horn from its mouth to the northwest. Say which body of water separates which two shores.
  2. Classify (5 min): Work through all twelve places. For each, say aloud what you know about the place (Greek, Byzantine, Ottoman, Genoese, or a ferry town) before choosing.
  3. Read the pattern (3 min): On the result map, notice that places 1 to 7, everything Byzantine and early Ottoman, sit on the historic peninsula, while the Genoese tower and the Asian-side towns sit across the water from it. Find the two gates of the land walls and notice that the walls cross the peninsula from water to water, rather than running along the Bosphorus.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: We take the ferry from Eminönü to Kadıköy on the evening of Day 1. Which body of water do we cross, and which continent are we on when we get off? A strong answer names the Bosphorus (near its mouth on the Sea of Marmara) and Asia.

docs.title: Knossos: Minoan, Evans, or Copy?
docs.text: Run the Knossos: Minoan, Evans, or Copy? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Knossos is the most famous case of reconstruction in Europe. What a visitor sees there comes from three different hands: the Minoans, who built the palace; Arthur Evans, who excavated it from 1900 and rebuilt parts of it between about 1905 and 1930, mainly in reinforced concrete from the 1920s; and the artists who painted copies of frescoes whose originals went to the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. This MicroSim asks one question of ten features: who made this?

Bin What belongs in it Minoan original Built or made by the Minoans and still at the site Evans reconstruction Built for Arthur Evans between about 1905 and 1930 Modern copy A painted copy at the site of an original now in the Heraklion museum

The cards come in a fixed order. Four are Minoan originals: the lower walls and floor plan around the central court, the gypsum throne, the storage jars in the West Magazines, and the drains and water channels. Three are Evans reconstructions: the red concrete columns at the North Entrance, the concrete upper floor over the Throne Room, and the large horns of consecration. Three are modern copies: the charging bull relief, the dolphin painting in the so-called Queen's Megaron, and the Cup-Bearer.

Each card is scored once, on the first answer. The reason appears at once and the card joins its correct bin, outlined green if the first choice was right and red if it was not. After answering, What to look for shows the material clue for that card, following the chapter's rule of thumb: check the material, then the color. Opening it is exploration, not part of the score.

docs.title: Knossos From Village to Decipherment
docs.text: Run the Knossos From Village to Decipherment MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The story of Knossos runs for 9,000 years, but almost all of its famous events crowd into two short stretches: the palace age of about 1900 to 1200 BCE, and the rediscovery that began in 1878. Between them lies a silence of more than 3,000 years in which no one could read the palace's records. This timeline is drawn to scale from 7000 BCE to 2030 CE, in two bands, Bronze Age Crete and Rediscovery, so those gaps show as distances.

The timeline starts almost empty: only the first village on the Kephala hill, about 7000 BCE. Four prediction questions, each answered once before its events appear, fill it in.

# Prediction Events added 1 Did the Thera eruption come before or after most palaces were destroyed? Thera erupts (c. 1600 BCE); Mycenaeans at Knossos (c. 1450 BCE) 2 About how many years separate the two? First palace, second palace, Phaistos Disc, Snake Goddess figurines 3 Did Knossos burn before or after the mainland palaces such as Pylos? Knossos burns (c. 1375 BCE); mainland palaces fall (c. 1200 BCE) 4 How many years passed between the first tablets and their reading? Kalokairinos (1878) through the UNESCO listing (2025)

After each answer the timeline zooms to the events just added and labels the gap the question asked about: about 150 years from Thera to the fall of the palaces, about 175 years between the fires at Knossos and at Pylos, and 52 years from Evans's first tablets in 1900 to Ventris's reading in 1952. In the full view, each band's events collapse into one bar that opens with a click, and after the last question a striped bar marks the more than 3,000 years in which Linear B went unread.

Bronze Age dates are approximate and debated. The sim uses the chapter's dates: the Thera eruption about 1600 BCE (radiocarbon dating; an older archaeological dating puts it near 1500 BCE), and the final destruction of the palace of Knossos about 1375 BCE, which some scholars place later.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the first question below the timeline and choose an answer. Each question counts once.
  2. Watch the timeline zoom to the new events, which are outlined in gold, and read the reason in the feedback.
  3. Click any event to read its description in the right-hand panel.
  4. Press Next question for the next prediction.
  5. Use Full span, Close-up: Bronze Age, Close-up: Rediscovery, and the Earlier and Later buttons to move around. Dragging the timeline also pans it; the mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the timeline.
  6. Start over hides the events again and resets the score.

  3. Compare (3 min): Press Full span. How does the real spacing compare with your sketch? Most people draw the palace age far too long and the village age far too short.
  4. Explain (3 min): Using the timeline, explain to a partner why the Thera eruption could not have destroyed the palaces all at once, and why Knossos and Pylos left baked tablets nearly two centuries apart.

docs.title: Reinforcing or Balancing? Loops From Ephesus to the Staff Room
docs.text: Run the Reinforcing or Balancing? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A causal loop diagram draws a chain of cause and effect that circles back on itself. Each arrow carries a sign: + when the two variables move in the same direction, − when they move in opposite directions. A loop is reinforcing when a change comes back around amplified, and balancing when it comes back pushing the other way. The rule for telling them apart is simple enough to apply without any intuition about the variables:

Count the minus signs around the whole loop. An even number, including zero, makes the loop reinforcing; an odd number makes it balancing.

This MicroSim gives six loops, one at a time:

# Setting Loop 1 School Student results → teacher confidence → quality of use → student results 2 School Rollout speed → teacher overload → resistance → rollout speed 3 School New initiatives → change fatigue → effort on each → student results → new initiatives 4 Ephesus Converts to Paul's message → sales of silver shrines → silversmiths' opposition → converts 5 Corinth Honor given to weaker members → sense of belonging → care for one another → honor 6 School Pressure for quick results → teachers' fear of mistakes → practice → student results → pressure

Loops 1 and 2 are the worked example in AI-Native Schools, Chapter 18, repeated in this chapter's section on systems thinking. Loop 4 comes from the silversmiths' riot in Acts 19 and from Pliny the Younger's letter to the emperor Trajan of about 112 CE, which reports the same economic pattern in Bithynia. Loop 5 is Paul's picture of one body with many parts (1 Corinthians 12). Loops 3 and 6 come from the chapter's sections on change fatigue and the implementation dip. All six are illustrative simplifications; real systems have many more links.

The set is built to break three habits. Reinforcing does not mean good: loops 3 and 6 are harmful, and both are reinforcing. A minus sign does not make a loop balancing: loops 3 and 6 each have two. And the number of boxes decides nothing: three-box loops appear among both the reinforcing and the balancing loops. Structure, not setting, decides behavior, which is why the Ephesus loop and the school rollout loop push back in the same way.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the loop. Hover over any arrow to read what the link means, for example "more fatigue, less effort on each." The +, −, and Reset view buttons zoom; drag the background to pan.
  2. Count the red minus signs around the whole loop, then select Reinforcing or Balancing (or press R or B) and press Submit.
  3. If the first answer is wrong, the sim gives a hint and one more try. The second answer does not change the score; after it, the correct type is shown and the loop counts as missed.
  4. Once a loop is answered, its marker turns into R or B and the minus signs are numbered, so the count is visible. Press Next loop.
  5. After loop 6, press See summary for a table of all six loops with their minus-sign counts and types. Try again restarts from loop 1.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers, especially teachers and school leaders, who have read Part Seven of Chapter 11. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: systems thinking, feedback loops, reinforcing and balancing loops, the counting rule, one body many parts, the economics of resistance, the implementation dip, and change fatigue (all in Chapter 11). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate reinforcing from balancing feedback loops by counting the minus signs around each of six causal loops, classifying at least 5 of 6 correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before starting, guess: is a loop that ends in falling student results reinforcing or balancing? Write the guess down.
  2. Classify (6 min): Work through the six loops. For each, trace one push around the loop out loud ("more initiatives, more fatigue, less effort...") before counting.
  3. Compare (4 min): Open the summary. Find the two harmful loops and their type. Then compare loops 2 and 4: what plays the role of resistance in Ephesus?
  4. Apply (3 min): Pick one loop from your own school or workplace. Draw it with three or four variables, mark each link's sign, and classify it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: A principal says, "Our results are dropping, so we are launching two new programs this year." Which loop is this, and what would weaken it? A strong answer names loop 3, identifies it as reinforcing because it has two minus signs, and proposes cutting the number of initiatives so that effort on each can recover.

docs.text:
Add ?edit=true to the URL to reposition the diagrams:

Open the Layout Editor

In edit mode we can drag every box and every loop marker, and the markers show R or B from the start. Use ← Loop and Loop → to move between the six loops. Click an arrow, or its sign, to select it, then use Flip Curve, Curve −, Curve +, or Straight to reshape it. The layout is kept in this browser as we work, so a reload does not lose it. Reset Layout discards it and reloads the layout from the JSON file. docs.title: Why Athens Looks the Way It Does
docs.text: Run the Why Athens Looks the Way It Does MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Most of what a visitor notices in Athens is not explained by antiquity. A bent iron gate on Patission Street, the name on a coffee menu, the metro to the airport, the empty shops and the new bakeries were all shaped by events of the last sixty years. This MicroSim puts fourteen of those events on one timeline, from the colonels' coup of 1967 to the Athens Declaration of 2023, and asks us to work backward from eight typical sights to the event that left each mark.

Sight Event that explains it Flowers at a twisted iron gate on Patission Street, and a march every November 17 Polytechnic uprising, November 14–17, 1973 "Greek coffee" on a menu where older Greeks remember "Turkish coffee" Cyprus and the fall of the junta, July 1974 Euro prices in a Plaka souvenir shop Euro notes and coins, January 1, 2002 A metro line to the airport and a tram to the sea Athens Olympics, August 2004 Memories of queuing for a daily €60 at a cash machine Banks close, June–July 2015 Empty shops, and a son who now works in Germany First rescue loan, 2010 (the October 2009 deficit revelation is also accepted) A Syrian bakery and an Afghan grocery Sea crossings of 2015 Greek and Turkish leaders promising regular meetings Athens Declaration, December 2023

Five events are context and explain none of the sights: the 1967 coup, joining the European Economic Community in 1981, the 1999 earthquakes, the EU–Turkey deal of March 2016, and the end of the rescues in August 2018. The sights are composites of things visitors commonly see, not specific places.

When all eight are matched, six of them point to events between 2002 and 2023. Much of the city a visitor walks through was shaped in the last two decades.

Before this timeline begins. The timeline starts in 1967, but the city it explains was made earlier. Athens became the capital of the new Greek kingdom in 1834, moving from Nafplio under the young Bavarian king Otto, and was replanned as a neoclassical capital around the small Ottoman town. It hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896, in the rebuilt Panathenaic Stadium. After the population exchange of 1923, which followed the Greek defeat in Asia Minor, about 1.2 million Orthodox refugees came to Greece, and Athens and Piraeus grew whole new districts, such as Nea Smyrni and Nea Ionia, named for the places they had lost. German forces occupied Athens from April 1941 to October 1944, and the famine of the first occupation winter killed tens of thousands in the capital. These events are told in Chapters 10 and 15.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the sight in bold and the question "Which event explains this?"
  2. Click an event on the timeline, or choose it from the list. Its date and description appear below the list. Selecting events to read them is exploration; nothing is scored until you commit.
  3. Press Commit (or Enter). A correct first choice adds to the score "n of 8 correct on the first attempt". A wrong first choice turns red and gives a hint; you get one more try. After a second miss the answer is revealed and the sight counts as missed.
  4. The matched event gets a gold badge with the sight's number (S1 to S8). Press Next sight to go on.
  5. Close-up: 2008–2019 spreads out the crowded crisis years; Full span returns to 1967–2023. Drag the timeline sideways to pan. Restart clears every match.

A strong answer names a specific sight and a dated event, for example the refugee neighborhoods of Nea Smyrni and the population exchange of 1923.

docs.title: Next-Word Prediction and Temperature
docs.text: Run the Next-Word Prediction and Temperature MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A language model writes one word at a time. For each next word it assigns a probability to every candidate, chooses one, adds it to the text, and repeats. The temperature setting controls how that choice is made. This MicroSim gives an imaginary small model four prompts, each with five candidate words, and lets us predict what the temperature will do before we see it.

The rule is the standard softmax-with-temperature rescaling. Raise each probability to the power \( 1/T \), where \( T \) is the temperature, and rescale so the five add up to 100 percent:

\[ p_i(T) = \frac{p_i^{1/T}}{\sum_j p_j^{1/T}} \]

This is the same as dividing the model's raw scores (its logits, here \( \ln p_i \)) by \( T \) before the softmax step. At \( T = 1 \) nothing changes. Below 1 the probabilities sharpen toward the favorite; above 1 they flatten. As \( T \) approaches 0 the favorite's share approaches 100 percent, so \( T = 0 \) is treated as "always take the most likely word" (greedy choice). The dashed outline on every bar keeps the temperature-1.0 probabilities in view, so we can see that the model's knowledge stays put while only its way of choosing moves.

Prompt Five candidate words at temperature 1.0 1. "Know ___" thyself 60, yourself 20, the 10, your 6, nothing 4 2. "Nothing in ___" excess 55, the 15, particular 12, life 10, common 8 3. "On Sundays the Grand Bazaar is ___" closed 45, open 30, busy 15, quiet 6, crowded 4 4. "The oracle at Delphi was ___" consulted 30, famous 25, a 20, closed 15, silent 10

Draw 20 makes 20 independent random picks, each weighted by the bars, and counts how often each word was chosen. The counts vary from draw to draw: at temperature 1.0, prompt 3 gives "open" about 6 times in 20 on average, but any one draw may give 3 or 9. The random numbers come from a fixed starting seed, so the same sequence of presses reproduces the same counts, and Try Again restarts the sequence.

What is simplified. All probabilities are invented to show the rule; the sim labels them "Illustrative probabilities, not from a real model." A real model scores tens of thousands of tokens, not five words, and products often combine temperature with other limits, such as sampling only from the most likely few tokens (top-k or top-p). Even at temperature 0, some hosted systems are not perfectly repeatable, because of small numerical differences in how the computation is run; the idealized rule in the sim is exactly repeatable.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge and choose one of the three answers (or press keys 1 to 3). Only the first choice counts.
  2. Press Reveal (or Enter). The temperature moves to the challenge's setting, the filled bars show the adjusted probabilities, and a draw of 20 appears, followed by the feedback.
  3. Press Draw 20 to draw again and watch the counts change, then press Next challenge.
  4. After challenge 5, free exploration unlocks: choose any prompt, move the Temperature slider from 0 to 2.0, and press Draw 20 as often as you like. Changing the prompt or the temperature clears the counts.
  5. Try Again returns to challenge 1 and resets the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers who use, or are curious about, AI chatbots. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: large language model, token, next-word prediction, temperature, and probability (Chapter 19, "Large Language Model" and "Next-Word Prediction"). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Infer how changing the temperature changes which next word a language model chooses and how often, answering at least 4 of 5 prediction questions correctly before the sampled results are revealed.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (8 min): Work through the five challenges in order. Say the reason for each answer out loud, or write it down, before pressing Reveal.
  2. Explore (4 min): Choose prompt 3 at temperature 1.0 and draw five times. How many draws contain at least one "open"? Now set the temperature to 0 and draw again.
  3. Discuss (3 min): The model "knows" the Grand Bazaar is usually closed on Sundays only in the sense that "closed" is its most likely word. Why can the same question get different answers on different days?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Moving the slider and drawing samples in free exploration is not evidence. As a follow-up, ask: Does raising the temperature make a model more creative or more accurate? A strong answer says that it makes the output more varied by giving unlikely words more chances, which can help with brainstorming but also makes wrong or odd words more frequent; it does not change what the model learned.

  2. Large language model — Wikipedia. Tokens, training to predict the next token, and how text is generated one token at a time.
  3. Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin, Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft (online). The chapter on large language models explains greedy decoding, random sampling, and temperature sampling.
  4. Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals and Jeff Dean, "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network" (2015, arXiv:1503.02531). Uses a softmax temperature above 1 to produce a "softer" probability distribution.
  5. Ari Holtzman and others, "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration" (ICLR 2020, arXiv:1904.09751). Why always taking the top word produces dull, repetitive text, and why pure sampling can wander; introduces top-p (nucleus) sampling.

docs.title: November Weather at Our Stops
docs.text: Run the November Weather at Our Stops MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A climate chart answers the packing question better than any forecast made weeks ahead: what is a typical November day like here? This MicroSim asks four prediction questions, and each chart appears only after we lock in an answer. Predicting first makes us read the pattern in the chart instead of looking up a single number.

Question What the chart shows Misconception it tests 1. Which stop has the coolest November afternoons? November highs and lows at all six stops Istanbul has the same weather as Athens because both are "Mediterranean." 2. Is November in Athens wetter or drier than August? Athens rainfall, month by month Summer is the wet season, as in many northern climates. 3. Which is the hottest month in Athens? Athens afternoon highs, month by month The hottest month is the month of the longest day. 4. How much colder is a November night in Istanbul than a November afternoon in Heraklion? Istanbul and Heraklion November highs and lows The Mediterranean is warm all year, so one set of clothes will do.

After the fourth question, an exploration view opens. Choose any stop to see its twelve months of afternoon highs and night lows as lines, rainfall as bars, and November shaded as "our month." Tooltips give every temperature in °C and °F (°F = °C × 9/5 + 32, rounded).

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Each stop's values are the mean daily maximum, mean daily minimum and mean monthly precipitation from the climate table in that city's English Wikipedia article, retrieved on November 24, 2026:

Stop Days on our trip Station and period Istanbul 1–5 Kireçburnu, 1991–2020 normals Çanakkale (Troy and Gallipoli) 6 Çanakkale, 1991–2020 normals İzmir (nearest major station to Ephesus) 7 İzmir, 1991–2020 normals Rhodes 8 Rhodes International Airport, Paradeisi, September 1996 – August 2026 averages Heraklion (Knossos) 9 Nikos Kazantzakis Airport, 1991–2020 normals Athens 10–13 Downtown Athens, 1991–2020 normals

For Heraklion, the article's first climate table is a short record from the harbor station (2007–2024); the sim uses the article's 1991–2020 airport normals instead, so that five of the six stops share the same standard period. Rhodes has no 1991–2020 table in its article, so its longest recent record is used. Weather in any single November can differ a lot from these averages.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question and choose an answer. The choice is locked in; each question allows one attempt.
  2. The chart for that question appears. The correct answer turns green, a different choice turns red, and the feedback explains the answer with the actual values.
  3. Press Next question. The score at the top right counts correct predictions.
  4. After question 4, press Explore the stops and choose any stop from the list. Hover over a month to read its values.
  5. Restart clears the score and returns to question 1.

docs.title: The Olympian Gods at Troy
docs.text: Run The Olympian Gods at Troy MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
In Book 20 of Homer's Iliad, as the fighting before Troy reaches its peak, Zeus lifts his ban and lets the gods go down to the battle while he watches from Olympus. Homer then names who went to each side. This MicroSim turns that passage into a sorting activity. Twelve god cards, shuffled, go into three bins:

Bin Gods (revealed at the end) Helped the Greeks Hera, Athena, Poseidon, Hermes, Hephaestus Helped the Trojans Ares, Apollo, Artemis, Aphrodite Above or outside the fight Zeus (watching from above), Demeter and Dionysus (no part in the Iliad's battles)

Each card shows the god's name and domains; hovering over a card turns it over to show the full domains and the symbol to look for on a vase or a relief. The domain is a clue but not the answer. The real reasons are stories: Hera and Athena lost the Judgment of Paris and Aphrodite won it; Poseidon remembers the wages a Trojan king never paid him; Apollo's priest was insulted by Agamemnon. Ares, the god of war himself, fights for the side that loses.

Before sorting, the sim asks for a prediction of the three totals. Many travelers expect all twelve gods to fight, or the war god to be on the winning side. At the end the true totals (5, 4, 3) appear beside the prediction, and the three cards whose sides follow the Judgment of Paris are outlined in gold.

The Iliad lists two more gods on the Trojan side who are not Olympians: Leto, the mother of Apollo and Artemis, and Xanthos, the river god. They are mentioned in the feedback but are not cards.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Type your predicted number of gods for Greeks, Trojans, and Outside in the three boxes below the canvas (whole numbers that add up to 12) and press Lock in prediction. Sorting starts only after that.
  2. Hover over a card to read its domains and symbol in the panel at the bottom.
  3. Drag each card into a bin. You can also click a card and then click a bin, or press 1, 2 or 3. Cards can be moved between bins, or dragged back to the tray, until you check.
  4. When all twelve are placed, press Check. Correct cards turn green and lock; misplaced cards turn red. After the first Check a red card shows only a hint; after the second it shows the story from the Iliad.
  5. You have up to three Checks. Only the first one counts for the score shown in the top right. After the last Check, any card still misplaced moves to its correct bin, and the tray shows your prediction beside the true totals.
  6. Start over reshuffles the cards and clears the prediction.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 6 at Troy. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Olympian gods, Mount Olympus, the Iliad, the Judgment of Paris, and the Trojan War. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify each of the twelve Olympian gods by the side they take in Homer's Iliad (helped the Greeks, helped the Trojans, or stayed above or outside the fight), using each god's domain and story, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first Check.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before touching a card, commit to three totals. Ask: did every god fight? Which side would the god of war choose?
  2. Sort (5 min): Place all twelve cards. For each one, name the story that decides it, not just the domain.
  3. Check and revise (3 min): Use the hint, "Think about the Judgment of Paris and old debts," to move the red cards.
  4. Compare (3 min): Read your prediction against the true totals. Which of your assumptions did the Iliad overturn?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is at least 10 of 12 correct on the first Check. A follow-up question for discussion: The gods in the Iliad are not impartial judges. What does that tell us about how the Greeks imagined the causes of a war? A good answer notes that the gods choose sides for personal reasons (wounded pride, unpaid debts, favorite heroes), so the war's outcome is not a verdict on who was right.

Common misconceptions this activity targets:

  • The gods acted as impartial judges of right and wrong.
  • The god of war must have been on the winning side.
  • Every Olympian fought at Troy.
  • Zeus was simply a Trojan partisan. (He helps the Trojans for a time only to keep his promise to Thetis, and stays above the fight in Book 20.)

docs.title: Can This Answer Lose?
docs.text: Run the Can This Answer Lose? MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The most famous answers attributed to the Oracle of Delphi seem astonishing because they "came true." This MicroSim asks a different question about each answer: could anything that happens prove it wrong? The test is simple. List two possible outcomes and ask whether the answer comes true under each.

Category Test Could be proven wrong At least one possible outcome would show the answer to be false. Comes true either way Every possible outcome can be read as fulfilling it. Not a prediction It tells someone what to do and says nothing about what will happen.

The eight cards come in a fixed order:

# Answer Source Category 1 "If you make war on the Persians, you will destroy a great empire." Herodotus 1.53, to Croesus, about 550 BCE Comes true either way 2 "Divine Salamis, you will destroy the children of women." Herodotus 7.141, to the Athenians, 481 or 480 BCE Comes true either way 3 "I say that you, son of Aeacus, the Romans can defeat." Cicero, On Divination 2.116, quoting a line said to be given to Pyrrhus Comes true either way 4 "No one is wiser than Socrates." Plato, Apology 21a, to Chaerephon Could be proven wrong 5 "Found a city in Libya." Herodotus 4.150, to the king of Thera, about 630 BCE Not a prediction 6 The gods to whom Xenophon should sacrifice for a safe journey Xenophon, Anabasis 3.1, about 401 BCE Not a prediction 7 "Your son will kill you." Sophocles, Oedipus the King, to Laius Could be proven wrong 8 "It will rain at Delphi between noon and 3 PM tomorrow." A modern weather forecast Could be proven wrong

The first three are the answers that "came true" most famously, and they are exactly the three that could not lose. The Pyrrhus line is the purest example: in Latin, Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse can mean either "you can defeat the Romans" or "the Romans can defeat you." Cicero himself mocked the story, pointing out that Apollo never spoke Latin and that the line comes from the poet Ennius. Cards 5 and 6 are a reminder that many real answers were not predictions at all but commands and approvals, which is what the answers recorded closest to their own time mostly look like.

What is uncertain. The quotations are the chapter's paraphrased translations. The famous hedged answers survive in stories written down long after the events, and some historians suspect that answers such as the second "wooden wall" response were polished afterward. Card 7 is from a tragedy, not a historical consultation. The categories describe each answer's structure, not whether the oracle actually gave it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card and its source, and ask: could anything that happens prove this answer wrong?
  2. Choose one of the three category buttons (or press keys 1 to 3). Only the first choice counts.
  3. Press Test both outcomes (or T or Enter). Two outcome boxes show whether the answer comes true, is proven wrong, or does not apply, followed by the reason.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 8, press See the totals.
  5. On the totals screen, click any card on the strip to read it again. Try Again starts over with card 1.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to visit Delphi. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: prediction, forecast, command, hedging, the Croesus prophecy, the wooden walls prophecy, Chaerephon's question, the Oedipus prophecy, and Xenophon's question (Chapter 17, Parts One, Three, Four and Five). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Distinguish answers that could be proven wrong from hedged answers that come true whatever happens and from answers that are not predictions at all.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 min): Before card 1, write down what Croesus probably took the answer to mean, without thinking about how the story ends.
  2. Classify and test (8 min): For each card, commit to a category, then use the two-outcome test to check it.
  3. Compare (3 min): On the totals screen, compare cards 1 to 3 with card
  4. Why is the weather forecast the bravest statement in the set?
  5. Transfer (2 min): Think of a horoscope, a market forecast, or a political promise you have heard recently. Which category does it fall in?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 6 of 8 correct on the first attempt, with cards 1 (Croesus) and 4 (Chaerephon) both correct. As a follow-up, ask: Why does an answer that cannot lose predict nothing? A strong answer says that if every outcome fulfills it, hearing the answer tells us nothing about which outcome to expect, and it protects the reputation of whoever gave it.

docs.title: Oracle, Gears, or Data?
docs.text: Run the Oracle, Gears, or Data? MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
People have asked about the future in three very different ways, and our trip has met all three. At Delphi, a person, the Pythia, gave an answer that the people asking had to interpret. In the National Archaeological Museum, the Antikythera mechanism turned centuries of counted sky records into gear teeth, so that anyone turning the crank got the same answer. On our phones, a learned model adjusts its own rules from millions of past examples.

This MicroSim gives twelve predictions, four of each kind, and asks one question: how was each answer produced? The three bins are defined on screen:

Bin How the answer is produced Oracle A person gives an answer that the people asking must interpret. Cycle model A rule built from regular cycles counted in past records, fixed in advance and the same for everyone. Learned model A rule that a computer adjusted for itself from a very large number of past examples. Prediction Bin Athens's envoys are told to trust the "wooden wall" (480 BCE). Oracle Croesus is told that if he attacks Persia, he will destroy a great empire. Oracle King Laius is told that his son will kill him. Oracle Chaerephon is told that no one is wiser than Socrates. Oracle The mechanism's lower back dial marks a possible eclipse in a month 18 years from now. Cycle model A Babylonian scribe's clay tablet lists the months, years ahead, when an eclipse may occur. Cycle model The mechanism's games dial shows that the Olympic Games fall in this year. Cycle model A stone peg calendar says that a certain star rises today and that a west wind will blow. Cycle model A phone keyboard suggests the next word of a message home. Learned model A bank's fraud system flags a card payment in Arachova as possibly not ours. Learned model A chatbot answers the question "Will the museum be open on Monday?" Learned model A map app predicts how long the drive back from Delphi will take. Learned model

The cards are shuffled once each time the page loads. The lesson is in the middle bin: a bronze dial, a clay tablet, and a stone calendar end up together because the method, counting a cycle, decides the bin, not the material or the age of the object.

Notes on the evidence. The four oracle stories are the ones told in Chapter 17. The eclipse dial on the mechanism's lower back is a spiral of 223 lunar months, the Saros cycle, and the games dial on the upper back follows the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games, as read from the 2005 X-ray scans. Babylonian astronomers predicted possible eclipse months from cycles of this kind, and the parapegma paired star risings with expected weather. The four modern cards are the everyday predictions of Chapter 19.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question and the three bin definitions. All twelve cards start in the tray at the top.
  2. Click a card to read it in full in the white panel. Then drag it into a bin, or press one of the three colored bin buttons (or keys 1, 2, 3). The next card is selected automatically.
  3. A placed card can be dragged to another bin, or back to the tray, until you press Check. Arrow keys move the selection.
  4. When all twelve are placed, press Check (or Enter). Each card is marked ✓ or ✗, and the panel explains how the selected card's answer was produced. The score "First attempt: n of 12" is fixed by this first Check.
  5. Move the red cards and press Check again for practice. Practice checks do not change the first-attempt score. Reset clears every placement but keeps the same card order.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 20, "Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today", after visiting the National Archaeological Museum. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: the oracle consultation and the Pythia (Chapters 17 and 18); the Antikythera mechanism, the Saros cycle, the four-year games cycle, Babylonian eclipse records, and the parapegma (Chapter 20, Part One); machine learning and the predictive model (Chapter 19). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate twelve predictions by how each answer is produced, as an oracle's answer, a cycle model, or a learned model, sorting at least 10 of the 12 correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (1 min): Before starting, decide which bin the Antikythera mechanism belongs in, and why it is neither an oracle nor a learned model.
  2. Sort (6 min): Place all twelve cards and press Check once. Note the first-attempt score, then fix the red cards.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Which cards did the material or the age of the source tempt you to misplace? What can a learned model do that the gears could not, and what could the gears do that the Pythia could not?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 10 of 12 cards in the correct bin on the first Check. A follow-up question: A weather app forecasts rain for tomorrow. Which bin does it belong in, and what would you need to know to be sure? A strong answer says it depends on the method: a model fitted to many past observations is a learned model, while a fixed rule such as "rain follows this star's rising" is a cycle model, and the material of the device does not decide.

docs.title: Where the Empire Withdrew, 1683–1923
docs.text: Run the Where the Empire Withdrew, 1683–1923 MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Ottoman Empire did not lose its lands in one collapse. It withdrew over 240 years, from the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 to the founding of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, and it withdrew unevenly. This MicroSim divides those years into four eras:

Era Years Turning points Era 1 1683–1829 Siege of Vienna; Treaty of Karlowitz (1699); Crimea independent (1774) and annexed by Russia (1783) Era 2 1830–1878 Greek independence and the French conquest of Algiers (1830); Congress of Berlin (1878) Era 3 1879–1913 British occupation of Egypt (1882); Italo-Turkish War (1911–1912); Balkan Wars (1912–1913) Era 4 1914–1923 World War I, the Arab Revolt, and the treaties that followed

Fourteen places are asked in a fixed order. Before we answer, we see only the place and a short description with no date of loss. We commit to an era, and only then does the sim show what happened, with dates, and color the place's dot by its era. Istanbul and Ankara are shown as reference cities and are not scored.

"Leaving Ottoman rule" here means the end of effective Ottoman government, which was not always the end of the sultan's formal title. Two places show the difference. Cyprus came under British administration in 1878 and Egypt under British occupation in 1882, but both stayed nominally Ottoman until 1914; the sim scores them by the earlier date and says so in its feedback. Crete is scored by its autonomy in 1898, not its union with Greece in 1913, and Serbia's three steps (1830, 1867, 1878) all fall in Era 2.

The sim also shows that a lost province did not always become a nation-state at once. Crimea went to Russia, Algiers to France, Rhodes to Italy, and Cyprus, Egypt, Baghdad and Jerusalem to Britain. The base map has relief and sea depths but no modern borders, so it does not draw today's frontiers onto the past.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question below the map, for example Buda: In which era did this place leave Ottoman rule? The place's dot is highlighted in yellow, and a short description appears in gray italics.
  2. Press Era 1, Era 2, Era 3, or Era 4 (or press 1 to 4). Each place has one attempt. The correct era turns green and a wrong choice turns red.
  3. Read the feedback: why the place left when it did, followed by what happened, with dates. The dot takes its era's color.
  4. Press Next place (or Enter). The score in the top right counts correct first answers.
  5. After place 14, press See result. Then replay the retreat with the By 1829, By 1878, By 1913, and By 1923 buttons, or press Replay next era. At each step, colored dots have left Ottoman rule and white dots are still Ottoman. Click any dot to read about it.
  6. Try Again clears every dot and the score. The mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the map; zoom with + and − and drag to pan.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: Ottoman decline, the treaties of Karlowitz (1699) and Küçük Kaynarca (1774), nationalism, the Congress of Berlin (1878), the Balkan Wars, and World War I. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify fourteen places on a map of the former Ottoman Empire by the era in which they left Ottoman rule, with at least 10 of 14 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict the shape (2 min): Before starting, say which region you think the empire lost first and which it lost last: the Balkans, North Africa, or the Arab Middle East. Write the guess down.
  2. Classify (8 min): Work through all fourteen places. For each, say aloud which power was pressing on it (Habsburg Austria, Russia, France, Britain, Italy, or a national movement) before choosing an era.
  3. Replay the eras (3 min): Step from By 1829 to By 1923 and compare the picture with your guess. Notice that the Balkan and Black Sea lands went before 1914, while Mecca, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Damascus stayed Ottoman until World War I.
  4. Who got it? (2 min): On the By 1913 map, name the place that became independent and the places that passed to another empire. Only Athens and Belgrade became capitals of new states before 1914.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 14 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: We visit Rhodes on Day 8 and Athens on Day 10. Which left Ottoman rule first, and which became Greek first? A strong answer says Athens left first (Greece independent in 1830) and became Greek first; Rhodes left in 1912 but went to Italy and became Greek only in 1947.

docs.title: The Parthenon's Five Lives
docs.text: Run the Parthenon's Five Lives MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Parthenon did not go straight from temple to ruin. For about 2,100 years after it was finished it was in use, first as Athena's temple, then as a church, then as a mosque, and it became a ruin only in 1687. This MicroSim asks us to sort twelve events into the building's five lives:

Life From To Temple of Athena 447 BCE End of the 4th century CE, when the old sacrifices were banned (the closing date is debated) Church (Orthodox, then Latin Catholic from 1204) Probably by the late 6th century CE (debated) 1458 Mosque 1458 (the conversion followed soon after; the exact year is not known) 1687 Ruin, with a small mosque inside 1687 1833 Protected monument, with its sculptures in museums 1833 Today

Each card shows a date and an event, such as 1018 CE: the emperor Basil II gives thanks for his victories in the building. We choose a life before any dates for the lives appear. Feedback gives the reason, and the card drops onto a timeline at its date. After card 12, the five lives appear as colored bands behind the cards. The years between the temple's closing and the church's opening are drawn as a striped band, because scholars disagree about when the conversion happened.

Two cards are traps, and mastery requires both:

  • Card 7, September 26, 1687. The Venetian shell that ignited the gunpowder stored inside ended the mosque's life, but it hit a working mosque, not a ruin.
  • Card 9, 1801–1812. Lord Elgin's agents worked on a roofless ruin with a small mosque inside, not on a complete building.

Dates. Card 8, Morosini's attempt to lower the horses of Athena's chariot from the west pediment, is dated early 1688 here. The specification gave 1687; most accounts place the attempt in the months after the explosion, before the Venetians left Athens in April 1688. Either way, the building was already a ruin. The 1674 drawings are traditionally credited to Jacques Carrey, though the attribution has been questioned.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card: its number, date, and event.
  2. Choose one of the five lives (or press keys 1 to 5). Only the first answer counts toward the score.
  3. Read the feedback. Correct. gives the reason; otherwise the feedback says which life the building was living and why. The card appears on the timeline; a red dashed border marks a card you missed.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 12, press Show the five lives.
  5. Use Full span and Close-up: 1400–2030 CE to change the view, and drag the timeline to move it. Hover over or click a card to read it again.
  6. Try Again clears all twelve cards.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to visit the Acropolis. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Parthenon, the Parthenon sculptures, the Parthenon as church and mosque, Lord Elgin, the Acropolis Museum, and restoration (Chapters 4, 7 and 15). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify twelve events in the Parthenon's history by which of the building's five lives it was living when each event happened, classifying at least 10 of 12 correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Name the lives (2 min): Before card 1, read the five choices aloud and guess roughly when each began.
  2. Classify (8 min): For each card, ask what the building was being used for on that date: was there a roof, a priest, an imam, a garrison, or a restoration crew?
  3. Read the bands (3 min): After card 12, compare the widths of the bands. The temple and church lives each lasted about a thousand years; the ruin began only in 1687.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt, including cards 7 and 9. As a follow-up, ask: Was the Parthenon a ruin when Lord Elgin's agents took its sculptures, and what made it one? A strong answer says yes: it had been a roofless ruin since a Venetian shell ignited the Ottoman gunpowder stored inside on September 26, 1687, while it was still in use as a mosque.

docs.title: Agreed Fact or Position?
docs.text: Run the Agreed Fact or Position? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
In a heated dispute it is tempting to think the facts themselves must be in doubt. The Parthenon Marbles dispute shows otherwise: Greece and the British Museum accept almost all the same facts and disagree about what those facts mean and where the sculptures should be. This MicroSim asks us to pull the argument apart into its pieces.

Twelve statement cards come one at a time. We sort each into one of three bins:

Bin Definition Agreed fact Something both sides accept as true. British Museum's position What the British Museum argues should be concluded or done. Greek government's position What the Greek government argues should be concluded or done.

After each answer the card joins its correct bin as a short label. At the end the three bins stand side by side: six agreed facts, three statements of the Museum's position, and three of the Greek government's.

Two cards are traps, and mastery requires both: the lost Ottoman permission document (card 6) and the British Museum Act of 1963 (card 10). Each is a fact that one side cites more often, but both sides accept it as true. A fact that helps one side is still a fact.

Fairness. The sim takes neither side. Each position is paraphrased from the side's own published statements (see References), and each side gets the same number of cards. The positions are summarized as of late 2026; talks between Greek officials and the British Museum have been reported since about 2022, so a position card may date if an agreement is announced.

Wording change. The chapter's specification phrased card 8 as In London the sculptures are seen free of charge beside the art of cultures from around the world. Read literally, that sentence is a fact both sides would accept (entry to the Museum is free), which would make the card unfair. The sim words it as the argument the Museum makes: The sculptures are best seen in London, free of charge, beside the art of cultures from around the world.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the three bin definitions at the top.
  2. Read the card in the panel and choose a bin with the buttons below (or press 1, 2 or 3). Only the first choice counts.
  3. Read the feedback. The correct bin is outlined in green; a wrong choice is outlined in red. The card joins its correct bin, with a red dashed border if you missed it.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 12, press See the bins.
  5. On the result screen, click any label in a bin to read its statement and reason again.
  6. Try Again clears the bins and reshuffles the twelve cards.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing to visit the Acropolis Museum. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: contested history (Chapter 4), the Parthenon sculptures, Lord Elgin, the Acropolis Museum, and the Parthenon Marbles dispute (Chapter 15). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate agreed facts from the British Museum's position and the Greek government's position in twelve statements about the Parthenon Marbles dispute, sorting at least 10 of 12 correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Test each card (8 min): Before choosing, ask: Would the other side deny this? If not, it is an agreed fact, even if one side quotes it more. If the sentence says what should happen or what the facts prove, it is a position.
  2. Read the bins (3 min): On the result screen, pair each position card with the facts it rests on. Which facts does the Museum use? Which does Greece use? Are any facts used by both?
  3. Discuss (4 min): Why will more evidence not settle this dispute? What kind of agreement could?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt, including cards 6 and 10. As a follow-up, ask: Is the British Museum Act of 1963 part of the Museum's position? A strong answer says no: the law's existence is an agreed fact; the Museum's position is the conclusion it draws from it, and Greece accepts that the law exists while arguing about what should be done.

docs.title: Paul's Journeys and Our Route
docs.text: Run the Paul's Journeys and Our Route MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Book of Acts tells one continuous story of Paul's travels. Study Bibles divide it into three numbered missionary journeys and a final voyage to Rome as a prisoner. The numbering is a modern convenience, and the dates are scholars' reconstructions that differ by a year or two.

Journey About Told in First 46–48 CE Acts 13–14 Second 49–52 CE Acts 15:36–18:22 Third 52–57 CE Acts 18:23–21:17 Voyage to Rome 59–60 CE Acts 27:1–28:16

This MicroSim asks one question about twelve places, in a fixed order: on which journey does Acts first bring Paul there? The answer is the first visit, not the longest stay. Ephesus is the classic trap: Paul spent two to three years there on the third journey, but Acts first brings him there briefly at the end of the second.

Before we answer, the map shows only the twelve places, our own route from Istanbul to Athens and Delphi, and three reference markers: Tarsus (Paul's birthplace, according to Acts), Damascus (his call), and Jerusalem (his arrest). The journey routes stay hidden, so each answer is a prediction. After the twelfth answer, all four routes appear and can be switched on and off one at a time. Each line joins the places Acts names, in Acts' order. The lines are not the actual roads or sea lanes, and where Acts names only a region ("Syria and Cilicia," "the region of Galatia and Phrygia"), the line passes through that region's main city.

The reveal also shows what Paul and our trip share: Athens, Rhodes, and the region of Ephesus, where our ship docks at Kuşadası. Acts never brings Paul to Byzantium (Istanbul), Heraklion, or Delphi, and his only time on Crete was as a prisoner, sheltering at Fair Havens on the south coast before the storm that wrecked his ship on Malta.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question below the map. The current place is the yellow dot.
  2. Press First, Second, Third, or Voyage to Rome (or keys 1 to 4). Each place has one attempt. The correct journey turns green and a wrong choice turns red.
  3. Read the feedback, which cites the passage in Acts. The place's dot takes the color of its correct journey; click it to read the feedback again.
  4. Press Next place (or Enter). After place 12, press Reveal the journeys.
  5. The score shows: "You placed n of 12. Mastery is 10." Use the four journey buttons to show or hide each route, and All (key 5) to show or hide them together. Click a route to list its stops, or a colored dot to see every journey that passes through it, with the first visit marked.
  6. The Our route checkbox shows or hides our cruise and land route. Try again clears all answers and hides the routes. The mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the map; zoom with + and − and drag to pan.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the visit to Ephesus. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: Paul's missionary journeys, the Book of Acts as the source for them, Roman roads and the sailing season, the Roman province of Asia, and our cruise route (Chapter 2). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify twelve places by the journey on which the Book of Acts first brings Paul there (first, second, or third journey, or the voyage to Rome), correctly placing at least 10 of 12.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before starting, guess which journey reached the most of the twelve places, and whether Paul ever came to Crete as a missionary.
  2. Classify (6 min): Work through the twelve places. For each one, say aloud the scene Acts tells there, if you know one (a vision, a convert, a stoning), before choosing.
  3. Compare the routes (4 min): After the reveal, show one journey at a time. Notice that the second journey reached the most places and first crossed into Europe, that Ephesus lies on two journeys, and that Paul reached Crete only as a prisoner.
  4. Connect to our trip (2 min): With Our route on, name the three places where our path and Paul's meet, and the stops on our trip that Acts never mentions.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: Tomorrow's guide in Ephesus says, "Paul's first visit to Ephesus lasted three years." What is wrong with that sentence? A strong answer says Acts first brings Paul to Ephesus briefly at the end of the second journey; the stay of two to three years came on the third.

docs.title: Where in Paul's Life Was Each Letter Written?
docs.text: Run the Where in Paul's Life Was Each Letter Written? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Nearly all scholars, of every faith and none, agree that Paul himself wrote seven of the thirteen letters that bear his name: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. None of them is dated. Historians place them in Paul's life the way a detective works, from clues inside each letter (who is with Paul, where he is, what has just happened) matched against the outline of his travels in Acts and a few fixed points such as the term of the proconsul Gallio in Corinth, about 51–52 CE, known from an inscription found at Delphi.

This MicroSim gives us the same clues. The timeline runs from 30 to 70 CE and shows six periods of Paul's life:

Band Period About A Call and early years 33–46 CE B First journey 46–48 CE C Second journey 49–52 CE D Third journey, including two to three years in Ephesus 52–57 CE E Prison in Caesarea 57–59 CE F Voyage and Rome 59–62 CE

Four events give fixed points: the meeting in Jerusalem about Gentile believers (about 49), Gallio in Corinth (51–52), Paul in Ephesus (about 52–55), and Paul's death in Rome according to later tradition (about 62–67). All the dates are scholars' reconstructions and differ by a year or two.

Most of the letters have one accepted period. Three do not, because scholars genuinely disagree. Galatians is usually placed in the third journey and sometimes in the second (a minority view, which the sim does not score as correct, dates it before the Jerusalem meeting, about 48). Philippians and Philemon were written from prison, and Paul does not say which prison: an Ephesian imprisonment that Acts does not mention, custody in Caesarea, or house arrest in Rome. The sim accepts every period that has wide scholarly support and, at the end, outlines the other accepted periods with dashed boxes. The order of the letters in the New Testament is by length, not date, so Romans, which comes first in our Bibles, was among the last written.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the six periods on the top row of the timeline and in the key below it. Hover over a period or an event for details, or click an event to read it in the panel.
  2. Choose a letter card in the tray. Its clue and passage appear in the panel at the top.
  3. Place the card: drag it onto the timeline over a period, or click a period in the card's own row. (Keys: 1 to 7 select a card; A to F place it.) We can move a card as often as we like before checking.
  4. When all seven are placed, press Check. Accepted cards turn green, lock, and show why. The others return to the tray with a hint.
  5. Place the returned cards again and press Check again. After the second Check, any card still wrong moves to its accepted period and is marked "shown" in amber.
  6. Select any card to read its reasoning. Start over clears everything.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the visit to Ephesus. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the seven undisputed letters, Paul's missionary journeys, the Book of Acts, Timothy and Titus, Phoebe and Cenchreae, and the Ephesian imprisonment theory (Chapter 9). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Organize the seven undisputed letters onto a timeline of Paul's life, using one clue from inside each letter, placing all seven in an accepted period within two attempts.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before reading any clues, guess which letter was written first. Many people guess Romans, because it comes first in the New Testament.
  2. Read and place (7 min): For each card, underline in your head the person and the place in its clue (Timothy, Athens; Ephesus; Titus, Macedonia; Phoebe, Cenchreae), then find the period when Paul was there.
  3. Check and revise (3 min): Press Check, read the reasons, and place any returned cards again.
  4. Look at the pattern (3 min): Count how many letters landed in period D. Notice that the seven letters come from about ten years, not thirty, and that only the prison letters remain debated.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is all seven placed in accepted periods within two Checks. As a follow-up, ask: Why can we say for certain that 1 Corinthians was written in Ephesus, but not Philippians? A strong answer says 1 Corinthians names Ephesus ("I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost"), while Philippians names only a praetorium and Caesar's household, which existed in any provincial capital as well as in Rome.

docs.title: Xerxes' Road to Salamis
docs.text: Run the Xerxes' Road to Salamis MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Persian Wars are easy to remember as one battle at Marathon. This map walks the whole war in order, from the burning of Sardis in 498 BCE to the Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE, and asks us to use the map as evidence. At five places we choose why the fighting or the crossing happened there before the explanation appears.

The ten places, in order:

Step Place Date Scored question? 1 Sardis 498 BCE; winter 481/480 BCE No 2 Marathon 490 BCE Yes 3 Abydos, on the Hellespont Spring 480 BCE Yes 4 The Athos canal Dug about 483–480 BCE No (context stop) 5 Thermopylae August or September 480 BCE Yes 6 Artemisium The same days as Thermopylae No (context stop) 7 The Acropolis of Athens September 480 BCE Yes 8 The strait of Salamis September 480 BCE Yes 9 Plataea August 479 BCE No 10 Mycale 479 BCE No

The map zooms to each place so that the ground itself is visible: the plain of Marathon, the narrows of the Hellespont, the pass at Thermopylae, and the strait between Salamis and the mainland. Colored lines are added as the war moves: Darius's fleet in 490 BCE, then Xerxes' army and fleet side by side in 480 BCE, then the Greek army and fleet in 479 BCE. The routes are simplified sketches through the places Herodotus names, not traced roads or sea lanes.

Two added stops. The chapter's specification lists eight places. This sim adds the Athos canal and Artemisium as unscored context stops, because they show what the eight alone hide: Xerxes' army and fleet moved together and depended on each other, and the Greeks defended a pass on land and a strait at sea on the same days.

Locations. Coordinates were checked against each place's Wikipedia article in November 2026. Artemisium, Salamis and Mycale mark the area of a sea or shore battle, not an exact spot, and the sim says so. At Thermopylae, the modern coastline lies several kilometers farther out than in 480 BCE, when the sea came almost to the foot of the cliffs; the sim notes this, because the modern plain would otherwise hide the very reason the pass mattered.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read step 1, Sardis, and the opening question: A Persian king wants revenge on Athens. How will he get there? Press Next place.
  2. At a numbered place with a question, look at the map first, then choose (a), (b) or (c) (or press A, B or C). Only the first choice counts.
  3. The feedback says Correct. or Not quite., gives the reason, marks the correct option in green, and shows the place's date and note.
  4. Press Next place (or Enter) to go on. Back returns to earlier places; answered questions show your choice but cannot be answered again.
  5. After place 10, press See the whole route for the full map and your score out of 5. Click any numbered marker to read its note again.
  6. Zoom with + and − and drag to pan; the mouse wheel scrolls the page. Start Again clears all answers.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 10 in Athens. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Persian Wars, the Ionian Revolt, Herodotus, the Battle of Marathon, Themistocles, the trireme, the Battle of Salamis, and the Hellespont (Chapters 7 and 15). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Infer, at five places in the Persian Wars, why the fighting or the crossing happened there, choosing the geographic reason before it is revealed and getting at least 4 of 5 correct.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict the road (2 min): At Sardis, before pressing Next, trace with a finger how a Persian army could reach Athens: by land around the north of the Aegean, or by sea across it. Both were tried.
  2. Infer from the map (8 min): At each question, name what you see on the map (a plain, a narrow strait, a pass between mountains and sea) before choosing a reason.
  3. Read the whole route (3 min): On the final map, follow the red army line and the blue fleet line from the Hellespont to Athens. Where do they run side by side, and what happened to the army after the fleet lost?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: Why could the Greeks, with fewer ships and soldiers, choose Thermopylae and Salamis as places to fight? A strong answer says that a narrow pass and a narrow strait let only a few men or ships fight at once, so the larger Persian numbers counted for less, and that the army depended on the fleet for its food.

docs.title: Place the Site in Its Era
docs.text: Run the Place the Site in Its Era MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Placing a site in its era comes down to one question: when was it built? This MicroSim gives fifteen cards, each naming a building or object we will see on the trip and the date it was built. Our job is to drop each one into the right period on the chapter's timeline:

Period Dates used in this guide Bronze Age c. 3200–1100 BCE Iron Age c. 1100–800 BCE Archaic Period c. 800–480 BCE Classical Period 480–323 BCE Hellenistic Period 323–31 BCE Roman Period 31 BCE–330 CE Byzantine Period 330–1453 CE Ottoman Period 1453–1922 CE

The ninth period, the Modern era, has no bin because none of the cards needs it. A boundary year belongs to the period it begins, so 480 BCE is Classical and 1453 CE is Ottoman.

Two of the cards are traps. The Palace of the Grand Master in Rhodes was built by crusader knights, not Byzantines, but its 14th-century date puts it in the Byzantine period: a period name tells when, not always who. The Stoa of Attalos in Athens was rebuilt in the 1950s, but it belongs to the Hellenistic period, when King Attalos II first built it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card in the white panel: what it is and when it was built.
  2. Click the period button under the bin where you think it belongs. The buttons sit in timeline order, under the bins they fill.
  3. The feedback appears at once. The correct bin is outlined in green, a wrong choice in red, and the card settles into its correct bin. Each card has one attempt.
  4. Press Next card to continue. The score in the top right counts correct first attempts.
  5. After the fifteenth card, press See result. All fifteen cards now sit in their bins along the timeline; missed cards have a red border. Hover over any card to read its date and explanation again.
  6. Restart reshuffles the cards and clears the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: historical timeline, BCE and CE dating, the nine periods and their dates, and the idea that a period name tells when, not always who. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Apply the chapter's period boundaries to assign each of 15 sites and objects on the trip to the period in which it was built, with at least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (2 min): Before starting, cover the bin headers and try to say the eight periods in order with their boundary years. Then check against the headers.
  2. Sort (6 min): Work through all fifteen cards. For each one, say the boundary years aloud before clicking: "537 is after 330 and before 1453."
  3. Review the traps (3 min): After the result, hover over the Palace of the Grand Master and the Stoa of Attalos. Explain in one sentence each why their period is not the one their builders or restorers might suggest.
  4. Extend (3 min): Apply the same rule to Hagia Sophia's later life. It was converted to a mosque in 1453. In which period was it built, and in which period did that first change happen?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: The Venetian Koules fortress in Heraklion was rebuilt in stone between 1523 and 1540. Which period holds that date, and who ruled Crete then? The date falls in the Ottoman period on our timeline, but Venice, not the Ottomans, ruled Crete until 1669: the same lesson as the Grand Master's Palace.
