docs.title: Who Was Exchanged in 1923?
docs.text: Run the Who Was Exchanged in 1923? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
On January 30, 1923, Greece and Turkey signed the Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations at Lausanne. It made the exchange compulsory: the Greek Orthodox Christians of Turkey were to move to Greece, and the Muslims of Greece to Turkey, and none could return. About 1.2 million Orthodox Christians, most of whom had already fled in 1922, and about 400,000 Muslims lost homes their families had lived in for generations. Both communities still remember it as a loss, and many families on both sides of the Aegean keep stories, recipes and keepsakes from the towns they left.

This MicroSim asks us to apply the convention the way its officials had to: case by case, by its written rules. The five rules at the top are simplified from the convention's first three articles and from Article 14 of the Treaty of Lausanne:

  1. Greek Orthodox Christians living in Turkey are exchanged to Greece.
  2. Muslims living in Greece are exchanged to Turkey.
  3. People of these two groups who had already left since 1912 count as exchanged, and may not return.
  4. Exempt: the Greek Orthodox established in Istanbul before October 30, 1918; the Muslims of Western Thrace; the Greek Orthodox of Imbros and Tenedos.
  5. The exchange applies only to Greece and Turkey.

The ten households are illustrative composites, not named families. They are built so that the obvious guess, from language or nationality, is often wrong. The convention's test was religion: a Turkish-speaking Orthodox family from Cappadocia was sent to Greece, and a Greek-speaking Muslim family from Crete was sent to Turkey. After each answer, the rule that decided the case is highlighted, and the case joins a summary grouped by outcome.

The simplified rules leave out the convention's details on property, nationality and the Mixed Commission that ran the exchange. In practice, officials also had to decide who counted as "established" in Istanbul, and those decisions were disputed for years.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the five rules at the top. They stay visible throughout.
  2. Read the case, for example A Greek Orthodox family whose grandparents settled in Istanbul in 1890.
  3. Press Sent to Greece, Sent to Turkey, or Not exchanged (or press 1, 2 or 3). Each case has one attempt.
  4. Read the feedback. The deciding rule is highlighted in yellow, and the case appears as a chip in its correct column, with a green border if we got it right and a red border if we did not.
  5. Press Next case (or Enter). After case 10, press See result.
  6. At the end, hover over any chip to review that case and its rule. Try Again repeats all ten.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Greco-Turkish War, the millet system (Chapter 6), the Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations and its exemptions, and Rhodes as an Italian possession in 1923. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Apply the rules of the 1923 population exchange convention to ten household cases, deciding whether each was sent to Greece, sent to Turkey, or not exchanged, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt, including cases 3 and 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the rules (2 min): Before case 1, say in one sentence what the convention used to decide who was "Greek" and who was "Turkish". Notice that the rules never mention language.
  2. Apply (8 min): Work through all ten cases. For each, name the rule you are using before choosing an outcome.
  3. Read the summary (3 min): At the end, count the households in each column. Half were not exchanged. Find the three different reasons why (an exemption, a religion the convention did not cover, and a territory outside Greece and Turkey).
  4. Connect to the trip (2 min): We see the Church of Agios Titos in Heraklion on Day 9, a mosque until 1923, and Rhodes on Day 8, which the exchange did not touch. Say which rule explains each.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt, including cases 3 and 4, which test the religion-not-language rule. As a follow-up, ask: A Turkish-speaking Orthodox family from Cappadocia and a Greek-speaking Muslim family from Crete each crossed the Aegean in 1923, in opposite directions. Why did each go where it went? A strong answer says the convention sorted people by religion, not by language, a legacy of the millet system.

  2. Population exchange between Greece and Turkey — Wikipedia. The numbers exchanged (about 1.2 million and about 400,000), the religious criterion, and the exemptions, including Imbros and Tenedos.

docs.title: When a Prediction Feeds Itself
docs.text: Run the When a Prediction Feeds Itself MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A weather forecast cannot change the weather, but a prediction about people can change the people, and the changed behavior becomes the data from which the next prediction is learned. This causal loop diagram takes three such loops apart link by link.

Loop Links Opposite (−) links Type 1 Predicted crime → patrols sent → crimes recorded → predicted crime 0 Reinforcing 2 Risk score → lower-level placement → challenging coursework → grades → risk score 2 (L5, L7) Reinforcing 3 Predicted 9 AM traffic → drivers who leave early or reroute → 9 AM traffic → predicted traffic 1 (L9) Balancing

A same direction (+) link means that if the first factor rises, the second rises, and if it falls, the second falls. An opposite direction (−) link means the reverse. A reinforcing loop sends a change around and brings it back larger, in the same direction: a self-fulfilling prediction. A balancing loop brings the change back opposed: a self-defeating prediction. The counting rule follows: an even number of opposite links, including zero, makes a loop reinforcing; an odd number makes it balancing.

Two results surprise most people. Loop 2 has two minus signs and still reinforces, because two reversals cancel. And Loop 3, where a forecast of heavy traffic is followed by a light road, is the loop in which the forecast did its job.

Loop 1 also shows an outside factor, true crime in the district, with a dashed arrow into crimes recorded. Records rise with true crime and with patrols, and a model trained on records cannot tell which. That is why a prediction that "comes true" in such a loop does not, by itself, show that the model was accurate.

What is simplified. The sim labels the diagram "Simplified causal model: directions only, no sizes." The link directions are the chapter's qualitative claims, not measured effects. Whether a real loop matters depends on how strong each link is, and real systems have more links than these. In particular:

  • Predictive policing. Lum and Isaac (2016) showed, by applying a published prediction algorithm to Oakland drug-arrest records, how such a loop could keep sending officers to the same neighborhoods, and Ensign and colleagues (2018) proved that the loop can run away when a model learns only from crimes that patrols discover. Supporters point to field trials, such as Mohler and colleagues (2015), that reported fewer crimes in predicted areas; critics note that such trials measure recorded crime, the quantity the loop distorts. The loop is a risk to design against, not proof that every system behaves this way.
  • Student risk prediction. A risk score harms only if it is used to lower expectations or placements. Used to bring extra help, the same score can break the loop, which is the point of question Q2.
  • The traffic loop is an illustration of a self-defeating forecast, not a model of the real Athens–Delphi road.

Other loops like these. The same structure appears elsewhere in computing. A recommendation system shows what it predicts we will click, our clicks are recorded, and the next model learns from those clicks, which can narrow what everyone is shown (Chaney and colleagues, 2018). Machine learning researchers call predictions that change the outcomes they predict performative (Perdomo and colleagues, 2020). A related loop is model collapse: when language models are trained, generation after generation, mostly on text written by earlier models, they gradually lose the rare and unusual parts of the original data (Shumailov and colleagues, 2024). How much this happens in practice depends on how much fresh human-written data stays in the mix, which is still being studied.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the two link definitions under the diagram. The current link is drawn in orange, and its two factors are outlined in orange.
  2. Choose Same direction (+) or Opposite direction (−) (or press S or O), then Submit (or Enter). Each link has one scored try. The feedback appears and the arrow takes its correct sign.
  3. Press Next link. After the last link of a loop, press Classify the loop, choose Reinforcing or Balancing (or press R or B), and submit. The R or B marker appears, and the counting rule is shown from then on.
  4. Repeat for Loops 2 and 3, then answer the three loop questions (keys 1 to 3 choose an answer).
  5. See results shows the scores for links, loops and questions. Start Over resets everything.

Hover over a box or a labeled arrow to read what it means. Drag the background to pan, and use +, − and Reset view to zoom.

docs.title: Editing the Layout
docs.text:
Add ?edit=true to the URL to reposition the diagrams:

Open the Layout Editor

In edit mode we can drag every box and every loop marker, and the arrows show their signs and the markers show R or B from the start. Use ← Loop and Loop → to move between the three loops. Click an arrow, or its sign, to select it, then use Flip Curve, Curve −, Curve +, or Straight to reshape it. The layout is kept in this browser as we work, so a reload does not lose it. Reset Layout discards it and reloads the layout from the JSON file. When the layout looks right, press Copy JSON or Download JSON and replace the contents of prediction-feedback-loops-cld.json with the result. All three loops live in that one file; each node's loop field says which loop it belongs to.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers curious about how AI predictions are used in schools, cities and everyday apps. Duration: 15–20 minutes. Prerequisites: predictive model, data bias (measurement bias), self-fulfilling prophecy, self-defeating prophecy, student risk prediction, and predictive policing (Chapter 19, Parts One and Four). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate reinforcing loops, in which a prediction helps bring itself about, from balancing loops, in which a prediction helps prevent itself, by labeling the direction of every link in three prediction loops and classifying each loop, with at least 9 of 10 links and all 3 loops correct.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 min): Recall Merton's bank run from the chapter. Which way does each link run: rumor of failure → withdrawals → bank's cash → failure?
  2. Label and classify (10 min): Work through the three loops. Say each link aloud as "if this rises, that rises" or "if this rises, that falls" before choosing.
  3. Answer the loop questions (3 min): For each question, name the link that the best answer changes.
  4. Discuss (5 min): Think of a prediction about people that affects you, such as a credit score, a recommended video, or a school placement. What do people do because of it, and does that action feed the next prediction?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 9 of 10 links, all 3 loops, and at least 2 of 3 loop questions correct on the first try. Opening a tooltip is exploration, not evidence. As a follow-up, ask: A forecast said "heavy traffic" and the road was light. Was it a bad forecast? A strong answer says that in a balancing loop a useful forecast can look wrong, because people acted on it, and that judging it fairly requires asking what would have happened without the forecast.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Robert K. Merton, "The Self-Fulfilling Prophecy," The Antioch Review 8, no. 2 (1948): 193–210. The paper that named the idea, with the example of a bank run.
  2. Kristian Lum and William Isaac, "To Predict and Serve?" Significance 13, no. 5 (2016): 14–19. The Oakland study of how predictive policing trained on arrest records can concentrate patrols.
  3. Danielle Ensign, Sorelle A. Friedler, Scott Neville, Carlos Scheidegger and Suresh Venkatasubramanian, "Runaway Feedback Loops in Predictive Policing," Proceedings of the Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency (2018). A mathematical model of the loop in Loop 1 and of ways to correct it.
  4. G. O. Mohler and others, "Randomized Controlled Field Trials of Predictive Policing," Journal of the American Statistical Association 110, no. 512 (2015): 1399–1411. Field trials that reported fewer crimes in predicted areas.
  5. Juan C. Perdomo, Tijana Zrnic, Celestine Mendler-Dünner and Moritz Hardt, "Performative Prediction," Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (2020). Predictions that change the outcomes they predict.
  6. Allison J. B. Chaney, Brandon M. Stewart and Barbara E. Engelhardt, "How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity and Decreases Utility," Proceedings of the 12th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (2018). The recommendation feedback loop.
  7. Ilia Shumailov and others, "AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data," Nature 631 (2024): 755–759. Model collapse.

docs.title: Read a Greek Sign
docs.text: Run the Read a Greek Sign MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Most Greek capital letters are the same as ours, and a few more are familiar from mathematics. A handful of look-alikes cause nearly all the trouble: Η is the vowel i, not h; Ρ is r, not p; Χ is ch, not x; Υ is y, sounding ee; and Ω is o, not w. This MicroSim gives twelve signs we are likely to see on the trip and asks us to type each one in Latin letters.

# Sign Spelled on signs Meaning Sounds like 1 ΑΘΗΝΑ athina Athens a-THEE-na 2 ΠΕΙΡΑΙΑΣ peiraias Piraeus, the port of Athens pee-reh-AHS 3 ΡΟΔΟΣ rodos Rhodes RO-thos 4 ΗΡΑΚΛΕΙΟ irakleio Heraklion ee-RA-klee-o 5 ΚΝΩΣΟΣ knosos Knossos kno-SOS 6 ΔΕΛΦΟΙ delfoi Delphi del-FEE 7 ΑΚΡΟΠΟΛΗ akropoli Acropolis a-KRO-po-lee 8 ΜΟΥΣΕΙΟ mouseio Museum moo-SEE-o 9 ΕΙΣΟΔΟΣ eisodos Entrance EE-so-thos 10 ΕΞΟΔΟΣ exodos Exit EX-o-thos 11 ΚΛΕΙΣΤΟ kleisto Closed klee-STO 12 ΑΝΟΙΧΤΟ anoichto Open a-nee-KHTO

The spellings follow ELOT 743, the standard used on Greek road and site signs. Common informal spellings are accepted too, such as pireas, knossos, delphi and klisto. Capital letters, spaces, hyphens and accent marks are ignored when checking an answer. Each pronunciation's stressed syllable matches the word's Wiktionary entry.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the sign and type it in Latin letters in the box below. Press Check or Enter.
  2. Press Letter key at any time to see all 24 Greek capitals with their sign spellings. Press Hide key to return.
  3. If the first try is wrong, the feedback names the sign's trap letters. Try once more.
  4. After a correct answer or a second miss, the sign appears letter by letter, each Greek letter above its Latin letter, with trap letters in red. A sign counts as read if it is correct within two tries.
  5. Press Next sign (or Enter) to continue. After the twelfth sign, the summary lists every sign and tallies the trap letters in the signs you missed at least once.
  6. Restart clears all answers.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: alphabet, the Greek language, the Greek capital letters and their sign spellings, and the letter pairs ΟΥ, ΑΙ, ΕΙ and ΟΙ. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Use the Greek letter table to transliterate twelve Greek signs from our route into Latin letters, with at least 10 of 12 correct within two attempts each.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (2 min): Open the Letter key and find the five look-alikes: Η, Ρ, Χ, Υ and Ω. Say what each one really is.
  2. Read (8 min): Work through all twelve signs. Type each one before opening the key; use the key only on a second try.
  3. Sound it out (3 min): For ΚΛΕΙΣΤΟ and ΑΝΟΙΧΤΟ, read the pronunciation aloud with the stress in the right place. These are the two words that matter most on a November afternoon.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 signs read within two tries. A follow-up question: A sign in Heraklion reads ΛΙΜΑΝΙ. Type it in Latin letters. It reads limani, "harbor."

docs.title: Read the Olive Oil Label
docs.text: Run the Read the Olive Oil Label MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The front of an olive oil bottle makes a claim; the back label holds the evidence. This MicroSim shows nine illustrative bottles, one at a time. For each, we read the claim on the front, turn the label to read the back, and judge whether the back supports the front. Beside the bottle is the standard we judge by:

Rule Standard Extra virgin Free acidity 0.8% or less (and no taste defects) Virgin Free acidity 2.0% or less Olive oil (refined and virgin blend) Free acidity 1.0% or less; never extra virgin Lampante Free acidity above 2.0%; not fit to eat until refined "Cold extraction" Only for virgin or extra virgin oil kept below 27 °C Freshness Read the harvest date, not the best-before date Origin Where the olives were grown and pressed, not where the oil was bottled Calories Every olive oil has about 120 kcal per tablespoon

Three labels support their claims and six do not. The pair of "cold extraction" labels, one at 25 °C and one at 32 °C, and the three honest labels keep us from rejecting every marketing phrase on sight: the skill is checking a claim against evidence, not distrusting all claims. After each judgment the back label's deciding detail is highlighted in yellow.

The labels are invented for practice and do not describe real products.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the claim on the front of the bottle.
  2. Press Turn the label (or T) to read the back, and compare each detail with the standard on the right.
  3. Choose Supports the claim (S) or Does not support the claim (D). Only the first judgment counts.
  4. Read the feedback and the highlighted detail, then press Next label (or Enter).
  5. After label 9, press See result for a summary of all nine. Hover over a numbered circle to review any label. Try Again starts over.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 8 on Rhodes, and anyone buying olive oil in a Greek shop. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: olive oil, the four grades and their free-acidity limits, malaxation, cold extraction below 27 °C, harvest date versus best-before date, and calories per tablespoon (all in the chapter section "Olive Oil"). Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Judge whether each of nine olive oil labels supports the claim on its front, using the EU grade limits, the cold-extraction rule, harvest dates, and origin wording, with at least 7 of 9 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the standard (2 min): Before the first label, name the one number that separates extra virgin from virgin oil.
  2. Judge the nine labels (8 min): For each, say aloud which back-label detail you are using before choosing.
  3. Find the pattern (2 min): In the summary, group the six unsupported labels by the kind of detail that decided them: acidity, temperature, ingredients, harvest, or origin.
  4. In the shop (on the day): Read the back of two real bottles in the Old Town and judge their front claims the same way.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 7 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Follow-up question: A bottle says "Extra virgin olive oil, cold extraction" and "best before March 2028," with no harvest date. What can and can't you conclude? The cold-extraction claim means it was kept below 27 °C, but without a harvest date we cannot tell whether the oil is from this season.

docs.title: Read the Ruin: Which Layer?
docs.text: Run the Read the Ruin: Which Layer? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Almost nothing we see on Day 2 stands as its first builders left it. This MicroSim practices one rule for reading a city of layers:

A thing belongs to the layer in which it arrived at this place, or, for a removal, the layer in which it was taken away.

The five layers are stacked like the ground itself, oldest at the bottom:

Layer Dates What it was Republic 1923–today The Turkish Republic Ottoman 1453–1922 The sultans' capital Latin occupation 1204–1261 Rule by the crusaders and Venice after the Fourth Crusade Byzantine 330–1453, except 1204–1261 The Christian imperial capital Roman before 330 CE The city before Constantine's capital

Twelve cards name things we see in the Hippodrome, Hagia Sophia and the Basilica Cistern. Three of them are trap cards: the Egyptian obelisk, the Serpent Column and the Medusa heads were all made long before they reached Constantinople, so their made date and their layer disagree. Other cards test the idea that a removal is a layer (the bare stone of the Walled Obelisk), that a European-looking monument can still be Ottoman (the German Fountain of 1900), and that not everything inside Hagia Sophia is Byzantine (the great calligraphic roundels and the ablution fountain).

The cards come in a fixed shuffled order, the same for every learner, so a group can compare answers card by card.

  3. The feedback shows when the thing was made and when it arrived or happened here, and the reason. The correct layer is outlined in green, a wrong choice in red, and the card settles into its correct layer.

  5. After the twelfth card, press See result. Hover over any card in the stack to review it; missed cards have a red border.
  6. Try Again repeats the same twelve cards in a new order.

docs.title: Rhodes Changes Hands, 1912–1948
docs.text: Run the Rhodes Changes Hands, 1912–1948 MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Rhodes became part of Greece only after World War II. Before that it was Ottoman for almost four centuries, Italian for three decades, German for twenty months, and British for almost two years. This timeline puts those rulers in one row and thirteen events in the row below, so the question "who governed Rhodes?" can be answered for any date.

Span Power governing Rhodes 1522 to May 1912 Ottoman Empire May 1912 to September 1943 Italy September 1943 to May 8, 1945 Germany (military occupation) May 8, 1945 to March 31, 1947 Britain (military administration) From March 31, 1947 Greece (formal union March 7, 1948)

Each event's number is colored by the power that governed Rhodes on that date. Three events, Ochi Day in 1940, the fall of Athens in 1941, and its liberation in 1944, happened on the Greek mainland; their hollow numbers show at a glance that Athens and Rhodes were on opposite sides of the war until 1945. Opening any event names the power that governed the island at that moment.

The timeline includes the deportation of the Jews of Rhodes on July 23, 1944. It is shown in the same plain style as every other event, with its date and the number deported, because the date is what the third question depends on: the deportation took place under German control, ten months after the Germans took the island from the Italians and less than a year before the war in Europe ended.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the prompt in the yellow bar, then compare the two rows from 1910 to 1949.
  2. Press Next event to read the events in date order, or click any event. Hover over an event or a colored span for its dates.
  3. Press Close-up: 1936–1949 to spread out the crowded war years, and Full span to return. ◀ Earlier and Later ▶ move the view; you can also drag the timeline sideways.
  4. Answer the five questions on the right. Each is scored once. The correct answer and its reason are shown, and the spans and events the question depends on are outlined in yellow on the timeline.
  5. Try Again clears the five questions and starts again.

docs.title: Who Built What We See in the Old Town?
docs.text: Run the Who Built What We See in the Old Town? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Rhodes is a layered city, and its layers do not sort themselves by style. A pointed Gothic arch may be the work of the knights in the 1480s, or of an Italian architect in the 1920s. This MicroSim asks one question of twelve buildings and features: who built what we see here today? Each card goes into one of four layers, stacked from oldest at the bottom to newest at the top.

Period Builders Dates Ancient The Greek or Roman city before about 400 CE Knights The Knights Hospitaller 1310 to 1522 Ottoman Builders under Ottoman rule 1523 to 1912 Italian Builders under Italian rule, new or rebuilt 1912 to 1943

The cards come in a fixed shuffled order, the same for every learner, with the four trap cards spread apart. Three traps are Italian buildings that look medieval: the Palace of the Grand Master, rebuilt from 1937 to 1940 after the explosion of 1856; the Liberty Gate, opened in 1924; and the Church of the Annunciation at Mandraki, a 1925 copy of the knights' lost cathedral. The fourth is the Kahal Shalom Synagogue, completed in 1577 by the Jewish community under Ottoman rule, which tests the idea that only Muslims built under the Ottomans. Two cards, the temple remains and the acropolis on Monte Smith, show that the ancient city survives even though the Colossus does not.

After each answer the reason appears and the card settles into its correct layer, outlined green if the first choice was right and red if it was not. After twelve cards the stack holds Ancient 2, Knights 3, Ottoman 4, and Italian 3.

  4. After the twelfth card, press See result for your score. Hover over any card in the stack to review it.
  5. Try Again repeats all twelve cards in a new order.

docs.title: From the Schism to the Sack, 1054–1261
docs.text: Run the From the Schism to the Sack, 1054–1261 MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Fourth Crusade was called to attack Egypt. It ended by sacking Christian Constantinople. This timeline lays out the seventeen events that explain how, in three rows:

Row What it follows Church The excommunications of 1054 in Hagia Sophia, a symbol of the drift between Rome and Constantinople Crusades From Urban II's call at Clermont in 1095 to the sack of April 1204 Byzantium and Venice Manzikert, Venice's trading privileges, the arrests of 1171, the massacre of 1182, and the Latin Empire to its end in 1261

Each event is numbered in date order. Clicking an event, or stepping through them with Previous event and Next event, shows its date and description. Four cause questions then ask which earlier event best explains a later one. The rows run separately for most of the period and converge in 1202 to 1204, when a debt to Venice, a Byzantine prince's unpaid promise, and a generation of anger at Western merchants met outside the city walls.

The timeline corrects four common ideas: that the Fourth Crusade set out to attack Constantinople; that the schism of 1054 was a single clean break felt by all Christians at once; that the Crusades were a single war; and that Venice and Byzantium were always enemies (event 3 shows them as allies).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the prompt in the yellow bar, then scan the three rows from 1054 to 1261.
  2. Press Next event to read the events in date order, or click any event. Hover over an event to see its title and date.
  3. Press Close-up: 1200–1205 to separate the crowded events of the Fourth Crusade, and Full span to return. Drag the timeline sideways to pan.
  4. Answer the four cause questions on the right. Each is scored once; the correct answer is shown, and the events it points to are highlighted.
  5. Restart clears the questions and starts again.

  3. Answer the cause questions (5 min): For each question, find the earlier event on the timeline before choosing.
  4. Explain it aloud (3 min): In three sentences, explain to a travel companion how a crusade bound for Egypt ended in Constantinople. Use at least three event numbers.

docs.text: Mastery is 3 of 4 cause questions correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: Why is it wrong to say that the Schism of 1054 caused the sack of 1204? The schism soured relations, but the direct causes were the crusaders' debt to Venice and Alexios IV's unpaid promise; the pope in fact excommunicated the crusaders for attacking a Christian city at Zara.

docs.title: Scribe or Press?
docs.text: Run the Scribe or Press? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A scribe and a printing press pay for a book in opposite ways. A scribe's cost is almost all marginal cost: every copy takes as long as the last. A press has a large fixed cost, casting type, building the press and setting every page, and after that each copy costs very little. So for one copy the scribe is cheaper, and for a hundred copies the press wins. This MicroSim asks where, exactly, the two lines cross.

The model uses one unit for everything: the workday, one person's day of skilled work. The book has 200 pages.

Method Rate Fixed cost Cost per copy Ordinary copyist 8 pages a day 0 200 ÷ 8 = 25 workdays Master calligrapher 2 pages a day 0 200 ÷ 2 = 100 workdays Printing press type set once 350 workdays 0.2 workdays

The press's fixed cost covers casting the type, building the press and setting all 200 pages; its cost per copy covers printing, paper handling and binding labor. These are round numbers chosen to show the shape of the comparison, an illustrative model, not historical prices.

The total costs for N copies are:

  • Scribe: cost per copy × N
  • Press: 350 + 0.2 × N

The crossover is the smallest whole number of copies at which the press is cheaper:

Scribe Inequality Solution Crossover Ordinary copyist 25 × N > 350 + 0.2 × N N > 14.1 15 copies Master calligrapher 100 × N > 350 + 0.2 × N N > 3.51 4 copies

The slower and more beautiful the handwriting, the sooner the press wins.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the table of the three methods. The highlighted rows are the scribe you are comparing and the press.
  2. With Ordinary copyist selected, type your prediction of the crossover into the box and press Check Prediction (or Enter). A prediction within one copy of the true crossover counts as correct. You get two tries; after a second miss the sim shows the worked inequality.
  3. The Copies slider is locked until your prediction is checked, so the chart cannot give the answer away. Then move the slider from 1 to 500 copies. Both total-cost lines grow from zero copies to the slider's value, the table shows each method's total, and the chart says which is cheaper. When the lines have crossed, a dashed line marks the crossover and a gold dot marks where they meet. The horizontal axis widens as the slider moves.
  4. Choose Master calligrapher, predict again and check.
  5. Move the slider to 200 copies and compare the costs: 5,000.0 workdays for the copyist, 20,000.0 for the calligrapher and 390.0 for the press.
  6. Reset clears both predictions.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 6, "Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses". Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: scribe, copyist, movable type, printing press, fixed cost and marginal cost, from the chapter sections "Scribes and Copyists", "Gutenberg" and "The Printing Press". Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Calculate the number of copies at which printing a 200-page book becomes cheaper than copying it by hand, for an ordinary copyist and for a master calligrapher, predicting each crossover within one copy.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the model (2 min): Which method has a fixed cost? Which has the larger cost per copy? At one copy, which is cheaper, and by how much?
  2. Predict and check (5 min): Set scribe cost equal to press cost, solve for N, and round up to the next whole copy. Check the prediction for the ordinary copyist, then for the master calligrapher.
  3. Compare (3 min): At 200 copies, how many times more does the copyist cost than the press? The calligrapher?
  4. Transfer (3 min): Suppose the press's fixed cost doubled to 700 workdays. Without the sim, estimate the new crossover for the ordinary copyist. (700 ÷ 24.8 ≈ 28.2, so 29 copies.)

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is both predictions correct, within one copy, in no more than two tries each. Follow-up questions:

  • Why was the scribe cheaper for a single copy? (The press must pay its whole fixed cost before it prints anything.)
  • Was the press's advantage only speed? (No: its cost per copy was over a hundred times lower than the copyist's.)
  • Why did beautiful handwriting make the press win sooner? (A slower scribe has a higher cost per copy, so the press's fixed cost is paid back in fewer copies.)

docs.title: Two Ends of the Serpent Column
docs.text: Run the Two Ends of the Serpent Column MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Serpent Column has two ends. It was cast after the Greek victory over the Persians at Plataea in 479 BCE and set up beside Apollo's altar at Delphi, where three intertwined bronze snakes held up a golden tripod. By 330 CE Constantine had moved it to the Hippodrome of his new capital, Constantinople, and it still stands there, in Istanbul, headless, in a pit. Its coils carry the names of the 31 Greek communities that fought, under the heading "These fought the war."

No single place tells its whole story. This MicroSim gives ten claims about the column and asks where each could be checked:

Claim Where to check it Bronze coils carry the names of the Greek cities that fought. In Istanbul A stone base by the great altar marks where the monument stood. At Delphi A bronze copy shows how the column looked in its setting. At Delphi The upper jaw of one serpent head survives. In Istanbul The column stands in a pit because the ground has risen since Byzantine times. In Istanbul The temple terrace where the monument stood is held up by the polygonal wall. At Delphi The Spartan commander Pausanias had his own name inscribed first, and it was erased. Only in a written source A golden tripod once sat on top of the three heads. Only in a written source The monument was made from a tenth of the spoils of Plataea. Only in a written source The Phocian leaders took the tripod's gold during the Third Sacred War. Only in a written source

The cards appear in a shuffled order. The totals carry the lesson: Delphi has the place (3), Istanbul has the object (3), and the writers have the story (4). Four of the ten claims rest on Herodotus, Thucydides, and the travel writer Pausanias, not on anything we can see at either end.

Notes on the evidence. Herodotus (9.81) says the Greeks set aside a tenth of the spoils of Plataea for Delphi and dedicated from it the golden tripod that stood on the three-headed bronze serpent next to the altar. Thucydides (1.132) says the Spartan regent Pausanias first had a couplet inscribed on the tripod naming himself as the victor, and that the Spartans erased it and inscribed the names of the cities instead. The travel writer Pausanias (10.13.9), in the 2nd century CE, says the Phocian leaders carried off the gold during the Third Sacred War (356–346 BCE) while the bronze remained. Ottoman pictures of the 16th century still show the three heads; accounts differ on exactly when they broke off, at the end of the 17th century or soon after. Card 6 simplifies slightly: the polygonal wall is the retaining wall along the south side of the temple terrace, the terrace on which the monument stood near the altar.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question and the three bin names. All ten cards start in the tray at the top.
  2. Click a card to read it in full in the white panel. Then drag it into a bin, or press one of the three colored bin buttons (or keys 1, 2, 3). The next card is selected automatically.
  3. A placed card can be dragged to another bin, or back to the tray, until you press Check. Arrow keys move the selection.
  4. When all ten are placed, press Check (or Enter). Each card is marked ✓ or ✗, and the panel shows why for the selected card. Only the first Check counts toward mastery.
  5. Move the red cards and press Check again until all ten are correct. The bins then show their totals and the summary. Reset clears every placement and returns the cards to the tray in the same order.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 18, "Day 12: Delphi", who saw the column's other end in Istanbul on Day 2 (Chapter 4). Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: the Serpent Column, Plataea and the Persian Wars (Chapter 15), the Hippodrome (Chapter 4), the Third Sacred War (Chapter 17), Herodotus, Thucydides and Pausanias as sources, the great altar and the temple terrace, and the polygonal wall (Chapter 18). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Attribute each of 10 claims about the Serpent Column to the place where its evidence can be checked, at Delphi, in Istanbul, or only in an ancient written source, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (1 min): Before starting, guess how many of the ten claims you could check by standing in front of the bronze in Istanbul.
  2. Sort (6 min): Place all ten cards and press Check once. Note the first score.

docs.title: Sèvres or Lausanne?
docs.text: Run the Sèvres or Lausanne? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Two treaties ended the Ottoman Empire's war with the Allies. The sultan's government signed the Treaty of Sèvres on August 10, 1920, but the Grand National Assembly in Ankara rejected it and it never took effect. After the nationalists' victories of 1921 and 1922, the Allies negotiated again, and the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on July 24, 1923, recognized an independent Turkey with roughly its present borders.

It is tempting to say that Lausanne simply cancelled Sèvres. It did not. This MicroSim shows ten terms of Sèvres with the Lausanne column hidden. For each term we predict Reversed (Lausanne undid the Sèvres term) or Kept (Lausanne left it in place, in substance), and only then see what Lausanne said. Six terms were reversed and four kept.

After the ten, we choose which of three explanations accounts for the pattern. The answer is the National Pact (Misak-ı Millî) of January 1920, which claimed the lands with an Ottoman Muslim majority still held by Ottoman forces at the armistice of October 1918, demanded the security of Istanbul and the Sea of Marmara, and left the Arab provinces to their inhabitants. Every term Lausanne reversed lay inside that claim, and every term it kept lay outside it.

The sim names some limits of that rule. The Straits stayed under an international commission until the Montreux Convention of 1936. The border with Iraq around Mosul, which Ankara did claim, was left open at Lausanne and settled in Iraq's favor in 1926. And the Pact's claim to eastern Anatolia as Muslim-majority land rested on a majority that existed only after most of the region's Armenians had been deported or killed in 1915–1916, as the chapter's World War I section describes. For Armenians and Kurds, Lausanne is remembered as the treaty that dropped the states Sèvres had promised; for Turks, it is the founding charter of an independent republic. The sim asks us to explain the treaty, not to judge it, but both memories are part of its history.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the prompt and the Sèvres column. The Lausanne column is hidden, and the current term's row is highlighted in yellow.
  2. Press Reversed or Kept (or press R or K). Each term has one prediction.
  3. The Lausanne term appears in the table with a badge, a green check if we predicted it and a red cross if we did not. The feedback below explains why.
  4. Press Next term (or Enter). After term 10, press See the tally.
  5. Choose explanation A, B, or C (or press A, B or C). The feedback tells us whether it fits, and why not if it does not.
  6. Try Again hides the Lausanne column and starts over.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Treaty of Sèvres, the Treaty of Lausanne, the National Pact, the Grand National Assembly, the Greco-Turkish War, the Dardanelles Strait, and the capitulations. Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate the terms of the 1920 Treaty of Sèvres that the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne reversed from those it kept, predicting at least 8 of 10 correctly and explaining the pattern by the National Pact.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. State the rule first (2 min): Before term 1, write down in one sentence what the National Pact claimed. Use it to make every prediction.
  2. Predict (8 min): Work through the ten terms. For each, say aloud whether the land or right lay inside the Pact's claim before choosing.
  3. Explain the pattern (3 min): Look down the finished Lausanne column and choose an explanation. If you chose B or C, find the term that breaks it.
  4. Two memories (2 min): Pick one reversed term, Smyrna or Armenia, and say how a Greek, an Armenian and a Turkish family might each remember what Lausanne decided.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 correct predictions and explanation A. As a follow-up, ask: We sail through the Dardanelles on this trip. Did Lausanne give Turkey full control of the Straits? A strong answer says no: Lausanne kept an international commission and demilitarized zones, and full Turkish control came only with the Montreux Convention of 1936.

docs.title: The Siege of 1453, Step by Step
docs.text: Run the Siege of 1453, Step by Step MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Constantinople did not fall to one cannon or one clever trick. It had five defenses, and Mehmed II's campaign took them apart one at a time over more than a year. This MicroSim walks through eight turning points, from the building of Rumeli Hisarı in 1452 to the final assault before dawn on May 29, 1453, and asks the same question at each one: which of the city's defenses does this defeat?

The six possible answers are the same at every step:

Answer A The strait: supply from the Black Sea B The chain across the Golden Horn C The land walls D Help from the West E The defenders' numbers and morale F None: the defenders held this time

Each step highlights its place on a schematic map of the historic peninsula, the land walls, the Golden Horn and its chain, Galata, the Bosphorus with Rumeli Hisarı and Anadolu Hisarı, and the Sea of Marmara. Two of the eight steps are days when the defenders won, so the answer is not always an Ottoman success. The summary at the end lists every step and counts how many fell under each defense.

The map is schematic: shapes and distances are simplified so that every place in the story fits in one small frame.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the step's date and event on the right, and find the highlighted place on the map.
  2. Choose one of the six answers (or press a letter key, A to F). The answer locks: the correct answer turns green, a wrong choice red, and the reason appears.
  3. Press Next step (or Enter, or the right arrow). Previous (or the left arrow) revisits an earlier step, but answers cannot be changed.
  4. After step 8, press See summary. The table shows the correct answer for each step and your answer, and the line below counts the steps under each defense.
  5. Restart clears all answers and returns to step 1.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: the Bosphorus Strait, the Golden Horn, the Theodosian Walls, moat, breach, Rumeli Hisarı, the chain across the Golden Horn, Janissaries, Mehmed II, Constantine XI, and Giovanni Giustiniani Longo. Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Attribute each of eight turning points of the 1453 siege to the defense of Constantinople it overcame, or recognize that the defenders held, with at least 6 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. List the defenses (2 min): Before starting, name the city's advantages from the chapter: water on three sides, the Golden Horn harbor, the land walls, supply from the Black Sea, and allies in the West.
  2. Step through (6 min): Work through all eight steps. Before choosing, say in one sentence what the event made harder for the defenders.
  3. Read the summary (3 min): Count the steps under each defense. Which defenses were already gone before the final assault? Which two steps were defenders' victories, and why did neither save the city?
  4. Discuss (3 min): A common story says the city fell because of the great cannon. Using the summary, write two sentences that explain why that story is incomplete.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 6 of 8 correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: The ships hauled over the hill on April 22 never attacked the sea walls. Why did they still matter? A strong answer says that they went around the chain, so the defenders had to move men from the land walls to guard the harbor walls, thinning a garrison of only about 7,000.

docs.title: Sort the Scripts
docs.text: Run the Sort the Scripts MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Writing systems differ most in what one basic sign stands for. This MicroSim gives twelve cards, each describing a script in two pieces of evidence: what one sign stands for, and how many signs the script uses. Our job is to sort each one into the right kind:

Kind What one sign stands for Typical sign count Logographic A word or part of a word Hundreds or more Syllabary A syllable About 40 to 100 Abjad A consonant; most vowels are left to the reader Under 40 Alphabet A vowel or a consonant Under 40

Three cards target the most common confusions. Egyptian hieroglyphs include some signs for single sounds, but a few sound-signs do not make an alphabet. Hebrew and Arabic are often called alphabets in everyday speech, but they leave most vowels unwritten, which makes them abjads. And Linear A, which no one can read, can still be classified: its sign count and its shared signs with Linear B mark it as a syllabary.

After the twelfth card, every card shows its sign count, sorted from most to fewest in each bin, so we can see the counts fall into the rule-of-thumb bands from the chapter's tip.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card in the white panel.
  2. Press the button under the bin where you think it belongs (or press 1 to 4). Each card has one attempt.
  3. The correct bin is outlined in green, a wrong choice in red, and the card settles into its correct bin. The feedback explains why.
  4. Press Next card to continue. The score in the top right counts correct first attempts.
  5. After the twelfth card, press See result. Each card now shows its sign count. Hover over any card to read it again; missed cards have a red border.
  6. Restart reshuffles the cards and clears the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: writing system, logographic script, syllabary, abjad, alphabet, the sign-count rule of thumb, and Linear A and Linear B from Part 1. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify twelve writing systems as logographic, syllabary, abjad, or alphabet from what one basic sign stands for and how many signs the script uses, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (2 min): Say the four kinds aloud with one example of each from the chapter before starting.
  2. Sort (6 min): Work through all twelve cards. For each, find the two pieces of evidence on the card before choosing: what one sign stands for, and how many signs there are.
  3. Read the counts (3 min): On the result screen, check that every count falls in its bin's band. Which script sits closest to a band's edge?
  4. Extend (3 min): Turkey switched from the Arabic script to a Latin alphabet in 1928. Using the Arabic and Modern Turkish cards, explain in one sentence why the switch made Turkish easier to read aloud.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: Japanese katakana has 46 basic signs, each a vowel, a consonant plus a vowel, or a final n. Which kind of script is it? A syllabary, like hiragana.

docs.title: Source, Myth, or Contested?
docs.text: Run the Source, Myth, or Contested? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every guide in Hagia Sophia tells stories, and they are not all the same kind of story. Some come from people who saw the building new. Some first appear centuries later. Some rest on dates nobody disputes, and some are arguments about what those dates should mean today. This MicroSim gives ten statements we are likely to hear on Day 2 and asks which of four kinds each one is:

Kind Definition used in the sim Primary source Evidence written or made at the time, by someone who was there or close to it. Myth A story first recorded long after the event, with no support from the time. Contested history The facts are agreed, but their meaning or proper use is disputed today. Settled history A fact agreed by the sources and by modern historians.

The statements are built to catch four common mistakes. A primary source is not the same as a true source: Procopius and Niketas Choniates were both close to what they described, and both wrote with a purpose. A myth is not worthless: the Solomon line tells us how proud later Byzantines were of their church. Contested history is not unknown history: the dates of Hagia Sophia's conversions are agreed, and the argument is about values. And a story told by every tour guide is not history just because it is told often.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the four definitions across the top.
  2. Read the statement in the white panel and press the button for its kind (or press 1 to 4). Each statement is scored once and cannot be changed.
  3. The correct kind is outlined in green, a wrong choice in red, and the reason appears below the statement.
  4. Press Next statement to continue. The numbered tiles show your answers so far.
  5. After the tenth statement, press See result. The panel shows your score and lists the statements you missed. Click any numbered tile to review that statement and its reason.
  6. Try Again reshuffles the same ten statements.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 2 in Istanbul. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: primary source, secondary source, myth, history and contested history, from Part One of the chapter, "Whose Story Is This?" Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Classify ten statements about Byzantine Constantinople as a primary source, a myth, contested history or settled history, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Three questions (2 min): Before starting, say aloud the question each kind of statement answers: who saw it, and why did they write?; when did this story first appear?; and who is this past important to now?
  2. Classify (6 min): Work through all ten statements. Before choosing, ask who is speaking and when. A named author from the time points to a primary source; "should" or "belongs" points to contested history.
  3. Review (3 min): On the result screen, click the tiles for the two eyewitness statements, Procopius on the dome and Choniates on the sack. Each is a primary source even though each is one-sided. Say what purpose each author had.
  4. On site (any time on Day 2): When a guide tells a story, ask which of the four kinds it is, and what we would need to know to be sure.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: A guide says the "weeping column" in Hagia Sophia grants wishes to anyone who turns a thumb in its hole. Which kind of statement is this, and how would we test it? It is a myth: we would look for the earliest source of the story and ask how long after the building it was written.

docs.title: What Did the Külliye Do?
docs.text: Run the What Did the Külliye Do? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Süleymaniye Mosque, built for Suleiman the Magnificent by Mimar Sinan between 1550 and 1557, is only the center of a much larger plan. Around it stand the buildings of its külliye, a complex of public services run as a single charitable endowment (vakıf). This MicroSim takes twelve of those buildings, one card at a time, and asks which public need each one served:

Need What it means 1. Worship Buildings for prayer 2. Learning Buildings for teaching and study 3. Health Buildings for treating the sick 4. Food and shelter Buildings that fed or housed people 5. Income Property whose rent or fees paid for the foundation 6. Remembrance Tombs of the founder and family

Two cards are traps. The medical school sounds like health, but it trained physicians; the patients were treated in the hospital next door. The public bath sounds like a free service, but bathers paid a fee, and the fee went to the foundation. Those two cards, with the rows of shops, show the idea at the heart of the vakıf: some buildings existed only to pay for the rest.

When all twelve are sorted, the summary reads Worship 1, Learning 4, Health 1, Food and shelter 2, Income 2, Remembrance 2. Four of the twelve served learning, the largest group.

docs.text:
1. Read the six needs in the colored column headers.
  2. Read the building on the card in the white panel and press the button for the need it served (or press 1 to 6). Each card has one attempt.
  3. The correct column is outlined in green, a wrong choice in red, and the card joins its correct column. The feedback gives the reason. The number at the bottom of each column counts its buildings.
  4. Press Next card to continue. The score in the top right counts correct first answers.
  5. After the twelfth card, press See result. Hover over any card in the columns to read its reason again; missed cards have a red border.
  6. Try Again repeats all twelve cards.

docs.text:

  2. Sort (6 min): Work through all twelve cards. For each one, ask two questions before choosing: who used this building? and who paid for it?
  3. Read the summary (3 min): On the result screen, count the buildings that spent money and the ones that earned it. Which group is larger, and why does the complex need both?
  4. Plan the walk (3 min): Using the chapter's walk around the Süleymaniye, decide which of these buildings we can still see from the street on Day 3, and which one we can eat lunch in.

docs.title: Layers of the Theodosian Walls
docs.text: Run the Layers of the Theodosian Walls MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Theodosian land walls, completed in 413 under Theodosius II, were not one wall but a defense in depth about 60 m deep. An army coming from Thrace, in the west, met five layers in turn:

Order Layer Approximate size 1 Moat About 20 m wide and several meters deep, with a low battlemented wall on its inner edge 2 Outer terrace A narrow strip between the moat and the outer wall 3 Outer wall About 8.5 m high and 2 m thick, with smaller towers of its own 4 Inner terrace (peribolos) About 15 to 20 m wide 5 Inner wall About 12 m high and nearly 5 m thick, with 96 towers up to about 20 m tall

The MicroSim shows a schematic cross-section with five numbered positions and the five layer names in random order. The drawing keeps the relative heights right (the moat below ground, the inner wall and its towers taller than the outer wall) but is not to scale, and all the sizes are approximate: they vary along the 5.7 km of wall, and sources give slightly different figures.

Part 1 asks us to place the names before anything is labeled. After one submission each position is marked, the sizes appear on the drawing, and each position's callout explains what the layer was for. Part 2 asks three questions: why the inner wall was taller, which emperor completed the walls, and how the crusaders got in in 1204.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question at the top: An army arrives from the west. What does it meet first, and what last?
  2. Click a name below the drawing, then click a numbered box to place it. You can also drag a name onto a box. Box 1 is the outside, toward Thrace; box 5 is next to the city.
  3. Rearrange freely: clicking a filled box sends its name back, and placing a name in a filled box swaps the old name out.
  4. When all five boxes are filled, press Submit. There is one submission. Each box turns green or red and shows the correct layer.
  5. Click any box, or any numbered marker on the drawing, to read that layer's size and purpose.
  6. Answer the three questions in Part 2, one attempt each, pressing Next question after each. The final line gives both scores.
  7. Restart clears both parts and reshuffles the names.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: moat, terrace, tower, breach, outer wall, inner wall, and peribolos. Learning objective (Bloom: Remember): Identify the five layers of the Theodosian land walls in the order an attacker from the west meets them, with no more than one placement error.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (3 min): Without looking back at the chapter, place the five names and submit.
  2. Read the callouts (3 min): Open all five callouts in order, 1 to 5. For each, say what an attacker standing there could and could not do.
  3. Answer Part 2 (2 min): Answer the three questions. Notice that question 1 asks about the design and questions 2 and 3 about the walls' history.
  4. Connect to the trip (2 min): At Yedikule or Edirnekapı, the moat is now gardens and the outer wall is broken in places. Predict which layers will still be easy to see, and which will need imagination.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 4 of 5 positions correct on the first submission. A follow-up question: In 1453 Mehmed II's cannon broke sections of the outer and inner walls near the Gate of St. Romanus. Why did each breach still leave the defenders a chance? A strong answer says that a breach in the outer wall put attackers on the inner terrace, under fire from the higher inner wall, and that the defenders rebuilt breaches at night.

docs.title: Thoughtful Traveler Choices
docs.text: Run the Thoughtful Traveler Choices MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The six thoughtful-traveler principles are easy to agree with and harder to use when a real person is standing in front of us. This MicroSim puts them to work on eight situations from our route. Each situation has three responses: a weak one, a tempting one, and the one that best fits the principles. We commit to one, and the MicroSim marks the best response and names the principle that decides it.

Principle Short form shown on screen Curiosity Ask and look closer Humility We are guests Consent People and sacred places are not scenery Reciprocity Fair exchange, no false promises Patience Fit the place's rhythm Many stories Listen to more than one account

The tempting answers are the interesting ones. Most of them sound polite: keeping a conversation with a steward short, refusing a carpet seller's tea, photographing a street vendor from far enough away that she does not notice, promising to "come back later." Each one quietly avoids contact with the person in front of us. The feedback explains why the best response treats that person as someone with a whole life rather than as part of the view.

All eight situations are illustrative, written for this guide. The Grand Bazaar's Sunday closing and Friday as the main day of congregational prayer come from our trip itinerary.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the situation and the three responses. The six principles stay at the top of the screen for reference.
  2. Press A, B or C (or type the letter) to commit to a response. Each situation allows one choice.
  3. The best response turns green, a different choice turns red, and the deciding principle lights up at the top. The feedback panel explains why.
  4. Press Next situation (or Enter) to continue. The score in the top right counts best choices.
  5. After the eighth situation, press See summary. It lists every situation, its deciding principle, our choice, and how many times each principle decided.
  6. Restart clears all answers and the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: thoughtful traveler, the six principles (curiosity, humility, consent, reciprocity, patience, many stories), tourist script, empathy, and cognitive and emotional empathy. Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Judge which of three responses best fits the six thoughtful-traveler principles in each of eight situations on our route, choosing the best response in at least 7 of 8 situations on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (2 min): Before starting, say each principle's question aloud from the chapter's table, for example "Whose home, workplace, or holy place is this?" for Humility.
  2. Judge (6 min): Work through all eight situations. Before pressing a button, name the principle that you think decides the case.
  3. Compare (3 min): On the summary, find the two principles that decided two situations each. What do the two Consent cases share? What do the two Patience cases share?
  4. Extend (3 min): Write a ninth situation for a stop we have not covered, such as the Day 9 visit to Knossos, with one weak, one tempting and one best response. Which principle decides it?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 7 of 8 best choices on the first attempt. A follow-up question: Response B in the Gallipoli situation, politely pointing out what the film said, sounds respectful. Which principle does it miss, and what would a better first move be? It misses Many stories: the better move is to listen first and ask what the battle means to the guide's own family.

docs.title: Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence?
docs.text: Run Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence? Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
How much should we trust a story about the past? The chapter offers a simple rule built on two questions: how long after the event was the earliest surviving evidence made, and did its author have a reason to shape it? This MicroSim applies the rule to eight stories from our two sites, Troy and Gallipoli, on a timeline that runs from the Late Bronze Age to the 20th century.

Verdict Rule Firm history Evidence within 10 years, no known reason to invent Real core, shaped telling Evidence within 10 years, but the author had a reason to shape it, or a detail is known to be invented Late or unsupported Earliest evidence more than 10 years after the event

For each story the event appears on the timeline as a blue dot. Before anything else is shown, we predict when the earliest surviving evidence was made and mark it with a gold ring. Then the evidence appears as a red square, joined to the event by a gap bar, together with the author and their stake. Only then do we judge.

Story Event Earliest evidence Gap Verdict A city on the Hisarlık mound burned c. 1180 BCE The Troy VIIa destruction layer itself 0 years Firm history A Hittite treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa c. 1280 BCE The treaty tablet from Hattusa 0 years Firm history A ten-year Greek siege to win back Helen c. 1180 BCE, if it happened Homer's Iliad, c. 700 BCE about 480 years Late or unsupported The wooden horse c. 1180 BCE, if it happened Brief mentions in the Odyssey, c. 700 BCE; fullest telling in Virgil, c. 19 BCE about 480 years Late or unsupported Mehmed II at Troy, avenging the Trojans 1462 Kritoboulos's history of Mehmed, c. 1467 about 5 years Real core, shaped telling Priam's Treasure and Sophia's shawl 1873 Schliemann's own account, 1874 1 year Real core, shaped telling Three Allied battleships lost on March 18, 1915 1915 Naval records of both sides 0 years Firm history The "Johnnies and Mehmets" words of 1934 1934 Şükrü Kaya's newspaper interview, 1953 19 years Late or unsupported

When all eight are judged, the timeline shows every gap at once. The longest bars belong to the most famous stories, the siege and the wooden horse.

Two stories ask for care. The losses of March 18, 1915, were men, not only ships: the French battleship Bouvet sank within minutes with most of her crew. And the "Johnnies and Mehmets" words are judged here only as a claim about who wrote them in 1934. As cultural memory, read at Anzac Day services and carved at Anzac Cove, they are real whoever wrote them, as the chapter explains.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Pick a story card above the timeline. Its event appears as a blue dot in its own row. Hover over any marker for details.
  2. Predict: click the timeline where you think the earliest surviving evidence was made, or type a year and choose BCE or CE. Your guess appears as a gold ring. Press Reveal the evidence.
  3. The timeline zooms to the story and shows the evidence, the gap bar, and the author's stake. The panel says how close your guess was (within 50 years counts as close for a BCE event, within 5 years for a CE event). The prediction is not scored.
  4. Judge: choose one of the three verdicts and press Check. A wrong first answer gives a hint; you get two tries. The rule that decides the story is highlighted on the right.
  5. Press Next story to continue. After all eight, press See all eight for the full timeline, then click any story card to review it.
  6. Full span returns to the whole timeline; Start over reshuffles the stories. Drag the timeline sideways to pan.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for Day 6 at Troy and Gallipoli. Duration: 15–20 minutes. Prerequisites: primary source and myth versus history (Chapter 4); Troy VIIa, Wilusa, the Iliad, the Odyssey, the Trojan Horse and Priam's Treasure (this chapter); the naval attack of March 18, 1915 (Chapter 7); the Johnnies and Mehmets words (this chapter); and the three verdicts. Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Judge each of eight stories about Troy and Gallipoli as firm history, a real core with a shaped telling, or late or unsupported, by comparing the date of the event with the date and author of its earliest surviving evidence, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first try.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): For each story, commit to a date for the earliest evidence before revealing it. Notice which famous stories you expected to have early sources.
  2. Judge (8 min): Apply both criteria, the gap and the author's stake, in that order.
  3. Look at the whole (3 min): On the final timeline, compare the longest bars with the shortest. Which stories are most famous, and which are best supported?
  4. Discuss (4 min): The Mehmed and Schliemann stories have tiny gaps but are still shaped. Why is an early source not automatically an honest one?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is at least 7 of 8 verdicts correct on the first try. A follow-up question: Hisarlık is a real Late Bronze Age city that burned around 1180 BCE. Does that make the ten-year siege of the Iliad firm history? No: a real place does not prove the story told about it; the earliest account of the siege is about 480 years later.

Common misconceptions this activity targets:

  • A famous story told everywhere must have an early source.
  • A source written by an eyewitness, or soon after, is automatically reliable.
  • A real place proves the story told about it.
  • A story with a late source must be false. (It may be true; it cannot be shown to be.)

docs.title: The Right Words at the Right Moment
docs.text: Run the Right Words at the Right Moment MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Knowing what a Turkish phrase means is not the same as knowing when to say it. This MicroSim puts fourteen of the phrases from the chapter's table into ten situations we will actually meet in Istanbul: walking into a café at 8 AM, buying a simit, asking a price, paying for dinner, answering a shopkeeper's welcome, greeting a fisherman at work, praising a home cook, getting past someone on a tram, leaving a restaurant in the evening, and accepting more tea.

Each situation offers three phrases, each with its pronunciation guide. One is the best choice; the other two are real Turkish that fits a different moment. Most of the traps are phrases that belong to the other person in the exchange: Afiyet olsun is what the cook says to us, and Hoş geldiniz is what the shopkeeper says, not our reply.

After the tenth situation, the MicroSim shows a phrase sheet: the ten best phrases with their pronunciations and meanings, which can be kept for the trip.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the situation and say the three phrases aloud, using the pronunciation guide under each one.
  2. Choose a phrase (or press 1, 2 or 3). Each situation has one attempt. The best phrase turns green, a wrong choice red, and the panel gives its meaning and the reason. A wrong choice also shows what the chosen phrase means.
  3. Press Next situation (or Enter). The score in the top right counts correct first choices.
  4. After situation 10, press See phrase sheet to see all ten best phrases, with a check or a cross for each of your first choices.
  5. Restart clears all answers.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: basic Turkish phrases and their meanings, and the Turkish pronunciation of c, ç, ş, ğ and ı. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Use the appropriate Turkish phrase in ten everyday situations from our Istanbul days, choosing the best phrase in at least 8 of 10 situations on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Say it first (2 min): Before choosing in each situation, say all three phrases aloud. The ı in Günaydın and Hayır is the "uh" sound, and ş in Teşekkür is "sh."
  2. Choose (5 min): Work through all ten situations. For each phrase, ask: who says this, and to whom?
  3. Find the pattern (3 min): On the phrase sheet, look at the situations you missed. How many of your wrong choices were phrases that the other person in the exchange would say?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: On the evening of Day 1, a waiter brings your balık ekmek and says Afiyet olsun. What could you say when you hand back the empty plate to the cook? Elinize sağlık, "health to your hands," or a simple Teşekkür ederim.

docs.title: Tutoring Effect Size Explorer
docs.text: Run the Tutoring Effect Size Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Studies of teaching report their results as an effect size: the gap between the program group and a comparison group, measured in standard deviations of the comparison group's scores (Cohen's d). The number is easy to quote and hard to feel. "Two sigma" does not mean the students learned twice as much, and 0.3 does not mean the effect was trivial.

This MicroSim translates effect sizes into a picture. Two normal curves share one axis of test scores: the conventional class, fixed at mean 0, and the program group, whose mean sits at d. If both groups are spread out in the same way, the average student in the program outscores the share of the conventional class lying below the program mean, which is

\[\text{percentile} = 100 \times \Phi(d),\]

where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The sim shades that share and prints it to one decimal place.

# Reported result d Model percentile 1 Bloom's studies, one-on-one tutoring with mastery learning (1984) 2.00 97.7 2 Bloom's studies, mastery learning in a class (1984) 1.00 84.1 3 VanLehn's review, human tutoring (2011) 0.79 78.5 4 Nickow, Oreopoulos, and Quan's review of randomized school tutoring trials (2020) 0.37 64.4 5 Nigeria after-school AI tutor pilot, six weeks (World Bank, 2025) 0.30 61.8

Reading these numbers with care. The five rows are not equally strong evidence, and the sim does not rank programs.

  • Bloom's 2.0 is an outlier. It came from a few small studies by Bloom's graduate students that lasted a few weeks, covered one unit, and tested exactly what had been taught. Later reviews of many trials find much smaller averages, and critics such as Paul von Hippel have argued that part of the gap came from the extra testing and feedback the tutored students received.
  • The 2020 review's 0.37 shrank on publication. The 2020 working paper pooled randomized trials of school tutoring and reported 0.37; the peer-reviewed version (2024) reports about 0.29, near the 61st percentile. Both are large by the standards of education research.
  • The AI tutor result is one short pilot. The World Bank team reported gains of about 0.3 standard deviations in English after six weeks of after-school sessions in Benin City, Edo State, with teachers present and a structured design. One randomized pilot is promising, not proof that AI tutoring in general works at that size; short studies with tests close to the material often report larger effects than long ones with broad tests.
  • The percentile is a model. It assumes normal curves with equal spread. Real score distributions are lumpier, and the percentile describes the average student, not every student.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the result, its study, and its d. The curves start together at d = 0, where the percentile is 50.0.
  2. Type the percentile you predict (a whole number from 0 to 100) and press Check or Enter. The program curve slides to d and the shaded share fills in. A prediction within 5 points of the model percentile counts as correct.
  3. If the first prediction is off, read the hint and try once more. The percentile stays hidden until you are right or have used both tries. Only the first attempt counts toward "n of 5 within 5 points on the first attempt".
  4. Press Next result to go on. After result 5, the free exploration slider unlocks: move d from 0.00 to 2.00 and watch the percentile change, with gold markers showing the five results.
  5. Restart returns to result 1 and clears the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 20, "Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today", in the section "Learning for All: The Prince's Tutor and the Philosopher's Warning". Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: standard deviation, effect size, and percentile (defined in "Bloom's 2 Sigma Problem"); one-on-one tutoring, mastery learning, and AI tutoring (defined in the sections around the sim). Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Interpret five reported effect sizes for tutoring and mastery learning, given in standard deviations, as the percentile of a conventional class that the average student in the program outscores, to within 5 percentage points.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): Work through the five results, predicting each percentile before the curves move. Note the first-attempt score.
  2. Explore (4 min): Use the slider to find the d that reaches the 75th percentile (about 0.67) and the 90th (about 1.28). Compare the gain from 0 to 1 with the gain from 1 to 2.
  3. Discuss (4 min): A company claims its AI tutor "delivers two sigma". What would you ask before believing it? Think about study size, length, the test used, and who was in the comparison group.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 4 of 5 predictions within 5 points on the first attempt. A follow-up question: An article says a program "raised scores by 0.25 standard deviations". About which percentile does the average student reach, and is that a small effect? A strong answer gives about the 60th percentile and notes that a quarter of a standard deviation is a meaningful gain for a whole school.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Benjamin S. Bloom, "The 2 Sigma Problem: The Search for Methods of Group Instruction as Effective as One-to-One Tutoring," Educational Researcher 13, no. 6 (1984): 4–16 (doi:10.3102/0013189X013006004). Results 1 and 2.
  2. Kurt VanLehn, "The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems," Educational Psychologist 46, no. 4 (2011): 197–221 (doi:10.1080/00461520.2011.611369). Result 3: human tutoring, d = 0.79.
  3. Andre Nickow, Philip Oreopoulos, and Vincent Quan, "The Impressive Effects of Tutoring on PreK-12 Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence," NBER Working Paper 27476 (2020) (nber.org). Result 4: pooled effect of 0.37.
  4. Andre Nickow, Philip Oreopoulos, and Vincent Quan, "The Promise of Tutoring for PreK–12 Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence," American Educational Research Journal 61, no. 1 (2024) (doi:10.3102/00028312231208687). The published version, with a pooled effect of about 0.29.
  5. Martín E. De Simone and others, "From chalkboards to chatbots: Transforming learning in Nigeria, one prompt at a time," World Bank Education blog, January 9, 2025 (blogs.worldbank.org). Result 5: about 0.3 standard deviations after a six-week pilot. The full study is World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125 (2025).
  6. Paul T. von Hippel, "Two-Sigma Tutoring: Separating Science Fiction from Science Fact," Education Next 24, no. 2 (2024) (educationnext.org). Why Bloom's 2.0 is an upper bound rather than a typical result.
  7. Jacob Cohen, Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed. (Lawrence Erlbaum, 1988). The standardized mean difference d and its percentile ("U3") interpretation.
  8. Effect size — Wikipedia. Cohen's d and how it is computed.
  9. Plotly JavaScript Open Source Graphing Library — Plotly documentation for the charting library used here.

docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:
