docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This map follows the Viking Star's seven-night Ancient Mediterranean Treasures voyage from Istanbul to Athens, November 14–21, 2026: the middle part of our November 11–23 trip. The cruise calls at six ports in Turkey and Greece, and the map ends with our overland day trip from Athens to Delphi:

  1. Istanbul, Turkey: Nov 14–15, overnight in port (trip days 4–5)
  2. Çanakkale, Turkey, the port for Troy and Gallipoli: Nov 16 (trip day 6)
  3. Kuşadası, Turkey, the port for Ephesus: Nov 17 (trip day 7)
  4. Rhodes, Greece: Nov 18 (trip day 8)
  5. Heraklion, Crete, Greece, the port for Knossos: Nov 19 (trip day 9)
  6. Athens (Piraeus), Greece: Nov 20, disembarking Nov 21 (trip days 10–11)
  7. Delphi, Greece, the sanctuary of Apollo and its oracle: Nov 22, a day trip by road from Athens (trip day 12)

The map labels the cruise ports by cruise day (Istanbul is cruise days 1–2) and Delphi by trip day. The daily chapters use trip days, which start with our own three days in Istanbul on November 11.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
• Step through the stops with the Next → and ← Previous buttons, the ← and → arrow keys, the numbered dots, or by clicking a numbered pin on the map. The map flies to each stop as you select it.
  • Read the stop card on the right. It shows the date, arrival and departure times, a short introduction, the key things to see, and a practical tip.
  • Follow the route. Legs already traveled are solid navy, the leg that brought you to the current stop is gold, and legs still ahead are dashed blue.
  • Click Whole route to zoom back out to the full itinerary.
  • Switch base maps with the layer control in the top-right corner of the map: street map, satellite imagery, or OpenStreetMap.

The route is approximate. The sea legs show the general track through the Dardanelles and around the islands, not the ship's exact navigation. The last leg follows the road north from Athens past Thebes and Livadeia, then up through Arachova to Delphi.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: This map is for us as travelers, not for a classroom. Here is how to get the most from it before and during the cruise.

docs.title: What We Will Get From It
docs.text:
• A clear picture of where each port is and which waters the ship sails through to reach it.
  • The one sight at each port that matters most, and the civilization that built it.
  • A realistic plan for each shore day that fits the port's arrival and departure times.

docs.title: Before We Leave
docs.text:
1. Route tour (5 minutes). Step through all seven stops in order. At each one, notice the water the ship crosses to get there: the Sea of Marmara, the Dardanelles, the Aegean Sea, and the Sea of Crete.
  2. Choose at Çanakkale. Troy and Gallipoli lie in opposite directions, so decide in advance which story we most want to stand inside: the Bronze Age city of Homer's Iliad, or the 1915 battlefields that shaped modern Turkey, Australia, and New Zealand.
  3. Book early. Check which included excursion Viking offers at each port. The Ephesus and Knossos tours fill up first.

docs.title: Each Evening Aboard
docs.text:
1. Look ahead. Open the next port, read its card, then read that day's chapter.
  2. Plan the day. Using the arrival and departure times and the tip, sketch a schedule that gets us back to the ship at least 30 minutes before it sails.
  3. Look closer. Switch to the satellite map and zoom in on tomorrow's port. At Rhodes, find the walls of the medieval town; at Heraklion, find the Venetian fortress guarding the old harbor.

docs.title: Looking Back
docs.text:
• On the flight home, sketch the route from memory and label all six ports and Delphi.
  • Put the main sight at each port in order of age, from Knossos (about 1900 BC) to Topkapi Palace (15th century AD), and note which empire built each one.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The old town of Heraklion, Venetian Candia, is small enough to walk in an hour, but its landmarks are easy to misplace. This map quiz asks us to find eight of them before we arrive. The base map shows streets, the harbor, and the shoreline, but no place names, so the map cannot give the answers away.

Eight cards come in a fixed order: Lions Square with the Morosini Fountain, the Loggia, the Church of Agios Titos, the Venetian arsenal, Koules Fortress, the Archaeological Museum, the Martinengo Bastion with the grave of Nikos Kazantzakis, and the Pantocrator (Chania) Gate. For each card we click where we think the landmark stands. A click within 150 m of the landmark counts as correct. Each card allows two tries, and only the first try counts toward the score.

Three cards target common mix-ups:

  • Koules Fortress stands out at the end of the harbor breakwater, not on the town's shore.
  • The Venetian walls ring the town on its landward side, not along the harbor, so the Martinengo Bastion and the Pantocrator Gate lie on the town's upper, southern and western edges.
  • The Venetian civic center is compact: the fountain, the Loggia, and Agios Titos stand within about 200 m of one another.

After card 8, all eight markers stay on the map and a dashed blue line joins the stops of our own walk on Day 9: the museum, the Lions, the Loggia, Agios Titos, the arsenal, and the Koules.

Reference points. Each reference point was checked against OpenStreetMap in November 2026. Six of the specification's points were within 30 m of the OpenStreetMap feature and were only rounded. Two were corrected:

Card Specification Used here Correction 7. Martinengo Bastion and Kazantzakis's grave 35.3317, 25.1311 35.3327, 25.1307 About 110 m, moved to the grave on top of the bastion 8. Pantocrator (Chania) Gate 35.3378, 25.1255 35.3370, 25.1249 About 100 m, moved to the gate itself

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card below the map, for example Lions Square: the Morosini Fountain and the Basilica of San Marco. Where would you find the Lions?
  2. Click the map where you think the landmark stands. A green ring means within 150 m; a red ring means a miss.
  3. After a first miss, the sim tells you how far away you were. Click again. After a correct answer or a second miss, the landmark's marker appears, a dashed line shows the distance from your click, and a note opens with the landmark's era and dates.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). The score in the top right counts correct first tries.
  5. After card 8, press See result to show all eight markers and the line of our walk. Click any marker to read its note again.
  6. Zoom with + and − and drag to pan. The mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the map. Try Again clears the map and the score.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: Candia, the Morosini Fountain, the Loggia, the Church of Agios Titos, the Venetian arsenal, Koules Fortress, the Venetian walls and bastions, the Martinengo Bastion, the Pantocrator (Chania) Gate, and the Heraklion Archaeological Museum (Chapter 13). Learning objective (Bloom: Remember): Locate eight landmarks of Venetian and Ottoman Heraklion on a street map of the old town, placing at least six of the eight within 150 m of the true position on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Find the edges (2 min): Before answering, find the old harbor and the long breakwater that encloses it, then trace the ring of streets and parks that follows the line of the walls around the town's landward side.
  2. Locate (6 min): Work through all eight cards. Before each click, say which part of the town the landmark belongs to: the civic center, the harbor, or the walls.
  3. Read the walk (2 min): On the result map, follow the blue line from the museum to the Koules. Notice that cards 1 to 5 lie on one short downhill route to the sea, less than a kilometer from the Lions to the Koules, while the walls ring the town's upper edge.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 6 of 8 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: We have one hour in the old town and want to see the Venetian civic center and the sea fortress. Which way do we walk from the Lions, and roughly how far? A strong answer says north, downhill along 25th August Street, past the Loggia and Agios Titos to the harbor, less than a kilometer.

docs.title: When Printing Arrived
docs.text: Run the When Printing Arrived MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
"The Ottomans had no printing until 1727" is one of the most repeated sentences about the empire, and it is wrong in an instructive way. Istanbul had a working press by about 1493, run by Sephardic Jewish refugees, and Armenian and Greek presses followed. What waited until 1729 was printing in the Arabic script for Muslim readers. This chart makes the difference visible.

Each bar is the number of years from 1455, the approximate date of Gutenberg's Bible, to the first printing named. Bars are ordered by year, earliest at the top, and colored by region.

# Bar Region First printing Years after 1455 1 Latin, Mainz Western Europe c. 1455 0 2 Latin, Venice Western Europe 1469 14 3 Hebrew, Italy Western Europe 1475 20 4 Greek, Milan Western Europe 1476 21 5 Hebrew, Istanbul Ottoman Empire 1493 38 6 Arabic script, Italy Western Europe 1514 59 7 Armenian, Istanbul Ottoman Empire 1567 112 8 Greek, Istanbul Ottoman Empire 1627 172 9 Arabic script, Aleppo Ottoman Empire 1706 251 10 Ottoman Turkish (Arabic script), Istanbul Ottoman Empire 1729 274

Notes on the dates. Several of these "firsts" carry scholarly caveats, which the infoboxes mention:

  • Bar 1. The first finished copies of the Gutenberg Bible were available in 1454 or 1455; about 180 copies were printed and about 49 survive.
  • Bar 3. 1475 is the year of the first dated Hebrew books: Rashi's commentary on the Torah at Reggio di Calabria (February 1475) and the Arba'ah Turim at Piove di Sacco (July 1475). Undated Hebrew books printed in Rome may be a few years older.
  • Bar 5. The Arba'ah Turim printed by David and Samuel ibn Nahmias carries a date equivalent to December 1493, but some scholars argue it was printed about ten years later, around 1503–1504.
  • Bar 6. The Kitab Salat al-Sawa'i, a book of hours for Arabic-speaking Christians, names Fano on its colophon, but it may have been printed in Venice. It is the first known book printed in Arabic with movable type. (Arabic text had been printed from carved blocks in the Islamic world centuries earlier, so even "first Arabic printing" depends on the technology counted.)
  • Bar 8. Nikodemos Metaxas's Greek press, backed by the Patriarch Cyril Lucaris, was closed by the authorities in 1628, within a year.
  • Bar 9. The Aleppo press of the Patriarch Athanasius Dabbas, for Christian books, is usually counted the first press for Arabic script inside the Ottoman Empire. It ran until about 1711.
  • Bar 10. Sultan Ahmed III's decree allowing İbrahim Müteferrika to print non-religious books came in 1727. The first book, the Vankulu Lügati, an Arabic–Turkish dictionary in two volumes, appeared in 1729. Its print run is usually given as 1,000 copies; Müteferrika's editions ran from 500 to 1,000 copies each.

The chart does not show why the wait was so long, and it cannot confirm the popular story that Sultan Bayezid II banned Arabic-script printing in 1485. No copy of such a decree survives, and many historians now doubt it was issued.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the chart title and the axis, Years after 1455. Each bar ends with its year and its gap in years.
  2. Hover over any bar, or tap it on a tablet, to open its infobox below the chart.
  3. Answer the four questions, one attempt each. After each answer, the bars the question depends on are outlined in gold, the correct choice turns green, and the infobox opens on the key bar.
  4. After question 4, press See my result. All the Ottoman bars are outlined so you can check who did the printing.
  5. Restart clears the score and the outlines.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 6, "Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses". Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: Gutenberg, the printing press, the Hebrew press of 1493, İbrahim Müteferrika, delayed Arabic-script printing and the millet system, from Chapter 6. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Interpret a chart of the years between Gutenberg's Bible and the first printing in ten scripts and places, answering at least 3 of 4 questions correctly.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the chart (2 min): Which bar is the shortest Ottoman bar? Which is the longest? Open both infoboxes.
  2. Answer the questions (5 min): Answer all four, then look at the gold outlines on the result screen.
  3. Explain the gap (3 min): In two sentences, say what the 274-year gap measures and what it does not. (It measures the wait for Arabic-script printing for Muslim readers in Istanbul; it does not mean the Ottomans had no presses, or that Arabic could not be printed.)

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. A follow-up question: Bar 6 shows Arabic printed in Italy in 1514. Why does that matter for explaining the Ottoman delay? Because the technology existed more than two centuries before 1729, the reasons for waiting must also have been cultural, economic and political, as the chapter's list of explanations suggests.

docs.text:

  3. Hebrew incunabula and Abraham Garton — Wikipedia. The first dated Hebrew books, Reggio di Calabria and Piove di Sacco, 1475, and the undated Roman editions (bar 3).

docs.title: Who Says So? Sorting Claims About Paul
docs.text:
Run the Who Says So? Sorting Claims About Paul MicroSim Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Almost everything we hear about Paul, from guides, sermons, paintings and films, mixes four kinds of statement:

Bin What belongs there Paul's own letters Stated in one of the seven letters scholars agree Paul wrote, whether or not Acts also says it. Acts only Stated in the Book of Acts, written a generation later (most scholars say about 80–90 CE), and not in Paul's letters. Scholars' inference Not stated in any source; reasoned from the evidence. Later tradition First told by writers after the New Testament.

This MicroSim gives us fourteen familiar claims, one at a time and in a fixed order, and asks of each one: who says so? One rule decides the close cases: when Paul's letters state a claim, it belongs in Paul's own letters even if Acts says it too, because a man's own words come first.

Sorting a claim is not the same as judging it true or false. Acts is an ancient source that is often accurate where it can be checked, and a claim that comes only from Acts or from tradition may well be true; some readers hold it as true on the authority of scripture or of the church. The sorter asks a narrower historian's question: where does this claim first appear? That question lets readers of faith and secular historians talk about the same evidence.

The result usually surprises people. Most of the vivid details of the familiar story (Tarsus, Roman citizenship, the name Saul, the light on the road) come from Acts. Paul's own letters give the inner story: a Pharisee and a persecutor, a retreat to Arabia after his call, and a man who worked with his hands so as not to burden anyone.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the four bin definitions under the colored headings.
  2. Read the statement in the white panel and ask: who says so?
  3. Place it: press one of the four buttons below the bins, click a bin, or press keys 1 to 4. Each card has one attempt and cannot be moved.
  4. Read the feedback, which cites the passage. The card stays in the bin we chose, marked ✓ or ✗; the correct bin is outlined in green and a wrong choice in red.
  5. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 14, press See result.
  6. The summary shows the score and regroups all fourteen cards by their correct bin. Hover over any card to read its reason again. Sort again clears the bins and restarts from card 1 in the same order.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the visit to Ephesus. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: primary sources and myth versus history (Chapter 4); the Book of Acts, the Pauline letters as Paul's own words, Paul as persecutor, the road to Damascus, Timothy and Titus, Roman citizenship, and Tarsus (Chapter 9). Learning objective (Bloom: Analyze): Differentiate claims about Paul by their source, sorting fourteen statements into Paul's own letters, Acts only, scholars' inference, or later tradition, with at least 11 of 14 correct.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before starting, write down three things you "know" about Paul. Guess which of them Paul says about himself.
  2. Sort (8 min): Work through the fourteen cards. Before each placement, say aloud which text you would open to check it: a letter, Acts, or neither.
  3. Read the summary (3 min): Compare the Acts-only bin with the letters bin. Notice which kind of detail each one holds.
  4. Test your own list (2 min): Return to your three claims and sort them with the same four bins.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 11 of 14 correct on the first attempt. As a follow-up, ask: In Ephesus tomorrow, a guide says, "Saul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, was struck blind by a light on the road and changed his name to Paul." Sort each part of that sentence. A strong answer says Tarsus, citizenship, the name Saul and the light all come from Acts only, and the name change is in no source at all: Acts simply begins calling him Paul (Acts 13:9).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Paul's letters (Galatians 1–2, Philippians 3, 1 Thessalonians 2, 1 Corinthians 4, 2 Corinthians 11, Philemon) and Acts 7–28, in any modern translation, for example the New Revised Standard Version. The passages cited in each card's feedback.
  2. Paul the Apostle — Wikipedia. Paul's life, the sources for it, and the questions scholars debate, including his citizenship and the dating of his call.
  3. Aretas IV Philopatris — Wikipedia. The Nabataean king whose death around 40 CE anchors the date of Paul's escape from Damascus.
  4. Acts of Paul and Thecla — Wikipedia. The 2nd-century story that gives the only physical description of Paul.
  5. Tertullian — Wikipedia. One of the earliest writers, about 200 CE, to say that Paul died by the sword, "a death like John's," in Rome.
  6. E. P. Sanders, Paul: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2001). A clear account of how historians weigh the letters against Acts.
  7. Wayne A. Meeks and John T. Fitzgerald, eds., The Writings of St. Paul, 2nd ed. (Norton, 2007). The letters with ancient and modern readings of Paul, from many traditions.

docs.title: With or To?
docs.text: Run the With or To? MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapter 2 drew a line that runs through the whole trip: a change in learning can be made with the people it affects or to them. This MicroSim asks us to judge eight cases against four questions that stay on screen the whole time:

  1. Who chose it?
  2. Whose language is it in?
  3. Who was consulted?
  4. Who keeps it going?
# Card Judgment From 1 Greek traders adopt the Phoenician letters and add vowels, about 800 BCE Done with people Chapter 2 2 The Roman Senate expels Greek philosophers and teachers of rhetoric, 161 BCE Done to people Chapter 12 3 Justinian's law forbidding pagans to teach, 529 CE Done to people Chapter 4 4 The ibn Nahmias brothers print a code of Jewish law in Istanbul, dated 1493 Done with people Chapter 6 5 Carnegie library buildings, given only if the town pays for books, staff, and upkeep, 1883–1929 Done with people Chapter 10 6 Turkey's Latin-based alphabet, imposed by law in 1928 with the old script banned Done to people Chapter 7 7 One English-language AI tutor installed in every primary school, without asking anyone Done to people Imagined AI project 8 Village teachers and parents choose and check their AI reading tutor's stories and language Done with people Imagined AI project

Two cards carry the lesson. The 1928 alphabet widened literacy and still sits in "Done to people", because whether a reform helped and how it was made are separate questions. The Carnegie libraries were paid for by one of the richest men of his age and still sit in "Done with people", because each town chose its library and kept paying for it. The two imagined AI projects carry the same judgment into our own time: AI is not top-down in itself; it depends on who chose it and who keeps checking it.

Notes on the evidence. Cards 1 to 6 summarize stories told in the chapters listed. Each is simplified to its decision. Historians debate how directly Justinian's law of 529 ended philosophical teaching in Athens, and the date of the Hebrew press is the one printed in its colophon, 1493, which some scholars place about a decade later. Cards 7 and 8 are illustrative scenarios written for this book, not reports of real projects, and the sim labels them "Imagined AI project".

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the four judging questions and card 1. The cards come in a fixed order, one at a time, and none can be skipped.
  2. Place the card: press Done with people or Done to people, click a bin, or press W or T. Feedback appears at once, and only this first placement counts toward the score "First try: n of 8".
  3. If the first placement was wrong, you may move the card to the other bin. It is marked "moved", and the score does not change.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter) to go on. After card 8, press See result to see the score and both bins with all eight cards. Hover over any card to read it and its feedback again.
  5. Start over clears every placement.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers reading Chapter 21, "Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them", on the flight home. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: costs of top-down reform, evangelism's shadow, education with communities, mother-tongue learning, and Chapter 2's with-versus-to distinction; the route stories in Chapters 2, 4, 6, 7, 10, and 12. Learning objective (Bloom: Evaluate): Judge whether each of eight efforts to widen or control learning, six from the trip and two imagined AI projects, was done with the people it affected or done to them, sorting at least 6 of 8 correctly on the first attempt.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (1 min): Before starting, decide whether a reform that worked can still be "done to people". Keep your answer in mind for card 6.
  2. Judge (6 min): Work through the eight cards, answering the four questions for each before placing it. Note the first-try score.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Pick a technology project at a school you know. Answer the four questions for it. Which answer would you most want to change, and who would need to be in the room to change it?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is at least 6 of 8 cards placed correctly on the first try. A follow-up question: A charity gives every school in a region free tablets in the children's home language, but teachers were not asked and no one is paid to repair them. With or to? A strong answer uses the questions: the language fits, but the choice, the consultation, and the upkeep all sit outside the community, so it leans toward "done to", and it names what would change that.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. History of the Greek alphabet — Wikipedia. The adoption of the Phoenician letters and the addition of vowels, around the 8th century BCE.
  2. Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 15.11. The decree of the Senate of 161 BCE expelling philosophers and rhetoricians from Rome.
  3. Edward Watts, "Justinian, Malalas, and the End of Athenian Philosophical Teaching in A.D. 529," Journal of Roman Studies 94 (2004): 168–182 (doi:10.2307/4135014). The law of 529 and the debate over how it ended teaching in Athens.
  4. Arba'ah Turim — Wikipedia. The code of Jewish law that David and Samuel ibn Nahmias printed in Constantinople, with its colophon date of 1493, among the first books printed in the Ottoman Empire.
  5. George S. Bobinski, Carnegie Libraries: Their History and Impact on American Public Library Development (American Library Association, 1969). Carnegie's conditions that a town provide the site and pledge a yearly sum for upkeep.
  6. Geoffrey Lewis, The Turkish Language Reform: A Catastrophic Success (Oxford University Press, 1999). The alphabet law of November 1928 and its costs.
  7. UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report, If You Don't Understand, How Can You Learn? Policy Paper 24 (2016) (unesdoc.unesco.org). Why teaching in the learner's own language matters.
  8. AI-Native Schools: AI-First Case Studies II, Lessons for Practice — the companion book's chapter on why school technology projects fail at planning, trust, and listening.

docs.title: World Literacy Over Two Centuries
docs.text: Run the World Literacy Over Two Centuries MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Most of us carry a rough mental timeline of literacy, and it is usually wrong by a century or more. This MicroSim tests that timeline with three predictions, each locked in before the chart reveals the data:

Question What the chart reveals Answer from the data 1. In 1820, what share of the world's people could read? The 1820 point Under 25% (12.1%) 2. In which period did more than half the world first become literate? The full line and its 50% crossing 1920–1969 or 1970–2020 (see below) 3. About 750 million adults cannot read. What share of the world's adults is that? The gap above the latest point About 10–15% (12.3% in 2024)

The line is the share of the world's people who can read, from 1820 to 2024. The shaded area above it is the share who cannot. Two gold markers mark events from the chapter: Sequoyah's Cherokee syllabary (1821) and Turkey's switch to a Latin-based alphabet (1928). After the third question, hover over any point or marker to read it.

The gap in the data. The series has no values between 1960 (41.6%) and 1975 (65.4%), so the line crosses 50% in that gap. A straight line between the two points crosses around 1965, while the first year in the data at or above half is 1975. Because the two readings fall in different periods, question 2 accepts both 1920–1969 and 1970–2020. Either way, the lesson is the same: mass literacy is mostly a 20th-century achievement.

Changing definitions. The older values are estimates built from very different sources, some of which counted anyone who could sign their name. The dip between 1940 (41.9%) and 1950 (36.0%) most likely reflects the switch to UNESCO's 1950 census-based world estimate rather than a real fall. Modern values count adults aged 15 and over who can read and write a short, simple sentence about everyday life.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question and choose an answer. Each question allows one attempt.
  2. The chart reveals the relevant data. The correct answer turns green, a different choice turns red, and the feedback explains the answer with the actual values.
  3. Press Next question. The score at the top right counts correct predictions.
  4. After question 3, press Explore the chart and hover over any point or either gold marker.
  5. Restart clears the score and the chart.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers preparing for the trip. Duration: 10 minutes. Prerequisites: literacy, functional literacy, the 1820 and present-day literacy estimates, and the UNESCO estimate of adults who cannot read. Learning objective (Bloom: Understand): Interpret a line chart of the share of the world's people who could read from 1820 to today, answering at least 2 of 3 prediction questions correctly before each answer is revealed.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (4 min): Before each question, sketch on paper what you expect the line to look like. Then answer and compare.
  2. Explore (3 min): Hover over 1900 and 2000. How much did the share change in each of those centuries?
  3. Connect (3 min): Find the 1928 marker. The Turkish alphabet reform is one of the "simpler scripts" the chapter credits with widening literacy. What else does the chapter name as a driver of the 20th-century rise?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 2 of 3 correct predictions. A follow-up question: The share of adults who cannot read fell from about 88% in 1820 to about 12% in 2024. Why can the number of adults who cannot read still be large? Because the world's adult population grew several times over, about 12% of roughly 6.1 billion adults is still about three-quarters of a billion people.

docs.text:

  3. World Population Prospects 2024 — United Nations. The source of the approximate figure of 6.1 billion people aged 15 and over.

docs.title: Graphic Novel Stories
docs.text:
These twenty-two short graphic novels follow the trip from Istanbul to Athens, so each one can be read the evening before or after standing in the place where it happened. Every story is built around something a traveler can actually see, and every one ends with a "Look Closer" pointer to a detail to find on site.

Series devices. Find Glaux, the little owl, hidden in one panel of each story. Look for the Myth or Evidence? callouts, which separate documented history from legend. Each story ends with a "Then and Now" view of the same place today.

Behind the scenes, every story shares one visual bible: Story Characters, Places and House Style. The idea list the stories came from is Story Ideas.

Every cover and panel image was generated from the detailed text-to-image prompt that sits under it on each story's page.

  • 1. Glaux and the Gods Who Moved In (14 panels)

    Glaux the little owl guides you through Athena's odd birth, her olive-tree duel with Poseidon, and how an owl ended up on the silver money of Athens, so you know the gods before the trip.

  • 2. Halfdan Was Here (12 panels)

    Justinian builds the biggest dome in the world, and about five hundred years later a bored Norse guard scratches his name into its marble railing. Find the runes, and meet the builders.

  • 3. Ships Over the Hill (16 panels)

    When an iron chain blocks the Golden Horn, a twenty-one-year-old sultan sails his ships over a hill. Follow the siege that ended the Byzantine Empire and made Constantinople into Istanbul.

  • 4. The Sultan's Sweet Tooth (12 panels)

    Follow one box of Turkish delight and one pinch of saffron through Istanbul's Spice Bazaar, past coffeehouses a sultan tried to close, and into the hands of two travelers heading home.

  • 5. The Press That Waited (12 panels)

    Istanbul had printing presses in the 1490s, yet the first Ottoman Turkish book in Arabic script appeared only in 1729. Meet the refugees, scribes and printer in a puzzle with disputed answers.

  • 6. The Head Teacher in the Park (10 panels)

    In August 1928 a head of state stood at a blackboard in an Istanbul park and taught a nation new letters. See how one alphabet sent adults back to school, and what that change cost and gave.

  • 7. The Horse at the Gates (16 panels)

    The wooden horse is not in the Iliad, and the man who found Troy dug through the city he sought. Follow the legend, the 1870s dig, and a gold hoard that went from Troy to Berlin to Moscow.

  • 8. The Soldier Who Carried His Enemy (12 panels)

    A famous statue shows a Turkish soldier carrying a wounded enemy officer to safety. Follow Gallipoli from the mines to the truce, and learn what is documented, what is legend, and why both matter.

  • 9. Great Is Artemis! (16 panels)

    A tentmaker teaches in a borrowed lecture hall, and two years later a city shouts for two hours. Meet Paul, Demetrius and the town clerk in Ephesus, and see why his letters outlived the temple.

  • 10. The Library With a Tomb (12 panels)

    A grieving son builds his father a library and lays him to rest beneath the reading room. Then the river quietly fills the harbor, and Ephesus slowly loses its sea. Look closer.

  • 11. The Giant Who Fell Down (12 panels)

    Rhodes pays for a bronze giant by selling its enemy's abandoned siege machines. It stands for only about 54 years, lies broken for centuries, and is almost certainly not what you imagine.

  • 12. The Knights' Last Stand (14 panels)

    For two centuries a military order holds Rhodes. In 1522 Suleiman arrives with an army, and after six months of tunnels and cannon the siege ends in an honorable surrender and a surprising rebuild.

  • 13. Into the Labyrinth (14 panels)

    Follow Theseus and Ariadne's thread through the myth of the Labyrinth, then meet Arthur Evans, who rebuilt Knossos in red concrete. What did the Minoans make, and what did Evans imagine?

  • 14. The Architect Who Cracked the Code (14 panels)

    A palace fire bakes the clay tablets of Knossos hard, and 52 years later an architect and a Brooklyn teacher's index cards turn them into words. The secret turns out to be a count of sheep.

  • 15. Twenty-One Years of Candia (12 panels)

    One of the longest sieges in history: Venice holds walled Candia for 21 years until Francesco Morosini surrenders it in 1669, and the same man turns up in Athens eighteen years later.

  • 16. The Jar Makers of Thrapsano (10 panels)

    In the Knossos storerooms stand clay jars taller than a person. In a Cretan village, potters still build them by hand. Follow one jar shape across about 3,500 years.

  • 17. Wooden Walls (16 panels)

    Delphi tells terrified Athens to trust a wooden wall. One politician says the wall is a fleet. Follow the Persian Wars from Marathon to Salamis, then to a bronze column now in Istanbul.

  • 18. Pericles' Building Site (16 panels)

    Pericles spends the allies' treasury on a temple with almost no straight lines. Follow the Parthenon from quarry to cranes, through church, mosque and a 1687 explosion.

  • 19. The Man Who Asked Too Many Questions (14 panels)

    An oracle says no one is wiser than Socrates, so he questions everyone in the Athenian Agora to prove it wrong, in a democracy run by raffles and broken pots, and the city eventually puts him on trial.

  • 20. The Pythia's Busy Day (16 panels)

    Follow a nervous farmer and a king's envoys through consultation day at Delphi, from a cold spring and a trembling goat to an answer that ruins an empire, and a question asked of a chatbot today.

  • 21. The Computer at the Bottom of the Sea (14 panels)

    Sponge divers sheltering from a storm find a sunken ship. In a crusted lump of its bronze, scientists find a 2,000-year-old machine of gears that predicted eclipses. Who built it?

  • 22. The Day the Imam Fainted (12 panels)

    A stuffed eggplant so good, or so rich in olive oil, that an imam fainted. Follow the vegetable from Ottoman kitchens to Greek tavernas, and through the exchange of 1923 that carried recipes across the sea.

docs.title: Story Characters, Places and House Style
docs.text:
This page is the single source of truth for anything that appears in more than one of the graphic-novel stories. Every story's index.md points here, and every image prompt in those stories reuses the paste-in blocks below word for word, so that Glaux, Athena or the Parthenon looks like the same person or place in every story, however many different images the text-to-image model makes.

Glaux's identity comes from the mascot's canonical file, docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md. The block for Glaux below is a compact copy of that sheet. If the two ever disagree, the character sheet wins; fix this page to match it.

docs.title: How the Prompts Use This Page
docs.text:
• Each image prompt is self-contained. A text-to-image model has no memory of this page, so every prompt that shows a recurring character, place or object pastes that item's block in full.
  • Each prompt opens with the house style line below, so all 22 stories share one look.
  • Each prompt ends with the guide's required sentence: Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.
  • No lettering in panels. Panel images contain no captions, speech bubbles, signs or labels, because image models misspell text. The story's words live in the paragraph under each panel. The cover is the one exception: it carries the story title.
  • All images are wide landscape, 16:9.

docs.title: House Style
docs.text:
Paste this sentence at the start of every prompt body, right after the identifier line:

Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image.

This is the same style as Glaux's own pose set, so the owl never looks pasted in from another book. Each story adds its own palette on top of the house style (see "Palettes by Era" below), but never replaces it. Real photographs, 3D renders, anime styles and photorealism are all off-brand.

docs.title: Safe-Image Rules
docs.text:
Image models refuse some content. These stories involve sieges, battles and a trial, so every violent moment is shown by its aftermath or its symbol:

  • No blood, wounds, corpses, weapons mid-strike, torture or executions.
  • A death is shown by an empty chair, a cup, a quiet room or mourners from behind.
  • A battle is shown by ships, smoke on the horizon, banners, dust and silhouettes at a distance.
  • No nudity. Greek statues and vase figures are shown draped, or shown only from a distance in soft focus.
  • Avoid swastikas and similar hate symbols entirely, even historically.

docs.title: Palettes by Era
docs.text: Era Palette to name in the prompt Myth time and Bronze Age Crete Terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green Classical Greece (500-300 BCE) Marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze Hellenistic and Roman (300 BCE-300 CE) Warm limestone, sea-green, deep red, bronze, evening gold Byzantine (300-1453 CE) Gold leaf, deep blue, imperial purple, candle amber, cream marble Medieval Rhodes and Venetian Crete Sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue, banner crimson Ottoman (1453-1922) Iznik turquoise, cobalt, tomato red, brass, saffron, white plaster Modern Turkey and Greece Natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta, olive

docs.title: Glaux the Little Owl (every story)
docs.text:
Glaux appears in every story. In historical scenes Glaux is an observer: an ordinary owl-sized little owl perched on a ledge, column, mast, gate or statue, never speaking to or touching the people of the past, and drawn small enough that a reader must hunt for the owl (the series' "Find Glaux" game). Only in myth-time scenes (Story 1) does Glaux act as a character. Glaux has no gender; write "Glaux" or "they."

Glaux the Little Owl: a true little owl (Athene noctua), small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts, warm earth-brown plumage with cream spots, bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream eyebrows, a cream-white throat patch and a short pale greenish-yellow beak. Glaux wears a small Aegean-blue scarf and a tan canvas satchel across the body with a small leather-bound travel notebook peeking out, and a sprig of three olive leaves tucked into the satchel strap. Alert, curious and warm expression.

For "Find Glaux" panels, add: Glaux is drawn small, perched at the edge of the scene, noticeable on a second look.

docs.title: The Travelers (the "Then and Now" panels)
docs.text:
Each story's final panel returns to the same place today. Two anonymous adult visitors stand in it, always seen from behind or at a distance, never in close-up, so no face needs to stay consistent.

Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail.

docs.title: Athena (Stories 1, 17, 18)
docs.text:
Goddess of wisdom and craft, patron of Athens. Calm, strong, not aggressive; weapons are shown at rest. Her owl is always Glaux-sized, and there should be only one owl in a scene.

Athena, goddess of wisdom: a tall, composed woman with dark wavy hair and calm gray eyes, wearing a bronze Corinthian-style helmet pushed up on her forehead with a tall crest, a long white wool peplos with a deep Aegean-blue border, and a scaled bronze-gold aegis cloak over the shoulders. She carries a tall spear held upright at rest and a round shield with a plain olive-wood face. Her expression is thoughtful and steady.

docs.title: The Olympians: Zeus, Poseidon and Apollo (Stories 1, 13, 20)
docs.text: Zeus, king of the gods: a broad, powerfully built older man with a full curled silver-white beard and thick white hair, wearing a gold-edged crimson himation draped over one shoulder, holding a short gilded scepter topped with an eagle; a faint storm-cloud glow behind him. Poseidon, god of the sea: a muscular man with a windswept sea-green beard and hair, a deep teal himation, holding a three-pronged bronze trident. Apollo, god of light and prophecy: a graceful, beardless young man with shoulder-length golden-brown hair crowned with a laurel wreath, a saffron-yellow chiton, holding a small laurel branch and a gold lyre.

docs.title: The Pythia, Apollo's Priestess at Delphi (Stories 17 and 20)
docs.text: The Pythia, Apollo's priestess at Delphi: a dignified woman of about fifty with gray-streaked dark hair under a simple white veil, wearing a plain long white linen gown with a wreath of laurel leaves in her hair, holding a laurel branch in one hand and a shallow bronze offering bowl in the other. Her expression is calm, inward and serious.

docs.title: Themistocles (Stories 17 and 19)
docs.text: Themistocles, Athenian statesman and admiral: a stocky, energetic man of about forty-five with a short dark curly beard, sharp dark eyes and a weathered, tanned face, wearing a plain cream chiton and a rust-brown himation draped over one shoulder, a bronze signet ring on his right hand; confident, restless, always mid-gesture.

docs.title: Pericles (Story 18, cameo in Story 19)
docs.text: Pericles, Athenian leader: a dignified man of about fifty-five with an unusually tall, long head, usually shown wearing a crested bronze helmet pushed back on his head, a trimmed gray-brown beard and a calm, commanding expression, dressed in a white himation with a dark-blue border draped over a cream chiton.

docs.title: Socrates (Story 19)
docs.text: Socrates, Athenian philosopher: a short, stocky man of about sixty with a bald, broad forehead, a wide flat nose, a thick gray beard and bright, amused eyes, barefoot, wearing a plain, worn, undyed wool himation and no jewelry; a curious, teasing expression.

docs.title: Francesco Morosini (Stories 15 and 18)
docs.text:
Venetian commander. In both stories he is seen in the same dress and age.

Francesco Morosini, Venetian commander: a lean man of about sixty with a long gray beard, a high forehead and a stern, tired expression, wearing a dark crimson velvet coat with gold braid over a steel breastplate, a wide white lace collar, a black cap with a small gold badge, and the red-and-gold sash of a Venetian captain-general.

docs.title: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (Stories 6 and 8)
docs.text:
Shown only as a young Ottoman officer in 1915 (Story 8) and as the mid-career head of state in 1928 (Story 6), never as an old man. Use the matching block.

Mustafa Kemal as a young Ottoman officer in 1915: a lean man of about thirty-four with light blue-gray eyes, light brown hair and a thin mustache, wearing a khaki Ottoman army field uniform with a peaked cap, binoculars at his chest and a calm, watchful expression.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1928: a man of forty-seven with penetrating light blue-gray eyes, short light-brown hair combed back and a thin mustache, wearing a well-cut dark Western suit with a white collar and tie, standing at a large portable blackboard with a piece of white chalk in his hand, a teacherly, patient expression.

docs.title: Arthur Evans (Stories 13 and 14)
docs.text: Sir Arthur Evans, British archaeologist: a short, energetic man in his fifties with a neat white beard, round wire glasses, a weathered face, wearing a rumpled cream linen jacket, a wide-brimmed straw hat and carrying a walking stick; he often carries a small ancient clay fragment in one hand and gestures eagerly.

docs.title: Paste-In Blocks: Recurring Places and Objects
The Parthenon and the Acropolis (Stories 1, 17, 18, 19, 21 and the Then-and-Now panels)
docs.text: The Acropolis of Athens: a steep, flat-topped, pale limestone rock rising above the city, crowned by the Parthenon, a long Doric temple of honey-colored marble with eight columns across the front, a low triangular pediment and a long carved frieze under the roof; to its left stands the smaller Erechtheion with its porch of six marble maidens. The sky behind is clear blue.

docs.title: Hagia Sophia (Stories 2 and 3)
docs.text: Hagia Sophia in Constantinople: a vast cream-and-ochre brick church crowned by one enormous shallow central dome ringed with a band of forty small arched windows, with a half-dome on either side and four tall minarets (add the minarets only in scenes after 1453); gold mosaics glowing inside.

docs.title: The Temple of Apollo and Sacred Way at Delphi (Stories 17 and 20)
docs.text: Delphi, the sanctuary of Apollo: a steep rocky terrace on the slope of Mount Parnassus with a paved winding Sacred Way lined with small treasuries and statues, leading up to the large Doric Temple of Apollo with six columns across the front; behind it steep gray limestone cliffs, below it a deep valley of silver-green olive trees stretching to a distant sea.

docs.title: The Owl Coin (Stories 1, 17, 18, 19)
docs.text: An ancient Athenian silver tetradrachm coin: a thick round silver coin showing the head of Athena in a crested helmet on one side and, on the other, a standing little owl beside an olive sprig and a crescent moon, with a rough, hand-struck edge.

docs.title: The Serpent Column (Stories 17 and 3)
docs.text: The Serpent Column: a tall bronze column made of three snakes twisted together in a spiral, which once held a golden bowl, now with the serpents' heads missing; weathered dark green-bronze, with a worn stone base.

docs.title: The Knossos Palace and the Giant Jar (Stories 13, 14, 16)
docs.text: The Palace of Knossos on Crete: a sprawl of low, flat-roofed, honey-colored stone buildings around an open central court, with distinctive red-painted, downward-tapering wooden columns (wider at the top than the bottom) with black capitals, and colorful frescoes; storerooms hold giant human-tall clay jars (pithoi) with rope-like ridged bands.
