docs.title: Story Ideas for the Mediterranean Travels Book
docs.text: These are twenty-two ideas for short graphic novels, each 8 to 16 panels long. They follow the trip from Istanbul to Athens, so a reader can meet each story the day before or the evening after standing in the place where it happened. Every story is built around something a traveler can actually see: a column drum in a wall, a scratch on a marble railing, a jar taller than a person.

docs.title: Series Conventions
docs.text:
These recurring devices tie the stories together and send readers out to look for themselves.

  • Then and Now. The first panel shows the place in its own era. The last panel shows the same view today, ideally matched to one of our trip photos.
  • Find Glaux. A little owl hides somewhere in one panel of every story: on a temple roof, on a ship's rail, on a coin. Little owls really do live on the Acropolis, so the hunt is not as far-fetched as it sounds.
  • Look Closer. Glaux closes each story by pointing at one specific detail to find on site.
  • Myth or Evidence? A small stamp marks any panel that shows legend rather than documented history. Several stories turn on exactly that question.
  • Crossovers. Some characters and objects appear in more than one story (see the table at the end), so readers who follow the whole series get "wait, it's him again" moments.
  • Learning for All. Where a story touches who got to read, write, or learn, the closing panel makes the connection, matching the thread that runs through the chapters.

docs.title: 1. Glaux and the Gods Who Moved In
docs.text:
Chapter: 1. The Long Timeline · Setting: Mount Olympus and the Acropolis, myth time · Panels: 14

Hook. Before we leave, Glaux introduces the gods we will keep running into on the trip, and explains how a small owl ended up on the money of the richest city in Greece.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Athena is born, fully armed, from the head of Zeus. Glaux, perched nearby, is unimpressed by the headache.
  • Panels 4–8: Athena and Poseidon compete to be patron of Athens. Poseidon strikes the rock and a salt spring bubbles up. Athena plants an olive tree. The citizens pick the tree, because you cannot drink seawater.
  • Panels 9–11: Athena's owl becomes the city's symbol and lands on the silver tetradrachm. People call the coins "owls."
  • Panels 12–14: A "where the gods live on our route" map: Zeus's birth cave on Crete, Artemis at Ephesus, Helios at Rhodes, Apollo at Delphi, Athena in Athens.

On the trip. The olive tree beside the Erechtheion stands where the myth says Athena's grew (it is a modern planting). Owl tetradrachms are on show in Athens museums.

Explore further. Which gods took sides at Troy? Try The Olympian Gods at Troy.

docs.title: 2. Halfdan Was Here
docs.text:
Chapter: 4. Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia · Setting: Constantinople, 532–537 CE and about a thousand years ago · Panels: 12

Hook. The emperor Justinian builds the biggest dome in the world. Centuries later, a bored Norse guard carves his name into its marble railing, and it is still there.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: The Nika riots of 532 burn the old church. Justinian decides to build something no one has seen before.
  • Panels 4–7: Two mathematicians, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, design a dome that seems to float on a ring of windows. In 537 Justinian walks in. A later legend gives him the line "Solomon, I have surpassed you."
  • Panel 8: The first dome collapses in 558 and is rebuilt higher.
  • Panels 9–11: A Norse soldier, probably of the emperor's Varangian Guard, standing through a very long service in the upper gallery, scratches runes into the parapet: a name, Halfdan.
  • Panel 12: A tourist today leans over the same railing and finds the runes.

On the trip. The runic graffiti in the south gallery, the seraphim in the dome's pendentives, and the building's change of use from church to mosque to museum and back to mosque.

Explore further. Readers try to read the runes from a photo, then compare their reading with the scholars'.

docs.title: 3. Ships Over the Hill
docs.text:
Chapter: 4. Byzantine Constantinople and 5. Ottoman Istanbul · Setting: Constantinople, April–May 1453 · Panels: 16

Hook. A great iron chain blocks the Golden Horn. Twenty-one-year-old Sultan Mehmed II solves the problem by sailing his ships over a hill.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: The Theodosian Walls, a thousand years unbroken. The last emperor, Constantine XI, has too few men to defend them.
  • Panels 4–6: The Ottoman cannons arrive, cast by a Hungarian founder named Orban who first offered his services to the Byzantines.
  • Panels 7–10: The chain holds. On April 22, Ottoman crews haul dozens of ships on greased log rollers over the hills behind Galata and launch them into the Golden Horn. Dawn reveals them inside the harbor.
  • Panels 11–14: The final assault on May 29. Constantine XI disappears in the fighting.
  • Panels 15–16: Mehmed rides to Hagia Sophia. The city becomes Istanbul.

On the trip. Surviving links of the chain are displayed in Istanbul museums. The land walls still run from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn.

Explore further. The Siege of 1453, Step by Step.

docs.title: 4. The Sultan's Sweet Tooth
docs.text:
Chapter: 6. Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses · Setting: Istanbul, 1660s to today · Panels: 12

Hook. Follow one box of Turkish delight and one pinch of saffron through the Spice Bazaar and three centuries of Ottoman taste.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: The Spice Bazaar opens in the 1660s as part of the New Mosque complex. Its Turkish name, Mısır Çarşısı, means "Egyptian Bazaar."
  • Panels 4–6: Coffee arrives in Istanbul in the 1500s, and coffeehouses become places of gossip and politics. Sultan Murad IV shuts them down. The coffee wins in the end.
  • Panels 7–9: In 1777 a confectioner remembered as Hacı Bekir opens a shop near the waterfront and makes lokum famous. His family's shop still sells it.
  • Panels 10–11: Saffron's journey: the town of Safranbolu is named for it, and it is worth more by weight than almost anything else in the bazaar.
  • Panel 12: Two travelers leave the bazaar with a box of lokum and a twist of saffron, which is exactly what we did.

On the trip. The L-shaped hall of the Spice Bazaar, the Hacı Bekir shop, and the price board for saffron.

Explore further. Reading Food in Layers: which dishes came from which era?

docs.title: 5. The Press That Waited
docs.text:
Chapter: 6. Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses · Setting: Istanbul, 1490s–1729 · Panels: 12

Hook. Istanbul had printing presses by the 1490s, so why did the first Ottoman Turkish book in Arabic script not appear until 1729?

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Jewish refugees from Spain set up a press in Istanbul in the 1490s. Armenian and Greek presses follow.
  • Panels 4–6: Ottoman scribes and calligraphers produce beautiful manuscripts. A popular legend says they blocked the press. Historians argue about whether that is true.
  • Panels 7–10: İbrahim Müteferrika, a convert from Transylvania, petitions the Sultan, wins permission in 1727, and prints a dictionary in 1729.
  • Panels 11–12: He prints a few dozen volumes before he dies. A Learning for All panel asks what a long delay costs a society, and who pays.

On the trip. Calligraphy in the mosques and at the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts; old books in the shops near the Grand Bazaar.

Explore further. Scribe or Press? and When Printing Arrived.

docs.title: 6. The Head Teacher in the Park
docs.text:
Chapter: 7. The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey · Setting: Istanbul, August 1928 · Panels: 10

Hook. A head of state stands at a chalkboard in a public park and teaches a nation a new alphabet.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–2: Ottoman Turkish is written in Arabic script, which fits Turkish vowels badly. Only about one person in ten can read.
  • Panels 3–5: In Gülhane Park, Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk) chalks up the new Latin-based letters for a crowd. He earns the nickname Başöğretmen, "Head Teacher."
  • Panels 6–8: Within months, the old script is replaced by law. Adults crowd into "Nation's Schools" to learn to read.
  • Panels 9–10: A grandmother who learned to read in 1929 reads a street sign aloud to her grandchild. A Learning for All closing panel.

On the trip. Every Turkish sign we read. Dolmabahçe Palace, where the clocks were stopped at 9:05, the minute Atatürk died in 1938.

Explore further. Sort the Scripts.

docs.title: 7. The Horse at the Gates
docs.text:
Chapter: 8. Troy and Gallipoli · Setting: Troy, myth time and the 1870s · Panels: 16

Hook. Everyone knows the Trojan Horse. Almost nobody knows that the Iliad ends before the horse ever appears, or that the man who "found" Troy dug right through the city he was looking for.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–6: The myth in quick cuts: ten years of siege, the Greeks pretend to sail away, the giant wooden horse, Laocoön's warning, soldiers climbing out at night, Troy burning.
  • Panel 7: A Myth or Evidence? stamp. The horse story comes from the Odyssey and Virgil's Aeneid, not the Iliad.
  • Panels 8–10: Frank Calvert, a British consul who owns part of the mound at Hisarlık, is sure Troy lies beneath it. Heinrich Schliemann arrives with money and a hurry.
  • Panels 11–13: Schliemann cuts a huge trench, finds gold in 1873, and names it "Priam's Treasure." It turns out to be about a thousand years older than any Troy of Homer's war. He smuggles it out of the country.
  • Panels 14–15: The treasure vanishes from Berlin in 1945 and turns up in a Moscow museum decades later.
  • Panel 16: Children climb the wooden replica horse at the site, and on the Çanakkale waterfront stands the horse built for a Hollywood film.

On the trip. Schliemann's trench, which slices through layers of nine cities stacked on top of each other, and both horses.

Explore further. Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence?

docs.title: 8. The Soldier Who Carried His Enemy
docs.text:
Chapter: 8. Troy and Gallipoli · Setting: Gallipoli peninsula, 1915 · Panels: 12

Hook. A famous statue shows a Turkish soldier carrying a wounded enemy officer to safety. Did it really happen? The story is about the battle, and about how nations decide what to remember.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–4: Allied ships fail to force the Dardanelles. Troops land at Gallipoli in April 1915, among them Australians and New Zealanders.
  • Panels 5–7: A young Ottoman officer, Mustafa Kemal, holds the high ground.
  • Panels 8–9: During a truce to bury the dead, soldiers from both sides trade cigarettes and food in no-man's-land.
  • Panels 10–11: The story behind the statue, told as a witness remembered it, with a Myth or Evidence? stamp: historians still debate its source.
  • Panel 12: Australian, New Zealand and Turkish visitors stand together at the same memorial today.

On the trip. The Mehmetçik statue, trenches that sit only meters apart, and the memorial words of reconciliation attributed to Atatürk.

Explore further. Readers sort which parts of the story are documented and which are remembered, the same skill as Source, Myth, or Contested?

docs.title: 9. Great Is Artemis!
docs.text:
Chapter: 9. Paul's Life and Letters and 11. Paul's Ideas and Leadership · Setting: Ephesus, about 52–55 CE · Panels: 16

Hook. A traveling tentmaker starts teaching in a lecture hall, and two years later the silversmiths of Ephesus riot because he is hurting their business.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Paul arrives in Ephesus, one of the largest cities in the Roman world, works at his trade, and teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus.
  • Panels 4–6: Letters go out and come in. He writes to the quarrelsome church in Corinth from here, and copies of his letters pass from hand to hand.
  • Panels 7–12: Demetrius the silversmith, who sells little silver shrines of the goddess Artemis, warns his guild that Paul's message will ruin trade. The crowd floods the theater and chants "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" for two hours.
  • Panels 13–14: The town clerk calms the crowd with a very Roman argument: we could be charged with rioting.
  • Panels 15–16: Paul leaves. His letters outlive both the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders, and the silversmiths' guild.

On the trip. The Great Theater, which held about 25,000 people. The single re-erected column that is all that stands of the Temple of Artemis.

Explore further. How Paul's Words Traveled and Where in Paul's Life Was Each Letter Written?.

docs.title: 10. The Library With a Tomb in the Basement
docs.text:
Chapter: 10. Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City · Setting: Ephesus, early 100s CE · Panels: 12

Hook. A son builds his father a library and buries him underneath it. Then the sea walks away from the city.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Celsus, a Roman governor born in the East, dies. His son decides a library is the best monument a learned man could have.
  • Panels 4–6: The façade rises, with four statues of the virtues: Wisdom, Excellence, Thought, and Knowledge. Inside, some 12,000 scrolls. Below, the father's marble coffin.
  • Panels 7–9: A day in Ephesus: the marble public latrines where people sat side by side and talked business, the terrace houses with painted walls.
  • Panels 10–11: River silt slowly fills the harbor. The coastline moves kilometers away and the port city dies.
  • Panel 12: Archaeologists rebuild the library façade in the 1970s from its fallen pieces.

On the trip. The library façade, the latrines, the street that once led to the harbor.

Explore further. One Walk, Seven Centuries and Documented, Debated, or Tradition?.

docs.title: 11. The Giant Who Fell Down
docs.text:
Chapter: 12. Rhodes · Setting: Rhodes, 305 BCE to the 650s CE · Panels: 12

Hook. Rhodes pays for a bronze giant about 33 meters tall by selling the siege machines its enemy left behind. It stands for barely sixty years, then lies on the ground for eight centuries as a tourist attraction.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: The siege of 305–304 BCE. Demetrius "the Besieger" brings an enormous siege tower, fails anyway, and leaves his equipment behind.
  • Panels 4–6: The sculptor Chares of Lindos spends twelve years raising a bronze statue of the sun god Helios.
  • Panel 7: An earthquake topples it about 226 BCE.
  • Panels 8–9: Visitors marvel that few people can wrap their arms around its fallen thumb.
  • Panel 10: A Myth or Evidence? stamp over the famous image of the Colossus straddling the harbor entrance: physically impossible.
  • Panels 11–12: In the 650s the bronze is sold for scrap. Today two bronze deer stand on columns at the harbor mouth.

On the trip. Mandraki harbor and its deer. Glaux asks where the statue really stood. Nobody knows for sure.

Explore further. Some think the Antikythera Mechanism was built on Rhodes (see story 21).

docs.title: 12. The Knights' Last Stand
docs.text:
Chapter: 12. Rhodes · Setting: Rhodes, 1309–1523, and the 1930s · Panels: 14

Hook. For two centuries a military order of knights holds Rhodes. In 1522 Süleyman the Magnificent arrives with an army, and the siege ends with a surprise: an honorable surrender.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: The Knights Hospitaller take Rhodes and build. Each "tongue" (France, Italy, Spain, England and others) gets an inn on the Street of the Knights.
  • Panels 4–9: The 1522 siege: tunnels and counter-tunnels under the walls, months of assaults, heavy losses on both sides.
  • Panels 10–11: Süleyman offers terms. The knights sail away on January 1, 1523, with their weapons, and end up on Malta.
  • Panels 12–14: A twist ending: the "medieval" Palace of the Grand Master that visitors tour was largely rebuilt by the Italian government in the 1930s.

On the trip. The Street of the Knights, the coats of arms over the inn doors, the walk through the dry moat.

Explore further. Who Built What We See in the Old Town? and Rhodes Changes Hands, 1912–1948.

docs.title: 13. Into the Labyrinth
docs.text:
Chapter: 13. Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B · Setting: Knossos, myth time and 1900 · Panels: 14

Hook. Theseus finds his way out of the Labyrinth with a ball of thread. Three thousand years later an English archaeologist rebuilds the palace in reinforced concrete, and visitors still struggle to find their way through which parts are ancient.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–6: King Minos, the Minotaur, Daedalus the inventor, Ariadne's thread, Theseus escaping.
  • Panel 7: Glaux points out the labrys, the double axe carved all over the palace, and the much-debated idea that "labyrinth" means "house of the double axe."
  • Panels 8–11: Arthur Evans buys the site, digs from 1900, and has artists "restore" frescoes from small fragments. He pours concrete columns and paints them red.
  • Panels 12–14: Side by side, the original fragments and the restored fresco. What did the Minoans make, and what did Evans imagine?

On the trip. The red columns, the "throne room," the fresco copies on site and the originals in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

Explore further. Knossos: Minoan, Evans, or Copy?

docs.title: 14. The Architect Who Cracked the Code
docs.text:
Chapter: 13. Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B · Setting: Knossos, London and Brooklyn, 1900–1952 · Panels: 14

Hook. A palace fire bakes thousands of clay tablets hard. A schoolboy hears a lecture about them, grows up to be an architect, and solves the puzzle that defeated the experts. The thrilling secret turns out to be a count of sheep.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–2: The fire that destroyed the palace saved its records by firing the unbaked clay.
  • Panels 3–4: Evans finds the tablets and calls the script Linear B. He never reads it.
  • Panels 5–7: In 1936 fourteen-year-old Michael Ventris hears Evans lecture and decides to crack it.
  • Panels 8–9: In Brooklyn, classicist Alice Kober builds the grids of related word endings that make the solution possible. She dies in 1950.
  • Panels 10–12: Ventris expects the language to be Etruscan. In 1952 his grid spells out Cretan place names in Greek. He announces it on BBC radio.
  • Panels 13–14: The tablets are inventories: sheep, wheat, chariot wheels. Glaux approves. Most of history is bookkeeping.

On the trip. Linear A and Linear B tablets in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

Explore further. Crack Linear B Like Ventris.

docs.title: 15. Twenty-One Years of Candia
docs.text:
Chapter: 14. Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today · Setting: Candia (Heraklion), 1648–1669 · Panels: 12

Hook. One of the longest sieges in history: the Venetians hold the walled city of Candia against the Ottomans for twenty-one years. The commander who finally surrenders it turns up again eighteen years later, in Athens.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Venetian Candia: fortress walls, a harbor castle, the winged lion of St. Mark over the gates. A century earlier a local boy, Domenikos Theotokopoulos, grew up here and left to become El Greco.
  • Panels 4–8: The siege drags on year after year as volunteers from across Europe come and go.
  • Panels 9–10: Francesco Morosini surrenders the city in 1669 and is allowed to sail home.
  • Panel 11: A teaser: Morosini in 1687, his guns aimed at the Acropolis (see story 18).
  • Panel 12: Today, on the Martinengo Bastion, the grave of the novelist Nikos Kazantzakis with its epitaph, "I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free."

On the trip. The walls, the harbor fortress, and the Lions Fountain, which carries the name of an earlier Francesco Morosini, a Venetian governor. Same name, different man.

Explore further. Walking Venetian Candia.

docs.title: 16. The Jar Makers of Thrapsano
docs.text:
Chapter: 14. Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today · Setting: Knossos storerooms, about 1600 BCE, and Thrapsano today · Panels: 10

Hook. In the Knossos storerooms stand clay jars taller than a person. In a Cretan village today, potters still make them by hand.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: A Minoan storeroom lined with giant pithoi holding olive oil, wine and grain.
  • Panels 4–6: Thrapsano potters build a pithos in coils on a wheel turned by an apprentice. For generations they traveled across Crete each summer, setting up wherever they found clay and customers.
  • Panels 7–8: The kiln firing.
  • Panels 9–10: Travelers sip wine at a village winery and watch the potters, as we did on the Villages of Crete excursion. A Then and Now split: the same jar shape, thousands of years apart.

On the trip. The pithoi in the Knossos storerooms; the Thrapsano workshops.

Explore further. Read the Olive Oil Label.

docs.title: 17. Wooden Walls
docs.text:
Chapter: 15. Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars · Setting: Delphi, Athens and Salamis, 490–479 BCE · Panels: 16

Hook. The oracle at Delphi tells the terrified Athenians to trust their "wooden wall." One clever politician decides that the wall is a fleet of ships.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Marathon, 490 BCE. Athens beats the first Persian invasion.
  • Panels 4–6: Ten years later King Xerxes returns with a far larger army. Athenian envoys at Delphi receive a grim prophecy and beg for a better one. The second answer mentions a "wooden wall."
  • Panels 7–8: Themistocles argues that the wall means the new fleet.
  • Panels 9–10: Athens is evacuated. The Persians burn the Acropolis.
  • Panels 11–13: The sea battle at Salamis in 480 BCE: Xerxes watches from a throne on the shore as his fleet is wrecked in the narrows.
  • Panels 14–15: After the final victory at Plataea, the Greeks send a bronze column of three twisted serpents to Delphi.
  • Panel 16: Crossover: that Serpent Column now stands in Istanbul's old Hippodrome, where Constantine moved it.

On the trip. Column drums from the earlier, burned temple built into the Acropolis north wall, visible from the streets of Plaka. The Serpent Column in Sultanahmet.

Explore further. Xerxes' Road to Salamis and Two Ends of the Serpent Column.

docs.title: 18. Pericles' Building Site
docs.text:
Chapter: 15. Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars · Setting: Athens, 447–432 BCE, and 1687 · Panels: 16

Hook. Pericles spends the allies' war chest on the most perfect building in Greece, a temple with almost no straight lines, and is accused of misusing the money.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: The treasury of the Delian League moves from the island of Delos to Athens. Pericles proposes rebuilding the burned Acropolis.
  • Panels 4–6: Ox carts haul marble from Mount Pentelikon. The architects Iktinos and Kallikrates check their plans; the sculptor Pheidias directs the sculpture.
  • Panels 7–9: The secret of the curves: the floor rises in the middle, the columns swell and lean inward. Glaux hunts for a straight line and fails.
  • Panels 10–11: Pericles' rivals accuse him of dressing Athens up in jewels bought with other cities' money.
  • Panel 12: The towering gold-and-ivory Athena stands inside.
  • Panels 13–15: A five-lives montage: temple, church, mosque, gunpowder store, and in 1687 a Venetian shell, fired under Morosini's command (see story 15), blows out its middle.
  • Panel 16: Scaffolding and cranes today. The restoration continues.

On the trip. The rising floor line, the swelling columns, and the frieze in the Acropolis Museum with gaps for the pieces held in London.

Explore further. The Parthenon's Five Lives and Agreed Fact or Position?

docs.title: 19. The Man Who Asked Too Many Questions
docs.text:
Chapter: 16. The Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus · Setting: The Athenian Agora, 480s–399 BCE · Panels: 14

Hook. The oracle says no one is wiser than Socrates. Socrates sets out to prove it wrong by questioning everyone in the marketplace, and Athens eventually votes to put him to death.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: How the democracy worked: officials picked by lot with a stone allotment machine, the kleroterion, and speeches timed by a water clock.
  • Panels 4–5: Ostracism: citizens scratch a name on a broken pot to exile a politician for ten years. Archaeologists found about 190 shards with Themistocles' name written by just a few hands. Someone was handing out ready-made ballots.
  • Panels 6–8: Socrates' friend asks Delphi whether anyone is wiser. The answer is no. Socrates is baffled.
  • Panels 9–11: He questions politicians, poets and craftsmen in the Agora and finds that they think they know more than they do.
  • Panels 12–14: The trial of 399 BCE before 501 jurors, the verdict, and the cup of hemlock.

On the trip. The kleroterion, the water clock and the ostraka in the Agora Museum, inside the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos.

Explore further. Who Could Vote in Athens?

docs.title: 20. The Pythia's Busy Day
docs.text:
Chapter: 17. The Oracle and 18. Delphi · Setting: Delphi, about 550 BCE · Panels: 16

Hook. Ride along with a nervous farmer and a very rich king on consultation day. One of them gets an answer that ruins him. A twist for modern visitors: in November, Apollo was believed to be out of town.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–2: Pilgrims climb the slopes of Mount Parnassus. Glaux notes that the oracle spoke only on set days, and traditionally not in winter, when Apollo was said to leave Delphi.
  • Panels 3–5: The Pythia purifies herself at the Castalian Spring. Priests sprinkle cold water on a goat; if it does not shiver, there is no oracle today.
  • Panels 6–8: The farmer pays his fee and asks whether to plant olives. The Pythia sits on her tripod in the inner chamber.
  • Panels 9–12: King Croesus of Lydia asks whether to attack Persia. The answer: he will destroy a great empire. He attacks, and the empire he destroys is his own.
  • Panels 13–14: The mystery of the vapors. Ancient writers describe a sweet smell; in 2001 geologists reported two faults crossing under the temple. A Myth or Evidence? stamp: the gas theory is still debated.
  • Panels 15–16: Today: "Know thyself," the stone navel of the world, and a reader asking a chatbot a question.

On the trip. The Temple of Apollo, the Castalian Spring, and the omphalos in the Delphi Museum.

Explore further. A Day at the Oracle and Can This Answer Lose?

docs.title: 21. The Computer at the Bottom of the Sea
docs.text:
Chapter: 20. Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today · Setting: Off Antikythera, the first century BCE and 1900–2005 · Panels: 14

Hook. Sponge divers sheltering from a storm find a sunken treasure ship. Inside a lump of corroded bronze from the wreck hides the oldest known geared calculator.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–2: A heavily loaded cargo ship sinks off a tiny island.
  • Panels 3–5: In 1900 Greek sponge divers find the wreck. Bronze and marble statues come up, and nobody pays much attention to a shoebox-sized lump.
  • Panels 6–7: The lump splits. Someone sees gear teeth.
  • Panels 8–10: Derek de Solla Price spends years with X-ray images and argues that it calculated the movements of the heavens.
  • Panels 11–12: In 2005 CT scans reveal tiny inscriptions: it predicted eclipses and even tracked the cycle of the Olympic Games.
  • Panels 13–14: Who built it? Rhodes? A follower of Archimedes? Glaux says, "Look closer."

On the trip. The fragments in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

Explore further. Antikythera Gears and the appendix Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism.

docs.title: 22. The Day the Imam Fainted
docs.text:
Chapter: 21. Going Home · Setting: Kitchens on both sides of the Aegean, 1600s to today · Panels: 12

Hook. A stuffed eggplant dish so good, or so extravagant with olive oil, that an imam fainted. Greeks and Turks both cook it, both name it, and argue over whose it is.

Panel beats:

  • Panels 1–3: Two versions of the legend of imam bayıldı, "the imam fainted": he fainted at the taste, or he fainted when he learned how much of his new wife's olive oil it used up.
  • Panels 4–6: More eggplant: karnıyarık ("split belly") and hünkâr beğendi ("the sultan liked it"), lamb served over smoky eggplant purée.
  • Panels 7–9: In Greece the first dish appears as imam baildi. In the 1920s the chef Nikolaos Tselementes tops moussaka with a French béchamel.
  • Panels 10–11: The 1923 population exchange carries cooks and recipes across the sea in both directions.
  • Panel 12: One table, two languages, one eggplant. A closing on learning with people rather than about them.

On the trip. Every menu from Istanbul to Athens. Order the eggplant on each side of the Aegean and compare.

Explore further. Reading Food in Layers and Who Was Exchanged in 1923?

docs.title: Crossover Characters and Objects
docs.text: Who or what Stories Connection Glaux Every story Hidden in one panel; closes each story with a detail to find Athena 1, 18 Patron goddess, then the giant statue inside the Parthenon The Delphi oracle 17, 19, 20 The "wooden wall," Socrates' wisdom, Croesus's mistake Francesco Morosini 15, 18 Surrenders Candia in 1669, shells the Parthenon in 1687 The Serpent Column 17 Made for Delphi after Plataea, now in Istanbul's Hippodrome Themistocles 17, 19 Hero of Salamis, then the target of ready-made ballots Rhodes 11, 12, 21 The Colossus, the knights, and a possible home of the Antikythera Mechanism Rebuilt ruins 10, 12, 13, 18 The Celsus façade, the Grand Master's palace, Evans's concrete, the Parthenon cranes

docs.title: More Ideas in Reserve
docs.text:
• The Unknown God: Paul in Athens trying to persuade Stoic and Epicurean philosophers on the Areopagus. See Paul's Speech Through Stoic Ears.
  • Two Homes: a Greek Orthodox family from Anatolia and a Muslim family from Crete in the 1923 population exchange, each moving into a house the other side left behind.
  • Sinan's Apprentice: the architect Mimar Sinan building the Süleymaniye mosque complex, told by a young stonecutter.
  • The Greek Books of Venice: Greek scholars in Venice printing the classics for a Greek world that had almost no presses of its own.
  • Spray Paint and Ruins: Athens street art after the debt crisis, told by the artists who paint the walls.

docs.title: Text to Image Prompt
docs.text:
Your task is to generate images for 22 graphic novel stories. The graphic novel stories are all stored in @docs/stories. Each story has it's own directory. Within the story directory you will find the main index.md for that story. Within the index.md file there are between 8 and 16 image descriptions including the cover image. Your task is to generate the images for each story from the image descriptions.

One important aspect is character consistency. There are many characters that appear in multiple panels and multiple stories. These characters must be consistent. To enable this you must read the character sheet @docs/stories/characters.md into the context window before you generate any story. This describes the house style and gives detailed descriptions of the shared houses and characters.

Things to know before you hand the prompts to the image model

  • Prompt length: the prompts are long, with a median of about 295 words and a maximum of about 510. The pasted character blocks make them long, but each prompt works on its own.
  • Images: the image links in each story are commented out, as the skill describes. Once the PNGs exist, run uncomment-images.sh on each story. The panel images contain no lettering because image models misspell text, so only the covers carry a title.

  • Safety: battles, the trial of Socrates and the 1687 Parthenon explosion are shown by smoke, silhouettes, empty chairs and objects. There is no gore, which should avoid the safety-filter refusals the skill warns about.

  • Facts the writers changed from my sketch:

  • They followed the chapters over the sketch where the two disagreed.

  • Story 19 says "about 500" jurors rather than 501.
  • Story 20 has Croesus's envoys, not Croesus himself, at Delphi.
  • The Colossus lay fallen for nearly nine centuries, not eight.

  • The Başöğretmen title dates from after the park scene.

  • Chapter gaps: the Mehmetçik statue story and the 1915 truce are not in Chapter 8, so those are sourced from web search and labelled as tradition. Story 4's coffee beat (arrival in the 1550s, closures about 1633) is from general history and hedged. The Greek Tselementes dating is left out.

  • Unverified links: every Wikipedia link returns 200, and I replaced one dead Wikipedia link. 32 Britannica and UNESCO links return 403 to automated requests, and one Metropolitan Museum link returns 429 (rate-limited), so I couldn't confirm them. Click through before publishing.

  • Anonymous travelers: the "Then and Now" panels show the travelers only from behind. I left out your names and faces, because the prompts go to an outside service.

Ask me any questions if the instructions are not clear to you.

docs.title: The Architect Who Cracked the Code
docs.text:
Cover Image Prompt (This is the Cover Image. Do not include this label in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a wide-landscape 16:9 cover image. Scene: a late-night desk lit by a single lamp. At the desk, bent over a large hand-ruled grid of small boxes, each holding an abstract incised sign, is Michael Ventris as an architect in his early thirties: a slim man with dark, slightly untidy hair, deep-set thoughtful eyes and a pale, intense face, wearing a gray tweed jacket over a white shirt with the sleeves pushed up, a loosened narrow tie, and a pencil behind one ear. Around him lie set squares, a drafting compass, stacks of index cards in plain cardboard cartons, and a small flat clay tablet with rows of tiny marks and a drawing of a three-legged cauldron. Behind him, on a shelf, a faint ghostly outline of a Bronze Age palace with red columns glows. Render the title as bold, hand-lettered text across the top: "THE ARCHITECT WHO CRACKED THE CODE" (exact spelling, no other text anywhere). Palette: warm clay red, cream, lamplight amber, ink black and lapis blue. Mood: quiet, intense, triumphant. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt **Story:** "The Architect Who Cracked the Code" tells how the clay tablets of Knossos, baked hard by the fire that destroyed the palace about 1375 BCE (some scholars argue for a later date), were found by Arthur Evans in 1900, called Linear B, and left unread for 52 years, until the English architect Michael Ventris showed in 1952 that they were written in Greek. It gives equal weight to the American classicist Alice Kober, whose roughly 180,000 index cards and grid of related word endings made the solution possible, and who died in May 1950, two years before it. **Places and eras:** Mycenaean Knossos (about 1400 BCE); the Knossos excavation (1900); London (1936 and the 1940s and 1950s); Brooklyn (the 1940s); a radio studio (July 1, 1952); the Pylos tablet (found 1952, read 1953); the Heraklion Archaeological Museum (today). Panels 1 and 2 use the Bronze Age palette (terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green). The other palettes extend the series table for modern eras and are named in each prompt: dig years (dusty ochre, straw yellow, spring green, faded sky blue, terracotta), London (gray stone, cream plaster, oak brown, amber lamplight), Brooklyn (paper cream, ink black, brick brown, lamplight amber). **House style:** hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, as in docs/stories/characters.md. No lettering anywhere in panels, including on the tablets, cards, grids and notebooks: write them as rows of tiny abstract incised marks and plain boxes, not readable letters. Only the cover carries the title. The fire is shown only as glow and smoke; nobody is in the burning room. **Legend versus evidence:** All of this story is documented history, with these cautions. The date of the palace fire is debated (about 1375 BCE in the most common dating). The story that fourteen-year-old Ventris heard Evans speak at a London exhibition in 1936 is a tradition about him, told as "the story goes." The tablets contain only accounts, never letters, laws, histories or poems. **Creative liberties:** The rooms, clothing and faces of the scribe, the schoolboy, Ventris, Kober and the others are invented for the series; no portrait was copied. Evans, in his eighties in 1936, is not drawn in panel 5 (only a tiny distant speaker at a lectern with no features), and the series' Evans block (a man in his fifties) is used only for 1900 to the early 1900s, in panels 3 and 4. The travelers visited the museum on Day 9; whether the Linear B tablets are on display on a given day varies, so the last panel is a display case of clay tablets in general. **Learning for All:** This story is part of the book's thread about who got to read and learn. Writing at Knossos was kept by a few dozen scribes, and then, in the 20th century, most of the Knossos texts were kept unpublished by Evans for decades; the decipherment moved quickly only after the texts were opened to others, and it needed Kober's patient groundwork, Emmett Bennett's careful sign list and edition of the Pylos tablets (1951), and John Chadwick's knowledge of early Greek. **Cast:** Recurring characters (see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md for Glaux): Arthur Evans (panels 3 and 4), the Palace of Knossos (panels 1, 2 and 3) and the Travelers (panel 14). Glaux hides in panel 13. Characters who appear only in this story: The Mycenaean palace scribe (panel 1): 
A Mycenaean palace scribe: a lean man of about forty with a trimmed black beard and short dark hair, wearing a plain linen tunic with a narrow blue border and a clay-stained leather apron, kneeling at a low table and pressing a pointed bone stylus into a small flat tablet of damp clay.
Cretan workmen of 1900 (panel 3): 
Cretan workmen of 1900: sun-browned men in dark baggy breeches, white shirts, red sashes and black fringed headscarves, carrying picks, wicker baskets and wooden wheelbarrows.
Michael Ventris as a boy (panels 5 and 6): 
Michael Ventris as a boy of fourteen in 1936: a thin, serious schoolboy with short dark hair parted at the side, large attentive dark eyes and a pale face, wearing a gray wool school blazer, gray flannel trousers, a white shirt and a thin striped tie, holding a small notebook and a pencil.
Michael Ventris as an architect (panels 7, 10, 11 and 12): 
Michael Ventris as an architect in his early thirties: a slim man with dark, slightly untidy hair, deep-set thoughtful eyes and a pale, intense face, wearing a gray tweed jacket over a white shirt with the sleeves pushed up, a loosened narrow tie, and a pencil behind one ear.
Alice Kober (panels 8 and 9): 
Alice Kober, American classicist, in her early forties: a slim, serious woman with dark hair pinned back in a plain bun, rimless round glasses, a gray wool dress with a white collar and a cardigan, and ink-stained fingers; patient and focused.

docs.title: Prologue - A Fire, a Boy and a Count of Sheep
docs.text:
The fire that destroyed the palace of Knossos baked its clay records hard, and for more than three thousand years nobody could read them. In 1936, so the story goes, a fourteen-year-old schoolboy heard the archaeologist who had found them say that they were unreadable. He grew up to be an architect, and in 1952 he proved that they were written in Greek, with help from a Brooklyn classics teacher who had died two years earlier. The thrilling secret turned out to be an inventory.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

docs.title: Panel 1: The Scribe Counts the Sheep
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 01. Do not include the panel number in the image.) I am about to ask you to generate a series of images for a graphic novel. Please make the images have a consistent style and consistent characters. Do not ask any clarifying questions. Just generate the image immediately when asked. Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 1 of 14. Setting: a palace archive room at Mycenaean Knossos, about 1400 BCE, warm lamplight on cream plaster. Palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster and olive green. Camera: a medium view from the doorway, looking in along a row of shelves. Mood: orderly, calm, ordinary. In the foreground, kneeling at a low table: A Mycenaean palace scribe: a lean man of about forty with a trimmed black beard and short dark hair, wearing a plain linen tunic with a narrow blue border and a clay-stained leather apron, kneeling at a low table and pressing a pointed bone stylus into a small flat tablet of damp clay. Around him: wicker baskets and wooden boxes stacked with long thin leaf-shaped clay tablets, a bowl of damp clay, a second tablet drying on a rack, a clay lamp with a small flame, a red-painted tapered column at the edge of the frame, and through a far doorway the rows of giant jars of a storeroom. The Palace of Knossos on Crete: a sprawl of low, flat-roofed, honey-colored stone buildings around an open central court, with distinctive red-painted, downward-tapering wooden columns (wider at the top than the bottom) with black capitals, and colorful frescoes; storerooms hold giant human-tall clay jars (pithoi) with rope-like ridged bands. Keep the surfaces of the tablets as rows of tiny abstract incised marks and small tally strokes, not letters. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

About 1400 BCE, a scribe at the Palace of Knossos presses a pointed stylus into damp clay. He is one of only a few dozen palace scribes, and he is not writing poetry: he is counting sheep, oil and wool for the palace. The tablets are working records for the current year, kept in baskets and boxes, and meant to be smoothed over and reused.

docs.title: Panel 2: The Fire That Saved the Records
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 02. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 2 of 14. Setting: the same archive room at Knossos as the previous image, seen from the same doorway, about 1375 BCE (some scholars date the fire later), at night. Palette: terracotta red, ochre and cream plaster, with deep orange firelight and dark smoke. Camera: the same medium view from the doorway as before. Then the palace burns, most likely about 1375 BCE, though some scholars argue for a later date. The scribes do not survive, and neither does their script. But the fire bakes the clay tablets as hard as pottery, and they lie under the rubble for more than three thousand years. We have them only because of disaster.

Evans began digging in March 1900, and within weeks the trenches yielded the Throne Room and the first clay tablets. He had come to Crete looking for early writing, and now he had thousands of tablets and fragments, more than at any other site. Nobody alive could read a word of them. The tablets were lists of people, flocks and goods, though no one knew it yet.

Evans sorts the tablets and gives the two scripts he finds their names. The signs are drawn with lines rather than pictures, so he calls them Linear A and Linear B. He spends the rest of his life on Knossos, and he never reads the tablets. He also publishes only a small part of them in his lifetime, so for decades almost nobody else can try.

In Brooklyn, a classics teacher called Alice Kober spends her evenings on the same puzzle. She teaches at Brooklyn College, carries a heavy teaching load, and works on Linear B in her spare time. With paper scarce in the war, she cuts scrap card by hand and builds a database of about 180,000 index cards in cigarette cartons, in a world with no computers. She refuses to guess what language the tablets were written in.

Kober found a pattern. Some words came in three forms with the same beginning and different endings, so the language was inflected, like Latin or Greek, and the sign before the ending shared its consonant with its partners. From pairs like that she started a grid of signs, without assigning a single sound. She died after an illness in May 1950, at 43, two years before the decipherment she had made possible. The chair is empty; the cartons remain.

Then he tries a guess about place names. Some words appear only on the Knossos tablets, never on those from Pylos, so they might be Cretan towns. The words come out as Greek: ko-wo, 'boy', ko-wa, 'girl', po-me, 'shepherd'. The guess was the key, but the grid was the lock that let one guess open everything.

The test comes from the ground. In 1952 the American archaeologist Carl Blegen finds a new tablet at Pylos, and when it is read with Ventris's values in 1953 it describes tripods and cups, with a little drawing beside each word: ti-ri-po-de, 'tripods', next to a three-legged cauldron; qe-to-ro-we, 'four-handled', drawn with four handles; a-no-we, 'without handles', drawn with none. No one could have arranged the match in advance. The secret that the Mycenaeans left was not poetry or prophecy but sheep, wheat and chariot wheels. Glaux approves: most of history is bookkeeping.

Nearby, in the museum, are the small clay tablets of Bronze Age Crete: accounts kept by a few dozen scribes, baked by the fire that ended their world. We know their words because a schoolboy listened, a teacher in Brooklyn made her cards, and an architect found a grid that worked. The next time we hear a discovery described as one person's lightning flash, we will ask who did the groundwork.

docs.title: Epilogue - The Groundwork Behind the Breakthrough
docs.text:
The decipherment of Linear B is usually told as one man's lightning flash. It was a relay. Evans found the tablets and gave the script its name, but locked most of them away. Alice Kober showed that the language had endings and built the grid's first rows. Emmett Bennett's careful sign list and edition of the Pylos tablets (1951) gave everyone reliable texts. Ventris made the leap, and John Chadwick brought the Greek. For half a century the story was told as Ventris's alone, until Margalit Fox's 2013 book The Riddle of the Labyrinth brought Kober back into view.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: Linear B was locked up twice, first by a palace that let only a few scribes write and then by a gatekeeper who published little. It opened when more people could look. This is the Learning for All thread in miniature: knowledge spreads when more people are taught to read it, and breakthroughs often come from the outsiders and the patient groundwork that no one thought to credit. In the museum, look at the tablets, and remember how many people it took to read them.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• Michael Ventris, radio talk, July 1, 1952 (as widely quoted; wording varies slightly between printings). Ventris said that he had come to the conclusion that the Knossos and Pylos tablets must be written in Greek, a difficult and archaic Greek, about five hundred years older than Homer and written in a rather abbreviated form.
  • The tablets themselves. The first words Ventris's grid produced are plain words from the palace's accounts: ko-wo ("boy"), ko-wa ("girl"), po-me ("shepherd"), ti-ri-po-de ("tripods"). They are not poetry; the Linear B tablets contain lists of people, livestock, land, goods and offerings, and no letters, laws or histories.
  • A book title. Documents in Mycenaean Greek (1956), by Ventris and Chadwick, is the first full handbook of the decipherment. No safe quotation from Alice Kober's own papers is given here; her work is best seen in her publications of 1945 to 1948 and in the cards that became the grid.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:

  • Where to look: the clay tablets of Linear A and Linear B in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, when on display (check on the day); the palace of Knossos itself; and the gypsum storerooms with their giant jars, which are where the palace kept the goods the tablets counted.

Narrative Prompt **Era and place.** Two layers of time share one story. The first is the Hellenistic and early Roman Aegean of about 100-60 BCE, when a heavily loaded merchant ship sinks near the small island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete. The maker's name is unknown, and the story keeps that as an open question, exactly as Chapter 20 and the appendix do: the evidence points to a skilled workshop, quite possibly on Rhodes, and the answer is still argued over. The Learning for All thread asks who gets to learn to make and read machines like this. **Series house style.** Every prompt opens with the series house-style line (a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded fills, a faint watercolor paper texture) and ends with the series consistency line. The later diving accidents of 1901 are not shown. **Creative liberties.** Faces of Valerios Stais, Derek de Solla Price and the 2005 team are imagined, because the prompts must not copy real portraits; they are drawn as likenesses of types, not portraits. The sponge-boat crew is anonymous. Panel 13's workshop is one possibility for where the mechanism was made, not a settled fact, and the two makers are invented types. The exact ship, route and owner of the mechanism are unknown. The CT-scan images in panel 12 are an artist's impression: tiny abstract engraved marks, never readable text. **Cast.** - **Glaux the Little Owl**, **the Travelers** (final panel): see [docs/stories/characters.md](../characters.md) and [docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md](../../img/mascot/character-sheet.md) (Glaux). docs.title: Prologue - A Lump Nobody Wanted
docs.text:
In a glass case in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens lies something that looks like a few pieces of rock. It is the Antikythera mechanism, a hand-cranked machine of bronze gears made in the 2nd century BCE, and it is the oldest known geared calculating device. It spent about 2,000 years on the seabed and two more years in a museum storeroom before anyone noticed what it was. This story follows the people who looked closer: sponge divers, an archaeologist, a historian with an X-ray machine, and a team with a scanner.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

About 65 BCE, a heavily loaded merchant ship works across the Aegean, probably bound west for Italy. Her cargo is a floating museum: bronze and marble statues, glass, fine pottery, jewelry and coins from Pergamon and Ephesus, which is how scholars date the voyage to about 70-60 BCE. Somewhere among the crates travels a wooden box about the size of a shoebox, already decades old. Nobody knows who ordered it, who carried it, or where it was going.

docs.text:

Wide underwater view of the seabed about 45 meters down off Antikythera, the same ship shown as a wreck, with no people or bodies anywhere in the frame. Time: a still, calm morning in about 65 BCE, after the storm has passed, with soft green light falling in slanting shafts from the surface. Palette: sea-green, deep teal, bronze, warm limestone and amber glints. The ship's broken wooden ribs and planks curve out of the sand like the ribs of a great animal. Around them lie scattered pointed clay amphorae, half buried; a marble horse's head rests on its side; a bronze hand and forearm reach out of the sand; a few glass bowls glint among the stones; and in the center foreground a small wooden box with a split lid lies half buried, a little dull bronze gleaming inside. Small silver fish drift through the scene, seaweed sways, and a single anchor stone sits to one side. Camera: low angle at sand level looking along the wreck toward the bright surface. The storm is over, and the sea is empty. On the seabed, about 45 meters down, the wooden hull slowly gives way and the cargo comes to rest in the sand: amphorae, statues, glass, and the small box with its bronze inside. Salt water begins its slow work on the metal, turning it into a crust of corrosion. Because the wreck stays buried, it escapes the fate of nearly all ancient bronze, which people melted down and reused.

Their gear is the standard dress of the age: a waterproofed canvas suit, a copper helmet, and air pumped down a hose by crewmen turning a hand crank. They have no idea what the delay is about to give them.

The crew finishes its fishing season, then returns to the island to dive on the heap. Hellenic Navy ships soon join the effort, and over the following months the divers bring up one of the great treasure finds of the ancient Mediterranean.

In the National Archaeological Museum, the statues get all the attention. The crust of corrosion on the shoebox-sized lump slowly dries and cracks, and for two years the pieces sit on a table among the more glamorous finds. This is how most discoveries are lost: not by being destroyed, but by being filed under "later." One May day in 1902, Valerios Stais is studying the finds from the wreck when his eye falls on the crumbling lump.

Palette: natural daylight, dusty cream, terracotta, olive and bronze glints, with a faint sepia warmth. Valerios Stais, Greek archaeologist, in 1902 (an imagined likeness, not a portrait): a man in middle age with a neat dark mustache and a high forehead, wearing a dark wool suit, a high white collar and a black tie, with dust on his sleeves and a magnifying glass in his hand; focused and quietly astonished. The Antikythera mechanism as found: a crusted, corroded, green-and-gray lump of bronze and wood about the size of a shoebox, cracked into several pieces, one broken face showing a flat bronze gear wheel with tiny triangular teeth and fine concentric rings, and faint scratches of tiny engraved marks; the marks are drawn as scratches, never as readable letters. Stais is seen in profile on the left, his eyes wide, holding the magnifying glass an inch above the broken face, where a perfectly regular ring of tiny triangular teeth shows in the crust. His other hand holds a small brush. On 17 May 1902, Stais sees a gear wheel embedded in the crust: a flat disk of bronze with regular, tiny triangular teeth. He guesses it is an astronomical clock. Most scholars of the day disagree, because a toothed machine seems far too complicated for the ancient Greeks, and the lump goes back to the shelf. Stais has seen something real; it will take most of the 20th century for the world to catch up.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: Stais noticed the gear on 17 May 1902, suggested an astronomical clock, and most scholars thought the object too complex for its period. Retelling: popular accounts often add a dramatic moment of the lump "splitting open"; the sources say only that the corroded crust cracked and shrank as it dried. The mechanism itself is simply evidence that Greek makers could cut gears.

The lump keeps its secret until the British science historian Derek de Solla Price, a professor at Yale, becomes fascinated by it in 1951. He studies the photographs, counts tooth after tooth, and in 1959 publishes an article calling it an "ancient Greek computer." He knows the photographs are not enough. To count teeth that are hidden inside the crust, he needs to see inside the stone itself.

In 1971, Price works with a Greek physicist, Charalampos Karakalos, in Athens. They take X-ray and gamma-ray images of all 82 fragments, laying each on film and exposing it. Each plate shows a faint ghost of the hidden structure: wheels within wheels, as if the crust had been made transparent. The pictures are blurry, but they show far more than anyone has seen before.

The Antikythera mechanism as found: a crusted, corroded, green-and-gray lump of bronze and wood about the size of a shoebox, cracked into several pieces, one broken face showing a flat bronze gear wheel with tiny triangular teeth and fine concentric rings, and faint scratches of tiny engraved marks; the marks are drawn as scratches, never as readable letters. Over the next years Price turns the shadows into numbers and the numbers into a gear train. In 1974 he publishes his conclusion: the box was a calendar-computer, a machine that modeled the movements of the Sun and Moon. Later researchers will correct many of his tooth counts, and add far more, but he has changed the question from "what is this lump?" to "how did they make it?"

In 2005 an international team, with scientists from Britain and Greece and the museum's own conservators, hauls a huge CT scanner into the museum. CT stands for computed tomography: the scanner takes hundreds of X-ray slices from every angle and a computer builds them into a 3D picture. A fragment too fragile to clean can now be seen layer by layer, in far more detail than any X-ray plate could show.

Over-the-shoulder shot at a computer desk in a dim laboratory in Athens in 2005, with the room lit mainly by the amber and white glow of a large monitor. Palette: cool white laboratory light, steel gray, deep blue shadow and the amber glow of a screen. The 2005 research team: an international group of three scientists and museum staff in the National Archaeological Museum, shown in profile or three-quarter view: a woman researcher in her forties with short gray hair and a white lab coat, a tall man in his thirties in a dark sweater holding a laptop, and an older museum conservator in a blue smock and white cotton gloves; all intent and quietly excited. The Antikythera mechanism as found: a crusted, corroded, green-and-gray lump of bronze and wood about the size of a shoebox, cracked into several pieces, one broken face showing a flat bronze gear wheel with tiny triangular teeth and fine concentric rings, and faint scratches of tiny engraved marks; the marks are drawn as scratches, never as readable letters. The three of them crowd close in profile, faces lit by the screen, looking at an enlarged scan slice of a bronze fragment in gray tones. On the screen, a ring of gear teeth and rows of tiny engraved marks appear in the metal, drawn only as tiny abstract scratches, never legible text. Above the screen, as an artist's glowing visualization, two faint translucent spiral dials hover like ghostly overlays: one with five tight turns, one with a wider coil, each marked with tiny symbols. Details: a mug of coffee gone cold, a keyboard, a ring of colored cables, and the real fragment on a foam cradle at the screen's edge. Emotional tone: breathless discovery, goosebumps. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The scans reveal what no one could see: thousands of tiny Greek letters, engraved over the surfaces of the box as a built-in user's manual. The text describes dials for the Sun and Moon, a spiral of 223 lunar months that predicts eclipses, and a dial that tracks the cycle of the Games, including the Olympic festival. The mechanism is not a clock and not a toy: it is a machine for reading the future of the sky. Turn the crank, and the dials show an eclipse before it happens.

docs.title: Panel 13: Who Made It?
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 13. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 13 of 14. Medium-wide shot inside an upper-floor bronze workshop in a harbor city of the eastern Aegean, imagined as Rhodes, about 100 BCE, warm late-afternoon light from a wide window overlooking a harbor with ships. Palette: warm limestone, sea-green, deep red, bronze and evening gold. The Antikythera mechanism as first built (a reconstruction): a shoebox-sized wooden case with a round bronze dial on the front ringed with fine engraved marks, a hand crank on the side, and a hinged back open to show a tightly packed train of small bronze gears with triangular teeth and two spiral dials; the marks are tiny scratches, never readable letters. The unknown makers, about 100 BCE: an older bronze-worker with a gray beard and a leather apron, and a younger worker with rolled sleeves holding a fine metal file, both in plain undyed linen tunics, shown mostly from behind, in profile or in shadow so that no face is recognizable. The two makers stand at a stout oak bench beside the open box, the younger one filing a single tiny tooth on a bronze gear held in a vise, while the older one points to a part of the mechanism. Details: racks of bronze files, calipers and compasses; a bronze sphere on a stand, a model of the heavens; a rolled papyrus of columns of tiny numbers on the bench; a small clay lamp; scraps of cut bronze sheet on the floor; and through the window the harbor, filled with ships. Emotional tone: quiet mastery, an unnamed craft whose names are lost. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Nobody signed the mechanism, and no ancient writer mentions this particular machine. The evidence points to a skilled workshop, quite possibly on Rhodes, in a tradition that ran from Archimedes to the astronomer Hipparchus and the philosopher Posidonius; the dials may have been set for a buyer from elsewhere in Greece. Other cities have been proposed, and the dating is still argued. Whoever the makers were, they combined astronomy, arithmetic and metalworking at a level nothing else we have matches for about 1,500 years.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: Cicero describes geared models of the heavens made by Archimedes and by Posidonius, so the tradition is real, and Hipparchus observed on Rhodes. Inference: a Rhodian workshop fits the lunar theory, the latitude and the cargo, but no inscription names the maker. Open: the Metonic dial uses month names from a different region, which is why researchers still debate where it was built and for whom.

Wide shot, from behind and slightly above, in a gallery of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens today, a November afternoon with soft daylight from high windows. Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive. Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. The Antikythera mechanism as found: a crusted, corroded, green-and-gray lump of bronze and wood about the size of a shoebox, cracked into several pieces, one broken face showing a flat bronze gear wheel with tiny triangular teeth and fine concentric rings, and faint scratches of tiny engraved marks; the marks are drawn as scratches, never as readable letters. The travelers stand small in the lower center of the frame, leaning slightly toward a softly lit glass case in front of them. Inside it rest the cracked, crusted green-and-gray bronze fragments of the mechanism on dark velvet, with one tiny gear wheel visible on a broken face, and the faint reflections of the two travelers in the glass. Details: a darkened gallery with a tall bronze statue of a youth standing at the back in soft focus, a long bench, a school group of small silhouettes far down the hall, and warm spotlights picking out the case. Emotional tone: quiet wonder, the sense of looking at a long-kept secret. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Today the fragments rest in a case in Athens, a shoebox of crust and bronze that changed how we see the ancient world. The question of who built it is still open, and so is how many other machines like it were melted down or lost. Glaux, perched on a windowsill in the storeroom of panel 6, has seen it all. "Look closer," they say, "at what everyone else walked past."

docs.title: Epilogue - What a Lump of Bronze Teaches
docs.text:
The Antikythera mechanism survives because the ship that carried it sank and because several generations of people refused to ignore it. A diver reported what he saw, an archaeologist noticed a gear, a historian counted teeth, and a team with a scanner read what a human eye never could. Each step depended on the last, and no single person solved it. What the box teaches is a pattern about knowledge itself: it is easy to lose, and it takes patient, shared looking to get it back.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today A crusted lump lay ignored among glamorous statues In 1902 Valerios Stais looked closely and noticed a gear wheel Discoveries often wait in plain sight for someone to look twice The gears were hidden inside corroded metal Price and Karakalos used X-rays in 1971; a team used CT scans in 2005 New tools can read what older ones could not; revisit old questions Nobody signed the machine, and the evidence is incomplete Researchers from many countries argue openly, and Rhodes is a leading candidate Say plainly what is known, what is inferred and what is open Skills held by a few workshops vanished for about 1,500 years Today the work is published and shared among researchers worldwide Knowledge that is written down, taught and shared survives

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: When you stand before the case in Athens, do the slow thing: look at the broken face of the largest fragment until you see the ring of tiny teeth. Then think about who in your own life makes or knows something valuable that only a few people understand, and ask whether it is written down or taught. The book's Learning for All thread asks who gets to learn to build and read machines like this one, and how to make sure the next such skill is shared with everyone who wants it.

"An Ancient Greek Computer" Derek de Solla Price, the title of his 1959 article in Scientific American, which gave the mechanism the name that stuck.

"Gears from the Greeks" Derek de Solla Price, the title of his 1974 study of the mechanism, based on the X-ray and gamma-ray images of the fragments.

Narrative Prompt **Era and place.** A food story told in layers. The legend panels (1 to 3) are set in an undated Ottoman household, and the story does not claim a year, because the tellings are tradition, not history. Panels 4 to 6 move through an Anatolian home kitchen, the palace kitchens of Topkapı in Istanbul, and a palace banquet of 1869. Panels 7 to 9 are in Greece: a village kitchen, a taverna and a hotel kitchen of the early 20th century. Panels 10 and 11 show the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey, and panel 12 is a table in the present day. **Themes.** Food as history you can eat; shared dishes with contested ownership ("the dishes are agreed, and the argument is over whom they belong to," as Chapter 15 puts it); the legends of imam bayıldı and hünkâr beğendi told honestly as legends; the human cost of the 1923 exchange, which carried cooks and recipes across the sea; and the Learning for All thread, learning with the people who hold the knowledge, not about them. The eggplant itself reached the Mediterranean in the early Middle Ages through Persian and Arab cooking, and the tomatoes in the dishes came from the Americas after 1492: the dish is a layer cake of history (see the Reading Food in Layers MicroSim). **Series house style.** Every prompt opens with the series house-style line (a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded fills, a faint watercolor paper texture) and ends with the series consistency line. Panels 7 to 9 (Greece in the early 20th century): natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive. Panels 10 and 11 (1923): muted pearl-gray dawn light, dusty ochre and weathered blue, with warm color kept for the cooking pots and kitchens. Panel 12: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive. **Safe-image decisions.** The 1923 exchange is shown with restraint: families with bundles on a quay, a cooking pot carried, ships at a distance, people seen from behind. docs.title: Prologue - The Vegetable That Crossed the Sea
docs.text:
An eggplant is not an obvious hero. It came from South or Southeast Asia, reached the Mediterranean through Persian and Arab cooking in the early Middle Ages, and then became the vegetable at the heart of more shared Greek and Turkish dishes than any other. Everyone agrees the dishes are delicious, and everyone disagrees about whom they belong to. This story follows one eggplant through legend, palace, tavern and quay, and ends at a table where both languages are spoken at once.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

Imam bayıldı means "the imam fainted," and there are two stories about why. In the first, an imam takes one bite of his wife's stuffed eggplant, cooked until it melts in olive oil, and swoons from pleasure. In the telling, his new wife watches him tip back among the cushions. The dish is real, and so is the name; the explanation is tradition.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: the dish, the name and the Turkish table it belongs to. Tradition: both stories about the fainting. Chapter 6 says that neither is history, "but both are true to the dish." No date, village or imam is named in any telling.

The imam of the legend: a stout, dignified man in his fifties with a short gray beard and a kind round face, wearing a tall white cloth-wrapped turban over a rounded cap, a long ankle-length cream robe over a pale blue under-robe, and holding a string of amber prayer beads; shown with gentle, respectful humor. The imam's new wife of the legend: a woman in her thirties with dark eyes and a proud, practical expression, wearing a long tomato-red dress with embroidered cuffs, a white headscarf pinned at the chin and a flour-dusted apron, her sleeves pushed up. The imam stands in the doorway of the pantry with one hand raised to his forehead and his eyes wide, staring at a row of tall clay oil jars, all standing empty with their lids off. His wife stands beside him holding a small empty jug and looking steadily back, unashamed. Details: a bunch of dried peppers hanging from a beam, a basket of eggplants and onions on the floor, a ladle lying beside a jar, a tiny oil stain on the stone, the long shadow of the imam on the wall, and a string of garlic by the door. The second story is about money, not manners. In this telling, the imam is not overcome by the taste but by the bill: the dish takes a great deal of olive oil, a precious ingredient, and he faints when he sees how much of the household's supply his new wife has used. Some tellers add that the jars were her dowry. Either way, the point of the story is the same: this dish is rich, and it is made with a generous hand.

Myth or Evidence? Both stories are legends. They explain a name, but no source names the imam, his wife, or the year. The Turkish name for the dish, "the imam fainted," is real and appears on menus today; the dish itself is documented by taste, by cookbooks and by generations of cooks.

The imam's new wife of the legend: a woman in her thirties with dark eyes and a proud, practical expression, wearing a long tomato-red dress with embroidered cuffs, a white headscarf pinned at the chin and a flour-dusted apron, her sleeves pushed up. Imam bayıldı: a whole purple eggplant split lengthwise down its belly and stuffed with soft onions, chopped tomatoes and garlic, glossy and golden with olive oil, served cool on a white plate with a sprig of parsley. In the center a deep copper tray holds a row of six eggplants like this, packed side by side in a shining pool of olive oil, cooling on the sill. Only the wife's forearms and hands are in frame at the right, lifting a spoon of oil over one eggplant. Around the tray, a still life of the layers of the dish: a clay jug of olive oil, a pile of ripe red tomatoes, a braid of garlic, a bowl of onions, and a bunch of parsley. The dish itself is simple and slow: a whole eggplant is split, stuffed with onions, tomatoes and garlic, cooked gently in olive oil and served cold. It is also a layer cake of history. Olive oil and garlic are ancient Mediterranean ingredients. The eggplant came in with Persian and Arab cooks in the early Middle Ages. The tomatoes are American, and reached the Mediterranean only after 1492; a recipe with tomatoes in it cannot be older than the voyages of Columbus. The Reading Food in Layers MicroSim lets us place other foods in their layers.

The second dish takes its name from what the cook does to it. Karnıyarık, "split belly," is an eggplant slit along its belly and filled with spiced minced meat, onion and tomato, then baked, often with a long green pepper on top. Unlike imam bayıldı, it is served hot and has meat in it. Its Greek cousin, papoutsakia, "little shoes," takes the same idea and adds a coat of béchamel.

The palace kitchens of Topkapı cook for several thousand people a day, and from them comes the empire's high cuisine. One of their dishes is hünkâr beğendi, "the sultan liked it": a stew of lamb spooned onto a smooth purée of eggplant roasted over a flame, then whipped with butter, flour, milk and cheese. It shows what the same vegetable looks like when it is dressed for a palace instead of a family table. The smoke you taste is the point.

The story says that hünkâr beğendi was created for the French Empress Eugénie when she visited Istanbul in 1869. It is a charming tale, and it is late and unproven. The dish itself is very real, and the idea that a great meal was served to a European empress fits the Ottoman palace's habit of showing its cooking to the world.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: the dish "the sultan liked it," its smoked eggplant purée, and Eugénie's 1869 visit. Legend: that the dish was invented for that dinner. Chapter 5 calls the story "late and unproven," and no early source ties the recipe to that banquet.

On the Greek side of the Aegean, the same vegetable meets the same fire. Melitzanosalata is eggplant roasted until the skin blackens, then mashed with garlic, olive oil and lemon or vinegar, and sometimes walnuts. It is the Greek cousin of the Turkish patlıcan salatası, and a visitor who has eaten one in Istanbul will recognize the other at once. The names change at the border, but the smoke does not.

In Greece the stuffed eggplant appears as imam baildi, and Athenian menus still list it under a Turkish name. Greeks and Turks both cook it, both name it, and both ask whose it is. Chapter 15 says it plainly: the dishes are agreed, and the argument is over whom they belong to. The honest answer is that each dish belongs to everyone who cooked it.

Wide shot of a busy hotel kitchen in Athens in the early 20th century, with a high ceiling, white tile walls and steam rising from copper pots under tall gas lamps. Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, terracotta, copper gold and olive. Nikolaos Tselementes, Greek chef of the early 20th century (an imagined likeness, not a portrait): a man in his forties in a white double-breasted chef's jacket and a tall white toque, with a neat mustache and a precise, proud expression, whisking a pale sauce in a copper pot. Moussaka: a thick square slice with layers of fried eggplant and spiced minced meat in tomato sauce under a tall golden-brown crust of béchamel, steaming on a white plate. The chef stands at center, whisking a pale, silky white sauce in a copper pot on a stove, in three-quarter view. In front of him on the steel table sits a large baking tin of layered eggplant and meat waiting to be topped, with a finished golden slice on a plate beside it. Details: young kitchen hands in white aprons chopping onions in the background, a rack of copper pans on the wall, a basket of eggplants, a bowl of cracked eggs, a sack of flour with a scoop, and a wooden cookbook stand holding a closed book with a blank cover. Emotional tone: pride, precision and a touch of French elegance. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story.
