Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive. Medium-wide shot from the street, matching panel 1's viewpoint. In the foreground stand Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. One lifts a hand toward a blue enamel street-name plate on the corner wall, shown edge-on so that nothing on it is legible, as if sounding it out; the other holds a small phrasebook. The mosque wall and a slender minaret stand behind them. Café tables with tulip-shaped tea glasses, a tram passing at the end of the street, a ferry on the water, a simit seller with his red cart and a cat on the wall complete the scene. Mood: pleased, curious and quietly moved. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Today every sign in Turkey is written in the alphabet of 1928, and two travelers can sound out the signs they pass, even without knowing the language. Giriş means "entrance," and Çıkış means "exit." The next time you read a Turkish sign aloud, you are using the tool the Head Teacher chalked on a board. It took years of schooling to read the old script and takes weeks to learn the new one, and that difference is the story.

docs.title: Epilogue - A Nation Goes Back to School
docs.text:
The alphabet reform of 1928 widened the circle of readers by lowering the cost of the first step: a script that fit the language, plus free classes for every adult. It also left costs behind. A generation lost easy access to its written past, the reform came from the top of a one-party state without a vote of the people, and its reach was uneven. The numbers behind it, a literacy rate of about one in ten in 1927, are a census answer to a particular question, which is why historians treat them with care.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today Script fits Turkish badly; about one in ten could read A 29-letter Latin-based alphabet, one letter for each sound, announced in 1928 Lowering the cost of the first step widens the circle Millions of adults could not read The Nation's Schools opened January 1, 1929, with free evening classes and certificates Pair a better tool with teaching and a place to learn Reach was uneven Classes reached towns before villages and men before women; many lost the skill without books Access needs books and practice, not just a classroom The change was ordered from the top A generation became cut off from Ottoman letters, fountains and gravestones Every big change has losses; ask who decided and who paid

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: When you read a Turkish sign today, say it aloud and notice that every letter has one sound. Then ask the question the book keeps asking: who is still locked out of reading, in any language, and what would open the door? Try the Sort the Scripts MicroSim to see the alphabets side by side, and look for the places in your own town where adults learn to read.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
No verbatim line from Mustafa Kemal or from the learners of 1929 is quoted here, because none could be confirmed in the sources used for this book. The documented words below are titles and names.

  • Türk Harflerinin Kabul ve Tatbiki Hakkında Kanun: the title of the law of November 1, 1928, usually translated as "Law on the Adoption and Application of Turkish Letters."
  • Başöğretmen: "Head Teacher," the title given to Mustafa Kemal as head of the Nation's Schools on November 24, 1928, and the reason Turkey celebrates Teachers' Day on that date.
  • Millet Mektepleri: "Nation's Schools," the name of the free adult literacy classes that opened on January 1, 1929.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:
• Chapter: 7. The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
  • Where to look: every Turkish sign you read, such as Giriş ("entrance") and Çıkış ("exit"); Gülhane Park below the walls of Topkapı; and Dolmabahçe Palace, where a clock in the room in which Atatürk died still shows 9:05, the minute of his death in 1938.
  • Explore further: Sort the Scripts puts the alphabets side by side.
  • Look Closer: Glaux's pointer: "Look up into the plane trees." Glaux hid in Panel 4, on a low branch above the blackboard in the park; today the plane trees of Gülhane Park still offer branches just the right height for a small owl.

docs.title: 7. The Horse at the Gates
docs.text: title: The Horse at the Gates: Myth, Troy and the Man Who Dug Too Fast description: The wooden horse is not in the Iliad, and the man who found Troy dug through the city he sought. Follow the legend, the 1870s dig, and a gold hoard that went from Troy to Berlin to Moscow. image: /stories/horse-at-the-gates/cover.png og:image: /stories/horse-at-the-gates/cover.png twitter:image: /stories/horse-at-the-gates/cover.png social: cards: false

docs.title: The Horse at the Gates
docs.text:
Cover Image Prompt (This is the Cover Image. Do not include this label in the image.) On the left, Troy in the Bronze Age at dusk, with The Wooden Horse of legend: a gigantic horse of rough-hewn pale pine planks, as tall as a three-story house, with a long arched neck, a plank body bound with rope-lashed beams, a mane of upright carved wooden spikes, a plain terracotta-red bridle, standing on a low timber platform with four heavy wooden rollers, with a small hidden hatch in its belly; no decoration and no lettering. standing before Troy in the Bronze Age, about 1180 BCE: a hilltop citadel on a low ridge above a windswept plain, ringed by a sloping wall of pale limestone about five meters thick, built in neat stepped sections, with a tall square stone tower at the northeast corner, a gate with a stone ramp, and small flat-roofed mud-brick houses crowded against the inside of the walls, in cream and ochre; below it a plain crossed by a winding river runs to a distant bay. and a crowd of tiny Trojans in ochre and cream clothing dragging it by ropes. On the right, a curve of the same ridge in the 1870s, where small figures in Victorian clothing and cloth caps work in an enormous trench in the mound, one man in a frock coat and pale cork sun helmet pointing. A diagonal seam of golden light runs between the two halves, with a few specks of gold in it. Across the sky, render the title in bold, hand-lettered title text: "The Horse at the Gates". Palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green on the left; sepia earth brown, dusty khaki, faded sky blue on the right. Emotional tone: mysterious, playful and a little mischievous. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt

This story runs on two timelines in one picture book. Panels 1-7 are myth and legend set in the Bronze Age, about 1180 BCE, on the plain and walls of Troy in northwest Anatolia (and one panel in Rome about 19 BCE where the horse story is written down). Panels 8-15 are documented history from the 1860s to 1993: Frank Calvert, Heinrich Schliemann, and the fate of the gold. Panel 16 is today.

Look and palette. The house style is the series' hand-drawn travel-sketchbook look. The myth panels use the Bronze Age palette from the series bible (terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green); the Roman panel uses the Hellenistic and Roman palette (warm limestone, sea-green, deep red, bronze, evening gold); the excavation panels use a Victorian palette (sepia earth brown, dusty khaki, faded sky blue, ochre, off-white linen) and Victorian-era clothing in the same ink-and-watercolor house style; the last two panels move to modern and Cold-War-era light. The two timelines must read as the same book, so keep the ink outline weight and watercolor texture identical.

Themes. How a war becomes a story; the difference between a poem and a layer of ash; who gets credit (Calvert and Schliemann); how an object can be famous for the wrong name; and the Learning for All thread, because the horse story survives only because Greek singers' songs were later written down in the Greek alphabet.

Safety. Troy's fall is shown by fire, smoke, silhouettes and ships, never by violence. Soldiers' weapons stay at rest. The 1945 panel shows only a truck, crates and a damaged building. The harbor-side horse in Çanakkale is not shown in any panel and, if mentioned, is described only as a big wooden horse built as a movie prop; name no studio or brand.

Creative liberties and uncertainties. No image of Laocoön, the Greek soldiers or the Trojan crowds exists; these are invented types. The architecture of Troy follows the late Bronze Age citadel, Troy VI and VIIa, with simplified walls; whether the Trojans ever pulled down a gate or saw a horse is legend. Schliemann's and Calvert's appearances are invented respectful likenesses based on their period, age and dress; the 1868 meeting is documented, its exact scene is imagined. The 1945 loading scene is generic and does not depict a documented event or place. No Cyrillic, German or Turkish lettering appears anywhere. The wooden horse always has the same plank, rope and spiked-mane look.

Cast. Paste each block below verbatim into every prompt where that character, place or object appears.

  • Glaux the Little Owl: see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md (Glaux). Glaux appears in exactly one panel, Panel 10, as a small hidden observer on a stone block.
  • The Travelers (final panel): see docs/stories/characters.md; seen from behind in Panel 16 only.

Laocoön (this story only)

Laocoön, priest of Troy: a lean, gray-bearded man of about fifty with deep-set, alarmed eyes, wearing a long white linen robe with a saffron border and a band of laurel leaves around his head, one arm raised and pointing, a short carved wooden ritual staff in the other hand.

Frank Calvert (this story only)

Frank Calvert, English consular agent at the Dardanelles in the 1860s: a lean, sun-browned man of about forty with a trimmed brown beard flecked with gray, wearing a worn tan linen suit, a soft wide-brimmed cloth hat and dusty boots, with a small leather notebook in his hand; quiet, patient and watchful.

Heinrich Schliemann (this story only)

Heinrich Schliemann, German excavator, in the 1870s: a stocky, restless man of about fifty with a high forehead, short thinning gray hair, a neat gray mustache and no beard, wearing a dark Victorian wool frock coat and waistcoat with a watch chain, high leather boots and a pale cork sun helmet, usually pointing or hurrying; energetic, impatient and sure of himself.

Sophia Schliemann (this story only)

Sophia Schliemann, in the 1870s: a young Greek woman of about twenty-two with dark hair parted in the middle and pinned back, a dark, high-collared Victorian dress, a straight posture and a solemn, composed expression.

A Roman poet (this story only)

A Roman poet of about 19 BCE: a thin, pale man of about fifty with a high forehead, short dark hair and tired, kind eyes, wearing a long cream wool mantle over a tunic, reading aloud from an unrolled papyrus scroll held in both hands.

Troy in the Bronze Age (place, this story only)

Troy in the Bronze Age, about 1180 BCE: a hilltop citadel on a low ridge above a windswept plain, ringed by a sloping wall of pale limestone about five meters thick, built in neat stepped sections, with a tall square stone tower at the northeast corner, a gate with a stone ramp, and small flat-roofed mud-brick houses crowded against the inside of the walls, in cream and ochre; below it a plain crossed by a winding river runs to a distant bay.

The Wooden Horse (object, this story only)

The Wooden Horse of legend: a gigantic horse of rough-hewn pale pine planks, as tall as a three-story house, with a long arched neck, a plank body bound with rope-lashed beams, a mane of upright carved wooden spikes, a plain terracotta-red bridle, standing on a low timber platform with four heavy wooden rollers, with a small hidden hatch in its belly; no decoration and no lettering.

The mound at Hisarlık in the 1870s (place, this story only)

The mound at Hisarlık in the 1870s: a long, low, grassy hill on a ridge above a wide plain, its top cut by one enormous straight trench with steep earth walls showing bands of dark ash, rubble and old stone walls, with spoil heaps beside it, wooden ladders and plank ramps, and a few canvas tents and a wooden hut along the rim.

The replica horse at Troy today (object, this story only)

The replica horse at Troy today: a large modern wooden horse of weathered gray-brown planks, about two stories tall, standing on a low wooden base beside a gravel path, with a small opening and wooden steps in its flank so visitors can climb inside.

docs.title: Prologue - A Horse That Is Not in the Poem
docs.text:
Everyone knows the Trojan Horse. Almost nobody knows that the Iliad, the great poem of the war, ends before the horse ever appears, or that the man who "found" Troy dug right through the city he was looking for. This story follows the legend from its siege to its burning, then follows the people who went looking for the real place in the 1860s and 1870s, and the gold that traveled from a trench in Turkey to Berlin and then to Moscow. Along the way we sort what is documented from what is legend, a habit worth having on the mound at Hisarlık.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

docs.title: Panel 1: Ten Years Under the Walls
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 01. Do not include the panel number in the image.) I am about to ask you to generate a series of images for a graphic novel. Please make the images have a consistent style and consistent characters. Do not ask any clarifying questions. Just generate the image immediately when asked. Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 1 of 16. Troy, northwest Anatolia, about 1180 BCE, late afternoon in the tenth year of a siege. Palette: Bronze Age palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green. Wide establishing view from the Greek camp on the plain looking up toward the citadel on its ridge: Troy in the Bronze Age, about 1180 BCE: a hilltop citadel on a low ridge above a windswept plain, ringed by a sloping wall of pale limestone about five meters thick, built in neat stepped sections, with a tall square stone tower at the northeast corner, a gate with a stone ramp, and small flat-roofed mud-brick houses crowded against the inside of the walls, in cream and ochre; below it a plain crossed by a winding river runs to a distant bay. Golden low light, a steady wind bending the grass, a weary, tense mood. In the foreground a row of dark ships drawn up on the sand behind a wooden palisade, curls of smoke from camp fires, three tired soldiers in bronze helmets and linen tunics mending a rope beside an upturned boat, a spear leaning at rest against it, and a pair of oxen resting in the shade of a tent of stretched hides. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

For ten years the Greeks have camped on the plain below the windy citadel, and for ten years the walls have held. The legend says an alliance of Greek kings crossed the sea to win back Helen, the wife of a king of Sparta, who had left with the Trojan prince Paris. The soldiers mend ropes and wait. Somewhere up on the ridge, the Trojans wait too.

docs.title: Panel 2: The Empty Beach
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 02. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Medium-wide view across the empty sand: The Wooden Horse of legend: a gigantic horse of rough-hewn pale pine planks, as tall as a three-story house, with a long arched neck, a plank body bound with rope-lashed beams, a mane of upright carved wooden spikes, a plain terracotta-red bridle, standing on a low timber platform with four heavy wooden rollers, with a small hidden hatch in its belly; no decoration and no lettering. It stands alone and enormous at the center of the frame. Behind it the Greek camp is empty, its tents collapsed and its fires still smoking, and a line of small dark ships sails out toward the horizon on a calm, pearl-colored sea. Footprints and wheel ruts cross the wet sand, a discarded rope coil lies near the horse's hooves, and gulls wheel overhead. In the far background the citadel stands on its ridge. Mood: eerie, quiet, suspicious relief. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

One morning the Trojans wake to silence. The camp is deserted, the ships are specks on the horizon, and on the beach stands a horse of timber taller than a house. In the legend the Greeks have only pretended to leave, hiding their fleet behind a nearby island, and the horse is a trap with soldiers inside. The Trojans do not know that yet.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 03. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Wide, slightly low-angle view of a joyful crowd hauling the wooden horse up the stone ramp toward the citadel gate. The Wooden Horse of legend: a gigantic horse of rough-hewn pale pine planks, as tall as a three-story house, with a long arched neck, a plank body bound with rope-lashed beams, a mane of upright carved wooden spikes, a plain terracotta-red bridle, standing on a low timber platform with four heavy wooden rollers, with a small hidden hatch in its belly; no decoration and no lettering. Beside it, the walls: Troy in the Bronze Age, about 1180 BCE: a hilltop citadel on a low ridge above a windswept plain, ringed by a sloping wall of pale limestone about five meters thick, built in neat stepped sections, with a tall square stone tower at the northeast corner, a gate with a stone ramp, and small flat-roofed mud-brick houses crowded against the inside of the walls, in cream and ochre; below it a plain crossed by a winding river runs to a distant bay. Dozens of Trojan men and women in linen tunics and long ochre dresses pull on thick ropes; children throw flower garlands over its neck, a lyre player walks ahead, and oxen are yoked to the rollers. Part of the gate's stone lintel has been pulled down to let the horse pass. Mood: festive, loud, dangerously confident. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. The Trojans take the horse for a gift. In the version the Roman poet Virgil tells, they decide to bring it inside as an offering to the goddess Athena, and they pull down part of the gate to fit it through. Children hang garlands on its neck. After ten years of war, a festival feels like a victory.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 04. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Palette: Bronze Age palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green. Medium shot, slightly low angle, centered on the priest warning the crowd while the horse looms behind him. Laocoön, priest of Troy: a lean, gray-bearded man of about fifty with deep-set, alarmed eyes, wearing a long white linen robe with a saffron border and a band of laurel leaves around his head, one arm raised and pointing, a short carved wooden ritual staff in the other hand. Behind him rises The Wooden Horse of legend: a gigantic horse of rough-hewn pale pine planks, as tall as a three-story house, with a long arched neck, a plank body bound with rope-lashed beams, a mane of upright carved wooden spikes, a plain terracotta-red bridle, standing on a low timber platform with four heavy wooden rollers, with a small hidden hatch in its belly; no decoration and no lettering. Around him the crowd of Trojans in linen tunics, some with garlands, turn their heads away or look doubtful; a young boy stares up at the horse; a woman clutches a child's hand; a Trojan elder shakes his head. A sacrificial bull is being led away along the street. Warm, dusty light and long shadows. Mood: urgent warning that nobody wants to hear. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

A priest named Laocoön steps out of the crowd and tells them to stop. In Virgil's poem he says the line still quoted in Latin, timeo Danaos et dona ferentes: "I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts." The crowd is not listening. Trojans who warn of danger are rarely as popular as Trojans who cheer.

docs.title: Panel 5: Down the Ropes at Night
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 05. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 5 of 16. A quiet courtyard inside Troy near the citadel gate, about 1180 BCE, deep night. Palette: Bronze Age palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green, deepened to indigo shadow with silver moonlight. Wide view, looking slightly up at the wooden horse in the middle of the courtyard: The Wooden Horse of legend: a gigantic horse of rough-hewn pale pine planks, as tall as a three-story house, with a long arched neck, a plank body bound with rope-lashed beams, a mane of upright carved wooden spikes, a plain terracotta-red bridle, standing on a low timber platform with four heavy wooden rollers, with a small hidden hatch in its belly; no decoration and no lettering. Its belly hatch is open and a rope ladder hangs down; six Greek soldiers in bronze helmets and dark cloaks climb down silently, one holding his sandals in his hand to be quiet, another helping the next, all with their weapons still sheathed. A Trojan guard sleeps sitting against the wall, a wine cup tipped over beside him. Houses are dark, a single oil lamp glows in one window, and a gate stands at the far end of the courtyard. Mood: hushed, tense, inevitable. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

That night, after the festival, the city sleeps. A hatch opens in the horse's belly and armed Greeks lower themselves down on ropes, and in the tradition they open the gates to the fleet that has sailed back in the dark. The tale is a master class in a single trick: the best way to get past a wall is to be invited in.

docs.title: Panel 6: Troy Burns
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 06. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 6 of 16. The plain below Troy, about 1180 BCE, before dawn. Palette: Bronze Age palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green, with orange fire-glow against deep indigo sky. Wide establishing view from the beach looking up at the citadel: Troy in the Bronze Age, about 1180 BCE: a hilltop citadel on a low ridge above a windswept plain, ringed by a sloping wall of pale limestone about five meters thick, built in neat stepped sections, with a tall square stone tower at the northeast corner, a gate with a stone ramp, and small flat-roofed mud-brick houses crowded against the inside of the walls, in cream and ochre; below it a plain crossed by a winding river runs to a distant bay. The houses inside the walls are ablaze, tall columns of smoke rise into the stars, and sparks drift on the wind. In the foreground, dark ships are drawn up on the sand again and a small group of Greek soldiers stands in silhouette, watching without moving. Along the road a line of Trojan families in silhouette flee with bundles and a donkey. No bodies, no fighting visible. Mood: solemn and sorrowful, the cost of the story. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

By morning the city is gone. Archaeologists do find a Troy that burned, the layer they call Troy VIIa, destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE, and in its ruins excavators found arrowheads and human remains. Whether Greeks, raiders or some war we cannot name set the fire, the stones do not say.

Myth or Evidence? Troy VIIa really burned, around 1180 BCE; that is documented. That it fell to a Greek army, after ten years, over Helen, is the legend. No evidence from the time says so.

docs.title: Panel 7: The Poet Who Built the Horse
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 07. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 7 of 16. Rome, about 19 BCE, early evening in a lamplit villa courtyard. Palette: Roman palette: warm limestone, sea-green, deep red, bronze, evening gold. Medium shot, over the shoulder of a listener, of a poet reading to a small circle of friends. A Roman poet of about 19 BCE: a thin, pale man of about fifty with a high forehead, short dark hair and tired, kind eyes, wearing a long cream wool mantle over a tunic, reading aloud from an unrolled papyrus scroll held in both hands. On the low table beside him sit a small clay model of a horse, a bronze lamp, a wax tablet and a stack of papyrus rolls tied with red cord; six listeners recline on couches in togas and long stolas, one leaning forward, one with eyes closed. An olive tree grows in a pot, a fountain trickles in the corner, painted red walls behind them. The scroll bears only faint, illegible marks. Mood: hushed absorption, a story being born. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Here is the surprise. The wooden horse is not in the Iliad, which ends with Hector's funeral, before Troy falls. The Odyssey mentions it three times, briefly. The fullest telling, including Laocoön and his famous warning, comes from the Roman poet Virgil in the Aeneid, written around 19 BCE, more than eleven centuries after Troy VIIa burned.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: the horse appears in the Odyssey (briefly) and in Virgil's Aeneid, written about 19 BCE. Tradition: that any such horse ever stood at Troy. Historians have suggested it might remember a siege engine or an earthquake (Poseidon was the god of both horses and earthquakes), but there is no evidence for either.

Frank Calvert, an Englishman who works as a consular agent at the Dardanelles, owns part of the mound at Hisarlık, and has been studying the plain for years. In the early 1860s he digs trial trenches on his own land and finds ancient walls. He is convinced that Homer's Troy lies inside, but he does not have the money for a full excavation.

In 1868 a wealthy German businessman, Heinrich Schliemann, comes to see Calvert. He listens, and he takes up the idea. Calvert has the knowledge and the land; Schliemann has the money and a great hurry. Historians would later use the letters of both men to give Calvert back his share of the credit.

Schliemann starts digging in 1871, and he digs big. His crews cut a huge trench straight through the middle of the mound. It is a spectacular piece of work, and it also slices through layers that lie close to Homer's age, so that he cuts away the very Troy he is looking for. The trench itself is now evidence: a cut is always younger than everything it cuts through.

In 1873 Schliemann finds a hoard of gold, silver and bronze objects, including two gold diadems made of thousands of small gold pieces. He names it Priam's Treasure, after Homer's king of Troy. The name is a wish. The hoard comes from Troy II, about a thousand years too early for Priam.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: a real treasure, found in 1873 and dated by later archaeologists to Troy II. The name 'Priam's Treasure' is Schliemann's hope, not a date.

Schliemann has a famous photograph made of his young wife, Sophia, wearing the diadems. In his book he says she carried the treasure away in her shawl. Years later he admitted that she had been in Athens at the time. The treasure was real, but the scene he told was a piece of publicity.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: the photograph, and Schliemann's later admission that Sophia was in Athens at the time of the find. Legend: the shawl scene, which Schliemann invented.

Schliemann has agreed to share the finds with the Ottoman government. He smuggles the treasure out instead. The Ottoman government sues him, and he pays a settlement. Most of the treasure goes to Berlin in 1881.

At the end of the Second World War, Soviet troops take the treasure from Berlin to Moscow. Then it vanishes. For decades nobody outside Russia knows whether it still exists.

In 1993 Russia confirms that the gold has been in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow all along, and it remains there today. A few pieces are in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, and the Troy Museum, opened in 2018, shows what the region still holds. A visitor who wanted to see the finds from Troy in one room would need tickets in four countries.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 16. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed clouds, sea blue, terracotta, olive. Wide establishing view from the plain looking up toward the low grassy ridge and mound, matching the viewpoint of panel 1 as closely as possible, with the exposed pale walls and the long cut of the old trench visible on the mound. The replica horse at Troy today: a large modern wooden horse of weathered gray-brown planks, about two stories tall, standing on a low wooden base beside a gravel path, with a small opening and wooden steps in its flank so visitors can climb inside. Children in colorful coats climb its steps and wave from its opening; a school group sits on the grass; a guide stands with a raised hand. On the plain in the foreground a gravel path and a few wild flowers. Two small figures in the foreground: Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. Mood: warm, windy, layered with time. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Today the legend and the dig sit side by side. Children climb the replica horse at the entrance and clamber about in it, while behind them the great trench still cuts through nine stacked cities. In Çanakkale, on the waterfront, a second horse stands: a big wooden horse built as a movie prop and given to the town. A Bronze Age war, a Roman poem, a Victorian excavation and a film: the horse is a layer of cultural memory all by itself.

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Horse Teaches
docs.text:
A horse that is not in the poem, a treasure that is not Priam's, and a discoverer who dug through his own prize: Troy is a place where names run ahead of evidence. The legend gives the city its meaning, and the layers of the mound give it its dates, and the two do not have to be forced into agreement. Calvert's patience and Schliemann's speed both left their mark, and the best of what the mound still tells us comes from reading the layers carefully, a habit the architect Wilhelm Dörpfeld began to bring to the site from 1882. This is also a Learning for All story. The horse reaches us only because Greek singers' songs were eventually written down in the Greek alphabet, the new script that made reading easier to learn.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today A name run ahead of the evidence Later archaeologists dated the treasure to Troy II, a thousand years before Priam's time Believe the layer number, not the label on the case. Credit given to the loudest voice Historians used Calvert's and Schliemann's letters to restore Calvert's share Ask who did the quiet work before the famous work. A discoverer in a hurry The great trench cut through layers close to Homer's age; a trained architect later brought careful recording Speed without method destroys the thing you are looking for. A story that outgrew its source The horse appears only in the Odyssey (briefly) and the Aeneid; the Iliad never mentions it Check the earliest source before trusting a famous scene.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: Before you climb the replica horse, walk over to Schliemann's trench and read its walls from the top down. Look for the bands of ash, then ask which of the nine cities each one belongs to. If you can, find the layer number beside any name on a label, and believe the number.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• "I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts" (timeo Danaos et dona ferentes): Laocoön's warning in Virgil's Aeneid, Book 2, written about 19 BCE. The line belongs to a Roman poem about the legend, not to anyone who lived at Troy.
  • Mēnin, "wrath": the first word of the Iliad in Greek, and its subject. The poem follows one hero's anger for about fifty days of the war's tenth year and ends with Hector's funeral, not with Troy's fall. We quote the word, not a translation.
  • No documented words of Calvert or of the Troy-era Trojans survive for this story, so we do not quote them. Schliemann's own books are rich sources, but he shaped his stories for publicity, as the shawl scene shows.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:
• Chapter: 8. Troy and Gallipoli
  • Where to look: Schliemann's great trench through the mound, where nine cities show in a single cross-section; the sloping Troy VI wall and tower; the replica wooden horse at the entrance, which visitors can climb inside; and, on the Çanakkale waterfront, a second, bigger wooden horse built as a movie prop.
  • Explore further: Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence?, which asks how old the earliest evidence is for stories from Troy and Gallipoli.
  • Look Closer: Glaux says: "Look closer. At the lip of the great trench, find a squared stone block." Glaux hid in Panel 10 (The Great Trench), perched on a squared stone at the trench edge, looking over the work. Little owls really do live in ruins like these.

docs.title: Into the Labyrinth
docs.text:
Cover Image Prompt (This is the Cover Image. Do not include this label in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a wide-landscape 16:9 cover image. Scene: a dramatic split view at golden hour. On the left, in a torchlit Bronze Age corridor of cream plaster painted with red and lapis bands, a single red thread winds across the floor and away into darkness, while a huge bull-headed shadow with long curved horns falls across the far wall (shadow only, no figure, no gore). On the right, in bright daylight, a row of smooth modern red-painted concrete columns, wider at the top than the bottom, stands beside rough ancient limestone blocks carved with a double axe. Between them, small in the frame, stands Sir Arthur Evans, British archaeologist: a short, energetic man in his fifties with a neat white beard, round wire glasses, a weathered face, wearing a rumpled cream linen jacket, a wide-brimmed straw hat and carrying a walking stick; he often carries a small ancient clay fragment in one hand and gestures eagerly. He holds up a clay fragment. Render the title as bold, hand-lettered text across the top: "INTO THE LABYRINTH" (exact spelling, no other text anywhere). Palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster and olive green. Mood: mysterious, adventurous, a little playful. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt **Story:** "Into the Labyrinth" retells the Greek legend of Theseus, Ariadne and the Minotaur (myth time, imagined at Bronze Age Knossos, about 1500 BCE) and then follows the English archaeologist Arthur Evans, who bought the hill of Kephala and began digging in March 1900 and went on to rebuild parts of the palace in reinforced concrete. The story asks one question: what did the Minoans make, and what did Evans imagine? **Places and eras:** Knossos, Crete (the palace in legend, the excavation of 1900, the rebuilding of about 1905 to 1930); the Heraklion Archaeological Museum (today). Panels 1 to 7 are myth time and use the Bronze Age palette from the series bible: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster and olive green. Panels 8 to 11 are 1900 to the 1920s and use dusty ochre soil, straw yellow, spring green, faded sky blue and terracotta (an extension of the "Modern" palette for the dig years). Panels 12 to 14 use natural museum and daylight tones with the Bronze Age colors in the frescoes. **House style:** hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, as in docs/stories/characters.md. No lettering anywhere in panels; only the cover carries the title. Safe-Image Rules apply: the Minotaur is only ever a shadow on a wall or a silhouette of horns, there is no combat, and every figure is draped or dressed. **Legend versus evidence:** The earliest written pieces of the Minotaur story are centuries younger than the palace, and the thread and the tribute of fourteen Athenians are first told in full by Roman-era writers. Panels 1 to 6 are legend; panel 7 mixes a documented symbol (the double axe) with a disputed word origin; panels 8 to 14 are documented history. The prompts mark which is which. **Creative liberties:** The legend gives no description of Minos, Daedalus, Ariadne or Theseus, so their appearance is invented for the series. Evans is drawn from the shared block only in panels where he is in his fifties (1900 to about 1905); in the 1920s rebuilding he was in his seventies, so he is not drawn in panel 11. Minoan men and women are dressed modestly in the prompts (the real frescoes show bare chests). The travelers visited the Heraklion Archaeological Museum on Day 9 and chose a village excursion instead of the palace, so the final panel is set in the museum, in front of the palace's scale model, not at the site. **Cast:** Recurring characters (see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md for Glaux): Arthur Evans (panels 8, 9 and 10 and the cover), Zeus (panel 1), the Palace of Knossos and the Travelers. Glaux hides in panel 7. Characters who appear only in this story: King Minos (panel 1): 
King Minos of Crete: a tall, stern man of about fifty with dark curled shoulder-length hair and a short black beard, a thin gold circlet on his head, a short embroidered ochre-and-lapis tunic with a broad woven belt, a long white cloak with a red border, gold bracelets and an ivory-headed staff; majestic and wary.

Ariadne (panels 4 and 6): 
Ariadne, princess of Crete: a young woman of about twenty with long black ringleted hair tied with a blue ribbon, wearing a flounced terracotta-and-ochre Minoan skirt with a fitted, high-necked blue-and-cream embroidered jacket and a gold bracelet, holding a ball of bright red thread.

docs.title: Prologue - A Maze, a Thread and a Bucket of Concrete
docs.text:
The legend says that beneath the palace at Knossos lay a maze so confusing that nobody who went in could find the way out, until a prince with a ball of thread did. Three thousand years later, an English archaeologist dug up the real palace, rebuilt much of it in reinforced concrete, and painted the columns red. Today's visitors find themselves in a second kind of maze: which of these walls are Minoan, and which are from the 1920s? This story walks through both.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

docs.title: Panel 1: The Palace of King Minos
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 01. Do not include the panel number in the image.) I am about to ask you to generate a series of images for a graphic novel. Please make the images have a consistent style and consistent characters. Do not ask any clarifying questions. Just generate the image immediately when asked. Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 1 of 14. Setting: the Palace of Knossos on Crete as the legend imagines it, about 1500 BCE, late-afternoon golden light. Palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster and olive green. Camera: a high bird's-eye view from the northwest, looking down across the whole palace, the same angle as looking down on a museum's scale model. Mood: majestic and faintly uneasy. The Palace of Knossos on Crete: a sprawl of low, flat-roofed, honey-colored stone buildings around an open central court, with distinctive red-painted, downward-tapering wooden columns (wider at the top than the bottom) with black capitals, and colorful frescoes; storerooms hold giant human-tall clay jars (pithoi) with rope-like ridged bands. Small in the foreground, on a rooftop terrace, stands King Minos of Crete: a tall, stern man of about fifty with dark curled shoulder-length hair and a short black beard, a thin gold circlet on his head, a short embroidered ochre-and-lapis tunic with a broad woven belt, a long white cloak with a red border, gold bracelets and an ivory-headed staff; majestic and wary. Below him the central court is dotted with tiny figures carrying jars, and a ramp leads to a North Entrance with a painted bull relief. Stone horns crown the roof edge, olive groves ring the hill, and far off a harbor glints with sails. In the Greek legend, King Minos rules Crete from a palace at Knossos, and tradition makes him a son of the god Zeus. Ships from across the Aegean owe him tribute, and his craftsmen are the finest anywhere. The real palace stood on this hill for more than a thousand years, and Arthur Evans will later name its people the Minoans after this king. In the legend, though, something troubling is growing in the palace cellars.

Minos calls on his master craftsman, Daedalus, to build a prison for a monster. The legend says the creature is the Minotaur, 'the bull of Minos', born after Poseidon sent the king a white bull and the king would not sacrifice it. Daedalus designs the Labyrinth so cleverly that no one who enters can find the way out, and Athens is made to send seven young men and seven young women into it as tribute. Whatever the Minotaur is, it is the poets' work: the Labyrinth is a story about a building that confuses.

Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, falls for the young prince and slips him a ball of thread. He ties one end to the doorway and unwinds it as he walks, so that the way back stays in his hand. The thread is first told in full by writers such as Plutarch and Apollodorus, in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. It is a very practical idea: if you cannot see the whole maze, at least leave a path you can follow home.

Myth or Evidence? Legend. The earliest scenes of Theseus and the Minotaur are on Greek pottery from the 7th century BCE, some 600 or 700 years after the palace fell, and the tribute and the thread are written down more than a thousand years after that.

Myth or Evidence? Legend. Bulls really are everywhere in Minoan art, in paintings, on seals and in the stone 'horns' on rooftops, so a Cretan monster with a bull's head is a natural thing for later Greeks to imagine. No bones, monster or maze have ever been found.

This is the labrys, the double-headed axe, carved on blocks all over the palace and treated as a sacred symbol. Since Evans, many writers have said that 'labyrinth' means 'house of the double axe'. Glaux, perched above the carving, would say: look closer.

Myth or Evidence? Documented, with a disputed word origin. The double axe is real, and a Linear B tablet from Knossos records an offering of honey to 'the Mistress of the Labyrinth', so a place or shrine of that name existed. But linguists are divided on whether the word really comes from labrys.

Arthur Evans first came to Crete in 1894 looking for early writing, after seeing tiny signs engraved on seal stones that Cretan women wore as charms. In 1878 a Heraklion merchant, Minos Kalokairinos, had dug trenches on this hill and found giant storage jars, but the Ottoman authorities, who still governed Crete, stopped him. Once Crete became autonomous, Evans bought the land and began digging in March 1900, with the Scottish archaeologist Duncan Mackenzie keeping the daily records and a large crew of Cretan workers. Within weeks they find the Throne Room and the first clay tablets.

In April 1900 the team uncovers a small room with a high-backed gypsum seat still standing against the wall. Evans calls it the throne of Minos, and it becomes famous as the oldest throne in Europe. It is one of the few things in the palace that is exactly where the Bronze Age left it.

Myth or Evidence? The throne is documented. The name is Evans's. The room in its present form dates from the last phase of the palace, after about 1450 BCE, and who sat there is unknown; some scholars think it was a priestess, not a king.

The palace's wall paintings did not survive on the walls. They fell when the palace burned and came out of the ground as heaps of fragments, often a few centimeters across. Evans hired artists, including a father-and-son team of Swiss painters both named Émile Gilliéron, to fit the pieces together and paint in the gaps. The results are lovely and partly guesswork: one figure, restored as a boy gathering crocuses, later turned out to be a blue monkey.

Wooden columns and beams had burned or rotted away, and the soft gypsum stone was dissolving in the rain, so from about 1905 Evans rebuilt, first in wood and stone and mainly from the 1920s in reinforced concrete. His architects, Christian Doll and later Piet de Jong, rebuilt the Grand Staircase, the North Entrance and an upper floor over the Throne Room, and painted concrete columns red in the Minoan shape, wider at the top than the bottom. The result is the only Bronze Age palace where visitors can feel a room's height, and also a palace partly designed in the 1920s.

A simple test works at almost any wall in Knossos: look at the material before the color. Rough rubble, worn limestone and pitted gypsum are almost always Minoan; smooth gray concrete and anything bright red or black above head height is almost always Evans; and a painting on an outdoor wall is a copy, because the originals are in the museum. Later conservation rules turned against rebuilding; the Venice Charter of 1964 says reconstruction should be ruled out on archaeological sites, and the iron inside Evans's concrete is now rusting. The concrete has itself become part of the site's history.

We have come back to the angle of the first panel, now through a glass case in Heraklion. On Day 9 we chose the village excursion over the palace, so our palace is the museum's scale model, and it is a good way to see how a maze-like plan could have started a legend. The next time we are at Knossos, we will know to ask the question that this story keeps asking: who made this, the Minoans, Evans, or a copyist?

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Labyrinth Teaches
docs.text:
The Labyrinth never existed as the legend tells it, but the palace that inspired it did, and so did the man who rebuilt it. Evans gave the world a vivid Minoan Crete, and he gave it a palace you can feel the height of; he also painted his own picture of the past onto the real one. The skill the legend rewards, leaving a path you can follow back, is the same skill a visitor needs at Knossos: always be able to trace what is original, what is rebuilt and what is guessed.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today Finding the way out of a maze Theseus tied a thread at the entrance and followed it back Keep a trail you can retrace A heap of tiny painted fragments Evans's artists fitted the pieces together and painted in the gaps Mark what is found and what is guessed Burned timbers and crumbling stone Evans rebuilt in reinforced concrete and painted the columns red A repair becomes history too, and later rules (the Venice Charter of 1964) discourage rebuilding Telling Minoan from Evans Visitors check the material first, the color second Ask who made it before you admire it

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: At Knossos, or in front of the scale model in Heraklion, find one wall and decide whether it is Minoan, Evans or a copy, then check your answer against the Knossos sim. Learning for All also means being told honestly what is original and what is a guess, so that anyone, not just an expert, can read the evidence for themselves.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• Homer, Iliad (Book 18), paraphrased. In the description of the shield of Achilles, the poet compares a dancing floor to the one that Daedalus once made in broad Knossos for Ariadne. This is the earliest written mention of the Knossos story that we have, set down some 600 or 700 years after the palace fell.
  • A Linear B tablet from Knossos. It records an offering of honey to "the Mistress of the Labyrinth" (as the chapter reads it). The tablet is documented evidence that a place or shrine called the Labyrinth existed at Mycenaean Knossos, and it says nothing about a Minotaur.
  • Arthur Evans, the title of his great work. The Palace of Minos (published in four volumes between 1921 and 1935) shows how Evans named the Bronze Age people of Crete after a king from the legend.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:
• Chapter: 13. Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
  • Where to look: the red-painted concrete columns, wider at the top than the bottom; the Throne Room, seen from the antechamber; the painted copies of frescoes on the palace walls; and the originals, including the Bull-Leaping Fresco and the fragments set in plaster, in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.
  • Explore further: Knossos: Minoan, Evans, or Copy?
  • Look Closer: Glaux was perched in panel 7, just above the carved double axe on the palace block. At the site, look for the labrys carved on the stone itself, and in the museum look for the darker edges of real fresco fragments inside the bright restored plaster.

Era and places. Two time layers joined by one object. The first is the palace of Knossos on Crete, in its storerooms (the "West Magazines" behind the Throne Room), about 1450 BCE; the great storage jars (pithoi) in use there date from roughly 1700 to 1450 BCE, so this date sits at the end of that range. The second is today, in the village of Thrapsano in the hills southeast of Heraklion and at a village winery on the same excursion afternoon. The story is told from the Villages of Crete excursion that followed a museum morning.

Themes. One skill, 3,500 years: a very large jar cannot be made in one piece, so the potter builds it in stages and fires it at high heat. The craft outlived every use it was invented for. Also: the palace economy (oil is wealth only if someone records it), and craft knowledge handed from hand to hand, a form of Learning for All that never needed a textbook.

Series house style. Hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills, faint watercolor paper texture. No lettering in any panel; only the cover carries the title. All images are 16:9. The full style line is pasted at the top of every prompt (see Story Characters, Places and House Style).

Palette. Panels 1 to 3 use the Bronze Age Crete palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster, olive green. Panels 4 to 10 use the modern Greece palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta, olive. Panel 10 shows both, split down the middle.

Creative liberties and uncertainties.

  • The storeroom date of about 1450 BCE is chosen so that a clay tablet can appear: the tablets we can read, in Linear B, date from about 1450 BCE onward at Knossos, and who ran the palace at that moment is still debated by scholars. The storekeeper and porters are invented, anonymous figures.
  • Minoan dress is drawn modestly (tunic, kilt, fitted bodice) rather than as in the famous frescoes.
  • The traveling potters of panel 4 belong to "the past" in the chapter's words; the exact period is left open, and the clothing is a generic Cretan village style of an earlier time.
  • The potter and apprentice are invented, anonymous composites. The traditional method (an apprentice turning a wheel while the potter shapes the jar) is drawn from how the craft is generally described. Our own visit saw freshly made pots drying in the shade, waiting for a kiln; panel 8, the firing, shows a step we did not witness.
  • Nothing here is a real brand or sign; the winery in panel 9 is drawn without any name or label.

Cast. Glaux the Little Owl hides in exactly one panel (panel 2): see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md (Glaux). The Travelers appear in panels 9 and 10 (see docs/stories/characters.md). The Knossos and giant-jar place block comes from docs/stories/characters.md. The following characters appear only in this story; their blocks are pasted verbatim into each prompt that shows them.

Minoan storekeeper and porters (panels 1 to 3):

Minoan palace storekeeper and porters, about 1450 BCE: a slim storekeeper with long curled black hair, a short patterned linen tunic and a wide embroidered belt, a small clay oil lamp in one hand and a clay tablet in the other; a porter in a plain kilt carrying a pointed clay jar on his shoulder; a woman porter in a long flounced banded skirt and fitted short-sleeved bodice, her hair in a thick braid, carrying a flat basket of barley.

The Thrapsano potter (panels 5 to 8, 10 and the cover):

The Thrapsano potter: a weathered Cretan man of about sixty-five with a thick gray mustache, a dark flat cap, a faded blue work shirt with rolled sleeves under a clay-stained canvas apron, and large hands gray with wet clay.

The potter's apprentice (panels 5 to 8, 10 and the cover):

The potter's apprentice: a lean young woman of about twenty with dark hair tied in a red kerchief, a gray work shirt with rolled sleeves and a clay-smeared apron; focused and patient.

A traveling team of Thrapsano potters from an earlier time (panel 4):

A traveling team of Thrapsano potters from an earlier time: four men in flat caps, dark waistcoats and baggy dark trousers, leading two mules loaded with a wooden wheel, wooden tools and wicker baskets.

docs.title: Prologue - A Jar Taller Than You
docs.text:
In the long storerooms of Knossos, behind the Throne Room, clay jars taller than a person still stand where they were found. They held the palace's wealth: olive oil, wine, grain. About 3,500 years later, in a hill village on the same island, potters still build jars that size by hand, one band of clay at a time. This story follows one shape across all those centuries, from a palace storeroom to a workshop we visited on an afternoon excursion. The craft has outlived every ruler in between.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

The air is cool, and it smells of oil and clay.

Porters bring the harvest in smaller, pointed jars and pour it through a funnel into the great ones. The giant jars held olive oil, wine, grain and pulses, and some carry raised bands of clay in a rope pattern, with rows of handles for lifting and tying on covers. Each jar is filled, covered and counted before the next one is opened.

Myth or Evidence? The raised bands and handles are documented on the jars themselves. That the bands imitate the ropes used to move the jars is a reasonable suggestion, not a certainty.

A jar of oil is wealth only if someone writes it down. The storekeeper presses a few signs and numbers into a damp clay tablet: the product, the amount, the place it came from. This is the palace economy, in which goods flow into a center and out again as rations, wages, gifts and offerings. The tablets we can read, written in Linear B, date from about 1450 BCE onward; they are bookkeeping, not literature.

In the past, teams of Thrapsano potters traveled the island through the summer. They set up temporary workshops wherever they found good clay and firewood, and they made jars for the villages around them. A village that needs a dozen big jars does not have to haul them up the mountain; the potters bring the workshop instead.

In the foreground a half-built jar, waist-high, sits on a low turntable; the potter lays a thick coil of wet gray clay around its rim and smooths the seam with his thumb, while the apprentice beside him holds a second soft coil across her forearms. The potter's apprentice: a lean young woman of about twenty with dark hair tied in a red kerchief, a gray work shirt with rolled sleeves and a clay-smeared apron; focused and patient. A very large jar cannot be made in one piece. The potter adds a band of clay, lets it stiffen, then adds the next, and the wall of the jar climbs a hand-width at a time. The Minoan potters worked in stages too, in coils or sections. In the workshop, the old rule is the same: patience first, height second.

The potter stands facing the jar with both wet hands cupped along its wall; the apprentice crouches at the wheel's edge and turns it steadily by hand, watching his hands. The potter's apprentice: a lean young woman of about twenty with dark hair tied in a red kerchief, a gray work shirt with rolled sleeves and a clay-smeared apron; focused and patient. In the traditional way of working, one person turns the wheel while the other shapes the wall, and the two have to trust each other. The apprentice's job is to keep the rhythm; the potter's job is to read the clay. Nobody writes the method down. It lives in the hands of whoever has done it a thousand times.

Rows of freshly made pots stand drying in the shade, still gray, waiting for the kiln that will turn them the orange of terracotta. This is what we saw on the day. The pots look finished and are not: a jar that dries too fast, or sits in a draft, can crack before it ever meets fire.

Fire turns clay into pottery, and at this size it takes real skill: the kiln must climb to a high heat slowly and hold it, and then cool slowly too. We saw pots waiting for the kiln, not a firing, so this panel shows the step we did not witness. Overnight the gray jars become terracotta orange, and by morning the potter knows which ones survived.

docs.title: Panel 9: The Wine and the Jar
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 09. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Setting: a village winery tasting room in the hills south of Heraklion, Crete, today, late autumn, soft afternoon light through a wooden doorway onto a stone floor. Camera: over-the-shoulder view from behind two visitors toward the host, who pours pale golden wine into a stemmed glass at a plain oak table. Cast: Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. Details: oak barrels along the back wall, unlabeled green bottles on a shelf, a plate of olives, bread and white cheese, bare grapevines glimpsed through the doorway with a few last yellow leaves, a string of dried red peppers. Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta, olive. Tone: warm, convivial, unhurried. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Before the potters, there is a glass of Cretan wine. Crete grows wine grapes found almost nowhere else, and the Minoans made wine here too: a Minoan country house at Vathypetro still has its stone wine press. Sitting with a glass a few hours after standing beside the palace jars, the morning's word "redistribution" suddenly makes sense. The wine was the wealth, and the jar was the bank.

docs.title: Panel 10: Then and Now
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 10. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image in the style above depicting panel 10 of 10, the "Then and Now" panel, as a split composition divided by one soft vertical band of golden light, no border lines or text. Left half, about 1450 BCE: the same Knossos storeroom as panel 1, same camera angle, looking down an aisle of giant jars. The Palace of Knossos on Crete: a sprawl of low, flat-roofed, honey-colored stone buildings around an open central court, with distinctive red-painted, downward-tapering wooden columns (wider at the top than the bottom) with black capitals, and colorful frescoes; storerooms hold giant human-tall clay jars (pithoi) with rope-like ridged bands. Right half, today: a Thrapsano workshop yard at the same low eye level, a freshly fired orange-terracotta jar of exactly the same shape and rope-pattern bands in the center, rows of gray unfired pots drying behind it. Cast: Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. They stand in the right half, small in the frame, looking at the jar. Palette: terracotta red, ochre, lapis blue, cream plaster on the left; natural daylight, whitewashed walls, terracotta, olive on the right. Tone: continuity across time, quiet wonder. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Same shape, about 3,500 years apart. Both jars are built in stages and fired at high heat. What changed is the job: the Minoan jar held a palace's oil and grain, the Cretan farmhouse jar held a family's wine and oil within living memory, and most big jars today hold flowers in a garden. The craft outlived every use it was invented for.

docs.title: Epilogue - What a Jar Remembers
docs.text:
A pithos is a small lesson in how knowledge survives. The palace that filled the Minoan jars fell, and the scribes' writing was lost for more than three thousand years. The jar-making did not fall, because it lived in the hands of families who passed it down, summer by summer. When the uses changed, the craft found new ones. Tablets, wheels and kilns come and go; the habit of making things well and teaching them to the next pair of hands is what lasts.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today A jar too large to make in one piece Build it in stages, letting each band of clay stiffen before the next Big results are often many small, patient steps Clay, firewood and customers scattered across the island Potters traveled in summer and built temporary workshops where the materials were Bring the skill to the people, not only the people to the skill Wealth that is easily lost or stolen The palace counted every jar on clay tablets Records turn stored goods into a system people can trust The old uses of the craft disappearing The same jar shape found a new life as garden pots A craft can outlive its original purpose

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: When you next pick up a bottle of olive oil, think of the jar it might once have lived in, then turn the bottle around and read the label: the harvest date and the origin tell you more than the picture on the front. The jar makers never needed a textbook, but they needed a teacher, and that is the Learning for All thread of this book: skills that stay open to whoever is willing to learn them. Try the Read the Olive Oil Label MicroSim, then ask a potter, a farmer or a cook near you how they learned what they know.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
No Minoan voice survives: the Minoans' own script, Linear A, has never been deciphered, and the Linear B tablets are accounts, not stories. Two ancient texts give the jar a voice instead.

  • Hesiod, an early Greek poet, tells in his Works and Days (about 700 BCE) how the first woman, Pandora, lifted the great lid of a pithos and let its troubles loose, leaving only hope inside. (Our paraphrase.) The "box" in the later phrase "Pandora's box" comes from a mistranslation made in the 16th century; the original vessel was a jar like these.
  • An ancient tradition, reported by the biographer Diogenes Laertius, says the philosopher Diogenes of Sinope lived in a large pithos in Athens. (An attributed tradition, not a quotation.)

docs.text:

A gap is newly broken in one bastion, crimson banners marked with a white eight-pointed cross still flying from the battlements, round stone cannonballs scattered in the moat, and a pale harbor with a line of galleys behind. In the foreground, A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He stands alone on the rampart looking toward the distant enemy camp of tents and red pennants. Across the top, render the story title as bold, hand-lettered title text in warm cream letters with a dark ink outline, reading exactly: "The Knights' Last Stand". Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Emotional tone: defiant and elegiac. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt **Era and place.** The island and city of Rhodes, in the Dodecanese off the southwest coast of Turkey: the arrival of the knights (1306-1310), the Street of the Knights and the walls rebuilt after 1480, the siege of June to December 1522, the departure of the knights on January 1, 1523, then the 1930s Italian rebuilding of the Palace of the Grand Master, and finally today. The story follows the chapter [Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights](../../chapters/12-rhodes/index.md). **Themes.** An order of monks who were also soldiers; walls built for cannon; a siege fought underground; an honorable surrender that both sides claimed as a victory; and the layers of the Old Town: the "medieval" palace is largely a 1930s Italian reconstruction. **House style.** Every prompt starts with the series house style line from [Story Characters, Places and House Style](../characters.md). All images are 16:9 with no lettering in the panels; only the cover carries the title. **Palette.** Medieval Rhodes: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Panels 5 and 7 (the sultan's camp and the tunnel mouths) use the Ottoman palette: Iznik turquoise, cobalt, tomato red, brass, saffron and white plaster. Panels 13 and 14 use natural daylight with sandstone and whitewash. **Safe imagery.** The siege is shown only by walls, smoke, the mouths of tunnels, cannonballs and banners, with no wounds, no bodies and no one mid-strike. Panel 10 shows the aftermath of the great assault of September 24. **Creative liberties and uncertainties.** The army's size is unknown; sources run from about 100,000 to 200,000 men, most of them laborers and support troops, and the story shows no numbers. The listening drum is told as "some say" in the chapter. Faces and ages of the Grand Master and sultan are artistic approximations. The Grand Master and the envoy in panel 11 are staged as a plausible moment, not a record. The 1856 explosion that wrecked the palace may have involved gunpowder stored "possibly since the siege of 1522"; this is hedged. **Cast.** Glaux the Little Owl and the Travelers follow [Story Characters, Places and House Style](../characters.md) and the [mascot character sheet](../../img/mascot/character-sheet.md); paste their blocks verbatim. Characters and places that appear only in this story are below; paste each block verbatim into every prompt where they appear. **The Grand Master (this story only)** 
Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam, Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes: a lean, weathered man of about fifty-eight with a long silvery-gray beard, a high forehead and deep-set, tired dark eyes, wearing a plain black monastic habit with a white eight-pointed cross on the chest, a steel breastplate over it and a long black mantle; dignified, resolute and exhausted.
**Sultan Suleiman (this story only)** 
Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1522: a slim man of about twenty-seven with dark eyes, a thin dark mustache and a short pointed beard, wearing a tall white turban with a small jeweled plume, a cobalt-blue silk caftan over a tomato-red robe and gold brocade; calm, young and watchful.
**A Knight Hospitaller (this story only)** 
A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined.
**Ottoman soldiers and miners (this story only)** 
Ottoman soldiers and laborers in 1522: infantrymen in tall white felt caps with a trailing back flap, dark-blue knee-length coats with red trim and sashes, and miners in plain brown tunics with cloth head wraps carrying baskets, picks and timber props.
**The Street of the Knights (this story only)** 
The Street of the Knights, Rhodes: a long, straight, narrow cobbled street climbing gently uphill between continuous two-story walls of honey-colored sandstone, with plain pointed-arch and rectangular doorways topped by carved stone coats of arms, small shuttered upper windows and plain flat buttresses; there are no shops, and at the top a large fortress-palace closes the view.
**The Palace of the Grand Master (this story only)** 
The Palace of the Grand Master, Rhodes: a large square fortress-palace of pale sandstone with massive round towers flanking its gate, a battlemented top, tall narrow windows and high plain outer walls, set on the high northwest corner of the walled town.
**The walls of Rhodes (this story only)** 
The walls of Rhodes: thick, low, sloped sandstone walls with rounded projecting bastions, battlements, a very wide dry moat below, a stone outer wall on the far side of the moat, and a gate tower reached by a bridge over the moat; the stone is honey-gold weathered to gray.

docs.title: Prologue - Six Months, Then a Handshake
docs.text:
In 1522 the Knights Hospitaller, a Catholic order that began as a hospital for pilgrims, hold the island of Rhodes against the Ottoman Empire. The young sultan Suleiman arrives with an enormous army, and for six months the knights and their Greek neighbors hold on behind the strongest walls in the Mediterranean. The ending surprises both sides: no massacre, but terms, a bow, and a fleet sailing out of the harbor. And the palace that visitors tour today? Mostly built by a government that did not exist when the knights left.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

docs.title: Panel 1: The Knights Arrive
docs.text:

Please make the images have a consistent style and consistent characters. Do not ask any clarifying questions. Just generate the image immediately when asked. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 1 of 14. Setting: the harbor of Rhodes, 1310 CE, hazy early morning. Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Wide view from the water up toward a hill crowned with a small Byzantine citadel above a Greek harbor town. A line of galleys with oars raised and crimson banners marked with a white cross arrives at a stone quay. In the foreground, A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He stands in the prow of the first galley beside a banner. Other details: Greek fishermen in small boats watching from the side, a ruined pier, a small domed church, gulls, dark cypress trees on the hill, calm blue water. Tone: uncertain arrival, a new home. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Between 1306 and 1310 the knights conquer Rhodes from the Byzantines. They are the Knights Hospitaller, officially the Order of the Hospital of St. John, a Catholic order that began as a hospital for pilgrims in Jerusalem and became a military order of knights who were also monks. They have lost every base they ever held in the Holy Land, and Rhodes, with its fine harbor, is now their own island state. On the hill above the town stands an old Byzantine citadel, which will one day become their palace.

docs.title: Panel 2: An Inn for Every Tongue
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 02. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image.
