Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Medium-wide shot of the street under construction. The Street of the Knights, Rhodes: a long, straight, narrow cobbled street climbing gently uphill between continuous two-story walls of honey-colored sandstone, with plain pointed-arch and rectangular doorways topped by carved stone coats of arms, small shuttered upper windows and plain flat buttresses; there are no shops, and at the top a large fortress-palace closes the view. It is still pale and new, with stonemasons carving shields in the stone above doorways, scaffolding against a wall, and a mule cart of cut blocks. A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He stands in the foreground talking with a master carver who holds a mallet and chisel. Other details: eight different colored banners hung from poles, each marking one inn, a Greek boy carrying a water jar, wood shavings on the cobbles, a cat on a windowsill, sun slanting down the street. Tone: confidence and community. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The knights come from all over Catholic Europe and are organized into national groups called langues, or tongues: by 1462 there are eight, among them Provence, Italy, Aragon and England. Each tongue has its own inn, an auberge, which serves as club, barracks and dining hall, and the inns line the street that climbs toward the palace. Look up and you see the carved coats of arms over the doors, because the knights signed their work. The town is divided: the northern part, the Collachium, is reserved for the knights, and the bigger southern part holds the Greeks, the Latin merchants and the Jewish community.

docs.title: Panel 3: Walls for the Age of Cannon
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 03. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 3 of 14. Setting: the land walls of Rhodes, about 1490 CE, hard bright light. Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Wide shot of masons building the walls. The walls of Rhodes: thick, low, sloped sandstone walls with rounded projecting bastions, battlements, a very wide dry moat below, a stone outer wall on the far side of the moat, and a gate tower reached by a bridge over the moat; the stone is honey-gold weathered to gray. They work on wooden scaffolds, laying massive sandstone blocks into a low, rounded, thick bastion beside an older tall square tower that looks thin and old by comparison. Laborers with baskets deepen and widen the dry moat. In the foreground, A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He and a master mason hold a small wooden model of a rounded bastion, seen in three-quarter view. Other details: wooden cranes, stacked round stone balls, banners of the tongues marking each stretch of the walls, cart tracks in the dust. Tone: sober preparation. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Cannon change everything. After surviving a siege in 1480 by the army of Mehmed II, the conqueror of Constantinople, the knights rebuild their walls. Tall, thin medieval walls shatter under cannon fire, so they make them lower and much thicker, and add rounded bastions that let defenders fire along the wall face. They deepen the dry moat as well, a killing ground between the outer and main walls. Each tongue defends its own stretch, so the defense is organized by nation, like the inns.

docs.text:

Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Wide shot over the shoulders of two defenders on the rampart. A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He and a Rhodian Greek militiaman in a brown tunic and cloth cap, both seen from behind, look out at hundreds of Ottoman ships with white sails and red pennants filling the blue sea to the horizon. On the beach boats unload troops and horses and a tent city begins to appear. Other details: smoke from signal fires on the hills, a flock of startled birds, a bronze cannon on the rampart, crimson banners stirring. Tone: dread and resolve. In late June 1522 an Ottoman fleet of perhaps 300 to 400 ships lands an army on the island. The size of the army is unknown, with estimates from about 100,000 to 200,000 men, most of them laborers and support troops. Against it the Grand Master, Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam, has about 600 to 700 knights and perhaps 6,000 or so other defenders: hired soldiers, Rhodian Greek militia and townspeople. Greeks fight on the walls beside the knights.

At the end of July the young Sultan Suleiman arrives to take command in person, two years into his reign. He is the Suleiman for whom Istanbul's Süleymaniye is named, and a mosque of his name will later stand inside these walls. Mehmed II failed to take Rhodes in 1480, and the young sultan means to finish the job. The siege will be fought with cannon and with shovels.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 06. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Wide shot of the walls under bombardment. The walls of Rhodes: thick, low, sloped sandstone walls with rounded projecting bastions, battlements, a very wide dry moat below, a stone outer wall on the far side of the moat, and a gate tower reached by a bridge over the moat; the stone is honey-gold weathered to gray. Clouds of white-gray smoke rise from distant rows of Ottoman cannon, round stone balls lie scattered at the foot of the bastions, a corner of the parapet is chipped and crumbling, and dust hangs in the air. In the foreground, A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He crouches behind a wall of earth-filled wicker baskets next to townswomen carrying stones in baskets. Other details: crimson banners still flying, a shattered battlement, a sunbeam through the smoke, rubble in the moat, a bucket of water. Tone: heavy, relentless. Nobody is injured and nobody is mid-strike. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The Ottomans bombard the walls with heavy cannon, but at first they do not try to climb them. The thick, low walls absorb much of the shot, and defenders, including women who carry stones and supplies, repair the damage. Round stone balls like these still lie in the grass of the moat today. The worst is still to come, and it comes from below.

docs.text:

Palette: Iznik turquoise, cobalt, tomato red, brass, saffron and white plaster. Medium-wide shot of three dark, timber-framed tunnel mouths opening in a long earthen mound, with spoil heaps of fresh pale earth beside them. Ottoman soldiers and laborers in 1522: infantrymen in tall white felt caps with a trailing back flap, dark-blue knee-length coats with red trim and sashes, and miners in plain brown tunics with cloth head wraps carrying baskets, picks and timber props. The miners carry baskets of soil and wooden props toward the openings. Beyond, the gray wall with a thin plume of smoke rises. Other details: coils of rope, oil lanterns, sacks, a mule with a timber load, a crow on a post, a line of stakes. Tone: patient menace. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Teams of Ottoman miners tunnel under the walls to blow them up with gunpowder, and the diggers' work shows only as dark mouths in the earth and growing heaps of spoil. A single mine, packed with powder, can bring down a section of wall in a moment. The defenders cannot see the miners, only the evidence they leave behind. To stop them, they must hear them.

docs.title: Panel 8: Listening
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 08. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Low close shot. A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He kneels with his ear near the floor beside a small parchment-skinned drum set on the stones, its skin trembling with fine dust dancing on it. Two defenders behind him hold lanterns. Other details: rough sandstone blocks, shoring beams, a rack of picks and shovels. Glaux the Little Owl: a true little owl (Athene noctua), small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts, warm earth-brown plumage with cream spots, bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream eyebrows, a cream-white throat patch and a short pale greenish-yellow beak. Glaux wears a small Aegean-blue scarf and a tan canvas satchel across the body with a small leather-bound travel notebook peeking out, and a sprig of three olive leaves tucked into the satchel strap. Alert, curious and warm expression. Glaux is perched on a wooden shoring beam in the upper right. Glaux is drawn small, perched at the edge of the scene, noticeable on a second look. The defenders listen for the digging, some say with drums whose skins tremble at the vibrations, and they dig their own tunnels to meet the enemy's.

Myth or Evidence? That the Ottomans mined under the walls and that the defenders dug countermines is documented. The trembling drum is a vivid detail some tellings add; the chapter marks it as "some say."

docs.title: Panel 9: Where the Tunnels Meet
docs.text:

Wide low view down a rough-hewn tunnel supported by timber props, a torch in an iron bracket on the wall, and at the far end a small ragged opening where a second tunnel meets it, with warm orange light and drifting dust on the other side. He and a Greek militiaman crouch, picks held down at their sides, listening. Other details: chisel marks on the stone, a bucket of earth, coils of rope, a wooden prop cracking, thin smoke along the ceiling. Tone: claustrophobic, tense. Nobody is fighting. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Underground, the siege becomes a game of nerves. When a countermine meets an enemy tunnel, the two sides are suddenly face to face in the dark, with only flickering torchlight between them. A tunnel found in time is a wall saved, and a tunnel found too late is a breach. We cannot know how many such meetings there were, only that the sources describe a war underneath the war.

Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Wide shot of the walls. The walls of Rhodes: thick, low, sloped sandstone walls with rounded projecting bastions, battlements, a very wide dry moat below, a stone outer wall on the far side of the moat, and a gate tower reached by a bridge over the moat; the stone is honey-gold weathered to gray. A broad gap in one bastion is piled with rubble, thick smoke drifting past, dozens of abandoned scaling ladders and wicker shields scattered on the slope below, and the order's crimson banners still flying from the top. In the foreground, A Knight Hospitaller: a man in a black monastic habit marked with a white eight-pointed cross, over which he wears a bright crimson surcoat in battle, with a steel helmet carried under one arm and a longsword resting in its scabbard; determined and disciplined. He sits wearily on a stone with his helmet in his hands while a Greek militiaman hands him a water flask; two townswomen carry stones in baskets behind them. Far below, Ottoman tents glow orange in the sunset. Other details: broken battlements, an overturned cart, long shadows. Tone: exhausted survival. No bodies. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Assaults through the breaches in September culminate in a great general assault on September 24, and the defenders throw it back with heavy losses on both sides. The picture shows only the aftermath: smoke, abandoned ladders, and banners still flying. But no help comes from Christian Europe, and food and gunpowder run low. The walls have bought time, and time is not rescue.

Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Medium shot. Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam, Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes: a lean, weathered man of about fifty-eight with a long silvery-gray beard, a high forehead and deep-set, tired dark eyes, wearing a plain black monastic habit with a white eight-pointed cross on the chest, a steel breastplate over it and a long black mantle; dignified, resolute and exhausted. He sits at a long table reading a folded document with a red wax seal, with a cold brazier, a burned-down candle and a map of the island on the table. An Ottoman envoy in a white turban and teal robe stands before him in side view, hands folded. Two knights stand behind the Grand Master, heads bowed. Other details: through a tall window a view of broken battlements, cracked stone, an inkpot, a bare stone floor. Tone: sorrow and dignity. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

By December the walls are broken in many places, and on December 20 the Grand Master accepts Suleiman's terms. A city taken by storm in this age can expect to be sacked, its people killed or enslaved. Rhodes instead surrenders on terms: the knights may leave with their arms, relics and honor, inhabitants who wish may leave with them, and those who stay keep their faith and their churches. Both sides can tell the story as a victory, and both do.

On January 1, 1523 the knights sail out with several thousand Rhodians. After seven years of wandering they receive Malta, where in 1565 they withstand another great Ottoman siege. For Suleiman, the terms end a siege that cost him dearly and give him the island intact. The Order of St. John still exists, as a medical and relief charity, more than nine centuries after it began.

docs.title: Panel 13: The Palace the Italians Built
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 13. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Wide shot of the palace under heavy timber scaffolding. The Palace of the Grand Master, Rhodes: a large square fortress-palace of pale sandstone with massive round towers flanking its gate, a battlemented top, tall narrow windows and high plain outer walls, set on the high northwest corner of the walled town. It is half still in rubble stumps and half already rebuilt in pale freshly cut stone, with masons and laborers in 1930s work caps, trousers and waistcoats on the scaffolds. In the foreground two men in light suits and hats, seen from behind, study large blueprints held open against the wind. Other details: carts with pale stone blocks, a hoist, crates of mosaic panels waiting to be installed, a clear sky, a whitewashed wall. Tone: ambition, a stage being set. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The palace that visitors tour is mostly not medieval. In 1856, under Ottoman rule, lightning struck the nearby Church of St. John and ignited gunpowder stored in its vaults, possibly since the siege of 1522, and the explosion wrecked much of the palace. The Italian governor had it rebuilt from 1937 to 1940, intended as a residence for the king of Italy and for Mussolini, and filled it with Hellenistic and early Christian mosaics brought from the island of Kos. It is a good museum, but it is an Italian reconstruction of the 1930s on medieval foundations.

docs.text:

Palette: natural daylight, honey sandstone, whitewash and Mediterranean blue. Wide shot looking uphill along the street toward the palace at the top, with long soft shadows and empty cobbles. The Street of the Knights, Rhodes: a long, straight, narrow cobbled street climbing gently uphill between continuous two-story walls of honey-colored sandstone, with plain pointed-arch and rectangular doorways topped by carved stone coats of arms, small shuttered upper windows and plain flat buttresses; there are no shops, and at the top a large fortress-palace closes the view. The Palace of the Grand Master, Rhodes: a large square fortress-palace of pale sandstone with massive round towers flanking its gate, a battlemented top, tall narrow windows and high plain outer walls, set on the high northwest corner of the walled town. In the middle distance: Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. Other details: carved coats of arms over the doors, a green tree leaning over a wall, shuttered windows, wooden doors painted blue, a cat on a step, pale blue sky. Early on a November morning, before the groups arrive, the Street of the Knights is quiet enough to hear our own footsteps. It is medieval in plan and largely medieval in stone, with careful modern repairs; the palace at the top, in contrast, is mostly a 1930s rebuilding. Look up at the coats of arms and ask which shield belongs to which Grand Master, and which layer built what we see.

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Walls Show
docs.text:
The knights held Rhodes for 212 years, then lost it after a six-month siege, and both sides could call the ending a win. What the story shows is how much of a "medieval" place is a later layer: Ottoman mosques, Italian restoration, and an Italian-built palace on the knights' foundations. Walls buy time, not victory, and a fortress is a promise that someone outside will come.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today A new weapon: cannon The knights made the walls lower, thicker and rounded, with a wider moat Defenders must adapt to new technology A siege fought underground Defenders listened for tunnels and dug their own Quiet, careful work can matter as much as bravery No help from Europe After six months, the Grand Master accepted terms Even the best defense needs someone coming to help A palace that burned and was rebuilt The Italian government rebuilt it in 1937-1940 Check the date on what is labeled medieval

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: On the Street of the Knights, read the coats of arms like date stamps, then walk down into the dry moat and find the round stone balls in the grass. At the palace, ask who built what you are standing in. The habit of asking which layer is original is the same habit that serves a learner anywhere, which is what Learning for All is about: a good question is available to everyone who walks through the gate.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• "Our lords the sick." The Hospitallers' rule required that the sick be treated as "our lords," and knights took turns serving in the wards of their hospital. This is documented in the order's rule and is why the building at the foot of the Street of the Knights is called a hospital.
  • Tuitio fidei et obsequium pauperum. The order's modern Latin motto, "defense of the faith and assistance to the poor." It is a motto the order uses today, not a quotation from the siege.
  • No words of Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam or Suleiman from December 1522 are quoted here, because the surviving reports are retellings made later and we cannot be sure of the exact words.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:
• Chapter: 12. Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
  • Where to look: the coats of arms over the inn doors on the Street of the Knights; the dry moat and the round stone balls in its grass; the d'Amboise Gate with its bridge; the Palace of the Grand Master, and the Hospital of the Knights (now the Archaeological Museum).
  • Explore further: Who Built What We See in the Old Town? and Rhodes Changes Hands, 1912-1948.
  • Look Closer: "Look closer at the carved shields over the doors, and ask which Grand Master put each one there." Glaux hid in panel 8, perched on a wooden shoring beam in the cellar where the knight listens.

docs.title: Prologue - A Gift That Is Also a Grave
docs.text:
Most families remember their dead with a statue or a carved stone. In about 110 CE a man in Ephesus, on the western coast of today's Turkey, chose something stranger: a public library, with his father's marble coffin waiting in a chamber below the reading room. Today the front of that building is the most photographed sight in the city. This is the story of why it was built, what happened to the sea that once lapped at the city, and how a ruin was put back together.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

About 110 CE, a funeral crosses the marble square at the foot of Curetes Street in Ephesus. The man on the bier is Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, a Greek from Sardis who rose to become a Roman consul in 92 CE, one of the first men from the Greek East to reach that rank, and later governor of the province of Asia. His son, Tiberius Julius Aquila, walks at the head of the mourners. Behind them lies only a cleared slope and a few stacked blocks, though not for long.

After the mourners leave, the study is quiet, and the chair at the desk is empty. A man of Celsus's rank might have been remembered with a statue or a grand tomb, and Aquila has the money for either. Historians cannot know what he felt, but the choice he made is written in stone: a monument that would keep working after its owner was gone, a public library.

Aquila begins the building around 110 CE and, the chapter tells us, leaves money in his will to finish it and to buy books. The inscription on the building records the sum: 25,000 denarii, enough to pay a Roman soldier for many decades. The architect here is imagined, since the chapter gives no name, but the plans, the pen and the silver are what such a project needed. A private grief is about to become public property.

The library goes up in marble: two stories of paired columns topped with richly carved Corinthian capitals, the leafy style Romans loved. The builders play a clever trick. The restorers later found that the columns and spaces near the center are slightly larger than those at the ends, and the lower columns stand on a podium, so the front looks taller and grander than its modest width. Aquila's heirs finish the job, because he does not live to see it complete.

Four statues stand in the niches of the lower story, each labeled in Greek with a virtue: Sophia (Wisdom), Aretē (Excellence), Ennoia (Thought) and Epistēmē (Knowledge). Statue bases on the steps carry texts in both Greek and Latin naming Celsus and his career, the bilingual voice of a Roman official in a Greek city. The statues a visitor sees today are copies, and the originals are in Vienna. The poses in the picture are imagined.

docs.title: Panel 6: Twelve Thousand Scrolls

Inside, the reading room is a single hall with niches in its walls for wooden cupboards that hold the scrolls. A reader asks the librarian for one, reads it on the spot and gives it back. In the ancient world a book is a hand-copied scroll, so a private library of thousands is a mark of great wealth, and here any Ephesian who can read can walk in.

Myth or Evidence? The usual figure of about 12,000 scrolls is a modern estimate from the size and number of the wall niches, not a number from an ancient source. It gives a fair sense of scale, nothing more.

Below the reading room, in a chamber of its own, lies the reason for the whole building. Celsus is buried in a marble sarcophagus there, a rare honor, since Romans did not normally bury the dead inside a city. The library is both a public library and a tomb, so every reader who comes to study walks over the governor's resting place. We can imagine Aquila standing here in the quiet, but the scene is a reconstruction, not a record.

Wide view of a large marble room with long benches along three sides, each bench with a row of keyhole-shaped openings, and a sunny open courtyard in the center with potted shrubs and a small fountain; a shallow channel of clean running water along the floor in front of the benches. A few steps from the library, the city's other kind of public space does a different job. In the public latrines beside the Baths of Scholastikia, built about the end of the 1st century CE, users pay a fee and sit side by side on marble benches, with water running continuously in a channel beneath. There are no partitions, and a visit is as social as a trip to the baths, so business deals and gossip pass from bench to bench.

Myth or Evidence? Guides often say wealthy citizens sent slaves ahead to warm the cold marble seats. We know of no ancient source for this: it looks like a modern joke that hardened into fact. The sponge-on-a-stick story has a few ancient references behind it, but how widely it was used is debated.

Up the street, wealthy families live in the terrace houses, and their walls tell us what they valued. In one house, excavators found a painted portrait of a bald, bearded man with his name written beside him in Greek: Sokrates. More than four centuries after Socrates died in Athens, the owner wanted the philosopher on the wall where guests would see him. The label also suggests that the owner and his guests could read it, or wanted to be seen as people who could.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 10. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Palette: sea-green turning to mud brown, warm limestone, bronze and evening gold. High bird's-eye shot over the colonnaded Harbor Street running toward the water: the harbor basin is shrinking, with brown silt plumes from a river clouding the blue-green water, mudbanks and reeds along the edges, and a merchant ship stuck at an angle on a sandbar. Dredging crews in shallow flat boats and on the shore pile mud into baskets and carry it away in lines. Other details: a long row of columns lining the street, a pale stone breakwater at the harbor mouth, gulls over the mudflats, a small ship waiting for deeper water. Tone: slow, inevitable loss. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The trouble with the harbor is already old when Aquila builds. The river we now call the Küçük Menderes carries mud down from the hills every winter and drops it where the current slows, so the coastline creeps west while the city chases it. The geographer Strabo, writing around the time of Jesus, says engineers narrowed the harbor mouth with a breakwater, hoping to deepen it, and trapped the silt inside instead. The Romans dredge again and again, but the silt wins.

The Library of Celsus at Ephesus: a two-story façade of warm cream limestone and marble, with paired Corinthian columns on both levels, a broad flight of steps leading up to three tall doorways, four niches between the lower columns holding draped female statues, three windows on the upper story, and gently curved and triangular pediments crowning the front; the building stands hard against a green hillside. It is shown ruined: the tall back wall still stands with empty niches, the front columns lie toppled with their carved capitals half buried in grass, and the stone is blackened by old fire. In the foreground a young shepherd seen from behind leans on a staff while a few goats graze among the fallen column drums. Other details: wildflowers among the blocks, a headless statue lying on its side, a cloud of mist over a marsh beyond where the sea once was, a small walled hill town on a far hill. The library burns in the 3rd century CE, and an earthquake later brings down the façade. The city shrinks, the sea draws away, and by the late Byzantine period the old harbor is a marsh and the people of Ephesus have moved up to the hill of Ayasuluk, where Selçuk stands today. The great marble front lies in pieces among the grass, with goats grazing where readers once climbed the steps. A library that outlived its owner has outlived its city as well.

Between 1970 and 1978, Austrian archaeologists re-erect the façade from its fallen pieces, one of the great reconstructions of the 20th century. Today we stand where Aquila stood and look up at the same four niches, though the statues in them are copies and the originals sit in Vienna. The sea is still out of sight. The library has returned, and so has a question the building asks of every visitor: how much of what we see is old, and how much is put back?

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Library Shows
docs.text:
A son's grief became a gift to a whole city, and the gift outlived the donor, the harbor and nearly the building. The library worked as a reading room for readers who could never have afforded the scrolls, and its endowment of 25,000 denarii shows how seriously Aquila took the job of keeping it going. Yet the story is also honest about limits: a library only helps those who can read and can reach the door, and in Roman Ephesus most people probably could not read at all.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: Standing in the square below the library, count the niches, find the copies of the four virtues, and then turn around and try to picture the sea. A gift of knowledge reaches only as far as the means to use it: literacy and the walk to the reading room then, a device, a connection and a reading level now, which is the question the companion textbook AI-Native Schools asks. Ask who is still outside the door.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• Sophia, Aretē, Ennoia, Epistēmē. The four Greek labels (Wisdom, Excellence, Thought, Knowledge) that identified the statues in the façade niches. This is documented: they are the actual words attached to the statues.
  • "The things to be seen." The Greek word theamata gave us the list we call the Seven Wonders, which began as a sightseer's list. In the 2nd century BCE the poet Antipater of Sidon wrote that after seeing the other wonders, he found the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus put them in the shade (paraphrased; this is the poet's judgment, as the chapter reports it).
  • Strabo on the harbor. The geographer reports that engineers narrowed the harbor mouth to deepen it and instead trapped silt inside. This is a paraphrase of the chapter's account, not a direct quotation. No words of Celsus or Aquila survive in our sources, so none are invented here.

Behind them, filling the sky: The Acropolis of Athens: a steep, flat-topped, pale limestone rock rising above the city, crowned by the Parthenon, a long Doric temple of honey-colored marble with eight columns across the front, a low triangular pediment and a long carved frieze under the roof; to its left stands the smaller Erechtheion with its porch of six marble maidens. Narrative Prompt **Era and place.** The Agora and Pnyx of Athens, and the sanctuary at Delphi in one flashback, spanning the 470s BCE to 399 BCE. The last panel is modern. **Theme.** A democracy that governed itself in person, picking officials by lot and voting exile on pieces of broken pottery, and the philosopher who treated every answer as the beginning of a question. The story shows how Athenian democracy worked, what the evidence of ready-made ostraka suggests about who could write, why an oracle's answer sent Socrates into the marketplace, and how a frightened city, just out of war and tyranny, put him on trial. **Series house style.** Hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded fills and faint watercolor paper texture. No lettering inside any panel; only the cover carries the title. All images are 16:9. **Story palette.** Classical Greece: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. The modern final panel uses natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive. **Restraint rule.** The trial and the hemlock are shown by symbols and aftermath only: a crowded court seen from a distance, bronze ballots, a cup on a table, an empty chair, friends seen from behind, lamplight. No death, body, struggle or poison scene is ever drawn. **Creative liberties and uncertainties.** - The chapter says the jury was about 500 citizens; the story follows the chapter. The count of 280 to 220 is an inference from Plato's report that a swing of 30 votes would have acquitted him. - The three examples (a politician, poets and craftsmen) come from Socrates' own account in Plato's *Apology*. The politician, the poet and the craftsman are unnamed composites and look the way the illustrator imagines them. - Chaerephon is a historical person, but nobody recorded how he looked. His drawn appearance is invented. Plato's Socrates calls him impulsive and says he had died before the trial. - What the Pythia said to Chaerephon differs in each ancient source (Plato, Xenophon, and a late verse quoted by Diogenes Laertius); the story follows Plato. - The "Prison of Socrates" shown to visitors on Philopappos Hill is a modern tradition with no ancient evidence, so the final scenes show an unspecified room; the chapter notes that a building at the Agora's southwest corner is a possible candidate. - Panels span different years: Pericles appears in the 440s BCE, Themistocles in the 470s BCE, and Socrates in the 410s to 399 BCE. docs.title: Prologue - The Marketplace That Ran a Government
docs.text:
In Athens the marketplace was also the government's office block, the courthouse and the town newspaper. Citizens picked officials by raffle, voted exile on broken pottery, and listened to speakers timed by dripping water. In this crowded square a short, barefoot man with a flat nose stopped anyone who looked wise and asked them what they meant. An oracle had told his friend that no one was wiser than he, and he set out to prove the god wrong, a project that took the rest of his life.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

On a morning in the 430s BCE the Athenian Agora wakes up as shop, courthouse and government office at once. Along the west side stand the offices of the democracy: the archive, the council hall, the round dining hall of the councillors on duty. The public notices go up on the long monument of the ten tribal heroes, so this is where an Athenian reads the news. In the shade of a stoa, a short man in a worn cloak is already talking to anyone who sits down.

docs.text:

Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. At left stands a tall rectangular stone slab pierced by rows of narrow slots (an allotment machine, the kleroterion) with a tube running down one side; a magistrate in a white himation drops black and white balls down the tube, and each ball decides whether a whole row of men will serve today. In front of it, a crowd of citizens in cloaks hold small bronze identity tickets, some pushing them into the slots, some waiting anxiously, a few looking disappointed as they are sent home. In the right background, striding past without waiting because he is an elected general rather than chosen by lot, is this man: Pericles, Athenian leader: a dignified man of about fifty-five with an unusually tall, long head, usually shown wearing a crested bronze helmet pushed back on his head, a trimmed gray-brown beard and a calm, commanding expression, dressed in a white himation with a dark-blue border draped over a cream chiton. Visible details: a bronze ticket flashing in the sun; a clerk holding a wax tablet with no writing; a boy selling figs; an old man laughing at his own bad luck; two councilmen carrying cushions; the Stoa's shaded colonnade behind. Tone: tense, comic, and fair. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The Athenians did not trust elections. A stone slab with rows of slots, the kleroterion, picked jurors and council members at random: each man pushed his bronze identity ticket into a slot, and black and white balls dropped down a tube settled whole rows of men at a time. Voting favored the rich, the famous and the good speakers, so the lot gave every citizen the same chance. The main exception was the ten generals, who were elected because war needed skill, and that is how Pericles could be chosen year after year.

In the center a citizen speaker in a white himation stands on a low stone platform, one hand raised, addressing rows of seated jurors on wooden benches. On a stand beside him sits a water clock: two clay pots, the upper one trickling a thin thread of water into the lower, watched by a court official with a staff. Visible details: two bronze ballot discs, one hollow-axled and one solid, in the palm of a juror; a tall urn waiting for ballots; an official with a wooden staff; a juror shading his eyes with his hand; a water jug passed along a bench; sunlight through the awning. Glaux the Little Owl: a true little owl (Athene noctua), small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts, warm earth-brown plumage with cream spots, bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream eyebrows, a cream-white throat patch and a short pale greenish-yellow beak. Glaux wears a small Aegean-blue scarf and a tan canvas satchel across the body with a small leather-bound travel notebook peeking out, and a sprig of three olive leaves tucked into the satchel strap. Alert, curious and warm expression. Glaux is drawn small, perched at the edge of the scene, noticeable on a second look: perched on the wooden fence rail near the water clock. Only one owl appears in this image. Tone: orderly, tense, fair. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Courts needed discipline, and the Athenians solved it with water. A water clock, two clay pots where water ran from one to the other, timed each speaker, about six minutes per filling. Juries of hundreds were chosen by lot on the morning of the trial and decided cases by secret ballot, using small bronze discs: a hollow-axled one for guilty, a solid one for not guilty. These are the things in the museum in the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos that turn the bare foundations of the Agora back into a working government.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 04. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. A crowd of citizens crouches and squats on the ground in small groups, each man scratching a few marks (unreadable scribbles) with a nail or stylus onto a broken piece of pottery, an ostrakon. At right, officials in white himations stand at wooden barriers beside tall heaps of sherds, sorting them into piles by hand. A broken amphora lies shattered at the edge as the source of more ballots. In the background stands a man at the edge of the crowd, mid-gesture, confident and unaware: Themistocles, Athenian statesman and admiral: a stocky, energetic man of about forty-five with a short dark curly beard, sharp dark eyes and a weathered, tanned face, wearing a plain cream chiton and a rust-brown himation draped over one shoulder, a bronze signet ring on his right hand; confident, restless, always mid-gesture. Visible details: potsherds stacked into a tall neat pile; a boy carrying a basket of shards; an old man peering at his shard with a squint; a stoa with long shadows; a goat nosing at a sherd; sweating officials. Tone: expectant, a little ominous, with the casual cruelty of a crowd. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Once a year the Assembly could vote on whether to hold an ostracism, a way of sending a leading politician into exile for ten years without a trial or any crime being charged. If it said yes, citizens gathered in the Agora weeks later and each scratched a name on an ostrakon, a broken piece of pottery, the scrap paper of the ancient world. If at least 6,000 votes were cast, the man with the most had ten days to leave Athens; he kept his property and his citizenship and could return after ten years. Themistocles, the victor of Salamis, was ostracized in the 470s BCE.

Myth or Evidence? Plutarch, writing about 600 years later, tells a story about the exile of Aristides, nicknamed "the Just": an illiterate countryman who did not recognize him asked him to write "Aristides" on a potsherd, because he was tired of hearing him called "the Just." Aristides wrote his own name. A story that late is a story. The ostraka themselves, however, are real evidence.

Palette: marble white, olive green, honey gold, bronze, dusk blue. In the foreground, seen from behind, a shrewd man in a plain hooded cloak holds a basket of broken-pottery shards, each marked with the same neat row of scratched lines (a pattern of strokes, not readable letters), and hands one to an older farmer in a patched tunic who stands blinking at it, unable to read. Behind them two more men hold identical shards and look around uneasily. Visible details: a farmer's calloused thumb and forefinger holding the sherd; a leather pouch on the hooded man's belt; another man waiting in line with his hands behind his back; broken pottery heaps in the distance; the long shadow of a plane tree; a sparrow on the ground. Tone: furtive, quietly troubling, a little sad. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

In a well on the north slope of the Acropolis, archaeologists found about 190 ostraka with the name of Themistocles, written by only a few different hands: ready-made ballots, apparently prepared for voters and never used. Two things follow. Someone was organizing a campaign against him, and some voters needed a ballot already written, because they could not write the name themselves. A democracy that voted in writing quietly assumed a literacy that not every citizen had.

In the middle distance, climbing the paved path with a white goat on a rope and a small honey cake in a cloth, an eager traveler: Chaerephon, Socrates' devoted friend: a lean, restless man of about forty with untidy dark curly hair, a short scruffy beard and quick, eager eyes, wearing a plain cream chiton and a faded blue-gray traveling cloak, dusty sandals and a straw hat hanging by its cord down his back; impatient and impulsive, always half-leaning forward. Behind him spreads the setting: Delphi, the sanctuary of Apollo: a steep rocky terrace on the slope of Mount Parnassus with a paved winding Sacred Way lined with small treasuries and statues, leading up to the large Doric Temple of Apollo with six columns across the front; behind it steep gray limestone cliffs, below it a deep valley of silver-green olive trees stretching to a distant sea. Socrates' friend Chaerephon, a man Plato's Socrates calls impulsive in everything he did, makes the long journey to Delphi. His question is simple and brash: is anyone wiser than Socrates? We know of this only because Socrates himself told it, years later, in his defense speech at his trial, as his student Plato wrote it down in the Apology. By then, Socrates says, Chaerephon was dead.

Interior medium shot, slightly low angle, the lamp-lit inner chamber of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, about 430 BCE, golden lamplight and deep shadow. Palette: marble white, bronze, honey gold, olive green, shadow blue. In the center, calm and still, seated on a tall bronze three-legged tripod, speaking: The Pythia, Apollo's priestess at Delphi: a dignified woman of about fifty with gray-streaked dark hair under a simple white veil, wearing a plain long white linen gown with a wreath of laurel leaves in her hair, holding a laurel branch in one hand and a shallow bronze offering bowl in the other. Her expression is calm, inward and serious. In the foreground, seen from behind, kneels this man: Chaerephon, Socrates' devoted friend: a lean, restless man of about forty with untidy dark curly hair, a short scruffy beard and quick, eager eyes, wearing a plain cream chiton and a faded blue-gray traveling cloak, dusty sandals and a straw hat hanging by its cord down his back; impatient and impulsive, always half-leaning forward. The setting is Delphi: Delphi, the sanctuary of Apollo: a steep rocky terrace on the slope of Mount Parnassus with a paved winding Sacred Way lined with small treasuries and statues, leading up to the large Doric Temple of Apollo with six columns across the front; behind it steep gray limestone cliffs, below it a deep valley of silver-green olive trees stretching to a distant sea. (Show it only as a pale bright doorway at the far end.) Visible details: a white-robed prophet standing at the tripod's side with his palm raised; a lit bronze hearth with a thread of smoke; a laurel wreath on the floor; a small honey cake on a bronze plate; Chaerephon's clasped hands; lamplight glinting on the tripod legs. Tone: hushed, solemn, expectant. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The Pythia answers that no one is wiser. In Plato's account, that is the whole of it. Notice what kind of answer it is: not a prediction, but a claim that could be tested.

Myth or Evidence? The three ancient sources disagree. Plato says the god said no one was wiser; Xenophon says no one was more free, more just or more sensible; a late verse quoted by Diogenes Laertius, about 600 years later and widely thought to be an invention, says Sophocles is wise, Euripides wiser, and Socrates wisest of all. Some scholars have wondered whether the whole episode is Plato's literary device. Most accept that Chaerephon asked something and got a flattering answer.

Medium shot in the shaded colonnade of the Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios in the Agora of Athens, about 428 BCE, mid-afternoon, with warm light slanting between the columns. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. At left, caught mid-sentence with arms spread wide, still dusty from the road: Chaerephon, Socrates' devoted friend: a lean, restless man of about forty with untidy dark curly hair, a short scruffy beard and quick, eager eyes, wearing a plain cream chiton and a faded blue-gray traveling cloak, dusty sandals and a straw hat hanging by its cord down his back; impatient and impulsive, always half-leaning forward. At right, sitting on the stone step with a hand scratching his bald head and a puzzled, amused frown, listening: Socrates, Athenian philosopher: a short, stocky man of about sixty with a bald, broad forehead, a wide flat nose, a thick gray beard and bright, amused eyes, barefoot, wearing a plain, worn, undyed wool himation and no jewelry; a curious, teasing expression. Visible details: two young men sitting cross-legged, leaning in; a shopkeeper peeking out between columns; a stray dog asleep in the sun; a clay cup of water at Socrates' feet; the colonnade's long shadows; pigeons on the roof tiles; the Acropolis blurred in the distance. Tone: amused, puzzled, the moment a mission begins. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The answer puzzles Socrates, he says, because he knows that he is not wise. So he does what he does best: he sets out to prove the god wrong. He will find someone who is wiser, and the quickest way to find one is to ask the people with the best reputations for knowing things. The stoa of Zeus the Freedom-Giver, which ancient writers name as a favorite spot for his conversations, becomes the headquarters of an investigation that will last the rest of his life.

At left, offering a patient, teasing look with one finger raised in a question, stands: Socrates, Athenian philosopher: a short, stocky man of about sixty with a bald, broad forehead, a wide flat nose, a thick gray beard and bright, amused eyes, barefoot, wearing a plain, worn, undyed wool himation and no jewelry; a curious, teasing expression. At right, stiff and increasingly uncomfortable, stands: A prominent Athenian politician (an unnamed composite): a handsome, self-assured man of about fifty with a carefully curled gray beard, wearing an expensive white himation with a purple border and a gold ring, carrying a polished walking stick, chest out and chin raised, flanked by two admiring young followers. Visible details: the politician's chin lowering by a fraction; his walking stick tapping the ground; a ring flashing in the sun; one follower smothering a smile behind his hand; a baker's stall in the background; a crowd of curious onlookers gathering at the margins; a bronze statue of a hero on its base in the middle distance. First comes a politician with a great reputation for wisdom. Socrates questions him, and in Plato's account the great man's answers fall apart under the next question. Socrates concludes that the man thinks he knows things that he does not, and is not even aware of it. The politician walks away offended, and the onlookers are delighted.

At left, mid-recitation, eyes half closed, one hand dramatically raised, stands: An Athenian poet (an unnamed composite): a dreamy man of about forty with long curly hair bound by a thin ribbon and a short beard, wearing a saffron-yellow chiton and a light-blue himation, holding a papyrus scroll in one hand and gesturing grandly with the other, eyes half closed. At right, head tilted and a faint smile on his face, leaning in with a curious question, is: Socrates, Athenian philosopher: a short, stocky man of about sixty with a bald, broad forehead, a wide flat nose, a thick gray beard and bright, amused eyes, barefoot, wearing a plain, worn, undyed wool himation and no jewelry; a curious, teasing expression. Next come the poets. Socrates reads their finest lines and asks them to explain what they mean, and finds that they cannot. They have written beautiful things, but they speak, Plato's Socrates says, rather like prophets who say fine words without understanding them. As in the first case, they think their talent in verse makes them wise about everything else.

Standing at center, proud, holding up a coin in the light: An Athenian coin-maker (an unnamed composite): a sturdy, soot-smudged man of about fifty with short gray hair and thick forearms, wearing a leather apron over a short rust-brown tunic, holding small iron tongs in one hand and a freshly struck silver coin in the other; proud, steady and open-faced. The coin he holds up is this object: An ancient Athenian silver tetradrachm coin: a thick round silver coin showing the head of Athena in a crested helmet on one side and, on the other, a standing little owl beside an olive sprig and a crescent moon, with a rough, hand-struck edge. In the doorway, leaning on the frame with his head cocked, listening: Socrates, Athenian philosopher: a short, stocky man of about sixty with a bald, broad forehead, a wide flat nose, a thick gray beard and bright, amused eyes, barefoot, wearing a plain, worn, undyed wool himation and no jewelry; a curious, teasing expression. Visible details: a small anvil and stamping die on a workbench; a tray of blank silver discs; glowing coals in a clay furnace; tongs hanging on the wall; shining coin dust on the apron; a young apprentice sweeping. Tone: warm, respectful, a different kind of knowing. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. The craftsmen are different. They really do know their crafts, and Socrates says so. But he finds that, because they do their own work well, they believe they are wise about everything else too. He concludes that the god meant something modest: Socrates is wiser only in that he does not think he knows what he does not know. And he takes the answer as a mission, to go on questioning people as the god's servant, even at the cost of making enemies.

docs.title: Panel 12: The Trial
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 12. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 12 of 14. Bird's-eye shot from a high angle over a large fenced open-air court of Athens, 399 BCE, a hot white morning, the light flat and unforgiving. Palette: marble white, bronze, honey gold, olive green, dust ochre. Hundreds of citizens in cream himations sit shoulder to shoulder on wooden benches in tight rows, almost five hundred of them, a sea of faces and robes. At the front, small in the frame and facing them, stands one barefoot man speaking: Socrates, Athenian philosopher: a short, stocky man of about sixty with a bald, broad forehead, a wide flat nose, a thick gray beard and bright, amused eyes, barefoot, wearing a plain, worn, undyed wool himation and no jewelry; a curious, teasing expression. (Here his expression is steady and unbowed.) Visible details: a water clock with two clay pots at the side, a thin thread of water between them; two tall bronze-banded urns for ballots waiting at the exit gate; a handful of accusers sitting together on the left; a small knot of his friends standing at the right edge of the crowd, seen from behind; a court officer holding a staff; dust motes in the light; the distant rock of the Acropolis visible above the rail. Tone: heavy, tense and quiet; no violence. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

In 399 BCE Athens had just lost the Peloponnesian War and survived the rule of a Spartan-backed junta called the Thirty Tyrants. Socrates is charged with not recognizing the city's gods, introducing new divine beings and corrupting the young, before a jury of about 500 citizens. In Plato's Apology, Socrates says that if only 30 votes had gone the other way he would have been acquitted, which suggests a vote of about 280 to 220. Asked to name his own penalty, he first proposes free meals at public expense, the honor given to Olympic victors; a later writer says even more jurors then voted for death.

Myth or Evidence? The trial is documented by two students, Plato and Xenophon, whose accounts differ. The count of 280 to 220 is an inference from one sentence in Plato. A common trap is to read the case as democracy versus philosophy. Socrates had questioned Athenians in public for decades, his students went on teaching in Athens, and the city remained the philosophy capital of the Mediterranean for nine centuries. A frightened city, just out of war and tyranny, looking for someone to blame, makes more sense of it.

docs.text:

Interior close-medium shot in a small plain stone room, Athens, 399 BCE, at dusk, lit only by a single oil lamp and a last band of orange sky through a high narrow window. Palette: marble white, bronze, honey gold, shadow blue, amber lamplight. In the center a plain wooden table holds a simple clay cup and a small jug, and beside it, pushed slightly back, stands an empty wooden chair with a worn undyed wool himation folded over its back. At the right edge, seen from behind in deep shadow, stand four or five friends in plain himations, heads bowed, one with a hand covering his face, a younger man leaning on the wall. The room is quiet and nobody is on the chair. Visible details: a wax tablet and a stylus on the floor; a small bronze lamp with a steady flame; sandals neatly set beside the chair; a stack of three unrolled scrolls; the long shadows of the standing men on the stone floor; bare plastered walls; a sleeping sparrow on the window ledge. Tone: grave, tender and still. Nothing is shown of the death itself. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

About a month after the verdict, Socrates drinks hemlock in the state prison. The delay came because no execution could take place while the sacred ship sent to the island of Delos was away; it had to return first. The final scene is told by his students, and this panel stays outside the room. A cup on a table, an empty chair and friends standing in the shadow are all the picture shows, and all it needs to.

Myth or Evidence? Visitors on Philopappos Hill are shown a "Prison of Socrates" cut into the rock; that is a modern tradition with no ancient evidence. The prison may have been a building at the southwest corner of the Agora, where excavators found small clay bottles of a size that would suit a dose of poison, but that too is a suggestion, not a certainty.

Small in the frame, standing together on a gravel path: Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. Ahead of them rises The Acropolis of Athens: a steep, flat-topped, pale limestone rock rising above the city, crowned by the Parthenon, a long Doric temple of honey-colored marble with eight columns across the front, a low triangular pediment and a long carved frieze under the roof; to its left stands the smaller Erechtheion with its porch of six marble maidens. Tone: quiet, reflective, with the old square still asking questions. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Today the Agora is a quiet field of foundations, olive trees and fallen marble, and the whole square becomes a working government again once you have seen the machine in the museum. Inside the reconstructed Stoa of Attalos, the allotment machine, the water clock and the potsherds are a few steps apart. Stand where the square once buzzed and you can still ask what Socrates asked: what do you mean, and how do you know?

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Man With Too Many Questions Shows
docs.text:
Athens built a government without kings: citizens ruled in person, drew lots for most offices and exiled leaders by scribbling on pots. Its great strength was that everyone had a chance to take part; its great flaw was how many people were left out. The city also showed how a democracy can be afraid. Socrates' habit of questioning the confident, taken as a mission from the god, is the other half of the story: the oldest answer in the Delphic tradition that is still worth having is the one he refused to take on trust.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today Ruling without kings Chose officials by lot and paid jurors, so the poor could serve Think about which of our own offices we would fill by drawing names A powerful rival Exiled by a vote on broken pots, with ready-made ballots handed out A written vote assumes everyone can write, and someone may be organizing the result An answer from an oracle Socrates tested it by questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen An answer is a claim to test, not an end to thinking A frightened city Convicted its most persistent questioner after war and tyranny Fear makes any society want to silence the person who keeps asking

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: Think about who in your own community can speak, who can write and who can read, and whose name never ends up on a ballot. Open Who Could Vote in Athens? to estimate how few of Athens's people the democracy actually included. The book's Learning for All thread asks the same question of every school and every tool: count the students it is not reaching, and be honest about that number too.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• "The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being." Attributed to Socrates in Plato's Apology (38a); the wording varies by translation, and the words are Plato's account of a speech given at the trial.
  • "I do not think I know what I do not know." Socrates' conclusion about his own wisdom in Plato's Apology, given here as the chapter's paraphrase of the Greek rather than a verbatim translation.
  • "Know thyself." The saying carved in the porch of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, which the travel writer Pausanias says was attributed to the Seven Sages; no ancient source names who wrote it.

Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a wide-landscape 16:9 cover image for a graphic novel. Exception to the no-text rule, for this cover only: render the title as bold, hand-lettered capital letters in honey-gold with a dark outline reading exactly "Pericles' Building Site" across the top, the only text in the image. Composition: a dramatic golden-hour view of the Acropolis of Athens in about 440 BCE as a vast building site. The Parthenon building site, about 440 BCE: the great temple platform on the Acropolis with half-raised honey-colored marble columns, some still stacked as separate drums, wooden scaffolds, timber cranes with ropes and pulleys, scattered blocks and carved fragments, and stonemasons at work. In the foreground, standing on a pile of marble blocks and gazing up at it with his arms folded, is Pericles. Pericles, Athenian leader: a dignified man of about fifty-five with an unusually tall, long head, usually shown wearing a crested bronze helmet pushed back on his head, a trimmed gray-brown beard and a calm, commanding expression, dressed in a white himation with a dark-blue border draped over a cream chiton. An ox cart carrying a pale marble column drum creaks up the ramp behind him, and the sea glints far below. Glaux the Little Owl: a true little owl (Athene noctua), small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts, warm earth-brown plumage with cream spots, bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream eyebrows, a cream-white throat patch and a short pale greenish-yellow beak. Glaux wears a small Aegean-blue scarf and a tan canvas satchel across the body with a small leather-bound travel notebook peeking out, and a sprig of three olive leaves tucked into the satchel strap. Alert, curious and warm expression. Glaux is drawn small, perched at the edge of the scene, noticeable on a second look. Glaux perches on a column drum in the lower corner. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze, with a warm gold sky. Tone: ambitious, awe-struck. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt

Era and places. Athens, 454 to 432 BCE, and the later lives of the Parthenon: the island of Delos (454), the burned Acropolis (about 447), the quarries of Mount Pentelikon and the road to Athens, the Acropolis building site (447 to 432), the Parthenon as church (probably from the late 6th century CE) and mosque (from soon after 1458), the Venetian siege of 1687, and today.

Themes. Who paid for a masterpiece, and who got to argue about it. The Parthenon was a public works program, voted by citizens, accounted for in public, and paid for in part with allies' money, a monument both to Athenian genius and to Athenian empire. Also: a building made of curves that look straight, a statue of gold and ivory, and a temple that spent about 900 years as a church and more than two centuries as a mosque and powder store before shell fire in 1687 blew out its middle. The Learning for All thread: the accounts were carved in stone for anyone to read, and the sculptures were designed to be read by any Athenian.

Series house style. Hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills, faint watercolor paper texture. No lettering in any panel; only the cover carries the title. All images are 16:9. The full style line is pasted at the top of every prompt (see Story Characters, Places and House Style).

Palette by era. Panels 1 to 12: Classical Greece (marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze). Panel 13: Byzantine (gold leaf, deep blue, imperial purple, candle amber, cream marble). Panel 14: Ottoman (Iznik turquoise, cobalt, tomato red, brass, saffron, white plaster). Panel 15: Venetian (sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue, banner crimson). Panel 16: modern Greece (natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta, olive).

Safe-image handling. The 1687 explosion is shown from a distance as a plume of smoke and flying dust, with no bodies and no people harmed on screen. The Athena Parthenos is shown draped, in gold and ivory, from a respectful distance.

Creative liberties and uncertainties.

  • Architect and sculptor names follow Chapter 15 (Ictinus, Callicrates, Phidias). Their faces and ages are invented. The architects' plans and the "curves" demonstrations are illustrative; only the measurements (platform rises about 6 cm at the ends and 11 cm along the sides) come from the chapter.
  • Plutarch's story that Pericles offered to pay for the buildings himself if the inscriptions named him may be polished; the stone accounts survive. Panel 11 says so.
  • Panel 12 shows the Athena Parthenos from descriptions and small Roman copies; the real statue is lost.
  • Our sources disagree about Phidias's end (Plutarch says he died in prison; another tradition says he went to work at Olympia), so the story leaves it open.
  • The date of the Parthenon's conversion to a church is debated; the story says "probably by the late 6th century."
  • In panels 13 to 16 the Parthenon block is pasted verbatim and followed by era-specific changes (cross and apse, minaret, smoke plume, scaffolding and missing roof). The block shows the building whole, which suits panels 13 to 15, as travelers saw it before 1687.
  • The chapter's casualty figure for the explosion, about three hundred, is given in the text only, never drawn.
  • A Chapter 14 note: the Francesco Morosini of the Heraklion fountain (1628) is a different man from the commander (1619 to 1694) who surrendered Candia in 1669 and led the 1687 army. This story shows only the commander.

Cast. Glaux the Little Owl hides in exactly one panel (panel 9): see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md (Glaux). Pericles, Athena, Francesco Morosini, the Owl Coin, the Parthenon and Acropolis, and the Travelers are in docs/stories/characters.md. The following appear only in this story; their blocks are pasted verbatim wherever they appear.

Ictinus (panels 6 and 7):

Ictinus, architect of the Parthenon: a lean man of about fifty with a short gray beard, a plain brown chiton, a rolled papyrus plan under one arm and a long wooden measuring rod in his hand; precise and quiet.

Callicrates (panels 6 and 8):

Callicrates, architect of the Parthenon: a sturdy man of about forty-five with a trimmed black beard, a white mason's apron over a cream chiton, holding a plumb line with a small lead weight; practical and good-humored.

Phidias (panel 6):

Phidias, sculptor: a vigorous man of about fifty with a long curly gray-brown beard, a marble-dusted tan work tunic with the sleeves pushed up, and a small iron chisel and a wooden mallet in his hands; absorbed and exacting.

The Venetian gunners of 1687 (panel 15):

The Venetian gunners of 1687: five sunburned artillerymen in shirtsleeves, leather aprons and red knitted caps, standing around two bronze cannons on wheeled wooden carriages behind a low wall of earth-filled wicker baskets, smoke still drifting from the muzzles; one holds a long stick with a smoldering match.

The Parthenon building site (panels 6 to 8 and the cover):

The Parthenon building site, about 440 BCE: the great temple platform on the Acropolis with half-raised honey-colored marble columns, some still stacked as separate drums, wooden scaffolds, timber cranes with ropes and pulleys, scattered blocks and carved fragments, and stonemasons at work.

The Acropolis in ruins, about 447 BCE (panel 2):

The Acropolis of Athens in ruins around 447 BCE: the pale limestone rock crowned by charred, broken columns and toppled column drums left standing thirty years after the Persian fire, weeds growing between the blocks and the city's red-tiled roofs far below.

docs.title: Prologue - The Money Question
docs.text:
In 454 BCE the treasury of an alliance of Greek cities moves to Athens, and Athens soon decides to spend part of it on the most perfect temple in Greece. The result is a building with almost no straight lines, and a political fight about whose money built it. Over the next two thousand years it becomes a church, a mosque and a powder store, and then a Venetian shell blows out its middle. Every fight over the Parthenon, from Pericles' day to ours, begins with the same question: who does it belong to, and who paid?

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

In 454 BCE Athens moves the treasury of the Delian League, the naval alliance of Greek cities it leads against Persia, from the island of Delos to Athens. The stated reason is that the money will be safer there. The allies' yearly payments, meant for defense, now sit in Athenian hands.

When the Persians left, Athens left the Acropolis in ruins. Later writers say the Greek allies swore to leave the burned temples as memorials, though that oath survives only in 4th-century versions and its authenticity is debated. Either way, the rock stands scorched for about thirty years. Pericles, an elected general who governs by persuading the Assembly, looks at the wreckage and sees a building site.

In 447 BCE the Assembly votes to rebuild. It is a public decision, made by citizens in the open air, and the work will be paid for out of public funds. Pericles has no throne and no permanent office; he has a gift for persuasion, and enough votes.

Setting: a marble quarry on the slope of Mount Pentelikon near Athens, 447 BCE, early morning with long shadows and white dust. Camera: wide, low angle looking up the terraced white face of the quarry. On the foreground ledge, a crew of eight quarrymen in short tunics drive iron wedges into a row of slots along a huge, newly cut block, while a ninth pours water over the wedges; others tilt the block's edge on a log lever. Details: wooden sledges and rollers, coils of rope, pale dust on their hair and arms, a mule carrying water jars, a foreman in a straw hat watching with a measuring rod, terraced pine slopes, the plain of Athens glinting far below. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold. Tone: effortful, rhythmic. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The marble comes from Mount Pentelikon, about 16 km from the Acropolis. Quarrymen cut it free in huge blocks with wedges, levers and patience; the white stone will turn honey-gold as it weathers. Every column drum on the Parthenon begins here as a lump of mountain.

A heavy four-wheeled wooden wagon pulled by four pairs of patient oxen carries a single pale marble column drum lashed with thick ropes; a driver in a wide straw hat walks at the lead ox with a goad held low, a boy runs beside the wheel with a bucket of water, and a mason walks behind steadying the load. Ox carts haul the blocks down the mountain to the city. Plutarch says Pericles defended the program by pointing to how many people it employed: carpenters, stonecutters, dyers, painters, merchants, sailors, teamsters, rope makers, road builders. It is a jobs program as much as a monument.

The architects Ictinus and Callicrates check their plans against the stone, and Phidias directs the sculpture. The temple will have 8 columns across each end and 17 down each side, and the stone arrives cut for its own place, so no two blocks are quite alike. Plutarch says Phidias oversaw the whole building program.

Almost nothing in the Parthenon is straight. The platform rises gently toward the middle of each side, by about 6 cm along the ends and about 11 cm along the long sides, so that it does not look as if it sags. A level floor would look as if it were sinking; a curved floor looks level.

The columns lean slightly inward, swell a little in the middle, a curve called entasis, and the corner columns are a bit thicker than the others, perhaps because a column seen against the bright sky looks thinner. Every block is cut for its own place in this curved geometry. That is one reason restoration takes decades, and why the building looks alive.

Glaux hunts for a straight line in the building and does not find one. Press a straightedge to the platform's edge and daylight shows between the board and the stone. The curves are too small to notice at a glance, which is exactly the point.

Myth or Evidence? Many books say the Parthenon was designed on the "golden ratio." No ancient source says so; the idea became popular in the 19th and 20th centuries. The platform measures about 30.9 by 69.5 m, a ratio of almost exactly 4 to 9, not the golden ratio. The curves, by contrast, are documented in the stone itself.

Pericles' rivals attack. Plutarch reports that they accuse him of decking out Athens with money that belongs to its allies. The building is both a monument to Athenian genius and to Athenian empire: the democracy at home is paid for, in part, by power over others abroad. Both things are true.

He stands at the edge of the frame watching the mason work, arms folded. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. Tone: orderly, quietly defiant. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Myth or Evidence? Plutarch says Pericles offered to pay for the buildings himself if the inscriptions would name him instead of the people, and the Assembly told him to spend what he needed from public funds. That story may be polished. What is not in doubt: fragments of the yearly building accounts, carved in stone on the Acropolis, survive, listing what the commissioners received and spent on the Parthenon and its statue.

The most famous building in Greece is also a public works program, voted on by citizens and accounted for in public. Anyone who walks up to the rock can read, in principle, where the money went.

In 438 BCE Phidias dedicates the statue of Athena Parthenos, about 12 m tall, built over a wooden core, with skin of ivory and armor and robes of gold. Thucydides reports that Pericles told the Athenians it carried 40 talents of refined gold, about a tonne, all of it removable and counted among the city's emergency reserves. Plutarch says Phidias' enemies later accused him of stealing gold; the plates were taken off and weighed, and the charge failed.

After the Christian Roman emperors ban the old sacrifices in the late 4th century CE, the temple's worship ends, and probably by the late 6th century it has become a church of the Virgin Mary, Our Lady of Athens. The builders move the entrance to the west, build an apse at the east, and cut windows; Christian inscriptions are still scratched into its columns. In 1018 the emperor Basil II gives thanks there for his victories, and after 1204 it becomes a Catholic cathedral.

In 1458 the Ottomans take the Acropolis, and soon afterward the cathedral becomes the city's main mosque, with a minaret at its southwest corner. Travelers in the 17th century describe the building as nearly complete, roof and all. In 1674 an artist with the French ambassador draws its sculptures, drawings that now give us our best record of what came next.

On September 26, 1687, during the Venetian siege of Athens led by Francesco Morosini, a shell strikes the Parthenon. The Ottoman garrison has stored its gunpowder inside; it ignites, blowing out the middle of the building, and about three hundred people are said to have died. Morosini is the same commander who surrendered Candia in 1669. He then tries to lower the horses of Athena's chariot from the west pediment as trophies; the ropes fail and the sculptures shatter.
