Today a bronze statue of a Turkish soldier carrying a wounded officer stands on the road between Kabatepe and Conkbayırı. It was put up in the late twentieth century, though sources differ on the year, and it is called the Mehmetçik monument, after the affectionate name Turkish people give their ordinary soldiers: "little Mehmet." Visitors from many countries stop to read it and to ask whether it happened.

Myth or Evidence? The statue is real, and the legend it commemorates is attested only as a retold story. What is documented is the truce of May 24, 1915, when soldiers from both sides sat down together. Both can be honored if each is labeled honestly.

docs.title: Panel 12: The Words on the Stone
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 12. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image depicting panel 12 of 12. Anzac Cove, Gallipoli, today, a bright, windy November morning. Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed pale sky, sea blue, terracotta, olive. Wide establishing view from near the water's edge looking toward the steep ridges, matching the viewpoint of panel 3 as closely as possible. Anzac Cove on the Gallipoli Peninsula: a small, narrow, stony beach curving around a bay of calm blue-gray water, with steep, dry, scrub-covered clay-and-gravel ridges rising almost straight up behind the beach, golden-brown grass, dark green scrub oak and a headland at the northern end. A low stone memorial stands at the right of the beach; a few distant visitors in coats and hats, including a small group with an Australian-style slouch hat, a family in coats with red poppies pinned on their lapels, and a Turkish family, stand in a loose group along the shore, quiet; a coach waits on the road behind. In the foreground, seen small: Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. Mood: quiet, reflective, shared. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Today, on the same beach, Australian, New Zealand and Turkish visitors stand together in the early morning wind. Words of reconciliation are carved on a memorial here: that the soldiers on both sides now lie together in the soil of a friendly country, and that there is "no difference between the Johnnies and the Mehmets." They are attributed to Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1934, but whether he wrote them is debated.

Myth or Evidence? The earliest source is a 1953 newspaper interview with Atatürk's former interior minister, nineteen years after the supposed 1934 message; researchers argue the most famous line was added in English in the late 1970s. As a claim about what he wrote, it is late and unsupported. As cultural memory it is real and powerful, and the honest way to read it is to hold both.

docs.title: Epilogue - How a Battlefield Becomes a Memory
docs.text:
Gallipoli is one place with several memories. For Turks it is Çanakkale geçilmez, the defense of the homeland at the gate of the capital, and the ordinary soldier is Mehmetçik. For Australians and New Zealanders it is a coming of age for two young nations, and Anzac Day is a sacred date. The documented events, the mines, the landing, the truce, are firm; the stories we tell about them, the carried officer and the carved words, are warmer and less certain. Telling them side by side, with honest labels, is what the book's tests for evidence are for, and it is a Learning for All habit: the more people can read the sources for themselves, the less any one story can claim to be the whole truth.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today A naval attack in a narrow strait A small minelayer laid a secret line of mines, and three battleships were lost A chokepoint rewards the defender who prepares quietly. A landing on the wrong beach Soldiers climbed steep ridges, and Mustafa Kemal's division reached the crest in time Plans fail on the ground; the people there decide. Two armies a few meters apart On May 24 they paused to bury the dead, and shared food and cigarettes Enemies are people, and sometimes they behave like it. A moving story with an uncertain source A statue and a carved message keep it alive, while historians label what is tradition Honor the memory, and label it honestly.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: If you walk the Gallipoli ridges, read at least one Turkish memorial as well as Anzac Cove, and ask each guide the two questions from the book: where does this come from, and how old is the earliest source? Then stand quietly at the statue, and decide for yourself how to hold both the legend and the truce.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• Çanakkale geçilmez, "Çanakkale cannot be passed": a phrase every Turkish child learns, according to the chapter; a slogan of national memory, not a quotation from one person.
  • "No difference between the Johnnies and the Mehmets": carved on a memorial at Anzac Cove and on Atatürk memorials in Canberra and Wellington, and traditionally attributed to Atatürk in 1934. Attribution is disputed: no 1934 source has been found, the earliest source is a 1953 interview, and researchers say the best-known line may be a later addition in English.
  • Mehmetçik, "little Mehmet": the affectionate Turkish name for the ordinary soldier, and the name of the monument whose statue is the subject of this story. We quote a word and a title, not a person, because no documented words of the soldier in the legend exist.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:

  • Where to look: the Mehmetçik monument on the road between Kabatepe and Conkbayırı; the trench lines, some of them only meters apart; Anzac Cove and its memorial; the Çanakkale Martyrs' Memorial near the southern tip, and the Nusret replica beside Çimenlik Castle in Çanakkale.
  • Explore further: Source, Myth, or Contested?, where readers sort which parts of a story are documented and which are remembered, and Mind the Gap: How Old Is the Evidence?.
  • Look Closer: Glaux says: "Look closer. Find a trench wall and a wooden stake." Glaux hid in Panel 8 (Cigarettes Across the Line), on a wooden stake at the edge of the trench. On site, look for how close the old trench lines really are.

docs.title: Prologue - A Box, a Twist and a Few Threads
docs.text:
Every traveler who walks the Spice Bazaar leaves with something small in a paper bag. This story follows two of those small things, a box of Turkish delight and a pinch of saffron, back through three centuries of Ottoman taste. Along the way a market is built to pay for a mosque, a sultan tries to close the coffeehouses, a confectioner opens a shop that is still open today, and a purple crocus turns out to be worth more by weight than almost anything on the stall.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

The market is no accident: the rent from its shops will help pay for the mosque's upkeep and charities, a common Ottoman way of funding a public building. Today the market is the Spice Bazaar.

The new hall smells of cumin, mint and cinnamon. Merchants arrange spices in cones, dried fruit in baskets and brass scales on boards, and the first customers wander in. The Turks call this market Mısır Çarşısı, "Egyptian Bazaar." The usual explanation links the name to Egypt, either through goods arriving by ship from Cairo or through Egyptian taxes that helped pay for the building, and nobody can say for certain which.

Within a generation the coffeehouse is the city's favorite place to talk. Men play backgammon, hear a storyteller, swap news and argue about the government over cups the size of an egg. Because most people cannot read, a room where news and stories pass by word of mouth is, in effect, a public classroom. Rulers notice that people who talk freely about the day's news may also criticize those in power.

Sultan Murad IV, who rules from 1623 to 1640, sees coffeehouses as places where people plot, and he orders them closed. The shutters go down, but the habit does not: people brew coffee at home, and after his reign the coffeehouses reopen. Coffee wins. A Turkish proverb says that a single cup of coffee commits you to forty years of friendship, and the story of the bans suggests why the cup was so hard to ban.

Saffron begins as a purple crocus that flowers in autumn. Each flower has only three red threads, called stigmas, and every one is picked by hand, so a single kilogram takes about 150,000 flowers. The Turkish town of Safranbolu is named after the spice, and the name is said to join safran with a Greek word for city. A few villages near the town are said to still grow the crop.

The things we buy here are the oldest things we carry home. Look closer next time you taste them.

docs.title: Epilogue - What a Box of Lokum Carries
docs.text:
A market, a drink and a sweet seem like small subjects, yet they answer large questions about how a city lives. The Spice Bazaar shows trade paying for charity, a sultan's ban shows the limits of control over habit, and Hacı Bekir shows how a good product becomes a name. For readers of the book's Learning for All thread, the coffeehouse adds a lesson: where reading is rare, places to listen and talk matter.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today A mosque needs lasting income Build a market beside it and use the shop rents to pay for the mosque Public goods often rest on ordinary commerce A sultan fears coffeehouse talk Close the coffeehouses; people kept drinking coffee and the shops reopened Habits and conversation are hard to ban A sweet older than any single maker Hacı Bekir made lokum famous from 1777; his family's shop is still open Fame often comes from craft and consistency, not invention Expensive saffron is easy to fake Buyers check the thread: deep red with pale tips, color released slowly in warm water Ask to see the evidence before you pay for a claim

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: Next time you taste lokum, ask the seller who made it and since when. Then look at a few saffron threads in warm water and notice how slowly the color arrives. Asking where a thing comes from, and how you can check, is the habit this whole book is trying to build.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
No spoken line from the merchants, confectioners or sultans in this story is documented in the sources used for this book, so none is invented here. Instead, three attested words and sayings stand in for their voices.

  • "Bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır." A well-known Turkish proverb, usually translated as "A cup of coffee has forty years of memory," meaning that a shared cup creates a lasting bond. Its author is unknown.
  • Mısır Çarşısı, "Egyptian Bazaar": the Turkish name of the Spice Bazaar, explained either by goods arriving from Egypt or by Egyptian taxes that helped pay for the building.
  • Lokum: the Turkish word for Turkish delight, said to come from an Arabic word for "morsels."

docs.title: Prologue - The Puzzle of the Late Press
docs.text:
Gutenberg printed his Bible in Germany around 1455. Istanbul, one of the largest cities in the world, had a working press by the 1490s, set up by refugees from Spain, and Armenian and Greek presses followed. Yet the first book printed in Ottoman Turkish in the Arabic script appeared only in 1729, almost three centuries after Gutenberg. This story follows that gap, tests the best-known explanation against the evidence, and asks what a long delay costs and who pays.

In 1492 the king and queen of Spain order every Jew to convert or leave. Tens of thousands go, and many find a welcome in the Ottoman Empire, where Sultan Bayezid II allows them to settle and practice their faith. They arrive on the Golden Horn with little more than what they can carry, but some bring skills in medicine, finance, textiles and printing. Those skills are about to change the city's skyline of ideas.

Within a year or two the brothers David and Samuel ibn Nahmias set up a press in Istanbul, the first in the Ottoman Empire. Their first known book, a code of Jewish law called the Arba'ah Turim, carries a date that corresponds to December 1493. Some scholars think it was printed about ten years later, so the exact year is debated. Either way, the capital had a working press within a few decades of Gutenberg.

The Ottoman authorities allow the empire's non-Muslim communities to print in their own scripts, and they do. Armenians in Istanbul start printing in 1567, and Greeks in 1627. In 1706 an Arabic press opens in Ottoman Aleppo, for Christian books. Printing is not unknown or forbidden in the empire; for Muslim readers in their own script, it simply has not started.

Beside them lie a bundle of reed pens, a brass inkwell with a silk cord, a pair of scissors, a polishing stone, a rolled license scroll and a finished page of flowing abstract calligraphic strokes pinned to dry. In Istanbul, handwriting is one of the highest arts. A calligrapher cuts a reed pen at an angle, mixes soot into ink and writes on paper polished with egg white and starch, and he signs his own work only after his master grants him a written license. An old saying holds that the Quran was revealed in Mecca, recited in Cairo and written in Istanbul. A craft this prestigious is not easily replaced.

Sunlight falls through the arch onto a sleeping tabby cat. On the top shelf among bound volumes perches a tiny owl. Glaux the Little Owl: a true little owl (Athene noctua), small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts, warm earth-brown plumage with cream spots, bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream eyebrows, a cream-white throat patch and a short pale greenish-yellow beak. The book market beside the Grand Bazaar stands on or near the old Byzantine market for paper and books, so the city has been selling books for more than a thousand years. Every volume here is a copy made by a trained hand. The master calligrapher Hafız Osman is said to have copied 25 complete Qurans in about forty years, or one every year and a half. The books are beautiful, and the number in circulation is limited by the number of trained hands.

docs.title: Panel 6: Did the Scribes Stop the Press?
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 06. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Palette: Iznik turquoise, cobalt, tomato red, brass, saffron yellow and white plaster, softened to a faded sepia storybook wash with a pale vignette edge, so that it looks like a legend told rather than a record. Medium-wide view. Six copyists in turbans and robes, each with a reed-pen case at the belt, stand in a loose row across the lane with their arms folded, facing a shut wooden door with an iron lock. A single open book lies on a stool. A lantern glows. A stray dog watches. On one side stands a stack of manuscripts tied with cord, on the other a small wooden press shown dark and still behind a barred window. No violence, no weapons. Mood: ambiguous, dramatic, legendary. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

A popular story says the scribes and calligraphers kept the press out, because printing threatened their livelihoods. It makes a good story, and it also has gaps. The scribes' jobs and craft were at stake, and handwriting a Quran was an act of devotion, but historians do not agree that organized scribes ever blocked a press.

Myth or Evidence? Documented: Hebrew, Armenian and Greek presses ran in Istanbul long before 1729, and copyists and calligraphers lived by handwriting. Tradition: that scribes physically stopped a press, and that Sultan Bayezid II banned Arabic-script printing in 1485 on pain of death. No copy of such a decree survives, and many historians doubt it was ever issued. Most now think several causes worked together: the sacred status of the handwritten Quran, the hundreds of pieces of type that joined Arabic letters demand, the scribes' livelihoods, a manuscript system that served a small reading public, and the state's control over what was written and taught.

İbrahim Müteferrika, born about 1674, comes from Kolozsvár in Transylvania, today Cluj in Romania, and probably grows up in a Unitarian Christian family. He comes to Istanbul as a young man, converts to Islam and serves the state as a diplomat and translator. His work takes him among books and maps from other countries, and he becomes convinced that the empire needs the press.

In 1726 Müteferrika and Said Efendi, the son of an Ottoman ambassador who had seen printing in Paris, present the government with a treatise on the benefits of printing. In 1727 Sultan Ahmed III issues a decree allowing them to print, supported by a ruling from the chief religious scholar. We imagine the audience as a single scene; the sources record the documents, not who stood where. The gate opens, but with strings attached.

Palette: Iznik turquoise, cobalt, tomato red, brass, saffron yellow and white plaster. Medium-wide interior. In the foreground İbrahim Müteferrika around 1727: a lean man of about fifty-three with a trimmed gray-brown beard, dark thoughtful eyes and a high forehead, wearing a cream turban and an olive-green kaftan with a narrow fur collar, ink on the fingers of his right hand; intense, patient and quietly stubborn. stands at a sloping wooden case divided into many small compartments filled with tiny metal type pieces, picking out one piece by hand. Beside him a heavy screw press stands ready and a rack of paper hangs overhead. At a table to the right two scholars in white turbans and gray robes bend over a freshly printed proof sheet, one of them holding a quill and pointing at a line. On the table sit an inkpot, a lamp, a stack of blank paper and a small brass bell. A narrow window shows the street. Mood: meticulous, supervised, hopeful. The permission comes with conditions: no religious books, so no Qurans, and a panel of scholars to proofread every book. The technical task is huge. Arabic script joins its letters, and each letter changes shape depending on its neighbors, so the printer needs hundreds of different pieces of type, where a Latin printer needs a few hundred in all. Müteferrika builds a press for a script that few had printed in this city.

Around him stacks of printed folded sheets rise on benches, pages hang on lines to dry, two helpers in plain tunics fold and bind pages, and a scholar in a white turban leans in to look over his shoulder. In 1729 the first book comes off the press: an Arabic-Turkish dictionary, printed in an edition of 1,000 copies. Where a scribe makes one copy at a time, a press can make a thousand. Ottoman Turkish in the Arabic script has its first printed book, almost 275 years after Gutenberg.

docs.text:

In the center İbrahim Müteferrika around 1727: a lean man of about fifty-three with a trimmed gray-brown beard, dark thoughtful eyes and a high forehead, wearing a cream turban and an olive-green kaftan with a narrow fur collar, ink on the fingers of his right hand; intense, patient and quietly stubborn., now aged about seventy with a white beard and a slightly stooped back, stands among tall stacks of bound printed books on wooden shelves, running a hand along one spine. Dust floats in a shaft of light from a high window. A single customer in a brown robe and cap examines a book near the doorway. A large map is rolled in a corner and a small brass compass lies open on a shelf. The press stands quiet in the background. Mood: tender, melancholy and dignified. By his death Müteferrika has printed 17 works: dictionaries, histories, a grammar and a geography with maps. Some of his editions are still being sold decades later. One reading is that his books sat unsold because too few people could read them: the press made copies cheap without making readers. A tool is only part of what it takes to widen the circle.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 12. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta, olive, with a few Ottoman accents. Wide shot of a quiet stone courtyard shaded by plane trees with bare autumn branches, lined with small bookshops under arcades. In the foreground by a book stall stand Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. One of them turns the page of an old illustrated book on a wooden table; the other studies a stack of antique prints. Rows of old books, maps and framed calligraphy panels fill the shelves, a shopkeeper sips tea from a tulip-shaped glass in a doorway, and a cat naps on a crate. Mood: reflective, affectionate, a long story still unfolding. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Today the Sahaflar courtyard still sells books, old and new. What did the long wait cost, and who paid? In our reading, the people outside the gates paid: the readers who never learned, the families without books and the scholars without cheap copies. Historians disagree about how much the delay mattered, but the pattern is clear: printing made copies cheap, and it took schools and a simpler alphabet to make readers. That second step comes in 1928.

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Wait Teaches
docs.text:
The press in Istanbul did not arrive late for lack of technology. By the 1490s the city had one; by 1706 Arabic script was being printed nearby. What delayed Ottoman Turkish printing was a mix of faith, craft, economics and control, and when it finally arrived it came with limits and met a public that mostly could not read. Seen through the Learning for All thread, the lesson is that tools, gatekeepers and readers all have to line up before the circle of learning widens.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: When you stand among old books in Istanbul, ask three questions of every new tool: who controls it, who does it leave out, and what else does the circle of learners need before it widens? Then try the two MicroSims to see the numbers behind the story for yourself.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
No documented spoken line from any scribe or printer in this story exists in the sources used for this book, so none is invented.

  • "The Quran was revealed in Mecca, recited in Cairo and written in Istanbul." An old saying about calligraphy, cited in the chapter; its author is unknown.
  • Attributed to Sultan Bayezid II: that the king of Spain had impoverished his own country and enriched the sultan's by expelling the Jews. The saying is repeated in almost every account but first appears in later sources, so treat it as a story. The welcome itself is documented history.
  • Vesîletü't-tıbâa ("The Means of Printing"): the title, as usually transliterated, of the treatise Müteferrika is recorded as writing in support of printing. The title survives; the story does not give us his spoken words.

docs.text:

docs.title: Twenty-One Years of Candia
docs.text:
Cover Image Prompt (This is the Cover Image. Do not include this label in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a wide-landscape 16:9 cover image. Scene: the bastioned walls of the Venetian city of Candia on Crete at golden hour. A great arrowhead-shaped sandstone bastion fills the foreground, its thick sloping face scarred by cannonballs, with a deep dry ditch below it and a carved winged lion of St. Mark (the lion holds a closed book) above a gate. Beyond the walls, a plain dotted with Ottoman tents and thin plumes of smoke; in the harbor behind, a Venetian galley slides toward a sea fortress at the end of a breakwater under a crimson banner. A small Venetian commander stands on the bastion looking out: Francesco Morosini, Venetian commander: a lean man of about sixty with a long gray beard, a high forehead and a stern, tired expression, wearing a dark crimson velvet coat with gold braid over a steel breastplate, a wide white lace collar, a black cap with a small gold badge, and the red-and-gold sash of a Venetian captain-general. Render the title as bold, hand-lettered text across the top: "TWENTY-ONE YEARS OF CANDIA" (exact spelling, no other text anywhere). Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Mood: stubborn, weary, grand. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt **Story:** "Twenty-One Years of Candia" follows the siege of the Venetian capital of Crete, Candia (today Heraklion), by the Ottomans, from 1648 to 1669 and one of the longest sieges in history, and the commander, Francesco Morosini, who surrendered the city in September 1669. A teaser shows the same man in Athens in 1687, and the last panel is the grave of the novelist Nikos Kazantzakis on the Martinengo Bastion today. **Places and eras:** Candia/Heraklion (the 1560s, the 1640s to 1669, today); Athens (1687, a teaser; the full story is told in another story of this series). All of the siege panels use the series palette for Medieval Rhodes and Venetian Crete: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson; the Ottoman camp adds tomato red, brass and saffron. The El Greco panel adds gold leaf. The last panel uses natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive. **House style:** hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, as in docs/stories/characters.md. No lettering anywhere in panels. Only the cover carries the title. Safe-Image Rules apply: the siege is shown only by walls, bastions, ships, tunnels, smoke and tents, with no wounds, corpses or weapons mid-strike. Soldiers are always at rest, watching, working or leaving. **Legend versus evidence:** All panels are documented history. Appearances and rooms are invented. Dates follow the book: the Ottoman landing in 1645, Chania in 1645, Rethymno in 1646, the siege before Candia from 1648, the vizier's personal command from 1667, the French expedition of 1669, the surrender in September 1669. The siege is called 21 years long (1648 to 1669). The Lions Square fountain was built in 1628 by an earlier Francesco Morosini, a Venetian governor, who is a different man from the commander of 1669; he is not drawn here, and the fountain is shown without him. **Creative liberties:** The text of the book says the Morosini of the siege was born in 1619, so he is about fifty at the surrender; the series' paste-in block for him (about sixty, lean, gray-bearded, stern and tired) is used unchanged in panels 9, 10 and 11, as the series requires, so he may look a little older than his years. He was about sixty-eight in 1687. The prompts for the Kazantzakis grave keep the cross plain and unlettered because panels have no text; the epitaph is printed in the narrative. **Cast:** Recurring characters (see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md for Glaux): Francesco Morosini (panels 9, 10 and 11 and the cover), the Acropolis and Parthenon (panel 11) and the Travelers (panel 12). Glaux hides in panel 2. Characters who appear only in this story: The young El Greco (panel 3): 
Domenikos Theotokopoulos, the young El Greco, in his early twenties: a slim young man with a long face, dark curling hair, a short dark beard and intense dark eyes, wearing a plain brown artisan's tunic with rolled sleeves and a paint-spattered linen apron, a fine brush in one hand.
Townsfolk of Candia (panel 2): 
Townsfolk of Candia: Greek women in long dark skirts and white headscarves carrying clay water jars, a Venetian merchant in a black cap and short cloak, and a boy leading a donkey, mixed together at the fountain.
Venetian soldiers (panels 4, 6 and 7): 
Venetian soldiers of Candia: sturdy men in short-brimmed steel helmets, buff leather jerkins over white shirts, crimson sashes and dark breeches, carrying long matchlock muskets at rest on their shoulders; tired and watchful, never shown fighting.
Venetian sappers (panel 5): 
Venetian sappers in a tunnel: stocky men in rolled sleeves, leather caps and dusty brown jerkins, one holding a small tin lantern, another a short pick, and one kneeling with an ear pressed to the earth wall.
Volunteers from across Europe (panel 7):

docs.title: Prologue - The Walls That Would Not Fall
docs.text:
For twenty-one years, from 1648 to 1669, the walled Venetian city of Candia held out against the Ottoman army, one of the longest sieges in history. The walls were designed so that no part of the ditch was out of the reach of a gun, and the Ottomans answered by digging under them. The man who finally negotiated the surrender, Francesco Morosini, would turn up eighteen years later in front of a very different wall. This story follows the city from its prosperous years to its end and then to a quiet grave on its southern bastion.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

Behind it, the long vaulted arches of the arsenal line the harbor, and above them the low, thick, angled walls of the city rise with arrowhead-shaped bastions. From 1211 to 1669 the Republic of Venice rules Crete as an overseas colony, the Kingdom of Candia, and the capital, Candia, gives its name to the whole island. Its harbor is guarded by a sea fortress, the Rocca a Mare, built between 1523 and 1540, and its landward side by a ring of low, thick walls with seven arrowhead bastions. Everything in the picture was designed so that no attacker could find a blind spot. In 1645 an Ottoman army lands in the west of the island, and the city's long test begins.

In Lions Square the city's water comes out of four stone lions. The fountain was built in 1628 by an earlier governor, also named Francesco Morosini, to bring fresh water from Mount Juktas to the city. He is a different man from the commander of 1669, but the two names will cause mix-ups for as long as anyone tells this story. Around the fountain, Greek townspeople and Venetian officials share the same square.

At an easel stands Domenikos Theotokopoulos, the young El Greco, in his early twenties: a slim young man with a long face, dark curling hair, a short dark beard and intense dark eyes, wearing a plain brown artisan's tunic with rolled sleeves and a paint-spattered linen apron, a fine brush in one hand. A century before the siege, a young painter grows up in this city. Domenikos Theotokopoulos, born in Candia in 1541, trains in the Cretan icon workshops, which paint in both a Byzantine and an Italian manner, and is already a master painter at home by 1563. About 1567 he leaves for Venice, and later Rome and Toledo in Spain, where the world will call him El Greco, 'the Greek'. Candia is a city of painters and scholars, and the siege will end that world.

Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue, banner crimson, with Ottoman accents of tomato red, brass and saffron. Camera: over-the-shoulder, looking out from behind two sentries toward the plain. Mood: tense, watchful, long-haul. In the foreground, standing on the wall, seen mostly from behind: Venetian soldiers of Candia: sturdy men in short-brimmed steel helmets, buff leather jerkins over white shirts, crimson sashes and dark breeches, carrying long matchlock muskets at rest on their shoulders; tired and watchful, never shown fighting. Beyond the deep dry ditch and the sloping face of the wall, the plain stretches out, covered with rows of tents, long raw-earth trench lines, earthen mounds for guns, and horses and wagons. Plumes of smoke rise from a distant fire on the far hills. Details: a crimson banner with the winged lion on a pole, a stack of cannonballs at the foot of a gun carriage, a sandbag, a gull circling, and the long shadow of the bastion across the ditch. The war begins in 1645, when an Ottoman army lands in western Crete. Chania falls that year and Rethymno in 1646, and in 1648 the Ottomans dig in before Candia. Within days the plain below the walls is a city of tents and trenches, and it will stay that way for years. The defenders on the bastions look out at it and realize that this will not be a quick war.

Mood: hushed, claustrophobic, listening. In the foreground: Venetian sappers in a tunnel: stocky men in rolled sleeves, leather caps and dusty brown jerkins, one holding a small tin lantern, another a short pick, and one kneeling with an ear pressed to the earth wall. They are working in silence, one with an ear pressed to the earth wall as if listening for digging on the other side. Details: timber props holding the roof, a wooden barrow of loose earth, a small bucket of water standing on the floor, little trickles of dust falling from the ceiling, a rolled plan of the bastion, a dim shaft of daylight at the far end, and the shadows of the men stretching long behind them. The fighting at the walls is mostly a war of tunnels. Ottoman miners dig under the bastions to blow them up, and Venetian counter-miners dig out to meet them underground, listening through the earth for the sound of a pick. This is why the arrowhead bastions were designed as they were: attackers could not simply walk up, so they spent twenty-one years digging.

Two Venetian galleys with oars raised slip between the sea fortress and the breakwater toward the quay, loaded with barrels and sacks. On the quay wait Venetian soldiers of Candia: sturdy men in short-brimmed steel helmets, buff leather jerkins over white shirts, crimson sashes and dark breeches, carrying long matchlock muskets at rest on their shoulders; tired and watchful, never shown fighting. with lanterns, who are hauling sacks of grain and barrels from a gangplank. For more than twenty years the city holds out because it can be supplied from the sea. Venetian galleys slip in at night with grain, powder and men, while Venetian fleets fight the Ottomans as far away as the Dardanelles to keep the lifeline open. As long as the harbor stays open, the walls can stand.

Volunteers come from across Christian Europe to help Venice hold the walls, and some stay for months, some for a season, and some for a single bad week. In 1669 a French expedition arrives, and its commander is killed in a failed sortie. Candia becomes a cause as well as a city: a Christian fortress on an island that the Ottomans want.

In 1667 the grand vizier Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha takes personal command and presses the siege harder than ever. The years of trenches and tunnels turn into a final, relentless push. By the late summer of 1669 the city is in ruins, and everyone in the camp and in the city knows that the end is near.

docs.text:

Palette: sandstone, steel gray, Mediterranean blue and banner crimson. Camera: a medium close view from across the table. Mood: grave, tired, resolute; no violence. At a heavy wooden table sits Francesco Morosini, Venetian commander: a lean man of about sixty with a long gray beard, a high forehead and a stern, tired expression, wearing a dark crimson velvet coat with gold braid over a steel breastplate, a wide white lace collar, a black cap with a small gold badge, and the red-and-gold sash of a Venetian captain-general. He holds a quill over an unrolled sheet of parchment, with no writing visible, and looks past it with a weary frown. Through the window beyond him, the broken bastions and a pall of smoke over the city are visible against a salmon sky. Details: a single candle in an iron stick, a small wooden chest with the red-and-gold sash folded on top, a map with no markings clearly visible, a cracked plaster wall, a goblet, a sealing wax stick, and the crimson banner on the wall behind him. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Francesco Morosini, the Venetian commander, has held the city for the last years of the siege. In September 1669 he negotiates a surrender. The terms are generous: the garrison and any inhabitants who wish to leave can do so with their property, and Venice keeps three small island fortresses off Crete at Souda, Gramvousa and Spinalonga, the last of them until 1715. Tens of thousands have died on each side.

At the stern rail of a Venetian galley stands Francesco Morosini, Venetian commander: a lean man of about sixty with a long gray beard, a high forehead and a stern, tired expression, wearing a dark crimson velvet coat with gold braid over a steel breastplate, a wide white lace collar, a black cap with a small gold badge, and the red-and-gold sash of a Venetian captain-general. Behind him, a crimson banner with the winged lion of St. Mark and a closed book is carefully folded in the hands of two sailors. In the foreground, two priests in dark robes carry a small gilded reliquary casket up the gangplank. Details: oars raised and dripping, the sea fortress at the end of the breakwater growing small, a line of ships with furled sails following, a thin trail of smoke from the city walls, crates and chests being loaded by townspeople leaving, gulls, and a long golden path on the water. The garrison and the people who choose to go sail out with their goods, and with them go the city's relics, among them the skull of Saint Titus, which will remain in Venice until it is returned to Heraklion in 1966. Candia becomes Kandiye, an Ottoman provincial capital, and Ottoman Crete begins, lasting until 1898. Morosini goes home to Venice, and his name will come back to the Aegean.

Eighteen years later the same man is in Athens, in command of the Venetian army that in 1687 attacks the city. Nobody in 1669 could have guessed where this commander would turn up.

Palette: natural daylight, whitewashed walls, sea blue, terracotta and olive, with the sandstone of the old walls. Camera: a wide view across the bastion's flat grassy top, looking toward the city and a distant mountain, at the same angle as the angled wall in the first panel. Mood: peaceful, open, unburdened. Today the Martinengo Bastion, the southernmost of the seven, is a quiet, grassy platform, and on it, under a plain wooden cross, lies the novelist Nikos Kazantzakis (1883 to 1957), who was born in Ottoman Candia. His epitaph, in translation, reads: 'I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free.' The walls that were built to stop an enemy are now the place where a free spirit is buried, and visitors climb them for the view.

docs.title: Epilogue - What a Long Siege Teaches
docs.text:
The siege of Candia ended in a negotiated surrender on generous terms, after tens of thousands had died on each side. Venice lost its Kingdom of Candia, and Crete gained an Ottoman provincial capital that lasted more than two centuries. The Cretan Renaissance that had produced El Greco and the scholar Marcus Musurus, who edited Greek texts for the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius, had already carried its learning out into Europe; the siege closed that chapter at home.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today Cannon had made tall medieval walls obsolete Low, thick arrowhead bastions leaving no dead ground Design for the actual threat, not the old one Attackers tunneling under the walls Counter-miners dug out to meet them underground A problem solved on paper still has to be solved underground A city cut off but not blockaded at sea Galleys brought supplies by night, and fleets fought far away to keep the sea lanes open A long effort needs a lifeline Whether to fight to the last or save the people Morosini negotiated terms that let the garrison and willing inhabitants leave with their property Knowing when to stop can be as hard as knowing how to hold on

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: If you are in Heraklion, walk the old walls and see for yourself why a bastion is shaped like an arrowhead, then climb the Martinengo Bastion to read the grave on the top. Cretan scholars such as Marcus Musurus helped put Greek texts into the small, portable books of Aldus Manutius in Venice, and knowledge that travels in a pocket outlasts the walls of any one city. Learning for All has always depended on who is allowed to carry knowledge out of a place, and who can read it when it arrives.

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
• The epitaph of Nikos Kazantzakis, on his grave on the Martinengo Bastion. In translation: "I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free." The wording is the translation given in the chapter.
  • The winged lion of St. Mark (a traditional Venetian inscription). The lion that watched over Venetian gates often holds an open book, traditionally inscribed with a Latin greeting to St. Mark, the city's patron saint. This is the symbol of Venice, not a record of any one lion in Candia.
  • El Greco's signature. Domenikos Theotokopoulos signed his paintings in Greek letters, and on some he added Kres, "Cretan", a documented sign of how he thought of his origins.

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:
• Chapter: 14. Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
  • Where to look: the Venetian walls and their seven bastions; the harbor fortress (the Koules) and the vaulted arsenal arches; the Morosini Fountain in Lions Square, which carries the name of an earlier Francesco Morosini, a governor, not the commander of the siege; and the Martinengo Bastion and Kazantzakis's grave on the southern edge of the old town.
  • Explore further: Walking Venetian Candia
  • Look Closer: Glaux was perched on the rim of the fountain basin in panel 2. At the real fountain, look at the lions' manes and mouths, and remember that the fountain's name belongs to a different Morosini.

Composition: a dramatic wide view of the narrows of Salamis at sunset in September 480 BCE, a long line of Athenian triremes with raised oars surging toward us across Aegean-blue water, their bronze rams glinting, with a smoky column from the distant burning Acropolis on the horizon and the dark mass of Mount Aigaleo on the right. In the lead ship, standing on the deck with one arm outstretched toward the sea, is Themistocles. Themistocles, Athenian statesman and admiral: a stocky, energetic man of about forty-five with a short dark curly beard, sharp dark eyes and a weathered, tanned face, wearing a plain cream chiton and a rust-brown himation draped over one shoulder, a bronze signet ring on his right hand; confident, restless, always mid-gesture. Glaux the Little Owl: a true little owl (Athene noctua), small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts, warm earth-brown plumage with cream spots, bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream eyebrows, a cream-white throat patch and a short pale greenish-yellow beak. Glaux wears a small Aegean-blue scarf and a tan canvas satchel across the body with a small leather-bound travel notebook peeking out, and a sprig of three olive leaves tucked into the satchel strap. Alert, curious and warm expression. Glaux is drawn small, perched at the edge of the scene, noticeable on a second look. Glaux perches on the curved stern post of the nearest ship. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions. Narrative Prompt

Era and places. The Persian Wars, 490 to 479 BCE, as told by Herodotus: the plain of Marathon (490), the Hellespont near modern Çanakkale (spring 480), Delphi (481 or 480), Athens and the Pnyx hill, the port of Piraeus, the Acropolis, the strait of Salamis (September 480), and Delphi again after Plataea (479). The last panel is the Hippodrome in Istanbul today.

Themes. An ambiguous oracle read by a democracy: the god spoke in a riddle and an Assembly of citizens argued over two words. A forecaster's judgment (Themistocles) beats a fixed rule. The wars are told by Herodotus, a man born a subject of the Persian king, which is part of why we trust his inquiry; we keep his account of what happened and treat his numbers as reported, not believed. Citizens, including the poorest, rowed the fleet that saved Athens (about 30,000 oarsmen): a Learning for All thread, because the city's survival depended on people who had no standing in older systems of rank.

Series house style. Hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills, faint watercolor paper texture. No lettering in any panel; only the cover carries the title. All images are 16:9. The full style line is pasted at the top of every prompt (see Story Characters, Places and House Style).

Palette. Classical Greece (marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze) for panels 1 to 3 and 5 to 15, with royal purple and saffron added wherever Xerxes or the Persian fleet appears (panels 4, 10 to 13). Panel 16 uses the modern Turkey palette: natural daylight, sea blue, terracotta, olive.

Safe-image handling. The battles are shown by dust, shields at rest, smoke, ships, oars, wreckage and mourners from behind. There is no combat, no wounds and no bodies. The Persian sack of the Acropolis is shown by smoke and ruined columns only.

Creative liberties and uncertainties.

  • The two oracle answers, Themistocles' reading of "divine Salamis" and the Assembly vote all come from Herodotus alone, who wrote about fifty years later. Some historians suspect the second answer was polished afterward. The story presents them as Herodotus tells them.
  • The legend of the runner who died after racing from Marathon to Athens appears centuries after the battle (Plutarch and Lucian) and is not in Herodotus. Panel 3 shows it as legend and says so.
  • Herodotus gives huge numbers for Xerxes' army; modern historians usually estimate far fewer, often about 100,000 to 300,000 fighting men. The number is not shown.
  • Where the Serpent Column was cast is not stated by Herodotus; we say "probably near Delphi." Its first appearance in panel 15 shows it new (bright bronze, three heads, golden bowl); the Serpent Column block describes its present weathered state.
  • Athena herself is not shown; she appears only as the head on the owl coin.
  • All Athenians and Delphians other than Themistocles and the Pythia are anonymous; the named Delphian Timon is not drawn.

Cast. Glaux the Little Owl hides in exactly one panel (panel 8): see docs/stories/characters.md and docs/img/mascot/character-sheet.md (Glaux). Themistocles, the Pythia, the Owl Coin, Delphi, the Serpent Column and the Travelers are in docs/stories/characters.md. The following appear only in this story; their blocks are pasted verbatim wherever they appear (in panel 8 the triremes are only half built, so they are described in the prompt rather than pasted).

Xerxes (panels 4 and 12):

Xerxes, Great King of Persia: a tall, broad-shouldered man of about thirty-eight with a long, carefully curled black beard, a tall upright cream felt tiara, a long saffron-and-purple embroidered robe with wide sleeves, gold bracelets and a gold-chain collar; an aloof, regal, unreadable expression.

The Athenian envoys (panels 5 and 6):

Two Athenian envoys: a gray-bearded man of about sixty in a travel-stained cream himation, and a younger man of about thirty with short dark hair in a faded rust himation, both with broad-brimmed traveler's hats hanging at their backs, dusty leather sandals and walking staffs; weary and anxious.

The Athenian trireme (panels 9, 11, 12, 13 and the cover):

An Athenian trireme: a long, narrow wooden warship, low in the water, with three staggered banks of oars, a bronze ram at the waterline of the bow, a curved raised stern post, a large painted eye on each side of the bow, a square sail furled on a single mast, and bronze-helmeted marines on the deck.

The burned Acropolis, 480 BCE (panel 10):

The Acropolis of Athens after the Persian sack of 480 BCE: the same steep, flat-topped, pale limestone rock above the city, but its old temples are smoking ruins, with blackened broken columns, toppled column drums, scorched marble, charred roof beams, tall columns of dark smoke drifting over the summit and a blackened stump where the sacred olive tree stood; the sky behind is hazy and brown-gray.

docs.title: Prologue - A Wall Made of Wood
docs.text:
In 480 BCE an enormous Persian army is marching on Athens, and the city has asked the god at Delphi what to do. The first answer tells them to run to the ends of the earth. The second is a riddle: Zeus will give Athena a wooden wall that will not fall. A city of stone temples has to decide what a wooden wall might be. The answer, and the man who argued for it, change the course of Greek history.

Find Glaux: Glaux hides in one panel of this story. Can you spot the little owl?

In 490 BCE a Persian fleet sent by King Darius lands on the plain of Marathon, about 40 km northeast of Athens. About 10,000 Athenian citizen soldiers march out to meet it, joined by about 1,000 men from the little town of Plataea; the Spartans cannot come in time. Herodotus says the Athenians attack at a run, and they win. Marathon is where the Persians first learn that Athens will fight.

By evening the Persian ships are rowing away. Herodotus counts 192 Athenian dead, and they are buried together under a mound that still stands on the plain, the Soros. Athens learns that it can win, and that the next invasion will be bigger.

Setting: the Athenian Agora at the foot of the Acropolis, 490 BCE, a bright hazy morning with a faint dreamlike glow around the edges to suggest a legend. Camera: medium-wide view as a lean, exhausted runner in a plain short tunic reaches the Agora, stumbling on to one knee with one arm raised, his sandals dusty, while a small crowd of citizens in cream and white himations looks on from the edges, some running toward him with water jars. Behind them rise the old temples on the rocky Acropolis. Details: a market stall of pottery, a plane tree, a herm statue on a pillar, startled doves. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. Tone: breathless, mythic. No one is shown dying. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Myth or Evidence? The documented feat is the one few people know: Herodotus says a runner named Pheidippides ran from Athens to Sparta to ask for help, about 240 km in two days. The runner who raced from Marathon to Athens with news of victory and then died appears centuries later, in Plutarch and Lucian, and Herodotus never mentions it. It is a legend. The modern marathon race honors it.

Setting: a hillside above the Hellespont at Abydos, spring of 480 BCE, bright cool morning; palette of marble white, Aegean blue, honey gold and bronze with royal purple and saffron for the Persians. Camera: wide, from behind and to one side of a white marble throne on a rocky ledge, looking out over the strait: two long bridges of boats lashed side by side stretch across the narrow water to the far shore, with dark columns of small marching figures and wagons crossing. Cast: Xerxes, Great King of Persia: a tall, broad-shouldered man of about thirty-eight with a long, carefully curled black beard, a tall upright cream felt tiara, a long saffron-and-purple embroidered robe with wide sleeves, gold bracelets and a gold-chain collar; an aloof, regal, unreadable expression. He sits on the throne watching, a tall purple parasol held over him by an attendant. Ten years after Marathon, Darius's son Xerxes comes himself. His army crosses the Hellespont, the narrow strait near modern Çanakkale, on two bridges of boats. Herodotus puts the army at 1.7 million infantry; modern historians, counting what roads, water and food could support, usually estimate far fewer, often 100,000 to 300,000 fighting men, though estimates vary widely. Whatever the number, it is far larger than Athens can match on land.

Herodotus tells the story in two acts. Athenian envoys ask the Pythia, Apollo's priestess, what to do about Xerxes. The first answer is terrifying: flee to the ends of the earth, for fire and war will destroy the city. A respected Delphian named Timon, Herodotus says, advises them to go back, carrying olive branches as suppliants, and ask again. The date is 481 or 480 BCE.

The second answer is hardly cheerful, but it leaves a door open. Zeus, the Pythia says, will grant Athena a wooden wall that alone will not be taken, and the answer ends: "Divine Salamis, you will destroy the children of women," at the time of sowing or of harvest. It names no side. Whichever fleet sinks, the line comes true.

Setting: the Pnyx hill, the open-air meeting place of the Athenian Assembly, autumn 480 BCE, bright midday; the old temples of the Acropolis stand in the distance with a thorn hedge and timber barricade along the rock's edge. Camera: medium-wide view over the shoulders of the crowd toward the speaker's rock. Cast: Themistocles, Athenian statesman and admiral: a stocky, energetic man of about forty-five with a short dark curly beard, sharp dark eyes and a weathered, tanned face, wearing a plain cream chiton and a rust-brown himation draped over one shoulder, a bronze signet ring on his right hand; confident, restless, always mid-gesture. He stands on the speaker's rock mid-gesture, one hand pointing out toward the sea. In the crowd, hundreds of men in cream and white himations sit on the sloping ground, some with raised hands; two gray-bearded oracle interpreters in white robes argue at the front with their hands spread. Details: a pile of voting pebbles on a bench, a boy selling water, a hawk circling, sharp shadows. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. Tone: heated, urgent. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Back in Athens the Assembly argues. Some older men say the wooden wall means the thorn hedge that once circled the Acropolis. The professional oracle interpreters say "divine Salamis" means defeat there. Themistocles replies that if the god had meant Athenian deaths he would have said "cruel Salamis," not "divine"; the dead will be the enemy's, and the wooden wall is the ships. The Assembly votes with him.

Myth or Evidence? Everything here comes from Herodotus, who wrote about fifty years later. Some historians suspect the second answer was polished afterward, or that Themistocles had friends at Delphi. What no one doubts is where the decision was made: in the Assembly, by citizens arguing over two words.

The "wooden wall" already exists, or nearly. In 483 BCE the state silver mines at Laurion strike a rich new vein. Herodotus says the Athenians are about to hand out the windfall, ten drachmas a citizen, when Themistocles persuades them to build 200 warships instead. Without that silver there would be no Greek fleet able to face Persia.

The Athenians do not defend their walls. Herodotus says they move their families to Salamis, Aegina and Troezen, and put their trust in the fleet. A few defenders barricade the Acropolis with timber, taking the oracle's wooden wall literally. The city is almost empty when the Persians arrive.

Palette: marble white gone gray, ash, charred brown and a hazy brown sky, with a hint of royal purple. The Acropolis of Athens after the Persian sack of 480 BCE: the same steep, flat-topped, pale limestone rock above the city, but its old temples are smoking ruins, with blackened broken columns, toppled column drums, scorched marble, charred roof beams, tall columns of dark smoke drifting over the summit and a blackened stump where the sacred olive tree stood; the sky behind is hazy and brown-gray. Far up the slope, tiny dark silhouettes of Persian soldiers with their purple-and-saffron banners move among the ruins without any fighting; empty streets of the city in the foreground, an overturned cart, scattered pottery, a stray dog. In the lower corner, a close detail: at the foot of a charred olive stump, one small green shoot has pushed up, bright against the ash. Tone: heavy, desolate, with a spark of hope. No people are harmed. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The Persians reach Athens and find it nearly empty. They burn the temples on the Acropolis and Athena's sacred olive tree. Herodotus says that on the very next day the Athenians who return to look find a new shoot already about half a meter long. The thirty years of ruins that follow will become Pericles' building site.

docs.title: Panel 11: The Trap in the Narrows
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 11. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Setting: the narrow strait between the rocky island of Salamis and the mainland of Attica at first light, September 480 BCE; a pink-gold sunrise, pale mist on the water, the dark hump of Mount Aigaleo on the right. Camera: wide view from the Greek shore on the island, raised slightly, looking across the strait. In the foreground, a line of Greek ships at the water's edge with rowers on the benches, oars raised in rest and marines taking their places. An Athenian trireme: a long, narrow wooden warship, low in the water, with three staggered banks of oars, a bronze ram at the waterline of the bow, a curved raised stern post, a large painted eye on each side of the bow, a square sail furled on a single mast, and bronze-helmeted marines on the deck. Across the narrow channel, rows and rows of Persian ships in red and gold crowd into the strait, their oars catching on one another; palette of Aegean blue, marble white, honey gold with royal purple and saffron for the Persians. Details: gulls, the glint of bronze rams, a man at the bow with an arm raised, tiny torches going out. Tone: tense, expectant. No fighting is shown yet. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Themistocles argues that in open water Persia's numbers would tell, but in the narrows they cannot. Herodotus says he sends a trusted man, an enslaved tutor named Sicinnus, to tell Xerxes the Greeks are about to flee. Xerxes believes it, and his ships spend the night closing both ends of the strait. At dawn the Persian fleet rows into the narrows.

Setting: the foot of Mount Aigaleo on the mainland shore of Attica, midday, September 480 BCE; palette of marble white, Aegean blue, honey gold and bronze with royal purple and saffron. Camera: medium-wide, from behind and slightly to one side of a gilded throne placed on a rocky ledge, looking over the water. Cast: Xerxes, Great King of Persia: a tall, broad-shouldered man of about thirty-eight with a long, carefully curled black beard, a tall upright cream felt tiara, a long saffron-and-purple embroidered robe with wide sleeves, gold bracelets and a gold-chain collar; an aloof, regal, unreadable expression. He sits stiffly forward on the throne, gripping its arms. Behind him, a line of attendants in long robes and a seated scribe with a wax tablet; a tall purple parasol. Far across the narrow water, small in the distance, crowded ships tangle their oars in the narrows, with drifting planks and broken oars on the surface and no figures visible. An Athenian trireme: a long, narrow wooden warship, low in the water, with three staggered banks of oars, a bronze ram at the waterline of the bow, a curved raised stern post, a large painted eye on each side of the bow, a square sail furled on a single mast, and bronze-helmeted marines on the deck. Tone: tense, then dawning dismay. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Xerxes watches from a seat at the foot of Mount Aigaleo. In the crush, Herodotus says, the Persian ships cannot turn or use their numbers, and the Greek rams find targets. One of the king's commanders that day is Artemisia, queen of Herodotus' own city of Halicarnassus, who had advised him not to fight in the narrows at all.

docs.title: Panel 13: Sunset in the Narrows
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 13. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image in the style above depicting panel 13 of 16. Setting: the strait of Salamis at sunset, September 480 BCE, a blazing gold-and-orange sky reflected on calm water. Camera: low wide view across the water. In the foreground a Greek ship glides home, its oars rising and falling in rhythm, its crew small silhouettes with helmets off. An Athenian trireme: a long, narrow wooden warship, low in the water, with three staggered banks of oars, a bronze ram at the waterline of the bow, a curved raised stern post, a large painted eye on each side of the bow, a square sail furled on a single mast, and bronze-helmeted marines on the deck. The strait is scattered with floating oars, planks, painted ship timbers and tangled rope; in the far distance a dark fleet of Persian ships withdraws toward the open sea, the smoke of the burned Acropolis a thin brown line on the horizon. Details: gulls over the wreckage, the glint of a lost bronze ram, a tattered purple sail. No bodies or people in the water are shown. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, honey gold, bronze, blazing sunset orange with a touch of royal purple. Tone: weary, triumphant, quiet. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

By evening the Persian fleet has withdrawn with heavy losses. Herodotus lists 378 Greek ships, 180 of them Athenian. With about 170 rowers a ship, Athens needed some 30,000 oarsmen, many of them from the poorest citizens, a fact whose consequences for Athenian democracy Chapter 16 follows. Without a navy to supply his army, Xerxes goes home with much of it.

docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 14. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Please generate a 16:9 image in the style above depicting panel 14 of 16. Setting: a bronze founder's yard on a rocky hillside, probably near Delphi, in 479 BCE, late afternoon, with steep gray limestone cliffs behind. Camera: medium wide view. In the foreground a stout founder in a leather apron and a young apprentice tip a crucible so a bright river of molten bronze pours into the mouth of a tall clay mold shaped like three twisted snakes; heat shimmers above it. Around them, details: bellows, a heap of captured bronze and shields set aside as melting stock, sacks of charcoal, a row of finished serpent heads, their tongues forked, laid on a cloth to cool, a brazier, an ox-cart. A small group of delegates from many cities in plain himations stands to one side watching. Palette: marble white, bronze, honey gold, ember orange, olive green. Tone: ceremonial, hot, proud. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

In 479 BCE the Greeks win at Plataea and Mycale, ending the invasion. They dedicate a tenth of the spoils to the god at Delphi, as Herodotus says: a bronze column of three intertwined snakes, probably cast near the sanctuary, to hold a golden tripod. The Greeks had won by standing together, and the monument will say so.

docs.title: Panel 15: These Fought the War
docs.text:
Image Prompt (This is Panel 15. Do not include the panel number in the image.) Style: a hand-drawn travel-sketchbook graphic-novel illustration, with clean dark ink outlines, flat softly shaded color fills and a faint watercolor paper texture, like a page from a traveler's journal; warm, sunlit, painterly lighting; no text, captions, signs, letters or speech bubbles anywhere in the image. Please generate a 16:9 image in the style above depicting panel 15 of 16. Setting: the Temple of Apollo terrace at Delphi, 479 BCE, a bright clear morning. Delphi, the sanctuary of Apollo: a steep rocky terrace on the slope of Mount Parnassus with a paved winding Sacred Way lined with small treasuries and statues, leading up to the large Doric Temple of Apollo with six columns across the front; behind it steep gray limestone cliffs, below it a deep valley of silver-green olive trees stretching to a distant sea. Camera: low angle from the Sacred Way looking up at the newly dedicated monument beside the temple's altar. The Serpent Column: a tall bronze column made of three snakes twisted together in a spiral, which once held a golden bowl, now with the serpents' heads missing; weathered dark green-bronze, with a worn stone base. In this scene it is brand new, a bright golden-bronze column with all three serpent heads intact and a large golden tripod bowl blazing on top, tiny incised marks covering the coils. In the foreground, a group of delegates from many cities, seen from behind in plain colorful himations, gaze up at it; a priest in white pours a libation from a bowl. Details: white doves, laurel garlands hung on the temple columns, the silver-green olive valley far below. Palette: marble white, Aegean blue, olive green, honey gold, bronze. Tone: triumphant, reverent. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

The column carries the names of the 31 Greek communities that fought, under a heading that means "These fought the war." The Spartan commander Pausanias first has his own name carved on it, and the Spartans erase his boast. The golden tripod does not last: the travel writer Pausanias says the gold was carried off in the Third Sacred War of 356 to 346 BCE, while the bronze serpents stood on.

docs.text:

Setting: the Hippodrome, Sultanahmet Square, Istanbul, Turkey, today, on a cool, clear November afternoon. Camera: low three-quarter view down into a shallow stone-edged pit where the monument stands, as closely matching panel 15's low upward angle as the pit allows. The Serpent Column: a tall bronze column made of three snakes twisted together in a spiral, which once held a golden bowl, now with the serpents' heads missing; weathered dark green-bronze, with a worn stone base. Behind it rise the pale stone Egyptian obelisk on its carved marble base and, further back, the gray domes and six slender minarets of the Blue Mosque against a pale blue sky. Two adult travelers seen from behind or in distant three-quarter view, dressed for cool November weather: one in a dark green rain jacket, the other in a charcoal wool coat with a rust-colored scarf, both with small daypacks, standing close together and looking at the view. Faces are never shown in detail. They stand at the low railing, small in the frame, looking down at the column. Details: bare plane trees, pigeons, a tram passing in the distance, a tea seller's cart. Palette: natural daylight, sea blue, terracotta, olive, weathered bronze. Tone: quiet wonder, continuity. Keep every character and place consistent with the other images in this story. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Constantine moved the column to his new capital by 330 CE, and it has stood in the Hippodrome ever since, in a pit because the ground has risen several meters. Its serpent heads are gone; the upper jaw of one lies in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. Two cities each hold half of the story: Istanbul has the object, and Delphi has the place.

docs.title: Epilogue - What the Wooden Wall Taught
docs.text:
A riddle from a god did not save Athens. A forecaster, a vote, a silver vein and thousands of ordinary rowers did. The oracle's words decided nothing by themselves; people decided what they meant, and then did the work. That is why the story rewards a careful reader: ask who decided, who paid and who rowed.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today An ambiguous oracle: "a wooden wall" and "divine Salamis" The Assembly argued over the words; Themistocles read them as the fleet Ambiguous guidance needs open argument and a clear decision-maker A much larger army with no hope on land Fight where numbers do not count: the narrows Choose the ground that cancels the enemy's advantage A silver windfall that could be shared out Spend it on 200 warships ten years before the need was proven Invest in the thing the future will demand A fleet that needed tens of thousands of rowers Poor citizens manned the oars and earned a claim on the city Those who carry the load deserve a voice

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text: When you next stand on the Acropolis, look at the north wall below the Erechtheion: column drums from the burned temples are built into it, a war memorial made of the war's own rubble. Then ask who in your own town gets to argue over the meaning of a riddle. The Learning for All thread of this book asks the same question about every classroom: who gets to read the evidence, and who gets to decide?

docs.title: Voices from the Sources
docs.text:
These are Herodotus' reports, in the paraphrased translations used in Chapters 15 and 17, not verbatim quotations.

  • The second Delphic answer, as Herodotus reports it: "Divine Salamis, you will destroy the children of women." Themistocles argued from the single word "divine."
  • The heading on the Serpent Column, as Herodotus and later writers report it: "These fought the war."
  • Herodotus on Darius, after Athens helped burn Sardis (about 498 BCE): he ordered a servant to say to him three times at every dinner, "Master, remember the Athenians." (As Herodotus reports it.)

docs.title: On the Trip
docs.text:
• Chapter: 15. Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
  • Where to look: column drums and carved blocks from the burned temples built into the Acropolis north wall, visible from the streets below in Plaka; the long island across the water from Piraeus, which is Salamis, and the strait beyond it; the bronze copy of the Serpent Column beside Apollo's altar at Delphi, and the original in its pit in Istanbul's Hippodrome.
  • Explore further: Xerxes' Road to Salamis and Two Ends of the Serpent Column
  • Look Closer: Glaux says: "Look closer at the north wall of the Acropolis, where round column drums sit among the building blocks." Glaux was perched on the carved stern post of a half-built trireme in Panel 8 (The Silver Fleet), beside a heap of silver coins.
